records.name: Actaea racemosa
records.description: Actaea racemosa (Cimicifuga racemosa, black cohosh): a cooling, relaxing herb in the herbal materia medica, used as analgesic, anodyne, anti-rhythmic, antidepressant; stimulates uterine contractions.
records.body:
*Actaea racemosa*, known as Cimicifuga racemosa, black cohosh, fairy candles, bugbane, bugwort, rattelroot, rattletop, rattleweed, is recorded in this section's herbal materia medica as follows. Its properties and uses are the herbal tradition's account, drawn from the sources listed; they are not clinical evidence, and the warnings should be read before any use.

## Energetics

- cooling
- relaxing

## Properties

- analgesic
- anodyne
- anti-rhythmic
- antidepressant
- antirheuamtic
- antispasmodic
- antivenomous
- emmenagogue
- hypotensive
- antibacterial
- antifungal
- alterative
- anti-inflammatory
- diaphoretic
- estrogenic
- mild sedative
- stomach tonic

## Indications

- muscular pains
- uterine pain with tenderness
- false pains
- irregular pains
- rheumatism of the uterus
- dysmenorrhea

## Dosage forms

- **standard decoction:**
  - 2-4 ounces up to 3 times daily
- **tincture:**
  - fresh root (1:2, 80% alcohol); dried root (1:5, 80% alcohol); 3-30 drops (0.1-1 ml) 3 times daily
  - fresh root produces better tinctures than dried root
- **glycerite:**
  - dried root (1:5); 6 drops to 1 ml (0.2 tsp.) 3 times daily
- **capsule:**
  - 1/2-1 capsule (250-500 mg) 2-3 times daily

## Warnings

- stimulates uterine contractions
- contraindicated with pregnancy
- large doses may cause headaches, dizziness, irritation of central nervous system, nausea, vomiting

## Notes

- **uses:**
  - reproductive health
    - It can work wonders for menstrual cramps, especially combined with black haw or wild yam.
    - phytoestrogens
    - has estrogen-like properties that may increase or decrease estrogen levels in different individuals
    - Black cohosh was taken to stimulate menstrual cycles and suppressed menstruation, treat uterine inflammation, relieve PMS, and to alleviate menstrual cramps and infertility.
    - regulate uterine contractions during childbirth
    - can be used in last weeks of pregnancy or in labor
    - may induce abortions
    - With menopause, black cohosh may help relieve hot flashes, irritability, and mood swings.
    - Depending on the ailment, healers sometimes mixed this herb with blue cohosh.
  - relaxant
    - Black cohosh is specific for tight and congested tissue states because it relaxes the structure as well as relaxing the blood vessels to allow for greater movement of blood (and therefore oxygen and nutrition) in an out of the tissue.
    - dull and achy pain
    - Its relaxant effect also affects the muscles surrounding the blood vessels, allowing them to dilate and lower blood pressure slightly.
    - This also helps relieve some migraine headaches, which are caused by spasms of the blood vessels of the head. Look for dull pain or headaches caused by eyestrain, cold, or congestion
    - whooping cough and spasmodic asthma
    - relaxes skeletal muscles
  - other
    - colds
    - coughs
    - sore throats
    - constipation
    - kidney disorders
    - rheumatism
    - fever
    - snake bites
- **over use:**
  - Black cohosh headaches can often be remedied with a strong cup of green tea.
  - do not take for more than five days
- **harvest:**
  - roots are best harvested from September through November when the weather starts turning cool and the leaves start dying back

## Sources

- The Modern Herbal Dispensatory
- Southeast Medicinal Plants
- Working the Roots

records.name: Action Potential
records.description: A brief electrical impulse that propagates along a neuron's axon, serving as the fundamental unit of neural signal transmission.
records.body:
An **action potential** is the brief electrical impulse that travels along a [neuron's](./neuron.md) axon, carrying information from one part of the nervous system to another. It is the basic unit of neural communication — every sensation you feel, every movement you make, every pain signal processed by the [nociceptive](../../../../../pain-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/nociception.md) system, involves action potentials traveling along neurons.

## How it works

A neuron at rest maintains a voltage difference across its [cell](../../../../../../../../content/text/glossary/terms/cell.md) membrane — approximately -70 millivolts (the inside is negative relative to the outside). This resting potential is maintained by ion pumps that keep sodium (Na+) concentrated outside the cell and potassium (K+) concentrated inside.

When the neuron receives sufficient stimulation (from a [synapse](./synapse.md), from a sensory receptor, or from an adjacent section of axon), voltage-gated sodium channels in the membrane open. Sodium ions rush into the cell, driven by both the concentration gradient and the electrical gradient. The membrane voltage rapidly rises from -70 mV to approximately +30 mV. This rapid depolarization is the action potential.

The sodium channels then close and voltage-gated potassium channels open. Potassium ions flow out of the cell, restoring the negative resting potential (repolarization). The ion pumps then restore the original ion concentrations.

The entire process takes about 1-2 milliseconds.

## All-or-none and propagation

Action potentials are **all-or-none**: if the stimulation reaches threshold, the action potential fires at full strength; if it does not reach threshold, nothing happens. There is no partial action potential. Information is encoded not by the size of individual action potentials (which are all the same) but by their frequency — a strong stimulus produces more action potentials per second, not bigger action potentials.

The action potential **propagates** along the axon because the depolarization in one region opens sodium channels in the adjacent region, triggering a new action potential there. In myelinated axons, the signal jumps between gaps in the myelin sheath (nodes of Ranvier), dramatically increasing speed — a process called saltatory conduction. This is why myelinated A-delta fibers conduct the fast, sharp aspect of pain much faster than unmyelinated C fibers conduct the slow, dull aspect.

## Clinical relevance

**Local anesthetics** (lidocaine, bupivacaine) work by blocking voltage-gated sodium channels. Without sodium influx, the action potential cannot be generated. The neuron cannot fire. No action potential means no signal transmission — which means no pain sensation from the blocked nerve. This is a direct, mechanism-based interruption of neural signaling.

**Anticonvulsants** (phenytoin, carbamazepine) also work by blocking sodium channels, reducing the excessive neuronal firing that produces seizures. Some of these drugs are used in [neuropathic pain](../../../../../pain-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/central-sensitization.md) because the same mechanism — excessive, sensitized firing — underlies both seizures and certain chronic pain states.

**Demyelinating diseases** (multiple sclerosis, Guillain-Barre syndrome) damage the myelin sheath, slowing or blocking action potential conduction. Symptoms depend on which neurons are affected: motor neurons produce weakness and paralysis; sensory neurons produce numbness, tingling, or pain.

## Related terms

- [Neuron](./neuron.md) — the cell that generates action potentials
- [Synapse](./synapse.md) — where the action potential triggers neurotransmitter release
- [Receptor](./receptor.md) — proteins that can initiate or modulate action potential generation

records.name: Acupressure
records.description: Manual stimulation of acupuncture points through sustained or rhythmic finger pressure without needles, applied according to TCM pattern diagnosis and acupoint indications.

lee2009.title: Stimulation of the wrist acupuncture point P6 for preventing postoperative nausea and vomiting

records.body: Acupressure (zhi ya, literally 'finger pressure') is manual stimulation of acupuncture points without needles. Within TCM, acupressure operates through the same meridian system and point functions as needle acupuncture. It is distinct from the broader therapeutic massage of tui na, though both are manual methods within TCM. Acupressure serves as an accessible tool for self-treatment and for patients unable or unwilling to receive needling. In traditional practice, acupressure techniques form part of the broader tui na repertoire, using finger pressure (an rou: pressing and rolling), pinching (nie), and percussion (pai) at specific points and along meridian pathways. The sustained pressure technique at acupoints is zhi ya—maintained pressure, usually with the thumb or index finger, held at one point for a specified duration. The key distinction is that acupressure targets specific points for their regulated functions, while tui na's broader massage techniques work along fascial lines and muscle groups. A tui na practitioner applying finger pressure to P6 (Neiguan) with the intention of treating nausea is performing acupressure; the same practitioner working along the forearm's flexor surface to release tension is performing broader tui na. P6 (Pericardium 6, Neiguan, literally 'inner gate') lies on the ventral forearm between palmaris longus and flexor carpi radialis tendons, approximately two cun above the wrist crease. In TCM terms, P6 governs the Pericardium's protective function and regulates the Heart's Shen (spirit/consciousness). Clinically, P6 is one of the most widely used points for nausea from all causes: motion sickness, medication-induced nausea, nausea from cancer treatment, post-operative nausea, pregnancy-related nausea, and functional nausea. Biomedical research on P6 acupressure and acupuncture for nausea found consistent effects through the Cochrane systematic review, showing reduced nausea incidence and severity. The mechanism involves vagal afferent stimulation altering brainstem centers regulating nausea and vomiting. From the TCM perspective, the point's traditional function—calming the Heart-Pericardium and restoring harmony—produces its clinical effect. Acupressure at P6 is readily self-administered for patients with chronic or recurrent nausea. The Kuznetsov applicator (a Soviet-era spiked mat) is sometimes marketed as an acupressure mat but is not part of TCM. It applies undifferentiated pressure to large skin areas without point-specific targeting, functioning as a reflex stimulus tool rather than TCM acupressure.

records.name: Acupressure Mat
records.description: A textile or foam mat embedded with hundreds of plastic or metal spikes that apply distributed mechanical pressure and pain stimulation to skin and superficial muscle tissue when a user lies or presses body parts on it, producing transient pain relief via gate-control mechanisms.

hohmann2012.title: The Benefit of a Mechanical Needle Stimulation Pad in Patients with Chronic Neck and Lower Back Pain: Two Randomized Controlled Pilot Studies

records.body:
An acupressure mat (also known as a Kuznetsov applicator, after its Soviet inventor) is a textile or foam base typically 30 × 60 cm embedded with hundreds of plastic or metal spikes. Users lie or press body parts on the mat, where the spikes apply distributed mechanical pressure to skin and superficial muscle tissue.

The mechanism is mechanical stimulation via spikes, which activate skin nociceptors (pain receptors) and mechanoreceptors (pressure sensors) simultaneously. Per gate control theory [@hohmann2012], this stimulation produces transient analgesia (pain relief) by suppressing pain signal transmission in the spinal cord through concurrent activation of non-painful tactile input.

Claims that the device stimulates acupressure points or activates meridians lack mechanistic support. The mat applies distributed pressure; it does not target anatomically identified acupoints. Claims that the device breaks up fascial adhesions or permanently changes tissue structure are not supported by evidence.

Evidence from small randomized trials [@hohmann2012] shows the device produces modest, transient pain reduction and muscle tension relief immediately after use. Pain typically returns to baseline within hours. No evidence supports long-term benefit or superiority over simpler mechanical pressure techniques such as massage or heat application.

Safety is generally good. Discomfort during use is expected; mild skin irritation and bruising are possible with prolonged contact. The device should be avoided on thin, fragile, or compromised skin and in users on anticoagulants.

records.name: Acute Pain
records.description: Pain that functions as a protective signal proportionate to tissue damage, time-limited and biologically adaptive
records.body:
**Acute pain** is pain that functions as a protective signal — proportionate to actual or imminent tissue damage, time-limited, and biologically useful. It is the pain that makes you withdraw from a hot surface, guard a broken limb, or seek medical attention for an abdominal emergency. Acute pain correlates reasonably well with [nociceptive](./nociception.md) input: the signal intensity roughly matches the tissue threat, and the pain resolves as the tissue heals.

Acute pain serves the organism. It directs attention to injury, motivates protective behavior (withdrawal, guarding, rest), and activates autonomic responses (increased heart rate, blood pressure, cortisol) that support survival. In this context, pain is adaptive — a system working as designed.

## Clinical features

Acute pain is typically:

- **Temporally linked** to an identifiable cause (injury, surgery, infection, inflammation)
- **Proportionate** to the severity of tissue involvement (though modulation means the correlation is imperfect)
- **Self-limiting** — it resolves as the underlying condition heals, usually within days to weeks
- **Responsive to treatment** — analgesics, anti-inflammatories, and treatment of the underlying cause produce predictable improvement

## Assessment

Clinical assessment of acute pain focuses on:

- **Location and character** — sharp, dull, burning, cramping; well-localized or diffuse
- **Severity** — patient-reported intensity (numeric scales, verbal descriptors)
- **Temporal pattern** — onset, duration, progression, aggravating and relieving factors
- **Associated findings** — vital sign changes, guarding, swelling, discoloration
- **Diagnostic significance** — acute pain patterns help identify the underlying pathology (chest pain in myocardial infarction, right lower quadrant pain in appendicitis, flank pain in renal colic)

The diagnostic value of acute pain depends on taking the patient's report seriously. Pain is what the patient says it is. Systematic undertreating of pain in Black patients, women, and people with disabilities — well-documented in the medical literature — represents a failure not just of compassion but of clinical reasoning. Dismissing a pain report means dismissing diagnostic information.

## The transition problem

The clinically critical question is when acute pain becomes [chronic pain](./chronic-pain.md). Most acute pain resolves. But in a significant minority of cases — estimates range from 10-50% depending on the type of injury or surgery — pain persists beyond the expected healing period. The nervous system undergoes changes ([central sensitization](./central-sensitization.md), altered descending modulation, structural reorganization) that decouple pain from tissue status. At that point, the pain is no longer a readout of ongoing damage but a self-sustaining neural process.

Early, adequate treatment of acute pain may reduce the risk of this transition. Undertreated acute pain — pain that persists at high intensity because of inadequate analgesia — may itself drive the neuroplastic changes that produce chronic pain. This is one of the mechanisms through which the systematic undertreating of pain in marginalized populations produces long-term harm.

## Related terms

- [Nociception](./nociception.md) — the neural process that acute pain usually reflects
- [Chronic Pain](./chronic-pain.md) — what acute pain becomes when the nervous system changes
- [Central Sensitization](./central-sensitization.md) — the mechanism of the acute-to-chronic transition

records.name: Adrenal crisis
records.description: Acute hemodynamic collapse with severe hypotension refractory to vasopressors alone, hypoglycemia, and hyponatremia, responding to parenteral glucocorticoid within 15-30 minutes and distinguishing adrenal crisis from other shock states by its specific treatment response.

nieman2016.title: Diagnosis of Cushing's syndrome in the modern era
nieman2016.publication: Endocrinology and Metabolism Clinics of North America

records.body:
An adrenal crisis is a state of acute hemodynamic collapse characterized by severe hypotension (systolic blood pressure below 80 mmHg) that does not respond to aggressive fluid resuscitation, profound hypoglycemia (blood glucose below 40 mg/dL), hyponatremia (sodium below 120 mEq/L), and altered mental status. The clinical presentation is sudden: the patient becomes profoundly weak or paralyzed, experiences severe abdominal pain and vomiting, and may lose consciousness. This is a medical emergency; without immediate treatment the patient enters refractory shock and dies within hours. The defining feature of adrenal crisis, distinguishing it from other causes of shock, is its specific treatment response: hypotension and hyponatremia that do not improve with maximum doses of vasopressors (norepinephrine, dopamine, epinephrine) but respond dramatically within 15–30 minutes to parenteral glucocorticoid (intravenous hydrocortisone or dexamethasone).

The underlying cause is sudden, severe deficit of glucocorticoid hormones, whether from primary failure of the adrenal gland, pituitary failure, or sudden withdrawal of glucocorticoid replacement therapy. The immediate trigger in a susceptible person is typically an acute stressor: infection (sepsis, pneumonia, meningitis), physical trauma, surgery, myocardial infarction, or unexpected medication discontinuation. But the essence of the crisis is not the trigger itself; it is the hemodynamic and metabolic failure that occurs when the body cannot sustain vascular tone and glucose production under acute demand. Without adequate glucocorticoid signaling, the cardiovascular system cannot maintain responsiveness to its own catecholamine surge, and the liver cannot mobilize glucose effectively. The result is paradoxical: sympathetic activation is present but produces erratic vasoconstriction and profound hypotension because the glucocorticoid permissiveness for catecholamine action is absent.

Treatment must be immediate: intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg or dexamethasone 4 mg is given on clinical suspicion alone, not delayed for test confirmation. This is one of the few medical emergencies where treatment is correct to begin on suspicion, because delay itself is the danger — the longer the patient remains untreated, the more likely irreversible shock and death. After glucocorticoid is given, aggressive fluid resuscitation with normal saline is administered, blood glucose and electrolytes are corrected, and any identified precipitating cause (infection, hemorrhage) is treated. Intensive care monitoring is mandatory. Hypotension typically begins to respond within 15–30 minutes of glucocorticoid administration; failure to respond raises the question of alternative diagnoses or complications.

In patients whose underlying condition is known, crisis is preventable: they are instructed to increase glucocorticoid doses during any acute illness or physiological stress, to keep injectable glucocorticoid immediately available, and to wear medical alert identification. In previously undiagnosed cases, the first crisis is often the event that reveals the underlying pathology and becomes the diagnostic turning point that enables subsequent appropriate management.

For clinical practice, the consequence is clear: any patient with acute unexplained hypotension, hypoglycemia, and altered mental status, in any clinical context, should receive glucocorticoid on suspicion if glucocorticoid deficiency is at all in the differential. The harm from unnecessary glucocorticoid use in acute settings is negligible; the harm from missed crisis is death.

## Related terms

- Cortisol — the glucocorticoid hormone whose deficiency is the proximal cause of crisis
- Glucocorticoid — the hormone class whose signaling fails in crisis
- Hypotension — the cardinal hemodynamic finding
- Hypoglycemia — a major metabolic component
- Hyponatremia — the electrolyte derangement that can cause seizures
- Shock — the hemodynamic state characterizing crisis
- Catecholamine — the hormone whose actions are rendered ineffective without glucocorticoid permissiveness

records.name: Adrenal insufficiency
records.description: Inadequate production of adrenocortical hormones (cortisol, and in primary insufficiency, also aldosterone), impairing the vascular and metabolic permissiveness needed to sustain a stress response, and characterized by morning cortisol <3 μg/dL, blunted or absent ACTH stimulation response, and symptoms of hypoglycemia, hypotension, and weakness.

cadegiani2016.title: Adrenal fatigue does not exist: a systematic review

records.body:
Adrenal insufficiency is inadequate production of adrenocortical hormones — primarily cortisol, and in certain forms also aldosterone — with sufficient reduction to impair the body's ability to sustain vascular tone, glucose homeostasis, and the metabolic permissiveness required for a normal stress response. It is a defined endocrine diagnosis, with specific diagnostic criteria, not a spectrum or a subjective state, and this distinction is essential because confusion between the clinical diagnosis and the informal concept of "adrenal fatigue" has muddied both the science and patient discussions.

Adrenal insufficiency is classified as primary, secondary, or tertiary based on where in the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis the failure occurs. Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease) is failure of the adrenal cortex itself: the gland cannot produce cortisol or aldosterone in response to ACTH, so both are profoundly reduced, and the loss of the negative-feedback signal causes ACTH and corticotropin-releasing hormone to rise uninhibited. The elevated ACTH stimulates melanocyte-stimulating hormone, a peptide produced from the same precursor, causing the characteristic hyperpigmentation — bronzing of the skin, especially in sun-exposed areas and in skin creases. Secondary adrenal insufficiency is loss of pituitary ACTH production (pituitary disease, pituitary surgery, pituitary apoplexy), so cortisol fails but aldosterone production is usually preserved via the renin-angiotensin system, and hyperpigmentation is absent because ACTH is low. Tertiary adrenal insufficiency is hypothalamic failure of corticotropin-releasing hormone production, producing the same pattern as secondary insufficiency — low cortisol, preserved aldosterone, no hyperpigmentation — but with distinguishable ACTH response to exogenous corticotropin-releasing hormone in testing.

Diagnosis requires specific tests: a morning cortisol below approximately 3 μg/dL (below 8 micromoles per liter) is generally considered insufficiently low for normal function; a corticotropin-releasing hormone or adrenocorticotropic hormone stimulation test establishes whether the adrenal gland or the pituitary can respond; and dexamethasone suppression testing (if secondary insufficiency is suspected) distinguishes pituitary from hypothalamic failure. Diagnosis is not made on a single cortisol measurement, because cortisol varies with time of day, stress, and recent glucocorticoid exposure. It is made by demonstrating persistent subnormal cortisol with failure of the gland or pituitary to respond to stimulation.

It is essential to address directly a widespread misconception: the "adrenal fatigue" concept popular outside medicine is not adrenal insufficiency and has no recognized medical definition. The systematic review by Cadegiani and Kater comprehensively found no substantiation for "adrenal fatigue" as a distinct pathological state. However, this does NOT mean the HPA-axis alterations reported in myalgic encephalomyelitis are unreal or unworthy of study. What the evidence shows is that myalgic encephalomyelitis presents with blunted or flattened HPA-axis responses — lower baseline cortisol, blunted awakening response, attenuated response to corticotropin-releasing hormone or adrenocorticotropic hormone stimulation — that are more modest than the profound insufficiency of diagnosed adrenal insufficiency. These alterations are real findings in peer-reviewed research but do not meet the threshold for a clinical diagnosis of adrenal insufficiency, and conflating "adrenal fatigue" with these axis alterations has been used both to dismiss legitimate findings and to overclaim clinical illness in people whose cortisol measurements are actually within normal range. The truth is: true adrenal insufficiency is a defined diagnosis that should be tested for and treated; blunted HPA-axis responses are real but distinct from true insufficiency; and neither one is the same as "adrenal fatigue."

Treatment of true adrenal insufficiency is glucocorticoid and (in primary insufficiency) mineralocorticoid replacement, with doses titrated to physiologic replacement — enough to restore vascular tone and glucose homeostasis without inducing iatrogenic glucocorticoid excess. The difference from management of blunted axis responses is crucial: patients with myalgic encephalomyelitis and mildly low cortisol do not necessarily benefit from glucocorticoid replacement, and blanket replacement of all "low cortisol" is a common clinical error that produces iatrogenic complications.

For clinical assessment and research, the consequence is clear: adrenal insufficiency must be diagnosed by the defined criteria (morning cortisol <3 μg/dL plus failure of stimulated response), not by symptoms or by the informal application of "adrenal fatigue." Findings of blunted axis responses in myalgic encephalomyelitis are scientifically meaningful and warrant further study, but they should not be conflated with clinical adrenal insufficiency or treated as though the diagnosis and treatment of one establishes the other.

## Related terms

- Hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis — the axis whose failure in primary, secondary, or tertiary forms defines adrenal insufficiency
- Cortisol — the hormone whose inadequate production defines the condition
- Adrenal crisis — the acute, life-threatening decompensation of untreated or undertreated adrenal insufficiency
- Glucocorticoid — the broader hormone class of which cortisol is the principal representative
- Myalgic encephalomyelitis — a condition associated with blunted HPA-axis responses, distinct from adrenal insufficiency
- Allostatic load — the cumulative cost of running physiological systems without adequate glucocorticoid support

records.name: Affective Reactivity Index
records.description: A brief, 7-item parent- and self-report scale (6 scored symptom items plus 1 impairment item) developed to give a dimensional, cross-setting measure of irritability in children and adolescents.

stringaris2012ari.title: The Affective Reactivity Index: a concise irritability scale for clinical and research settings
stringaris2012ari.publication: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry

records.body:
The Affective Reactivity Index (ARI) is a brief, 7-item parent- and self-report scale — 6 scored symptom items plus 1 impairment item — developed by Stringaris, Goodman, Leibenluft, Brotman, and colleagues (2012) to give a concise, dimensional measure of irritability usable in both highly specialized research settings and general child mental health settings. It was validated in two samples of children and adolescents: a U.S. sample of 218 recruited at the National Institute of Mental Health (bipolar disorder n=39, severe mood dysregulation n=67, children at familial risk for bipolar disorder n=35, healthy volunteers n=77), and a U.K. sample of 88 drawn from a general mental-health setting and from primary/secondary schools. In both samples, the parent- and self-report ARI scales loaded on a single factor and showed internal consistency the original validation study describes only as "excellent" — the exact alpha and test-retest coefficients are not given in the abstract text this dossier drew from, and were not independently re-derived from the paper's full-text tables.

The ARI measures irritability as a dimensional trait — a graded score, not a categorical diagnosis — and in the U.S. validation sample of children and adolescents, scores graded upward from healthy volunteers through children with severe mood dysregulation, with parent-rated (but not self-rated) irritability significantly higher in severe mood dysregulation than in bipolar disorder. This distinguishes the ARI from a diagnostic instrument like the criteria for disruptive mood dysregulation disorder: the ARI gives a continuous irritability score usable across clinical and non-clinical populations, while DMDD is a categorical yes/no diagnosis requiring specific duration, frequency, and setting criteria to be met.

Because the ARI was validated in children and adolescents only, using it to characterize irritability in adults — for example, alongside the STAR*D depression-trial irritability threshold or the adult anger-attack literature — extends the instrument beyond its validated population without established psychometric support in adults. And because the original 2012 validation paper's own abstract reports internal consistency only qualitatively, later cross-cultural replication studies that report specific alpha values (for example, an Italian-sample study reporting alphas of 0.79 and 0.78) describe those particular samples' psychometrics, not the original validation study's own numbers, and should not be substituted for them when citing the instrument's founding reliability figures.

records.name: Agitated Depression
records.description: A depressive syndrome with prominent psychomotor agitation, traced from Kraepelin and Weygandt's mixed-state descriptions to Athanasios Koukopoulos's revival of the concept as a bipolar mixed state. In Koukopoulos's later scheme it is distinguished from mixed depression specifically by the presence of psychomotor agitation.

koukopoulos2005.title: Toward a validation of a new definition of agitated depression as a bipolar mixed state (mixed depression)
koukopoulos2005.note: PMID 15051107; numeric results not independently retrieved beyond secondary characterization in Verdolini et al. 2015

verdolini2015.title: The State of the Art of the DSM-5 'with Mixed Features' Specifier
verdolini2015.note: PMC4562096; source for the Kraepelin/Weygandt historical characterization

records.body:
Agitated depression names a depressive syndrome combining depressed mood with prominent psychomotor agitation. The clinical lineage runs from Kraepelin, who described "excited depression" as one of his mixed states of manic-depressive insanity, through his student Weygandt, who coined "agitated depression" for a mixed state combining depressed mood, psychomotor agitation, and flight of ideas. Athanasios Koukopoulos revived and extended this lineage in his own later nosological scheme.

The distinction that matters is internal to Koukopoulos's own usage, not a distinction from an outside rival: in his later scheme, Koukopoulos distinguished "agitated depression" — mixed depression with psychomotor agitation present — from "mixed depression" proper, defined by the absence of psychomotor agitation, rather than treating the two labels as synonyms. This split places agitated depression on the side of exactly the symptom (psychomotor agitation) that the DSM-5 mixed-features specifier deliberately excludes from its own criteria, which is why agitated depression sits outside the DSM-5 specifier's admitted symptom set even though it is described in the same excitatory-depression literature. Different authors have used "agitated depression" and "mixed depression" inconsistently across the wider literature, a terminological variability this dossier flags rather than resolves.

For clinical observation, the practical stakes of the distinction are treatment-relevant: agitated depression, framed by Koukopoulos as a bipolar mixed state, is proposed to warrant mood-stabilizer rather than antidepressant-only treatment, on the reasoning that antidepressant monotherapy in a state already carrying an excitatory (agitated) process risks worsening rather than resolving it. The primary validation papers for this reframing are conceptual and clinical-validation papers proposing and defending a nosological distinction rather than large epidemiological studies, and their full numeric results were not independently verified beyond what secondary review (Verdolini et al. 2015) reports.

records.name: Airway
records.description: The anatomical passage carrying gas between the environment and the lungs, assessed clinically through four functions: patency, oxygenation, ventilation, and protection.
records.body:
The **airway** is the anatomical passage that carries gas between the environment and the lungs. In clinical practice it is divided into upper and lower segments, a distinction that organizes both assessment and intervention.

The **upper airway** extends from the nose and mouth through the pharynx (nasopharynx, oropharynx, hypopharynx) to the larynx and vocal cords. It is responsible for filtering, warming, and humidifying inspired air and for protecting the lower airway from aspiration. Upper-airway problems tend to produce [stridor](./stridor.md) — a high-pitched inspiratory sound indicating narrowing above or at the level of the vocal cords.

The **lower airway** extends from the trachea through the bronchi and bronchioles to the alveoli, where gas exchange occurs. Lower-airway problems tend to produce [wheeze](./wheeze.md) — a musical expiratory sound indicating narrowing below the vocal cords, typically from bronchospasm or mucus plugging.

The clinical significance of the airway is defined by four bedside functions:

1. **Patency** — Is the passage open? Obstruction at any level threatens all downstream functions.
2. **[Oxygenation](./oxygenation.md)** — Is oxygen reaching arterial blood?
3. **[Ventilation](./ventilation.md)** — Is carbon dioxide being eliminated?
4. **Protection** — Is the airway defended against aspiration of gastric contents, blood, or secretions?

Each function can fail independently. A patient can have a patent airway but inadequate oxygenation (as in pneumonia). A patient can be well-oxygenated but poorly ventilated (as in early opioid toxicity, where supplemental oxygen may mask rising CO2). Assessing all four functions — not just one — is the foundation of airway management.

## Related terms

- [Oxygenation](./oxygenation.md) — oxygen delivery to arterial blood
- [Ventilation](./ventilation.md) — gas movement and CO2 elimination
- [Stridor](./stridor.md) — upper-airway narrowing sound
- [Wheeze](./wheeze.md) — lower-airway narrowing sound

records.name: Akathisia
records.description: A drug-induced movement disorder of inner restlessness and compulsion to move, most classically linked to antipsychotic exposure but also named in FDA warning language for antidepressants, whose presentation as agitation is routinely mistaken for a worsening of the underlying psychiatric illness rather than recognized as an adverse drug effect.
records.body:
Akathisia is a movement disorder of subjective inner restlessness and a compulsion to move — pacing, rocking, shifting weight from foot to foot, an inability to sit or stand still — associated with dopamine-receptor-blocking and other psychotropic medications. It is named, alongside agitation, hostility, aggressiveness, impulsivity, hypomania, and mania, as a reported symptom following antidepressant initiation in the U.S. FDA's black-box warning language issued in 2004 (regulatory text characterized via search results for this entry, not independently re-fetched from FDA.gov) — evidence that akathisia is treated, even by regulators, as its own distinct entity where it co-occurs with, and can be confused with, generalized agitation.

The clearest evidence that akathisia is separable from ordinary agitation, rather than a synonym for it, comes from Crowner and colleagues' 1990 observational study. A closed-circuit television camera was installed in each corner of the dayroom of a locked unit for violent psychiatric patients; incidents of assault, together with the five minutes preceding each assault, were recorded on videotape, and all parties present were rated for akathisia's motor component. The finding — "both victims and assailants were akathisic before about half of all incidents; bystanders rarely were" — is described as the first observational study of the akathisia-violence relationship, and its design is what makes the distinction operational: akathisia was scored as its own rateable variable, not inferred backward from the presence of agitation or violence. This is a single small-unit observational study, not a controlled trial, and the causal evidence linking akathisia to violence more broadly is limited, even in favorable secondary descriptions, to case reports and small case series. A 2021 systematic review, characterized via search result and not independently fetched for this entry, is reported as concluding that akathisia cannot be reliably linked to suicidal behavior in patients treated with antipsychotic medication — a more recent, systematic look at an adjacent question that found the evidence insufficient for a reliable causal link.

The practical consequence, and the reason this term is entered separately from psychomotor agitation rather than folded into it, is that akathisia is routinely mistaken for a worsening of the underlying psychiatric illness rather than recognized as an adverse effect of its treatment. Because akathisia presents as restlessness and motor agitation, and can co-occur with irritability, the same surface phenotype as a genuine psychiatric agitation or activation state, a clinician who does not separately assess for akathisia's specific motor component — as Crowner and colleagues' rating protocol did — risks reading a medication-induced state as evidence that the underlying illness, or the dose of an antipsychotic or antidepressant already given, needs to be increased rather than reconsidered. The evidence base for treating akathisia as a validated general cause of aggression remains thin — case reports and small case series, not controlled studies — so the correct clinical inference from observed agitation is not that akathisia is present, but that akathisia is one alternative explanation that must be actively assessed for and ruled in or out before attributing new agitation to illness progression.

records.name: Allodynia
records.description: Pain produced by stimuli that are not normally painful, such as light touch or mild temperature changes
records.body:
**Allodynia** is pain produced by stimuli that are not normally painful — light touch, gentle pressure, mild warmth or coolness, the brush of clothing on skin. The stimulus is innocuous; the pain is real. This dissociation between stimulus and response is the clearest clinical demonstration that pain is not a simple readout of [nociceptive](./nociception.md) input but a product of nervous system processing.

Allodynia is classified by the type of stimulus that provokes it:

- **Mechanical (tactile) allodynia** — pain from light touch or pressure. A cotton swab brushed across the skin, the weight of a bedsheet, a gentle handshake — all produce pain. This is the most common form in [central sensitization](./central-sensitization.md) states.
- **Thermal allodynia** — pain from mild temperature changes that would normally feel neutral or mildly warm/cool. Lukewarm water on the skin produces burning pain.
- **Movement allodynia** — pain produced by normal joint movement or muscle contraction within the physiological range.

## Mechanism

In normal processing, touch and pressure signals travel on large-diameter A-beta fibers, which do not produce pain. In allodynia, these signals are being interpreted by a sensitized spinal cord as nociceptive — the same A-beta input that normally produces the sensation of touch now activates pain circuits. The peripheral nerve is sending the same signal it always sends. The change has occurred centrally.

This can happen through several mechanisms:

- **Loss of inhibitory gating** — normally, A-beta fiber activity inhibits nociceptive transmission in the dorsal horn (the gate-control mechanism). When inhibitory interneurons are damaged or suppressed, this gating fails, and touch input passes through pain pathways.
- **Phenotypic switching** — A-beta fibers may begin expressing neuropeptides (substance P, CGRP) normally produced only by nociceptive fibers, effectively turning touch neurons into pain-signaling neurons.
- **Central sensitization** — hyperexcitable dorsal horn neurons respond to inputs they would normally ignore, treating innocuous afferent input as noxious.

## Clinical significance

Allodynia is a hallmark of several [chronic pain](./chronic-pain.md) conditions:

- **Fibromyalgia** — widespread mechanical allodynia is a defining feature
- **Migraine** — cutaneous allodynia (scalp tenderness, pain from wearing glasses or earrings) develops during attacks and may persist between them in chronic migraine
- **Complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS)** — severe allodynia in the affected limb
- **Postherpetic neuralgia** — allodynia in the dermatome affected by shingles
- **Chronic low back pain** — mechanical allodynia in the painful region and sometimes beyond it

The presence of allodynia tells the clinician that central sensitization is active — that the problem is not in the peripheral tissue but in the nervous system's processing. This matters for treatment: anti-inflammatories targeting peripheral tissue will not help; interventions targeting central mechanisms (descending modulation, neuroplastic retraining, centrally acting medications) are more appropriate.

Allodynia also has profound implications for daily life. When light touch hurts, clothing hurts. Being held hurts. The casual physical contact of social life becomes a source of pain. [Access intimacy](../../../../../../content/text/glossary/terms/access-intimacy.md) — the felt ease when access needs are met without negotiation — becomes particularly significant for people whose access need is that touch, the medium of most human connection, has become dangerous.

## Related terms

- [Hyperalgesia](./hyperalgesia.md) — amplified pain from normally painful stimuli (allodynia's companion concept)
- [Central Sensitization](./central-sensitization.md) — the mechanism that produces allodynia
- [Nociception](./nociception.md) — the peripheral process from which allodynia dissociates

records.name: Anger Attack
records.description: A sudden, situationally disproportionate episode of anger with autonomic or panic-like features, first described as a subgroup phenomenon in outpatients with major depressive disorder and reported, in uncontrolled open-label case series, to resolve with antidepressant treatment.

fava1993angerattacks.title: Anger attacks in unipolar depression, Part 1: Clinical correlates and response to fluoxetine treatment

fava1991angerattacks.title: Anger attacks in depressed outpatients and their response to fluoxetine

fava1999review.title: Anger attacks in patients with depression

rosenbaum1993neuroendocrine.title: Anger attacks in unipolar depression, Part 2: Neuroendocrine correlates and changes following fluoxetine treatment

records.body:
An anger attack is a sudden, out-of-proportion spell of anger accompanied by autonomic or panic-like features — tachycardia, sweating, flushing, a subjective sense of loss of control — first characterized by Fava, Rosenbaum, and colleagues in outpatients being treated for major depressive disorder at the Massachusetts General Hospital Depression Research Program. Across their case series, anger attacks were reported at rates depending on sample and definition: 44% of 127 medication-free depressed outpatients in the 1993 report (PMID 7848377), and, in an earlier, smaller subgroup comparison, 48% of 31 younger depressed patients versus 21% of 29 age-matched healthy controls (PMID 1775598, p = .048).

An anger attack is not a DSM-III-R, DSM-IV, or DSM-5 diagnostic criterion for major depressive disorder — it is a research construct, defined and measured by the Anger Attacks Questionnaire developed within this one research program. It should also be distinguished from irritability as a trait or mood state: irritability names a standing proneness to anger or a period of elevated angry mood, while an anger attack is a bounded, panic-attack-like spell with its own autonomic signature, closer in phenomenology to a discrete panic attack than to a mood state. Fava and Rosenbaum's own 1999 review describes the construct as "sudden intense spells of anger that resemble panic attacks but lack the predominant affects of fear and anxiety associated with panic attacks" (PMID 10418810).

Every quantitative finding about anger attacks in this literature comes from the same research program's open-label, uncontrolled case series (no placebo arm in either the 1991 or 1993 reports), conducted at a single U.S. academic center in adult depressed outpatients already seeking treatment — so the reported resolution of anger attacks in 71% of patients who had them, after 8 weeks of open-label fluoxetine in the 1993 report, cannot be separated from a general antidepressant response, a placebo response, or regression to the mean, and the 1999 summary review restates the same program's own accumulated observations rather than an independent replication. A neuroendocrine pilot finding — blunted prolactin response to TRH in patients with anger attacks (n=12) versus without (n=13) — is likewise a small mechanistic study whose authors frame their own conclusion as suggestive ("may have... greater central serotonergic dysregulation"), not an established mechanism, and blunted TRH-prolactin response is a nonspecific finding reported across other psychiatric conditions. Any use of the anger-attack construct in current research or practice should therefore treat its treatment-response and mechanism findings as hypothesis-generating from one program's uncontrolled series, not as replicated causal evidence.

records.name: Anhedonia
records.description: Reduced capacity to experience pleasure from an obtained reward, a consummatory/hedonic deficit that the effort-based decision-making literature treats as empirically and conceptually separable from motivational anergia (reduced effort allocation).

salamone1994.title: Anhedonia or anergia? Effects of haloperidol and nucleus accumbens dopamine depletion on instrumental response selection in a T-maze cost/benefit procedure

salamone1991.title: Haloperidol and nucleus accumbens dopamine depletion suppress lever pressing for food but increase free food consumption in a novel food choice procedure

treadwayzald2011.title: Reconsidering anhedonia in depression: Lessons from translational neuroscience

treadway2009.title: Worth the 'EEfRT'? The Effort Expenditure for Rewards Task as an Objective Measure of Motivation and Anhedonia

husainroiser2018.title: Neuroscience of apathy and anhedonia: a transdiagnostic approach

records.body:
Anhedonia is reduced capacity to experience pleasure from a rewarding stimulus once obtained — a deficit in consummatory, hedonic response, not in the drive to pursue reward in the first place. The distinction the effort-based decision-making literature turns on is between anhedonia and motivational anergia: reduced willingness or capacity to mobilize effort toward reward, independent of how pleasurable the reward is once obtained.

Salamone, Cousins, and Bucher (1994) posed the distinction directly, in a paper titled "Anhedonia or Anergia?": in a T-maze cost/benefit procedure, disrupting nucleus accumbens dopamine transmission in rats (via haloperidol or 6-hydroxydopamine lesion) shifted choice away from a high-reward, high-effort arm toward a low-reward, low-effort arm, while the same animals continued to consume the high-value food normally once effort was removed from the choice — dopamine loss reallocated effort, it did not blunt the reward's value. A companion design (Salamone et al., 1991) found the same dissociation from the other direction: accumbens dopamine depletion and haloperidol suppressed lever-pressing for a preferred food while increasing free consumption of a less-preferred one, with total food intake and preference-when-free both intact. Treadway and Zald (2011) generalized the argument to human depression research: the field's "underspecified definition of anhedonia has failed to dissociate between consummatory and motivational aspects of reward behavior," with substantial preclinical evidence implicating dopamine "primarily in motivational aspects of reward" rather than consummatory pleasure.

The consequence for clinical measurement is that a self-report anhedonia scale, which typically asks about anticipated or experienced pleasure, does not distinguish these two deficits, and a behavioral finding of reduced effort for reward should not automatically be read as evidence of reduced hedonic capacity. The Effort Expenditure for Rewards Task (EEfRT; Treadway, Buckholtz, Schwartzman, Lambert, & Zald, 2009) was built specifically to separate the two: in a nonclinical sample of 61 undergraduates, trait anhedonia scores predicted reduced willingness to choose a harder task for a larger reward, giving the effort measure construct validity against self-reported anhedonia while still targeting a motivational, not consummatory, construct. Husain and Roiser (2018) find shared mechanisms across apathy/anergia and anhedonia within a transdiagnostic effort-based framework without collapsing the two into one construct — they are correlated and co-occurring across many patients, not mechanistically identical, and the later finding that anhedonia severity independently moderates effort-based choice (see effort-based decision-making) is itself evidence the two dimensions are separable enough to interact rather than being one thing measured twice.

records.name: Anthraquinone
records.description: A class of aromatic organic compounds with a tricyclic ring structure, found in rhubarb, senna, aloe, and Japanese knotweed — characterized by laxative, anti-inflammatory, and antimicrobial activity
records.body:
Anthraquinones are a class of aromatic organic compounds based on the 9,10-anthracenedione skeleton — a tricyclic structure consisting of three fused six-membered rings with two ketone groups. They are produced by several plant families, most notably [Polygonaceae](../../../../../../../botany-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/polygonaceae.md) (knotweed, rhubarb), Fabaceae (senna), Asphodelaceae (aloe), and Rhamnaceae (cascara sagrada).

Anthraquinones are the chemical basis of the oldest known class of laxative drugs. Senna, rhubarb root, cascara, and aloe have been used as purgatives across multiple medical traditions for millennia. The laxative mechanism is well characterized: anthraquinone glycosides pass through the small intestine unabsorbed, are hydrolyzed by colonic bacteria to release the potential aglycone, which then stimulates colonic motility and inhibits water reabsorption — producing the cathartic effect.

## Key anthraquinone compounds

**[Emodin](emodin.md)** (1,3,8-trihydroxy-6-methylanthraquinone): Found in [Japanese knotweed](../../../../../../../botany-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/japanese-knotweed.md), rhubarb, and senna. The most pharmacologically studied anthraquinone, with anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, and anticancer activity beyond its laxative effect.

**Chrysophanol**: Found in rhubarb and senna. Laxative and hepatoprotective.

**Rhein**: Found in rhubarb. Anti-inflammatory and nephroprotective in animal studies.

**Aloe-emodin**: Found in aloe. Laxative and potentially anticancer; classified by IARC as possibly carcinogenic to humans (Group 2B).

**Physcion**: Found in Japanese knotweed. Hepatoprotective and antifungal.

## Safety

Chronic use of anthraquinone laxatives can cause electrolyte depletion (particularly potassium), melanosis coli (darkening of the colonic mucosa), and potential hepatotoxicity and nephrotoxicity at high doses. Traditional formularies limit treatment duration and combine anthraquinone-containing herbs with harmonizing agents to buffer their drastic action — a practice that modern toxicology confirms as prudent.

## See also

- [Emodin](emodin.md) — the principal anthraquinone in Japanese knotweed
- [Polyphenol](polyphenol.md) — the broader chemical class
- [Japanese Knotweed](../../../../../../../botany-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/japanese-knotweed.md) — a major source
- [Hu Zhang](../../../../../traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/hu-zhang.md) — TCM use of anthraquinone-containing knotweed

records.name: Antibody
records.description: An immunoglobulin protein produced by B cells and plasma cells that binds a specific antigen shape; the adaptive immune system's primary secreted recognition molecule.
records.body:
An antibody (immunoglobulin) is a Y-shaped protein with two functionally distinct regions: a constant region (Fc), which determines the antibody's class and effector behavior, and a variable region (Fab), which forms the antigen-binding site. The variable region's shape is generated by V(D)J recombination — random splicing of gene segments during B cell development — producing a repertoire of binding specificities large enough to cover essentially any antigen shape the body might encounter, without any single antibody being pre-specified for any single pathogen.

## Classes

- **IgM** — the first antibody produced in a primary response; forms pentamers, efficient at complement activation.
- **IgG** — the dominant antibody in blood and the main mediator of long-term humoral memory; crosses the placenta, conferring passive immunity to the fetus.
- **IgA** — secreted at mucosal surfaces (gut, airway, breast milk); the front line against pathogens at epithelial barriers.
- **IgE** — bound to mast cells; mediates allergic reactions and anti-parasite defense.
- **IgD** — present on naive B cell surfaces; role less fully characterized than the others.

## Affinity maturation

On first exposure to an antigen, B cells produce antibodies of modest affinity. In germinal centers — structures that form within lymph nodes and spleen during an active response — activated B cells undergo somatic hypermutation: their antigen-receptor genes accumulate point mutations at a rate far above the genomic background. Mutated B cell clones compete for antigen and for survival signals from helper T cells; clones whose mutated receptors bind antigen more tightly outcompete their neighbors and are selected to proliferate and differentiate into antibody-secreting plasma cells or long-lived memory B cells. Repeated over cycles, this variation-and-selection process raises the average binding affinity of the antibody population across an immune response — the molecular basis of why a second exposure to a pathogen produces a faster, stronger, better-fitting response than the first.

## Effector functions

Binding an antigen is rarely the whole story — what the antibody does once bound depends on its class and context:

- **Neutralization** — physically blocking a pathogen's ability to attach to or enter host cells.
- **Opsonization** — coating a pathogen so that phagocytes (which have receptors for antibody Fc regions) engulf it more efficiently.
- **Complement activation** — antibody binding can trigger the complement cascade, a sequence of plasma proteins that can punch holes directly in pathogen membranes.

## A framing from outside immunology

The founding note for this section's theory arc reads an antibody as "a charged claim (this shape: refused) carrying its provenance" — germinal-center affinity maturation read as an evidence-accumulation process, and Niels Jerne's [idiotypic network](./idiotypic-network.md) theory (antibodies that bind other antibodies) read as identity constituted by claims about claims. See ["Immunity as Belief Board"](../../../../../../../../../../../../content/text/documents/articles/notes/2026/08/21/2026-08-21-note-on-immunity-as-belief-board.md) for the full framing — presented there as a draft hypothesis, not as settled immunology.

## Related terms

- [Self/non-self discrimination](./self-non-self.md) — what antibody specificity is selected against during development
- [Idiotypic network](./idiotypic-network.md) — Jerne's theory of antibodies recognizing other antibodies' binding regions
- [Immunological tolerance](./immunological-tolerance.md) — why most antibody clones are never produced against the body's own antigens

records.name: Approach Motivation
records.description: The directional (approach-versus-withdrawal) aspect of a motivated state, historically indexed to relative left frontal cortical activity but treated in this glossary as orthogonal to affect's valence and arousal dimensions.

harmonjones1998.title: Anger and frontal brain activity: EEG asymmetry consistent with approach motivation despite negative affective valence
harmonjones1998.publication: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

harmonjones2001.title: State anger and prefrontal brain activity: Evidence that insult-related relative left-prefrontal activation is associated with experienced anger and aggression
harmonjones2001.publication: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

harmonjones2003a.title: Clarifying the emotive functions of asymmetrical frontal cortical activity

authors: M. J. A. M. van Putten
vandervinne2017.title: Frontal alpha asymmetry as a diagnostic marker in depression: Fact or fiction? A meta-analysis

paul2025.title: Frontal alpha asymmetry as a marker of approach motivation? Insights from a cooperative forking path analysis
paul2025.publication: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

carverwhite1994.title: Behavioral inhibition, behavioral activation, and affective responses to impending reward and punishment: The BIS/BAS scales
carverwhite1994.publication: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

records.body:
Approach motivation is the directional aspect of a motivated state — whether behavior is organized toward engaging and obtaining a goal (approach) or toward disengaging and avoiding it (withdrawal) — treated in this literature as a dimension that can vary independently of an affective state's valence. This section's ruling on affect fixes valence (pleasant to unpleasant) and arousal (calm to activated) as the two dimensions locating a felt state; approach motivation names a third, orthogonal axis: motivational direction. The paradigm case establishing the two are not the same construct is anger, a negatively valenced state that behaves, empirically, like an approach-motivated one rather than a withdrawal-motivated one.

The primary physiological evidence for this claim is relative left-frontal cortical activity. Harmon-Jones and Allen (1998) correlated resting EEG frontal alpha-power asymmetry with trait anger in an unselected undergraduate sample and found dispositional anger associated with greater left- than right-anterior activity, concluding that "anterior asymmetry varies as a function of motivational direction rather than affective valence." Harmon-Jones and Sigelman (2001) extended this to a state manipulation: participants insulted by a confederate showed greater relative left-frontal activity than neutrally treated participants, and this activation was itself associated, by regression, with more self-reported anger and more aggressive behavior toward the confederate. Harmon-Jones's own later review (2003) narrowed the claim considerably: left-frontal activation appeared specifically when participants believed they could act on their anger, and did not appear when the anger-producing situation was framed as one they could do nothing about — anger did not raise relative left-frontal activity unconditionally, by the author's own account.

Independent of the research group that produced these findings, the general validity of frontal alpha asymmetry as an approach-motivation marker is now seriously disputed. A meta-analysis of 16 studies (van der Vinne et al., 2017; pooled major depressive disorder n = 1,883, controls n = 2,161) found a non-significant, negligible effect size for frontal asymmetry as a depression marker. More directly on point, a large cooperative multi-lab reanalysis (Paul et al., 2025; N = 740, spanning resting, picture-viewing, and guessing-task paradigms, with many independent teams each choosing a defensible analysis pipeline) reported that "frontal asymmetry was not reliably affected by task manipulations and did not relate to self-reported traits," concluding the data "could not support the validity of frontal asymmetry as a marker of approach motivation, neither as a reliable state nor as a trait marker." This is a direct, large-sample, multi-team non-replication of the general construct that the anger-EEG findings sit inside, though it does not name the anger studies specifically.

Approach motivation is also operationalized as a self-report trait construct, independent of any EEG measure: the Behavioral Activation/Approach System (BAS) scales (Carver & White, 1994) ask directly about reward sensitivity and drive. Anger correlates positively with self-reported BAS in the same research tradition that produced the EEG claims, but this is a different measurement channel with its own, separately documented validity history — the EEG-asymmetry claim and the self-report BAS claim should not be merged into one effect size or read as replicating one another.

The consequence for research design and clinical observation is direct: resting or task-related frontal EEG asymmetry should not, on its own, be read as evidence of an approach-motivated state, and should especially not be used as a diagnostic or trait marker in depression, where the pooled meta-analytic effect is negligible. A finding of relative left-frontal activity accompanying a negative-valence state is consistent with the approach-motivation hypothesis but is not, given the 2025 multi-lab non-replication, sufficient evidence for it on its own; convergent behavioral or self-report evidence should be sought before the construct is asserted from an asymmetry measure alone.

records.name: Attachment
records.description: The innate system by which infants bond with caregivers, and the lifelong relational patterns — secure, anxious, avoidant, disorganized — that result from early attachment experiences.
records.body:
Attachment theory (John Bowlby, Mary Ainsworth) describes the biological system by which infants seek proximity to caregivers when distressed, and the relational patterns that develop from how caregivers respond. These patterns persist into adulthood, organizing how a person experiences intimacy, manages distress, and relates to others — including therapists.

Four primary attachment patterns:

- **Secure** — the caregiver is consistently responsive. The child learns that relationships are reliable and distress signals produce comfort. Adults with secure attachment can tolerate closeness and separateness, can ask for help without excessive anxiety, and can offer support without losing themselves.
- **Anxious-preoccupied** — the caregiver is inconsistently responsive. The child learns to amplify distress signals to ensure response. Adults with anxious attachment are hypervigilant to relational cues, fear abandonment, and may cling or demand reassurance in ways that strain relationships.
- **Avoidant-dismissive** — the caregiver is consistently unresponsive to emotional needs. The child learns to suppress distress and manage alone. Adults with avoidant attachment prize independence, minimize emotional needs, and may struggle with intimacy.
- **Disorganized** — the caregiver is the source of both comfort and threat. The child faces an irresolvable paradox: the person who should provide safety is the person who generates danger. This produces incoherent attachment behavior and is strongly associated with dissociation and complex [trauma](./trauma.md).

Attachment patterns are not fixed. They can be modified through sustained relational experience — most notably through the [therapeutic relationship](./therapeutic-alliance.md), which provides a context for new relational learning. A therapist who is consistently present, attuned, and non-retaliatory offers an experience that can gradually update the client's relational templates.

Attachment is relevant beyond psychotherapy. In [Somatic Experiencing](../concepts/somatics/somatic-experiencing.md), the concept of neuroception — the [nervous system's](../../../../../human-body-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/the-nervous-system.md) subconscious evaluation of safety and threat — maps directly onto attachment: a person whose early environment was unpredictable has a nervous system calibrated for threat-detection, not for the social engagement that secure attachment supports.

## Related terms

- [Trauma](./trauma.md) — disorganized attachment and complex trauma
- [Therapeutic Alliance](./therapeutic-alliance.md) — the relational context for attachment repair
- [Psychotherapy](../../documents/articles/notes/psychotherapy.md) — attachment patterns in the therapeutic relationship
- [Somatic Experiencing](../concepts/somatics/somatic-experiencing.md) — neuroception and the autonomic basis of attachment

records.name: Auricular Acupuncture
records.description: Acupuncture, acupressure or electrical stimulation at points on the external ear, read as a map of the whole body; developed in its modern form by Paul Nogier in 1950s France and taken up in Chinese practice.

oleson2014.title: Auriculotherapy Manual: Chinese and Western Systems of Ear Acupuncture

records.body:
Auricular acupuncture treats points on the outer ear, the auricle, which it reads as a map of the whole body. In the French physician Paul Nogier's 1950s account, the ear resembles an inverted fetus, with the head at the lobe and the feet toward the top. Chinese practitioners adopted and extended the map, and today both a Chinese and a Western system of ear points are in use [@oleson2014]. Points are needled, pressed with seeds or pellets, or stimulated electrically, as in [electroacupuncture](electroacupuncture.md).

Its best-known standardized use is the five-point NADA protocol (sympathetic, Shen Men, kidney, liver and lung points), widely used alongside addiction and trauma care.

The ear is also where other methods converge. [taVNS](../../../../../medical-technology-services-section/services/electrotherapy-devices-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/transcutaneous-auricular-vagus-nerve-stimulation.md) targets the cymba conchae and the tragus because the [vagus nerve](../../../../../../../physiology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/vagus-nerve.md)'s auricular branch supplies them. [Cranial electrotherapy](../../../../../medical-technology-services-section/services/electrotherapy-devices-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/cranial-electrotherapy-stimulation.md) clips its electrodes to the earlobes. Whether ear points act through a body map, as the tradition holds, or through the ear's rich sensory innervation, as a physiological reading proposes, the two accounts meet at the same anatomy and can be studied side by side without either settling the other.

records.name: Autoimmunity
records.description: The clinical and mechanistic failure of self-tolerance: immune cells or antibodies targeting the body's own tissue as though it were foreign, producing diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, type 1 diabetes, and lupus.
records.body:
Autoimmunity is the immune system's regulatory apparatus failing on its own constituency: T cells or antibodies that escaped central and peripheral tolerance mechanisms mount a sustained response against a self-antigen, and the body's own tissue is treated as though it required elimination. See [the immune system](../../../../../human-body-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/the-immune-system.md) for the clinical presentation of specific autoimmune diseases (rheumatoid arthritis, type 1 diabetes, multiple sclerosis, lupus); this entry focuses on how tolerance fails.

## Mechanisms of failure

- **Escape from central tolerance** — thymic negative selection is imperfect; some self-reactive T cell clones are never presented with the self-antigen they target (because it is expressed only in a specific peripheral tissue, not broadly enough to appear during thymic selection) and so are never deleted.
- **Failure of peripheral tolerance** — regulatory T cell insufficiency, or costimulatory signals reaching an otherwise-anergic self-reactive cell (inflammation from an unrelated infection can supply the missing costimulation).
- **Molecular mimicry** — a pathogen antigen structurally resembles a self-antigen closely enough that antibodies or T cells raised against the pathogen cross-react with host tissue after the infection resolves. Rheumatic fever following streptococcal infection (cross-reactivity between streptococcal M protein and cardiac myosin) is a classic case.
- **Epitope spreading** — an immune response that begins narrowly targeted (one self-antigen, one epitope) broadens over time to target additional epitopes on the same or nearby proteins, as tissue damage from the initial response releases more self-antigen for presentation.
- **Genetic susceptibility** — particular HLA (MHC) alleles are strongly associated with specific autoimmune diseases, because the allele shapes which self-peptides get displayed during thymic selection and which get presented to potentially self-reactive T cells in the periphery.

## Treatment logic

Because autoimmunity is excess or misdirected immune activity rather than immune insufficiency, treatment runs the opposite direction from treating infection: immunosuppression (corticosteroids, biologic agents targeting specific inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α or IL-6) rather than immune stimulation.

## A framing from outside immunology

Autoimmunity has a separate, older sense in political philosophy: Roberto Esposito's use of the biological metaphor to describe communities whose protective mechanisms turn on their own members (see [immunitas](../../../../../../content/text/glossary/terms/immunitas.md), and the vault's philosophical [auto-immunity](../../../../../../../../../philosophy-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/auto-immunity.md) entry). This entry is the clinical/mechanistic sense; that entry is the political-philosophical extension of the same figure.

The founding note for this section's theory arc offers a third, narrower reading, proposing autoimmunity be understood specifically as "false conflict-naming" — a classifier that should route a self-antigen signal into [tolerance](./immunological-tolerance.md)'s residual-uncertainty bucket instead promotes it to a named refutation. See ["Immunity as Belief Board"](../../../../../../../../../../../../content/text/documents/articles/notes/2026/08/21/2026-08-21-note-on-immunity-as-belief-board.md) — a draft awaiting the section's owner review, with an explicit falsifier attached (the tolerance/autoimmunity line should be re-derivable as a conflict-naming threshold in a fusion model, checked against published tolerance data).

## Related terms

- [Immunological tolerance](./immunological-tolerance.md) — the mechanism whose failure produces autoimmunity
- [Self/non-self discrimination](./self-non-self.md) — the classification autoimmunity misapplies
- [Immunitas](../../../../../../content/text/glossary/terms/immunitas.md) — Esposito's political-philosophical extension of the immune metaphor, including the autoimmune figure
