records.name: Baduanjin
records.description: The "Eight Pieces of Brocade": a moving qigong sequence of eight standing or seated exercises, among the most practised and most studied forms.

kohn2008.title: Chinese Healing Exercises: The Tradition of Daoyin

records.body:
Baduanjin (八段錦), the "Eight Pieces of Brocade", is a moving [qigong](./qigong.md) sequence of eight exercises. Brocade is a fine, many-coloured silk, and the name praises the set's value. The set appears in Song-dynasty sources, and a seated version and a standing version have both been transmitted since [@kohn2008].

The eight movements of the standing set, in the common modern order and naming:

1. Holding up the heavens with both hands, to regulate the [san jiao](./san-jiao.md).
2. Drawing the bow, left and right, as if shooting a vulture.
3. Separating heaven and earth, raising one hand and pressing down the other, to regulate the spleen and stomach.
4. The wise owl gazes backward, turning the head, to relieve the five strains and seven injuries.
5. Swaying the head and swinging the tail, to calm heart-fire.
6. Two hands reach down to the feet, to strengthen the kidneys and waist.
7. Clenching the fists with angry eyes, to increase strength.
8. Rising and dropping onto the heels, seven times, to dispel the hundred illnesses.

Each movement's traditional name states its intended action on the organ-function systems of [zang-fu](./zang-fu.md) theory. The set is a daoyin sequence in the strict sense: posture, breath, and attention are coordinated in every movement, as the [three regulations](./san-tiao.md) require.

In 2003 the Chinese Health Qigong Association issued a standardized Baduanjin together with three other forms: Yijinjing, Wuqinxi, and Liuzijue. Because it is short, low in intensity, and fixed in form, it is the qigong most often used as the intervention in clinical trials. That evidence is weighed in the [2026-09-24 note on the clinical evidence for qigong and taiji](../../documents/articles/notes/2026/09/24/2026-09-24-note-on-the-clinical-evidence-for-qigong-and-taiji.md).

records.name: Bioavailability
records.description: The fraction of an administered drug dose that reaches systemic circulation in pharmacologically active form, expressed as a percentage
records.body:
**Bioavailability** is the fraction of an administered drug dose that reaches the systemic circulation in an unchanged, pharmacologically active form. It is expressed as a percentage: a drug with 100% bioavailability delivers its entire dose to the bloodstream; a drug with 50% bioavailability delivers half.

Intravenous administration has 100% bioavailability by definition — the drug is placed directly into the bloodstream. Every other route of administration has lower bioavailability because the drug must cross biological barriers and may be degraded or metabolized before reaching systemic circulation.

## Factors affecting oral bioavailability

Oral administration — the most common route — subjects drugs to several barriers:

- **Dissolution and absorption** — the drug must dissolve in the gastrointestinal fluid and cross the intestinal wall. Drugs with poor water solubility, large molecular size, or vulnerability to acid degradation have reduced absorption. Food, gastric pH, and gut motility all influence this step.
- **First-pass metabolism** — after crossing the intestinal wall, orally administered drugs enter the portal vein and pass through the liver before reaching systemic circulation. The liver's CYP enzymes may metabolize a significant fraction of the drug on this first pass, dramatically reducing bioavailability. This is why some drugs (like nitroglycerin, which is almost entirely destroyed by first-pass metabolism) cannot be given orally and must be administered sublingually, transdermally, or intravenously.
- **Intestinal metabolism** — the gut wall itself contains metabolic enzymes that can degrade drugs before they reach the portal circulation.
- **Efflux transporters** — membrane proteins (like P-glycoprotein) in the intestinal wall actively pump drugs back into the gut lumen, reducing the fraction absorbed.

## Clinical significance

Bioavailability matters because it determines the relationship between the dose administered and the dose that actually reaches the drug's target. When switching between routes of administration (e.g., from IV to oral), the clinician must adjust the dose to account for bioavailability differences. A drug with 50% oral bioavailability requires twice the oral dose to achieve the same plasma concentration as an IV dose.

Bioavailability also explains variability between patients and between different formulations of the same drug. Generic drugs are required to demonstrate "bioequivalence" — similar bioavailability to the branded version — but small differences can matter for drugs with narrow [therapeutic indices](./therapeutic-index.md).

In [harm reduction](../../../../../public-health-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/harm-reduction.md) contexts, bioavailability explains why route of administration dramatically affects both the effect and the risk of a substance. Smoking or injecting a drug bypasses first-pass metabolism, producing higher peak concentrations and faster onset than oral use — which explains both the more intense subjective effect and the higher overdose risk of these routes.

## Related terms

- [Pharmacokinetics](./pharmacokinetics.md) — the broader framework of which bioavailability is one component
- [Half-Life](./half-life.md) — how long the drug remains in the body once it has reached circulation
- [Therapeutic Index](./therapeutic-index.md) — the margin of safety that bioavailability variability can narrow

records.name: Biomedicine
records.description: The medicine grounded in the biological and physical sciences that explains disease by anatomical, physiological, cellular, and molecular mechanism and judges treatment by controlled trial; the dominant medical system of hospitals and universities worldwide.

engel1977.title: The need for a new medical model: a challenge for biomedicine

records.body:
Biomedicine is medicine grounded in the biological and physical sciences. It explains disease by mechanism: anatomical lesion, disturbed physiology, cellular and molecular pathology, infectious agent. It locates illness in the body of the individual patient. It judges treatments by controlled comparison, with the randomized controlled trial as its strongest evidence.

It took its modern form in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries through pathological anatomy, cell theory, germ theory, and experimental physiology. In the twentieth century it became the medicine of hospitals, universities, and state health systems across the world.

The name is used mainly by those who compare it with other medical systems: anthropologists, historians, and practitioners of other traditions. It names biomedicine as one system among several rather than as "medicine" without qualification. "Western medicine", the common gloss in China and elsewhere, is inexact, since the system is practised and developed worldwide. "Allopathic" is a nineteenth-century homeopathic coinage.

From within, its best-known critique is Engel's argument that a purely biological model cannot account for illness as people live it, and his proposal of a biopsychosocial model [@engel1977]. In this forest it is the frame through which the medical sections read other systems, such as [traditional Chinese medicine](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/traditional-chinese-medicine.md), from the outside. Those sections keep the two readings side by side instead of letting either adjudicate the other.

records.name: Blinding
records.description: Keeping participants, and where possible clinicians and outcome assessors, unaware of who received the active treatment, so that expectation cannot bias results.
records.body:
Blinding, also called masking, withholds from people in a trial which group each participant is in. In a single-blind trial only the participants are unaware. In a double-blind trial the clinicians and assessors are too. Blinding exists because knowing shapes both what participants report and what observers see, especially for subjective outcomes [@kaptchuk2015].

Drug trials blind with identical pills. Practice and device trials often cannot. No one can be given a sham [qigong](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/qigong.md) without knowing it, so movement trials fall back on comparing active controls (the evidence in the qigong note is read that way). Stimulation trials depend on a convincing [sham](sham-stimulation.md). When blinding fails, [placebo effects](placebo-effect.md) and a device's specific effect cannot be told apart.

records.name: Blood Stasis
records.description: 血瘀 (xue yu) — a pathological condition in which blood flow is impeded, stagnant, or obstructed, producing fixed sharp pain, dark complexion, and purple tongue — one of the most clinically significant pathological products in TCM

chen2004.title: The integration of traditional Chinese medicine and Western medicine

records.body:
Blood stasis (xue yu 血瘀) is a pathological condition in [Traditional Chinese Medicine](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/traditional-chinese-medicine.md) in which blood flow is impeded, slowed, or obstructed. It is not merely "poor circulation" in the colloquial sense — it is a specific diagnostic category with characteristic signs, defined causes, predictable complications, and targeted treatment principles. Blood stasis is one of the most clinically important pathological products in TCM because it both results from and causes further disease, creating self-reinforcing cycles of obstruction and dysfunction.

## Diagnosis

Blood stasis has a distinctive clinical presentation. The cardinal signs are:

**Pain**: Fixed, stabbing, sharp, and well-localized — as opposed to the wandering pain of Wind or the dull pain of deficiency. The pain is typically worse at night and worse with pressure. The TCM axiom is: "where there is no flow, there is pain" (bu tong ze tong 不通则痛). Blood stasis is the paradigmatic "no flow" condition.

**Complexion**: Dark, dusky, or purple. The area of the body affected by stasis may show dark discoloration. Facial complexion in chronic blood stasis is characteristically dark and lusterless.

**Tongue**: Purple or dark-red tongue body, often with dark spots or petechiae. The sublingual veins (visible when the tongue is curled upward) may be engorged, dark, and tortuous. Tongue diagnosis is the single most reliable clinical indicator of blood stasis.

**Pulse**: Choppy (se 涩) — a pulse that feels rough, uneven, and "catching," as if the blood flow encounters resistance. The choppy pulse reflects the impeded flow that defines the condition.

**Other signs**: Fixed masses or lumps (abdominal masses, uterine fibroids), varicose veins, spider angiomata, dark or clotted menstrual blood, bleeding that is dark in color, skin that bruises easily and heals slowly.

## Causes

Blood stasis does not arise spontaneously. It is always secondary to another pathological process:

**[Qi](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/qi.md) stagnation**: The most common cause. Qi moves blood — it is the motive force behind circulation. When Qi stagnates (from emotional constraint, particularly frustration and unexpressed anger), blood movement slows and eventually stagnates. Liver Qi stagnation leading to blood stasis is an extremely common clinical progression, particularly in gynecological conditions.

**Cold congealing blood**: External or internal cold causes blood to congeal, just as cold solidifies liquids. Cold-type blood stasis produces severe cramping pain that is relieved by warmth — the classic presentation of dysmenorrhea (painful menstruation) from cold in the uterus.

**Heat scorching blood**: Extreme heat can damage blood vessels and cause blood to extravasate (leave the vessels) or become thick and viscous. This is blood stasis from heat — less intuitive than cold-type stasis, but clinically significant in febrile diseases and hemorrhagic conditions.

**Trauma**: Physical injury directly damages blood vessels and produces localized blood stasis — the bruise, the swelling, the hematoma. Traumatic blood stasis is the most straightforward type and the easiest to understand in biomedical terms.

**Chronic deficiency**: In long-standing [Qi deficiency](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/qi.md), the motive force driving blood movement weakens progressively. Blood stasis from deficiency is characteristic of elderly patients, the chronically ill, and postpartum women — all states where the body's operational force is depleted.

## Treatment principle: invigorate blood, dispel stasis

The treatment of blood stasis involves herbs that **invigorate blood** (huo xue 活血) — literally "enliven the blood," restore its movement — and **dispel stasis** (qu yu 祛瘀) — break up the stagnant accumulation. [Hu Zhang](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/hu-zhang.md) (Japanese knotweed root) belongs to this category. Other major blood-invigorating herbs include:

- **Dang Gui** (Angelica sinensis) — nourishes and moves blood simultaneously; the most widely used blood herb in the TCM materia medica
- **Chuan Xiong** (Ligusticum chuanxiong) — moves blood and Qi; reaches the head (treats headaches from blood stasis)
- **Tao Ren** (peach kernel) — breaks blood stasis; used for severe fixed masses and amenorrhea
- **Hong Hua** (safflower) — invigorates blood, dispels stasis, alleviates pain
- **Dan Shen** (Salvia miltiorrhiza) — invigorates blood, cools blood, calms the spirit; widely studied for cardiovascular applications

The choice of herb depends on the type and location of stasis. Hu Zhang is selected when blood stasis co-occurs with [damp-heat](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/damp-heat.md) (as in jaundice or hepatobiliary disorders), because it addresses both pathologies simultaneously — a dual classification that most blood-invigorating herbs do not share.

## Blood stasis and modern medicine

Blood stasis is the TCM concept with perhaps the strongest correspondence to modern biomedical understanding. The clinical presentation — fixed pain, dark discoloration, masses, abnormal bleeding, choppy pulse — maps onto conditions characterized by:

- **Microcirculatory dysfunction**: Impaired blood flow through capillary beds, measurable by laser Doppler flowmetry and nail-fold capillaroscopy
- **Hypercoagulability**: Elevated fibrinogen, increased platelet aggregation, elevated D-dimer — laboratory markers that correlate with TCM blood stasis diagnoses
- **Chronic inflammation**: Elevated CRP, IL-6, TNF-α in patients diagnosed with blood stasis patterns
- **Endothelial dysfunction**: Impaired nitric oxide production, increased endothelin — the vascular endothelium's failure to maintain normal blood flow

Recent research has identified a particularly striking structural correlate: **fibrinaloid microclots** — anomalous, dense clots resistant to fibrinolysis that block microcapillaries and reduce oxygen transfer. These microclots occur in chronic inflammatory and vascular diseases and are now understood to be mechanistically responsible for many of the symptoms TCM has attributed to blood stasis for centuries. The parallel with Virchow's triad (vessel wall damage, blood flow stasis, hypercoagulable state) is direct.

Research programs in China, Japan, and integrative medicine centers have established statistically significant correlations between TCM blood stasis diagnosis and these biomedical markers [@chen2004]. The classical formula **Xue Fu Zhu Yu Tang** (血府逐瘀汤, "Drive Out Stasis from the Mansion of Blood"), developed by Wang Qing-Ren in the 1830s, has been the subject of randomized controlled trials and is available as an FDA-approved capsule in China (since 2002) for coronary heart disease and hyperlipidemia — a rare example of a traditional formula validated through modern clinical trial methodology.

This convergence does not mean blood stasis "is" microcirculatory dysfunction — the concepts operate at different levels of description — but it validates that TCM's clinical observation identified a real pathological phenomenon through functional assessment that biomedicine later described through molecular mechanisms.

The pharmacology of blood-invigorating herbs aligns with this correspondence. [Hu Zhang's](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/hu-zhang.md) [resveratrol](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/resveratrol.md) inhibits platelet aggregation and improves endothelial function. Dan Shen's tanshinones are anticoagulant and anti-inflammatory. Chuan Xiong's tetramethylpyrazine improves microcirculation. The herbs that TCM selected over centuries for "invigorating blood" turn out to contain compounds that address the biomedical correlates of impaired circulation.

## Related

- [Pattern Diagnosis](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/pattern-diagnosis.md) — the diagnostic method that identifies blood stasis
- [Zang-Fu](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/zang-fu.md) — the organ systems through which blood stasis manifests

records.name: Bush-Francis catatonia rating scale
records.description: A 1996 operationalized rating scale and standardized examination for catatonic signs, comprising a 23-item severity/treatment-response scale and an embedded 14-item screening instrument, validated for high interrater reliability.

bush1996a.title: Catatonia. I. Rating scale and standardized examination

bush1996b.title: Catatonia. II. Treatment with lorazepam and electroconvulsive therapy

records.body:
The Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale (BFCRS) is a 1996 instrument developed to give catatonic signs operationalized definitions and a standardized examination procedure, so that presence and severity can be rated systematically rather than impressionistically. It comprises a 23-item rating scale, used to describe severity and track treatment response, and an embedded 14-item screening instrument (the Bush-Francis Catatonia Screening Instrument), used with a cutoff of two or more of the fourteen signs present to flag a patient as catatonic.

The BFCRS is a measurement instrument, not a diagnostic nosology: it operationalizes and rates the presence and severity of individual catatonic signs — including hypokinetic items such as stupor and waxy flexibility and hyperkinetic items such as agitation — but it was not designed or validated as a discriminator between "retarded" and "excited" catatonia as diagnostic categories; a single patient can score highly on hypokinetic and hyperkinetic items at once. In its validation study — 44 simultaneous ratings of 28 cases, each meeting the two-of-fourteen screening threshold — the 23-item total score had an interrater reliability of 0.93 (mean per-item agreement 88.2%, SD 9.9), and the 14-item screening instrument's total score had a reliability of 0.95 (mean per-item agreement 92.7%, SD 4.9), indicating close agreement among trained independent examiners using the scale's operationalized definitions.

The consequence for research design is that a study wanting to characterize a patient's pole — retarded, excited, or mixed — must derive that classification itself from the scale's item-level scores, since the instrument does not output a pole label, and the high reported reliability applies to the scale as validated (single-timepoint ratings by trained raters against its own item definitions), not to any downstream pole-classification scheme built on top of it. The 23-item total score is also the instrument used in the companion literature to track treatment response, including the graded, non-universal response to lorazepam and electroconvulsive therapy: in the study that formalized this treatment protocol, 16 of 21 patients (76%) who completed a full lorazepam trial had resolution of catatonic signs, tracked using this same scale.

## Related terms

- Catatonia — the syndrome this instrument rates
- Retarded catatonia — the hypokinetic pole, described through some of the scale's items
- Excited catatonia — the hyperkinetic pole, described through others
- Lorazepam challenge test — a diagnostic-and-therapeutic use of catatonia response commonly tracked with this scale

records.name: Capnography
records.description: Continuous monitoring of exhaled carbon dioxide concentration via waveform and numerical value, serving as the primary bedside confirmation of tube placement and ventilation adequacy.
records.body:
**Capnography** is the continuous monitoring of exhaled carbon dioxide (CO2) concentration, displayed as both a numerical value (end-tidal CO2, or EtCO2) and a waveform over time. In airway care, it serves as the primary confirmation tool for tracheal tube placement and the most reliable bedside monitor of [ventilation](./ventilation.md) adequacy.

The capnography waveform displays CO2 concentration throughout the respiratory cycle. A normal waveform shows near-zero CO2 during inspiration, a rapid rise during early expiration as dead-space gas mixes with alveolar gas, a plateau representing alveolar CO2 (whose end-point is the EtCO2 value), and a rapid return to baseline with the next inspiration. Normal EtCO2 ranges from approximately 35-45 mmHg.

Clinical applications in airway management:

- **Tube placement confirmation** — a consistent waveform with appropriate EtCO2 values over multiple breaths is the most reliable confirmation that a tracheal tube is in the trachea, not the esophagus. An esophageal intubation produces no waveform or a rapidly diminishing one. This single application prevents one of the most dangerous airway complications.

- **Ventilation monitoring** — rising EtCO2 indicates hypoventilation or increased CO2 production; falling EtCO2 may indicate hyperventilation, decreasing cardiac output, or circuit disconnection. Capnography detects ventilation changes before pulse oximetry does.

- **Cardiac arrest monitoring** — during CPR, EtCO2 reflects the adequacy of chest compressions (which drive pulmonary blood flow and therefore CO2 delivery to the lungs). A sudden rise in EtCO2 during arrest may indicate return of spontaneous circulation.

- **Waveform pattern recognition** — abnormal waveform shapes indicate specific pathology. A sloped plateau suggests bronchospasm. A gradually rising baseline suggests rebreathing. A sudden loss of waveform suggests extubation, circuit disconnection, or cardiac arrest.

Capnography complements pulse oximetry but provides fundamentally different information. Pulse oximetry monitors [oxygenation](./oxygenation.md); capnography monitors ventilation. Together they cover both sides of gas exchange.

## Related terms

- [Ventilation](./ventilation.md) — the process capnography monitors
- [Oxygenation](./oxygenation.md) — the companion process monitored by pulse oximetry
- [Airway](./airway.md) — the passage whose integrity capnography confirms

records.name: Catatonia
records.description: Catatonia is a transdiagnostic psychomotor syndrome diagnosed by three or more of twelve DSM-5-TR signs and seated as a specifier attached to an underlying disorder rather than coded as a stand-alone diagnosis. Its motor presentation spans a hypokinetic (retarded) pole and a hyperkinetic (excited) pole that modern cohort data show commonly co-occurring rather than defining two mutually exclusive subtypes.

goldar1995.title: Karl Ludwig Kahlbaum's concept of catatonia

dawkins2022.title: Catatonia Psychopathology and Phenomenology in a Large Dataset

records.body:
Catatonia is a psychomotor syndrome defined by the presence of three or more of twelve clinical signs: stupor, catalepsy, waxy flexibility, mutism, negativism, posturing, mannerism, stereotypy, agitation not influenced by external stimuli, grimacing, echolalia, and echopraxia. DSM-5 replaced DSM-IV's standalone "catatonic schizophrenia" subtype with this single, transdiagnostic sign-count threshold, applied through three diagnostic routes: catatonia associated with another mental disorder (a specifier attachable to mood, psychotic, neurodevelopmental, and other disorders), catatonic disorder due to another medical condition, and unspecified catatonia. DSM-5-TR, published in 2022, made no substantive change to this definition. In every route, catatonia is seated as a specifier or qualifier attached to an underlying diagnosis rather than coded as a stand-alone disease category.

This transdiagnostic framing reverses an older, narrower assumption that catatonia belongs chiefly to schizophrenia. Karl Ludwig Kahlbaum's 1874 monograph, *Die Katatonie oder das Spannungsirresein*, first described the syndrome as running a cyclic course across melancholic, manic, stuporous, and confused phases in the same patients, rather than as a fixed feature of one disease. A prospective study of 55 catatonic inpatients found only 4 (about 7%) met research criteria for schizophrenia, while over two-thirds had diagnosable affective disorders, usually mania — directly at odds with the historical catatonia-schizophrenia linkage. A separate review of the affective-disorder literature reports catatonic-sign prevalence at 13% to 31% of affective-disorder inpatient samples, and, across acute psychiatric admissions generally, a wide and study-dependent range running from 6% to 38% historically down to 2% to 8% in more recent estimates — a spread the review does not resolve into a single figure.

Catatonia's motor presentation spans two poles: a retarded (hypokinetic) pole of stupor, immobility, and mutism, and an excited (hyperkinetic) pole of purposeless agitation unresponsive to external stimuli. In a retrospective cohort of 1,456 validated catatonia diagnoses across 2,130 episodes, stupor/immobility was recorded in 925 patients, of whom 105 (11.4%) also showed excitement, while of 196 patients with excitement, 105 (53.6%) also showed stupor/immobility — the same 105 co-occurring patients counted from each side. The authors describe this as psychomotor "alternation": stupor and excitement, though seemingly opposite states, frequently co-occur within the same episode rather than marking two mutually exclusive subtypes.

Two consequences follow for clinical observation and research design. First, the DSM-5-TR sign-count threshold is phenomenological rather than mechanistic, and it is agnostic to which pole the qualifying signs come from — meeting "3 of 12" says nothing by itself about whether a patient's presentation is retarded, excited, or mixed; clinical assessment operationalizes the individual signs through instruments such as the Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale rather than through a pole label. Second, because catatonia is coded as a specifier rather than a free-standing diagnosis, clinical and research records must separately track the disorder it attaches to; and because retarded and excited signs demonstrably co-occur within episodes, any study design that forces a single-timepoint classification into one pole risks misclassifying the substantial minority of patients — roughly half of those with excited signs, and about one in nine of those with stuporous signs, in the cohort above — who show both.

## Related terms

- Retarded catatonia — the hypokinetic pole of the syndrome
- Excited catatonia — the hyperkinetic pole of the syndrome
- Malignant catatonia — the hyperthermic, autonomically unstable variant carrying substantial risk of death if untreated
- Bush-Francis catatonia rating scale — the operationalized instrument used to rate catatonic signs
- Lorazepam challenge test — the diagnostic-and-therapeutic probe used to support the diagnosis and predict treatment response

records.name: Central Sensitization
records.description: Amplification of neural signaling within the spinal cord and brain that produces pain hypersensitivity beyond what peripheral input warrants
records.body:
**Central sensitization** is the amplification of neural signaling within the central nervous system (spinal cord and brain) that produces pain hypersensitivity. In a centrally sensitized state, the gain on the pain system has been turned up: normal inputs produce exaggerated responses, and inputs that should not produce pain at all begin to do so.

The concept was developed by Clifford Woolf in the 1980s through experiments demonstrating that injury-driven input from the periphery could induce lasting changes in spinal cord excitability — changes that persisted after the peripheral input stopped. This was a paradigm shift. It meant that the central nervous system was not a passive relay for peripheral signals but an active processor that could be fundamentally altered by its own experience.

## Mechanisms

Central sensitization involves several interacting processes:

- **Wind-up** — repeated C-fiber stimulation at the same intensity produces progressively larger responses in dorsal horn neurons. The same input generates increasing output — a neural amplification that does not require any change in the peripheral stimulus.
- **NMDA receptor activation** — under normal conditions, NMDA receptors on dorsal horn neurons are blocked by magnesium ions. Sustained nociceptive input removes this block, allowing calcium influx that triggers intracellular cascades leading to long-term changes in neuronal excitability. This is structurally similar to the long-term potentiation (LTP) involved in learning and memory — the nervous system is literally learning to produce pain more efficiently.
- **Expanded receptive fields** — dorsal horn neurons begin responding to input from areas beyond their normal receptive field. A neuron that previously responded only to input from the thumb may begin responding to input from the entire hand. This produces the clinical phenomenon of pain spreading beyond the site of original injury.
- **Loss of inhibitory interneurons** — sustained nociceptive input can damage or suppress inhibitory interneurons in the dorsal horn that normally act as brakes on pain transmission. When these brakes fail, excitatory signals pass through unchecked.
- **Glial activation** — microglia and astrocytes in the spinal cord become activated by sustained nociceptive input, releasing pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IL-6) and other mediators that maintain neuronal hyperexcitability. This neuroinflammation can persist long after the original peripheral stimulus has resolved.

## Clinical manifestations

Central sensitization produces recognizable clinical features:

- **[Allodynia](./allodynia.md)** — pain from stimuli that are not normally painful (light touch, gentle pressure, mild temperature changes)
- **[Hyperalgesia](./hyperalgesia.md)** — increased pain from stimuli that are normally painful (a mildly painful pinch produces severe pain)
- **Temporal summation** — repeated identical stimuli at the same intensity produce progressively increasing pain
- **Expanded pain distribution** — pain that spreads beyond the site of original injury or develops in areas remote from any identifiable pathology
- **After-sensations** — pain that persists or intensifies after the stimulus is removed

These features are present across many [chronic pain](./chronic-pain.md) conditions: fibromyalgia, chronic low back pain, chronic tension-type headache, temporomandibular disorders, irritable bowel syndrome, and chronic pelvic pain syndromes. The conditions differ in their peripheral triggers but share central sensitization as a maintaining mechanism.

## Implications for treatment

If central sensitization is the mechanism sustaining chronic pain, then treatments targeting peripheral tissue alone will be insufficient. The target must include the sensitized central nervous system itself:

- **Neuroplasticity-based approaches** — [somatic practices](../../../../../somatics-services-section/content/text/glossary/topics/somatics.md) that retrain the nervous system's processing of sensation (graded motor imagery, mirror therapy, [somatic awareness](../../../../../somatics-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/somatic-awareness.md) training) address the cortical and spinal components of sensitization
- **Descending modulation** — exercise, sleep optimization, stress reduction, and mindfulness-based interventions can shift descending modulation from facilitation back toward inhibition
- **Pharmacological modulation** — medications targeting central mechanisms (gabapentinoids, SNRIs, NMDA antagonists) rather than peripheral inflammation (NSAIDs) or peripheral nociception (opioids) may be more appropriate for centrally driven pain
- **Context modification** — because psychosocial factors (stress, isolation, threat perception) drive descending facilitation, addressing these factors is not adjunctive but mechanistically central to treatment

In TCM terms, central sensitization is a state in which [Qi](../../../../../traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/qi.md) stagnation has become self-perpetuating — the system's operational flow is disrupted not by an ongoing obstruction but by the pattern of disruption itself. The system has learned dysfunction.

## Related terms

- [Nociception](./nociception.md) — the peripheral process that central sensitization amplifies and distorts
- [Chronic Pain](./chronic-pain.md) — the clinical condition sustained by central sensitization
- [Allodynia](./allodynia.md) — pain from non-noxious stimuli, a cardinal feature
- [Hyperalgesia](./hyperalgesia.md) — amplified pain response, another cardinal feature

records.name: Channel Entry
records.description: 归经 (gui jing) — the concept that each medicinal herb has an affinity for specific meridians and organ-function systems, directing its therapeutic effects to particular body regions and functions
records.body:
Channel entry (gui jing 归经, literally "returning to the channel") is the concept in [Traditional Chinese Medicine](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/traditional-chinese-medicine.md) that each medicinal herb has a natural affinity for specific [meridians](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/meridians.md) and [organ-function systems](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/zang-fu.md). When an herb "enters" a channel, it means the herb's therapeutic effects are directed preferentially toward the organs and body regions associated with that channel. Channel entry is one of the three primary classification axes for herbs in the TCM materia medica, alongside the four natures (thermal character) and five tastes.

## What channel entry means clinically

Channel entry answers the question: *where does this herb go?* Two herbs may share the same nature (cold) and taste (bitter), but if they enter different channels, they treat different conditions. This is the concept that makes Chinese herbal medicine a precision system rather than a crude "hot herb for cold pattern" approach.

For example, [Hu Zhang](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/hu-zhang.md) enters the **Liver, Gallbladder, and Lung** channels. This means:
- Its blood-invigorating action is directed toward Liver-related conditions (menstrual disorders, hypochondriac pain, eye disorders)
- Its damp-heat-clearing action is directed toward the Gallbladder (jaundice, gallstones, bitter taste)
- Its phlegm-resolving action is directed toward the Lung (cough with thick sputum)

If a practitioner needed to clear damp-heat from the Bladder (urinary tract infection), they would choose a different herb that enters the Bladder channel — not because Hu Zhang cannot clear damp-heat, but because its therapeutic action is directed elsewhere.

## How channel entry was determined

Channel entry was determined empirically over centuries of clinical observation. When practitioners consistently observed that a particular herb relieved headaches along the Gallbladder meridian (temporal region), improved vision (Liver opens to the eyes), and resolved rib-side pain (Liver/Gallbladder region), they recorded that herb as entering the Liver and Gallbladder channels. The classification is a condensation of clinical observation, not a deduction from theory.

Modern pharmacological research provides partial mechanistic explanations for some channel affinities. Herbs that "enter the Liver channel" often contain compounds that affect hepatic metabolism, bile secretion, or the smooth muscle of the biliary tract. Herbs that "enter the Lung channel" often contain volatile compounds that reach the respiratory tract or affect bronchial smooth muscle. These correspondences are not universal — channel entry describes functional targeting, not receptor pharmacology — but they suggest that the traditional classification identified real tissue-level affinities through functional observation.

## Channel entry and formula design

Channel entry is essential to [formula](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/herbal-medicine.md) design. The **envoy herb** (shi 使) in a formula's hierarchical structure often serves as a channel guide — directing the other herbs to the target organ system. Platycodon (jie geng) guides formulas upward to the Lung. Achyranthes (niu xi) guides formulas downward to the Kidney and lower body. Bupleurum (chai hu) guides to the Liver.

When [Hu Zhang](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/hu-zhang.md) is combined with Yin Chen Hao (Artemisia capillaris) for jaundice, both herbs enter the Liver/Gallbladder channel — their therapeutic actions converge on the same target system. When Hu Zhang is combined with Bei Mu (Fritillaria) for phlegm-heat cough, both enter the Lung channel. The formula's coherence depends on channel entry alignment.

## Related

- [Zang-Fu](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/zang-fu.md) — the organ-function systems targeted by channel entry
- [Herbal Medicine](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/herbal-medicine.md) — the therapeutic system that uses channel entry for formula design

records.name: Chronic Pain
records.description: Pain persisting beyond tissue healing, sustained by central sensitization and neuroplastic changes rather than ongoing peripheral injury
records.body:
**Chronic pain** is pain that persists beyond the expected period of tissue healing — conventionally defined as pain lasting longer than three months, though the temporal boundary is less important than the underlying mechanism. In chronic pain, the nervous system has undergone changes that decouple the pain experience from ongoing tissue damage. The pain is real, neurophysiologically grounded, and often severe — but it is no longer a readout of peripheral injury. It is a self-sustaining process within the nervous system itself.

This is the single most important concept in pain medicine, and the one most frequently misunderstood. Chronic pain is not [acute pain](./acute-pain.md) that forgot to stop. It is not the patient's failure to recover. It is a distinct neurophysiological state characterized by [central sensitization](./central-sensitization.md), altered descending modulation, neuroinflammation, and structural reorganization of pain-processing circuits. The nervous system has learned to produce pain — and it continues to produce it even after the original stimulus is gone.

## Mechanisms

Several overlapping processes sustain chronic pain:

- **Central sensitization** — dorsal horn neurons become hyperexcitable, amplifying signals and responding to inputs that would not normally produce pain ([allodynia](./allodynia.md)) or producing exaggerated responses to mildly painful stimuli ([hyperalgesia](./hyperalgesia.md))
- **Descending facilitation** — brainstem circuits that normally inhibit pain transmission shift toward facilitating it, creating a pro-nociceptive state
- **Neuroinflammation** — glial cells (microglia, astrocytes) in the spinal cord and brain become activated, releasing inflammatory mediators that maintain sensitization
- **Cortical reorganization** — pain-processing regions in the brain undergo structural and functional changes; the somatosensory map may blur or expand, and the affective (emotional/suffering) dimension of pain may become amplified relative to the sensory-discriminative dimension
- **Autonomic dysregulation** — chronic pain states are often accompanied by sympathetic nervous system changes that feed back into the pain cycle (sleep disruption, stress-axis activation, immune dysfunction)

## The biopsychosocial reality

The biopsychosocial model of pain — which recognizes that biological, psychological, and social factors all contribute to the pain experience — is not a polite way of saying chronic pain is partly psychological. It is a statement about how nervous systems work. Stress, sleep deprivation, social isolation, economic precarity, and trauma all measurably alter the neurophysiology of pain processing. A patient whose chronic pain worsens during periods of financial stress is not imagining the increase — their descending modulation shifts under stress, their inflammatory markers rise, their sleep architecture deteriorates, and their pain amplifies through identifiable neural mechanisms.

This means that effective treatment of chronic pain requires addressing the conditions in which the nervous system operates, not just the nerve fibers that carry the signal. [Somatic practices](../../../../../somatics-services-section/content/text/glossary/topics/somatics.md) that retrain [interoceptive](../../../../../somatics-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/interoception.md) processing and [somatic awareness](../../../../../somatics-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/somatic-awareness.md) address the neuroplastic dimension. [Harm reduction](../../../../../public-health-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/harm-reduction.md) frameworks address the pharmacological dimension without demanding abstinence. [Disability justice](../../../../../../content/text/glossary/terms/disability-justice.md) addresses the structural conditions that concentrate chronic pain in specific populations.

## Chronic pain as political phenomenon

Chronic pain is not distributed randomly. It concentrates in populations subject to:

- **Structural poverty** — economic precarity produces chronic stress, inadequate nutrition, poor sleep, limited access to care, and exposure to environmental toxins — all of which drive the neurophysiological processes that sustain chronic pain
- **Racial and gender discrimination** — systematic undertreating of pain in Black patients and women is well-documented; but beyond acute undertreating, the chronic stress of discrimination itself alters pain processing through allostatic load
- **Disability** — many disabling conditions involve chronic pain; and the social conditions of disability (isolation, poverty, barriers to access, medical abandonment) worsen pain through the biopsychosocial mechanisms described above
- **Occupational injury** — workers in physically demanding, poorly compensated jobs sustain injuries that transition to chronic pain, then face a medical system that questions their pain reports and an insurance system that pressures return to work

[Disability justice](../../../../../../content/text/glossary/terms/disability-justice.md) activists insist that these patterns are not incidental. Chronic pain is a [syndemic](../../../../../public-health-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/syndemic.md) condition — it interacts synergistically with the structural conditions that produce it, creating feedback loops that no single-point intervention can break.

## Related terms

- [Acute Pain](./acute-pain.md) — the protective pain that chronic pain diverges from
- [Central Sensitization](./central-sensitization.md) — the primary mechanism sustaining chronic pain
- [Allodynia](./allodynia.md) — pain from non-painful stimuli, a hallmark of sensitized states
- [Hyperalgesia](./hyperalgesia.md) — amplified pain from normally painful stimuli

records.name: Coagulation Cascade
records.description: The series of serine-protease-mediated reactions by which tissue factor, platelets, and clotting factors assemble on an anionic phospholipid membrane surface to generate thrombin and fibrin, with the essential membrane requirement being phosphatidylserine externalization on the platelet surface.

osterud1977.title: Activation of Factor IX by the reactions of blood coagulation

records.body:
The coagulation cascade is the series of enzyme-catalyzed reactions by which
blood clotting is initiated and propagated. Classically it is described in
three stages: the intrinsic pathway (initiated by contact with tissue damage
or foreign surfaces), the extrinsic pathway (initiated by tissue factor
exposure), and the common pathway, all converging on the generation of
thrombin, which then cleaves fibrinogen to fibrin and activates fibrin-
stabilizing factor XIII. Each stage consists of serine proteases activating
downstream serine proteases in a cascade of amplification.

The classical cascade model describes these reactions as occurring in bulk
aqueous phase. However, modern cellular and biophysical studies have
established that the coagulation cascade does not function as a soluble
cascade. Instead, it is a membrane-localized process: the critical amplification
step, the activation of factor X to factor Xa, and the subsequent formation of
thrombin-generating complex (the tenase complex), occur exclusively on the
surface of activated platelets. More specifically, these complexes assemble on
an anionic phospholipid bilayer with calcium and vitamin K-dependent factors
anchored to the membrane via calcium bridges. The essential anionic phospholipid
is phosphatidylserine.

## The prothrombinase complex and the membrane requirement

The prothrombinase complex itself is the assembly of factor Xa and factor Va
on a phospholipid surface in the presence of calcium. This complex catalyzes
the activation of prothrombin (factor II) to thrombin at a rate roughly 200,000
times faster than factor Xa alone in solution. This enormous rate enhancement —
the factor of 200,000 — is not because the enzyme has become more active; it is
because the enzyme and substrate are now constrained in two dimensions on the
membrane surface. The membrane brings them into proximity and holds them there.
Without the membrane, the reaction rate is negligible.

This has a crucial consequence: phosphatidylserine availability is not a
modifier of coagulation; it is a location requirement. Coagulation cannot occur
without it. In healthy hemostasis, phosphatidylserine is normally restricted to
the inner (cytoplasmic) leaflet of cell membranes by ATP-dependent flippase
activity. Upon platelet activation — by thrombin, collagen, ADP, or thromboxane
— this lipid is externalized to the outer leaflet through calcium-activated
scramblase activity. This externalization occurs on a seconds-to-minutes
timescale and exposes the anionic charge that the coagulation complexes require.

## The cell-based model replaces the cascade model

The classical cascade model has been superseded in modern hematology by the
cell-based model of coagulation, which describes coagulation as occurring on
the surfaces of platelets, tissue factor-bearing cells, and red cells. In this
model:

1. **Initiation phase** — Tissue factor on the surface of an injured cell
   encounters factor VII in the blood. Factor VII binds tissue factor, and the
   complex activates factor X. This occurs on the tissue factor-bearing cell
   surface.
2. **Amplification phase** — The small amount of thrombin generated in
   initiation is amplified by the "tenase complex" (factor IXa + factor VIIIa)
   assembling on the platelet surface, which then activates factor X to factor
   Xa at much higher rates than soluble factor VII can.
3. **Propagation phase** — The prothrombinase complex (factor Xa + factor Va)
   assembles on the phosphatidylserine-bearing platelet surface and generates
   large amounts of thrombin from prothrombin.
4. **Fibrin formation** — Thrombin cleaves fibrinogen to fibrin and cross-links
   the clot via factor XIII.

The advantage of the cell-based model is that it explains why clotting is
spatially localized. Coagulation does not happen throughout the entire blood
volume; it happens where platelets are activated and where phospholipid
surfaces are exposed. This spatial confinement is the whole purpose — to arrest
bleeding at the site of injury without ocluding the entire vascular tree.

## Consequence: phospholipid availability as a coagulation determinant

Because the prothrombinase complex absolutely requires a phosphatidylserine-
bearing surface, anything that causes phosphatidylserine to externalize more
widely — either on more cells or for longer periods — has the potential to
shift coagulation in a procoagulant direction. Conversely, anything that
impairs phosphatidylserine externalization (such as flippase gain-of-function,
ATP depletion that impairs scramblase, or deficiency of calcium signaling
cascades that normally trigger externalization) shifts toward an
anticoagulant phenotype. This is why phosphatidylserine externalization is not
a curiosity of cell biology; it is a load-bearing fact of hemostasis.

## Related terms

- Phosphatidylserine — the anionic membrane lipid on which coagulation
  complexes assemble
- Platelet activation — the process producing phosphatidylserine externalization
- Prothrombinase complex — factor Xa + factor Va assembling on phosphatidylserine
- Fibrin — the final product of the coagulation cascade
- Thrombin — the final active serine protease in the cascade, produced from
  prothrombin

records.name: Conditioned Pain Modulation
records.description: A pain-suppression mechanism in which one noxious stimulus suppresses pain from a second noxious stimulus, mediated by descending inhibitory brainstem pathways.

yarnitsky2010.title: Conditioned pain modulation (the diffuse noxious inhibitory control-like effect): its relevance for acute and chronic pain states

records.body: Conditioned pain modulation (CPM) is a psychophysical phenomenon in which activation of one painful stimulus reduces perceived intensity of a second painful stimulus. The mechanism involves descending inhibitory pathways: painful input from one body region reaches the brainstem (periaqueductal gray, rostral ventromedial medulla), which sends inhibitory signals down the spinal cord, suppressing nociceptive transmission from a second region. CPM is also known as diffuse noxious inhibitory control (DNIC). The classical demonstration is cold-water immersion: immersing one hand in cold water reduces pain from simultaneous pressure to the foot. In acute pain, CPM is typically efficient, with painful input triggering strong descending inhibition. In chronic pain states, CPM efficiency is often reduced, contributing to pain amplification and central sensitization. CPM is distinct from distraction, which suppresses pain through attentional mechanisms. Clinically, CPM can be quantified by measuring pain perception with and without a conditioning stimulus. Efficient CPM is associated with better pain tolerance. Reduced CPM is found in many chronic pain conditions including fibromyalgia and persistent post-injury pain.

records.name: Cranial Electrotherapy Stimulation
records.description: Small pulsed alternating currents (microamperes to a few milliamperes) through electrodes on the earlobes, behind the ears or at the temples, for 20–60 minutes, used for anxiety, insomnia and depression; a prescription device class in the US with modest, low-certainty evidence for anxiety.

shekelle2018.title: Benefits and Harms of Cranial Electrical Stimulation for Chronic Painful Conditions, Depression, Anxiety, and Insomnia: A Systematic Review

kavirajan2014.title: Alternating current cranial electrotherapy stimulation (CES) for depression

barclay2014.title: A clinical trial of cranial electrotherapy stimulation for anxiety and comorbid depression

datta2013.title: Cranial electrotherapy stimulation and transcranial pulsed current stimulation: a computer based high-resolution modeling study

voroslakos2018.title: Direct effects of transcranial electric stimulation on brain circuits in rats and humans

records.body:
Cranial electrotherapy stimulation (CES) passes a small, usually pulsed and biphasic [alternating current](../../../../../../../../../../../physical-science-services-section/services/physics-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/alternating-current.md) through electrodes clipped to the earlobes, or placed behind the ears or at the temples, typically for 20–60 minutes a day. Devices differ widely in their dose. Some run at a fraction of a milliampere and low frequency, often below the level a user can feel. Others deliver several milliamperes on a higher-frequency carrier. It descends from the "electrosleep" research of the mid-twentieth century and is used chiefly for anxiety, insomnia and depression.

**Regulation.** In the US, CES devices fall under 21 CFR 882.5800. Since the FDA's 2019 reclassification they are Class II, prescription devices for anxiety and insomnia. Claims for depression remain Class III, which requires premarket approval.

**Mechanism.** Several routes are proposed, and none is settled.
- *Transcranial:* current-flow modelling of ear-clip montages shows that part of the current crosses into the brain, including toward deep structures, producing small [electric fields](../../../../../../../../../../../physical-science-services-section/services/physics-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/electric-field.md) [@datta2013]. Their magnitude is at or below the range where [transcranial stimulation](transcranial-electrical-stimulation.md) reliably affects neurons [@voroslakos2018]. The original claim, that CES shifts the EEG toward [alpha](../../../../../../../../../neuroscience-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/alpha-rhythm.md), is a statement of this route.
- *Peripheral:* the electrodes sit on skin supplied by sensory nerves, including the auricular branch of the [vagus nerve](../../../../../../../../../physiology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/vagus-nerve.md), so part of any effect could run through the same pathways [taVNS](transcutaneous-auricular-vagus-nerve-stimulation.md) targets.
- *Expectancy:* the conditions it is used for are ones where [placebo effects](../../../../../../../../content/text/glossary/terms/placebo-effect.md) are large [@kaptchuk2015]. Subsensory devices can be compared against a genuinely indistinguishable [sham](../../../../../../../../content/text/glossary/terms/sham-stimulation.md). Higher-current devices that tingle are harder to blind.

**Evidence.** A systematic review for the US Veterans Affairs Evidence Synthesis Program pooled 26 randomized trials [@shekelle2018]. It found low-strength evidence of a modest benefit in patients with anxiety and depression, and insufficient evidence for depression alone, insomnia, headache, fibromyalgia and other pain conditions. A Cochrane review of CES for acute depression found no adequate evidence either way [@kavirajan2014]. Individual sham-controlled trials report benefit, such as a five-week trial in outpatients with anxiety [@barclay2014], but they are mostly small and often industry-linked.

**Safety.** Adverse effects are mild and uncommon: skin irritation under the electrodes, headache, and dizziness at higher currents.

For a structured path from the physics to this evidence, see the [note on studying cranial electrotherapy stimulation](../../documents/articles/notes/2026/09/24/2026-09-24-note-on-studying-cranial-electrotherapy-stimulation.md).

records.name: Critical Appraisal
records.description: A structured method for judging the trustworthiness, relevance, and applicability of evidence before using it in clinical reasoning or care decisions
records.body:
**Critical appraisal** is a structured method for judging the trustworthiness, relevance, and applicability of evidence before using it in clinical reasoning or care decisions.

The practice originates in evidence-based medicine (EBM) and centers on a systematic set of questions applied to any piece of evidence — whether a randomized controlled trial, an observational study, a clinical guideline, or a [FOAM](./foam.md) blog post:

1. **Is the source trustworthy?** Who produced this content? What is their expertise? Do they cite primary evidence? Are conflicts of interest disclosed?
2. **Is the evidence valid?** What study design was used? Was the methodology sound? Are the results statistically and clinically significant? Could bias explain the findings?
3. **Is the evidence relevant?** Does this apply to my patient population? Were the study participants similar to the patients I treat? Does the clinical context match?
4. **Is the evidence applicable?** Can I implement these findings in my practice setting? Do I have the resources, skills, and institutional support? Does this conflict with existing local protocols?

In the context of FOAM consumption, critical appraisal takes on additional dimensions. FOAM content is typically not peer-reviewed, may not cite primary sources, and is shaped by the same platform incentives (engagement, novelty, shareability) that distort information in other domains. Red flags for FOAM content include:

- Strong recommendations without cited evidence
- Generalization from single cases to broad clinical populations
- Novel techniques presented without safety language or acknowledgment of limitations
- Recommendations that conflict with established guidelines without explicit justification

Critical appraisal is not skepticism for its own sake. It is the discipline that allows clinicians to learn from distributed sources without being misled by them. The goal is not to reject FOAM but to consume it with the same rigor applied to any other source of clinical evidence.

## Related terms

- [FOAM](./foam.md) — the open-access movement that makes critical appraisal essential
- [FOAMed](./foamed.md) — educational FOAM content requiring appraisal
- [Pretest Probability](./pretest-probability.md) — supports appraisal by anchoring interpretation

records.name: Critical Slowing Down
records.description: Critical slowing down is a dynamical-systems signature — rising autocorrelation and rising variance in a system's fluctuations as it approaches a bifurcation — first described in ecology and climate science, and proposed as a possible marker of an approaching transition between depressive and non-depressive mood states.

vandeleemput2014.title: Critical slowing down as early warning for the onset and termination of depression
vandeleemput2014.publication: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

bosdejonge2014.title: 'Critical slowing down in depression' is a great idea that still needs empirical proof
bosdejonge2014.publication: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

records.body:
Critical slowing down names a general property of dynamical systems approaching a bifurcation: as a stable equilibrium loses its resilience, the system's return rate to equilibrium after small perturbations slows, which shows up statistically as rising temporal autocorrelation and rising variance in the system's fluctuations over time. The concept originates in dynamical-systems theory and was developed and empirically tested in ecology and climate science, where it has been studied as a candidate generic early-warning indicator for approaching tipping points in systems such as lake eutrophication and climate subsystems.

Van de Leemput and colleagues (2014) imported this framework into psychiatry, testing whether rising autocorrelation, rising variance, and rising cross-correlation between momentary emotion ratings (collected by Experience Sampling Method) were associated with a person's later transition into or out of a depressive episode. Across two independent samples — 535 women from a general-population twin cohort, of whom 13.5% went on to a clinical MDD diagnosis, and 93 patients with MDD tracked for treatment response — the subgroups with an upcoming mood transition showed a significant upward trend in baseline autocorrelation, variance, and cross-emotion correlation relative to the subgroups without (p < 0.05 for each indicator). The authors themselves described this as a first empirical bridge between dynamical-systems theory and psychopathology, not a validated predictive model, and cautioned in their own words that accurate dynamical models are hard to build even for physical systems such as lakes or the climate, let alone psychiatric disorders.

This finding is directly disputed on statistical grounds. Bos and de Jonge (2014) pointed out that van de Leemput et al.'s three indicators were each measured once per person — a single snapshot of that person's own autocorrelation, variance, and cross-correlation across one week of sampling — not repeatedly across time within each person. The published result is therefore a between-subject association (people who later transition have higher autocorrelation than people who do not), but it was written up, and widely read, as though it demonstrated a within-subject dynamical process — an individual's own autocorrelation rising as they approach their own tipping point — which the design cannot distinguish from a simple confound: the higher-risk subgroups' higher baseline mean levels of negative emotion could themselves produce higher measured autocorrelation and variance without any genuine loss of resilience. Van de Leemput and coauthors published a reply defending the between-subject design as informative, though its specific arguments were not accessible for this review. What critical slowing down is nearest to, and must be kept distinct from, is mood instability: mood instability describes how much a person's affect fluctuates in magnitude, while critical slowing down describes a specific pattern in the rate and structure of those fluctuations — their autocorrelation and variance trending upward — that is hypothesized, not established, to precede a discrete state transition.

The consequence for research design is that a cross-sectional or single-timepoint measurement of autocorrelation and variance across subjects cannot establish that any individual's own mood dynamics are slowing down before a transition; only genuinely within-subject, repeated-over-time monitoring of one person's own indicators, tracked up to and through an actual transition, can test the within-person claim. None of this literature identifies a neural, hormonal, or other physiological mechanism for a mood switch: every model here is a formal statistic or dynamical-systems description fitted to self-reported mood time-series data, not a demonstrated biological switch mechanism.

records.name: Cupping
records.description: A therapeutic method applying suction-sealed cups to the skin to move stagnant Qi and Blood through meridians, understood in Traditional Chinese Medicine as a treatment for stagnation patterns.

cao2012.title: An Updated Review of the Efficacy of Cupping Therapy

kim2011.title: Cupping for Treating Pain: A Systematic Review

lauche2012.title: The Effect of Traditional Cupping on Pain and Mechanical Thresholds in Patients with Chronic Nonspecific Neck Pain: A Randomised Controlled Pilot Study

nielsen2012.title: Safety protocols for Gua sha (press-stroking) and Baguan (cupping)

records.body:
Cupping (ba guan, "pulling cups") is a therapeutic method in Chinese medicine that applies negative pressure to the body surface. Within traditional practice it is selected through pattern diagnosis and may be used to move constrained Qi and Blood, warm or open a region, or address pain and other patterns of obstruction.

Methods include fire cupping, wet cupping, sliding cupping, and rapid repeated or flash techniques. These differ materially and should not be treated as one identical intervention.

The circular red-to-purple marks produced by dry cupping are often read traditionally in relation to stagnation and treatment response. From a biomedical perspective, suction changes local perfusion and can produce petechiae or ecchymosis through superficial microvascular blood extravasation. These descriptions concern the same treated surface but are not equivalent diagnostic categories.

Earlier versions of this entry described the marks as "not vessel rupture" and attributed broad anti-inflammatory effects to increased prostaglandins. That wording was too strong. The defensible biomedical description is local vascular and tissue response to negative pressure, with clinical pain evidence that remains heterogeneous and generally limited by study quality.

Wet cupping deliberately breaches the skin and therefore has additional infection-control and blood-exposure requirements. Even dry cupping and [gua sha](./gua-sha.md) can create petechiae/ecchymosis; safety literature treats contaminated instruments and bloodborne-pathogen exposure as relevant concerns [@nielsen2012].

## Related

- [Gua Sha](./gua-sha.md)
- [Sha](./sha.md)
- [Qi](./qi.md)
- [Xue (Blood)](./xue.md)
- [Meridians](./meridians.md)

records.name: Cytochrome P450
records.description: A superfamily of heme-containing enzymes — primarily in the liver — that metabolize the majority of pharmaceutical drugs, dietary compounds, and environmental toxins through oxidation reactions
records.body:
The cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes are a superfamily of heme-containing monooxygenases found primarily in the endoplasmic reticulum of hepatocytes (liver cells) and enterocytes (intestinal cells). They catalyze the oxidation of a vast range of substrates — pharmaceutical drugs, dietary compounds, endogenous hormones, and environmental toxins — and are responsible for the metabolism of approximately 75% of all clinically used drugs.

The name reflects their biochemistry: "cytochrome" (colored cellular protein), "P450" (the protein absorbs light at 450 nm wavelength when bound to carbon monoxide). Humans have 57 CYP genes organized into 18 families and 44 subfamilies.

## The major drug-metabolizing CYPs

Five CYP enzymes account for the metabolism of most drugs:

| Enzyme | % of drug metabolism | Key substrates | Notable inhibitors |
|---|---|---|---|
| **CYP3A4** | ~50% | Statins, calcium channel blockers, immunosuppressants, many antibiotics | Grapefruit juice, ketoconazole, [resveratrol](resveratrol.md) |
| **CYP2D6** | ~25% | Codeine, tamoxifen, many antidepressants, beta-blockers | Fluoxetine, paroxetine |
| **CYP2C9** | ~10% | Warfarin, NSAIDs, phenytoin | Fluconazole |
| **CYP2C19** | ~5% | Proton pump inhibitors, clopidogrel, diazepam | Omeprazole |
| **CYP1A2** | ~5% | Caffeine, theophylline, some antipsychotics | Fluvoxamine, [resveratrol](resveratrol.md) |

## Drug interactions

CYP enzymes are the primary mechanism of pharmacokinetic drug interactions. A compound that inhibits a CYP enzyme slows the metabolism of all other drugs that enzyme processes, effectively increasing their blood levels — sometimes to toxic concentrations. A compound that induces a CYP enzyme accelerates metabolism of other drugs, reducing their efficacy.

This is clinically relevant for herbal-drug interactions. [Resveratrol](resveratrol.md) inhibits CYP3A4 and CYP1A2, meaning Japanese knotweed preparations can increase blood levels of drugs metabolized by these enzymes. [Emodin](emodin.md) also affects CYP-mediated metabolism. These interactions are the pharmacological basis for the contraindication of [Hu Zhang](../../../../../traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/hu-zhang.md) with certain pharmaceutical medications.

## Genetic variation

CYP genes are highly polymorphic — different individuals carry different versions of CYP genes, producing enzymes with different metabolic capacity. CYP2D6 polymorphism is particularly well studied: "poor metabolizers" (lacking functional CYP2D6) accumulate drugs that the enzyme normally clears, while "ultra-rapid metabolizers" (with duplicated CYP2D6 genes) clear drugs so quickly they may not achieve therapeutic levels at standard doses.

## See also

- [First-Pass Metabolism](first-pass-metabolism.md) — the process CYP enzymes drive
- [Bioavailability](bioavailability.md) — what CYP metabolism reduces
- [Resveratrol](resveratrol.md) — inhibits CYP3A4 and CYP1A2

records.name: Cytokine
records.description: A class of small, secreted signalling proteins produced by immune and other cells that coordinate inflammatory, antiviral, and immune responses through multiple receptor mechanisms; defined by context-dependence where the same cytokine can act as pro- or anti-inflammatory depending on target cell type, receptor subtype, and concentration.

rose-john2014.title: Trans-signaling is a dominant mechanism for the pathogenic actions of interleukin-6 in the brain

records.body:
Cytokines are small secreted proteins produced by immune cells (primarily T cells, B cells, and macrophages) and other cell types (endothelial cells, fibroblasts, tissue-resident cells) that act as extracellular signalling molecules in immune responses, inflammation, hematopoiesis, and wound repair. The class includes interleukins (IL-1β, IL-6, IL-10), tumor necrosis factors (TNF-α), interferons (IFN-γ, type I interferons), and chemokines (CXCL8, CCL2) — a functionally defined grouping rather than a single biochemical family. A cytokine is distinguished from a hormone by its source and mode of action: hormones are synthesized in specialized endocrine glands and transported via circulation to distant target tissues; cytokines are induced rapidly in response to local tissue damage or pathogen exposure and act primarily on nearby cells (paracrine signalling) or on the producing cell itself (autocrine signalling). The boundary blurs pragmatically — some cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6) can reach systemic levels and produce distant effects — but the conceptual distinction holds: a hormone is constitutive and glandular; a cytokine is inducible and distributed.

The mechanistically essential feature of cytokine biology is context-dependence and pleiotropy: a single cytokine binds multiple receptor subtypes on different target cells, and the same cytokine can produce opposite effects depending on which receptor is engaged, which cell type expresses it, and the ambient concentration and presence of costimulatory signals. IL-6 exemplifies this sharply. When IL-6 binds membrane-bound IL-6 receptor (IL-6Rα) on hepatocytes and some immune cells, it promotes acute-phase protein synthesis and supports immune activation — broadly anti-inflammatory in functional consequence. When IL-6 is shed as soluble IL-6R (sIL-6R) in circulation and the IL-6/sIL-6R complex activates gp130 on neurons, astrocytes, and endothelial cells that express gp130 but not membrane IL-6Rα, it drives bloodbrain barrier disruption, synaptic loss, and depressive-like behavior — broadly pro-inflammatory and pathogenic. The same molecule, same ligand-receptor family, opposite functional outcomes determined by target-cell identity and receptor subtype. This context-dependence means cytokine redundancy — multiple cytokines can activate overlapping downstream pathways — is a fundamental feature, not a limitation: TNF-α and IL-1β both activate NF-κB and can each upregulate the other, creating amplification loops where a single cytokine trigger can recruit multiple mediators.

The consequence for biomarker work and clinical assessment is severe and underappreciated: a single serum-cytokine measurement is a weak and potentially misleading instrument because (1) cytokine concentrations are highly variable between individuals and across time, (2) the same measured level can reflect opposite functional states depending on which cytokine and which target-cell responses matter for the disease being studied, and (3) cytokine panels, despite producing two decades of ME/CFS and related-condition research, have shown inconsistent findings across studies — meta-analyses of IL-6, TNF-α, IL-8, and other cytokines in ME/CFS patients report positive associations in some cohorts, null findings or opposite directions in others, and the heterogeneity appears robust to reasonable corrections for measurement error and publication bias. The inconsistency is not primarily a failure of measurement technique or statistical power; it reflects that serum cytokine levels, untethered from the cellular and receptor context in which those cytokines exert effects, are epidemiologically and mechanistically underdetermined as markers of disease state. Functional assays — the ability of a patient's stimulated immune cells to suppress cytokine production when exposed to dexamethasone or glucocorticoid, for instance — predict clinically relevant outcomes more consistently than absolute cytokine concentration does, and are the appropriate experimental readout for testing mechanistic hypotheses about inflammation's role in symptom generation.

## Related terms

- Interleukin — one major subfamily of cytokines
- Inflammation — the coordinated response cytokines help organize
- Receptor — the molecular target through which cytokines act
- Glucocorticoid-immunosuppression — how cortisol restrains cytokine transcription

records.name: D-Dimer
records.description: A fibrin degradation product, the fragment of cross-linked fibrin released into the blood when plasmin cleaves fibrin during fibrinolysis; elevated levels indicate recent or ongoing fibrin formation and degradation, with high sensitivity but poor specificity for thrombosis, and age-adjusted cutoffs required for clinical interpretation.

kearon2006.title: In reply: D-dimer cutoff can be raised for older patients

records.body:
D-dimer is a fragment of cross-linked fibrin released into the blood during
fibrinolysis. When thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin, factor XIII
(fibrin-stabilizing factor) catalyzes the formation of covalent cross-links
between fibrin molecules. When plasmin subsequently degrades this cross-linked
fibrin, one of the major products is a fragment consisting of two fibrin D
domains held together by these cross-links — the D-dimer. It is released into
the circulation as a soluble protein and can be measured in blood plasma.

## What an elevated D-dimer indicates — and does not

An elevated D-dimer level indicates that fibrin has been formed and degraded
somewhere in the body within the preceding hours to days. This is the highest-
sensitivity test for venous or arterial thrombosis. If a patient with suspected
deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism has a normal D-dimer, thrombosis is
highly unlikely, and further imaging (ultrasound or CT angiography) is usually
not needed.

However, D-dimer elevation is not specific to thrombosis. Fibrin formation and
degradation happen in many physiological and pathological states besides clotting:

- Inflammation and infection elevate D-dimer, because inflammatory cytokines
  upregulate coagulation
- Pregnancy elevates D-dimer as a normal physiological change
- Recent surgery or trauma elevates D-dimer for days to weeks
- Liver disease elevates D-dimer because the liver produces both fibrinogen and
  its clearance mechanisms
- Sepsis, malignancy, and disseminated intravascular coagulation produce massive
  D-dimer elevation
- Intensive exercise, acute stress, and epinephrine administration elevate D-
  dimer acutely
- Aging itself elevates D-dimer; a 70-year-old healthy person can have a higher
  D-dimer than a 30-year-old with a pulmonary embolism

The consequence is that while D-dimer is sensitive (if negative, thrombosis is
ruled out), it is not specific (if positive, thrombosis is not ruled in). A
positive D-dimer requires either further testing to confirm thrombosis or, in
the presence of a low clinical probability, may be a false positive. For this
reason, modern clinical use of D-dimer relies on a two-step process: first,
assess clinical probability (Wells score or similar), then use D-dimer to
refine that assessment.

## Age-adjusted cutoffs

The D-dimer cutoff used to distinguish "normal" from "elevated" has major
implications for clinical practice. Using a fixed cutoff (e.g., 0.5 μg/mL) for
all ages means that older patients will exceed the threshold more frequently,
leading to more imaging studies and more false-positive findings in the elderly.
Studies since the early 2000s have documented that age-adjusted D-dimer
thresholds improve specificity in older patients. A common recommendation is to
use an age-adjusted cutoff of (patient age × 0.01) μg/mL for patients over 50
years old. This acknowledges that D-dimer rises with age, and that the mere
fact of being older does not warrant imaging if the D-dimer is elevated only
modestly above what is expected for age.

## What a normal D-dimer does and does not exclude

A normal D-dimer value has high negative predictive value: it makes acute
thrombosis very unlikely. However, a normal D-dimer does not exclude:

- Chronic thrombosis (a clot that formed weeks or months ago and is now stable)
- Microclot burden that is not currently being lysed
- A clot that is partially organized (no longer actively degrading)

This is especially relevant to hypotheses about microclots in long COVID and
ME/CFS. If microclots are present but not currently being actively lysed by
plasmin, they would not produce elevated D-dimer. Some studies report normal or
low-normal D-dimer in cohorts where microclot counts are reported as elevated.
This finding is either evidence that (1) the microclots are not actively being
degraded, consistent with their proposed resistance to fibrinolysis, or (2) the
microclots do not exist, and the D-dimer result is the true finding. This
ambiguity — that normal D-dimer does not resolve whether microclots are present
or absent — is itself a source of uncertainty in the field.

## Related terms

- Fibrin — the protein being cleaved
- Fibrinolysis — the process generating D-dimer
- Plasmin — the enzyme cleaving fibrin to produce D-dimer fragments
- Thrombosis — the condition D-dimer is used to detect
- Fibrin degradation product — the broader category of fragments produced by
  plasmin cleavage

records.name: Damp-Heat
records.description: 湿热 (shi re) — a compound pathological pattern combining the heaviness and stickiness of dampness with the inflammation and urgency of heat, characteristically affecting the Liver/Gallbladder, Bladder, and digestive systems
records.body:
