These features are present across many [chronic pain](../../../../services/pain-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/chronic-pain.md) conditions: fibromyalgia, chronic low back pain, chronic tension-type headache, temporomandibular disorders, irritable bowel syndrome, and chronic pelvic pain syndromes. The conditions differ in their peripheral triggers but share central sensitization as a maintaining mechanism.

## Implications for treatment

If central sensitization is the mechanism sustaining chronic pain, then treatments targeting peripheral tissue alone will be insufficient. The target must include the sensitized central nervous system itself:

- **Neuroplasticity-based approaches** — [somatic practices](../../../../services/somatics-services-section/content/text/glossary/topics/somatics.md) that retrain the nervous system’s processing of sensation (graded motor imagery, mirror therapy, [somatic awareness](../../../../services/somatics-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/somatic-awareness.md) training) address the cortical and spinal components of sensitization

- **Descending modulation** — exercise, sleep optimization, stress reduction, and mindfulness-based interventions can shift descending modulation from facilitation back toward inhibition

- **Pharmacological modulation** — medications targeting central mechanisms (gabapentinoids, SNRIs, NMDA antagonists) rather than peripheral inflammation (NSAIDs) or peripheral nociception (opioids) may be more appropriate for centrally driven pain

- **Context modification** — because psychosocial factors (stress, isolation, threat perception) drive descending facilitation, addressing these factors is not adjunctive but mechanistically central to treatment

In TCM terms, central sensitization is a state in which [Qi](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/qi.md) stagnation has become self-perpetuating — the system’s operational flow is disrupted not by an ongoing obstruction but by the pattern of disruption itself. The system has learned dysfunction.

records.name: Chronic Pain
records.body:
Pain persisting beyond tissue healing, sustained by central sensitization and neuroplastic changes rather than ongoing peripheral injury

Requires
central-sensitization

**Chronic pain** is pain that persists beyond the expected period of tissue healing — conventionally defined as pain lasting longer than three months, though the temporal boundary is less important than the underlying mechanism. In chronic pain, the nervous system has undergone changes that decouple the pain experience from ongoing tissue damage. The pain is real, neurophysiologically grounded, and often severe — but it is no longer a readout of peripheral injury. It is a self-sustaining process within the nervous system itself.

This is the single most important concept in pain medicine, and the one most frequently misunderstood. Chronic pain is not [acute pain](../../../../services/pain-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/acute-pain.md) that forgot to stop. It is not the patient’s failure to recover. It is a distinct neurophysiological state characterized by [central sensitization](../../../../services/pain-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/central-sensitization.md), altered descending modulation, neuroinflammation, and structural reorganization of pain-processing circuits. The nervous system has learned to produce pain — and it continues to produce it even after the original stimulus is gone.

## Mechanisms

Several overlapping processes sustain chronic pain:

- **Central sensitization** — dorsal horn neurons become hyperexcitable, amplifying signals and responding to inputs that would not normally produce pain ([allodynia](../../../../services/pain-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/allodynia.md)) or producing exaggerated responses to mildly painful stimuli ([hyperalgesia](../../../../services/pain-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/hyperalgesia.md))

- **Descending facilitation** — brainstem circuits that normally inhibit pain transmission shift toward facilitating it, creating a pro-nociceptive state

- **Neuroinflammation** — glial cells (microglia, astrocytes) in the spinal cord and brain become activated, releasing inflammatory mediators that maintain sensitization

- **Cortical reorganization** — pain-processing regions in the brain undergo structural and functional changes; the somatosensory map may blur or expand, and the affective (emotional/suffering) dimension of pain may become amplified relative to the sensory-discriminative dimension

- **Autonomic dysregulation** — chronic pain states are often accompanied by sympathetic nervous system changes that feed back into the pain cycle (sleep disruption, stress-axis activation, immune dysfunction)

## The biopsychosocial reality

The biopsychosocial model of pain — which recognizes that biological, psychological, and social factors all contribute to the pain experience — is not a polite way of saying chronic pain is partly psychological. It is a statement about how nervous systems work. Stress, sleep deprivation, social isolation, economic precarity, and trauma all measurably alter the neurophysiology of pain processing. A patient whose chronic pain worsens during periods of financial stress is not imagining the increase — their descending modulation shifts under stress, their inflammatory markers rise, their sleep architecture deteriorates, and their pain amplifies through identifiable neural mechanisms.

This means that effective treatment of chronic pain requires addressing the conditions in which the nervous system operates, not just the nerve fibers that carry the signal. [Somatic practices](../../../../services/somatics-services-section/content/text/glossary/topics/somatics.md) that retrain [interoceptive](../../../../services/somatics-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/interoception.md) processing and [somatic awareness](../../../../services/somatics-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/somatic-awareness.md) address the neuroplastic dimension. [Harm reduction](../../../../services/public-health-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/harm-reduction.md) frameworks address the pharmacological dimension without demanding abstinence. [Disability justice](../../documents/articles/research/2026/07/31/lenticule-import/library/terms/disability-justice.md) addresses the structural conditions that concentrate chronic pain in specific populations.

## Chronic pain as political phenomenon

Chronic pain is not distributed randomly. It concentrates in populations subject to:

- **Structural poverty** — economic precarity produces chronic stress, inadequate nutrition, poor sleep, limited access to care, and exposure to environmental toxins — all of which drive the neurophysiological processes that sustain chronic pain

- **Racial and gender discrimination** — systematic undertreating of pain in Black patients and women is well-documented; but beyond acute undertreating, the chronic stress of discrimination itself alters pain processing through allostatic load

- **Disability** — many disabling conditions involve chronic pain; and the social conditions of disability (isolation, poverty, barriers to access, medical abandonment) worsen pain through the biopsychosocial mechanisms described above

- **Occupational injury** — workers in physically demanding, poorly compensated jobs sustain injuries that transition to chronic pain, then face a medical system that questions their pain reports and an insurance system that pressures return to work

[Disability justice](../../documents/articles/research/2026/07/31/lenticule-import/library/terms/disability-justice.md) activists insist that these patterns are not incidental. Chronic pain is a [syndemic](../../../../services/public-health-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/syndemic.md) condition — it interacts synergistically with the structural conditions that produce it, creating feedback loops that no single-point intervention can break.

records.name: Hyperalgesia
records.body:
Increased pain response to stimuli that are normally painful, where the magnitude of pain exceeds what the stimulus warrants

**Hyperalgesia** is an increased pain response to stimuli that are normally painful — the gain on pain is turned up, so that a mildly painful stimulus produces severe pain. Unlike [allodynia](../../../../services/pain-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/allodynia.md) (pain from non-painful stimuli), hyperalgesia involves stimuli that would produce some pain in anyone; the difference is in the magnitude of the response.

Hyperalgesia is classified by location relative to the original injury:

- **Primary hyperalgesia** — increased pain sensitivity at the site of tissue damage. This is partly driven by peripheral sensitization: inflammatory mediators lower nociceptor thresholds, so nerve fibers in the injured area fire more readily. The inflamed area around a cut or burn being exquisitely tender to touch is primary hyperalgesia.

- **Secondary hyperalgesia** — increased pain sensitivity in uninjured tissue surrounding the site of damage. This is driven by [central sensitization](../../../../services/pain-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/central-sensitization.md): the spinal cord amplifies signals from the broader region, not just from the injury site. The area around a burn being painful to light pressure, even where the skin is intact, is secondary hyperalgesia.

The clinical distinction matters. Primary hyperalgesia may respond to anti-inflammatory treatment targeting the peripheral sensitization. Secondary hyperalgesia will not — because the amplification is occurring centrally.

## Opioid-induced hyperalgesia

A particularly significant form is **opioid-induced hyperalgesia (OIH)** — a paradoxical state in which opioid use itself increases pain sensitivity. Rather than producing more analgesia, continued opioid exposure activates pronociceptive mechanisms (NMDA receptor activation, glial activation, descending facilitation) that amplify pain. The patient reports worsening pain, the clinician increases the opioid dose, the hyperalgesia worsens, the dose increases again — a cycle that can produce severe, widespread pain driven entirely by the treatment intended to relieve it.

OIH is clinically distinct from tolerance (which requires more drug to achieve the same effect) and from disease progression (which involves worsening of the underlying condition). It is one of the mechanisms through which the opioid crisis has harmed chronic pain patients — patients whose pain worsened precisely because of the medications prescribed to manage it, then faced dose reductions that produced withdrawal on top of iatrogenic hyperalgesia.

This dynamic connects directly to [harm reduction](../../../../services/public-health-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/harm-reduction.md). Patients experiencing OIH need careful, compassionate dose management — not abrupt discontinuation (which produces withdrawal and rebound pain) and not dose escalation (which worsens the hyperalgesia). The harm reduction principle of meeting people where they are, reducing immediate danger, and treating survival as the first priority applies directly to opioid taper in hyperalgesic patients.

records.name: Nociception
records.body:
The neural process of encoding and processing noxious stimuli, distinct from the conscious experience of pain

**Nociception** is the neural process of encoding and processing potentially harmful (noxious) stimuli. It is the nervous system’s threat-detection mechanism — peripheral nerve fibers responding to mechanical, thermal, or chemical stimuli that exceed a threshold indicating potential tissue damage.

Nociception is not pain. This distinction is foundational. Nociception is a neural event: a signal traveling from the periphery through the spinal cord to the brain. Pain is a conscious experience: what the brain produces when it interprets nociceptive and other inputs as indicating threat. The two can dissociate in either direction — nociception without pain (a soldier wounded in combat who feels nothing until the threat passes) and pain without nociception (a person with [central sensitization](../../../../services/pain-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/central-sensitization.md) experiencing severe pain from light touch).

## Nociceptive pathways

Nociceptors are free nerve endings distributed throughout the body (skin, muscle, viscera, joints) that respond to stimuli threatening tissue integrity:

- **A-delta fibers** — thinly myelinated, fast-conducting fibers that carry sharp, well-localized “first pain.” These produce the immediate, precise pain that makes you withdraw your hand from a hot surface.

- **C fibers** — unmyelinated, slow-conducting fibers that carry dull, diffuse, aching “second pain.” These produce the throbbing, poorly localized pain that follows the initial sharp sensation.

The nociceptive signal travels from the peripheral nerve to the dorsal horn of the spinal cord, where it undergoes the first stage of modulation. The dorsal horn is not a passive relay station — it is a processing center where descending signals from the brain, local interneuron activity, and input from other sensory fibers can amplify or suppress the nociceptive signal before it reaches higher centers.

From the dorsal horn, ascending pathways (primarily the spinothalamic tract) carry the signal to the thalamus and then to multiple cortical regions: the somatosensory cortex (localization and intensity), the anterior cingulate cortex (affective/unpleasantness dimension), the insular cortex ([interoceptive](../../../../services/somatics-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/interoception.md) integration), and the prefrontal cortex (cognitive evaluation and context).

## Modulation at every level

The clinical significance of nociception is that it is modulated at every stage of transmission. The intensity of the peripheral stimulus does not determine the intensity of the pain experienced. Modulation occurs through:

- **Peripheral sensitization** — inflammatory mediators (prostaglandins, bradykinin, substance P) lower the threshold of nociceptors, making them fire more easily. This is why inflamed tissue is more painful than healthy tissue, even to gentle touch.

- **Spinal gating** — activity in large-diameter mechanoreceptive fibers (A-beta fibers, which carry touch and pressure information) can inhibit nociceptive transmission in the dorsal horn. This is why rubbing a bumped elbow reduces pain — the touch input “closes the gate” on nociceptive input.

- **Descending modulation** — brainstem nuclei (periaqueductal gray, rostral ventromedial medulla) send signals that can either facilitate or inhibit nociceptive transmission at the spinal level. Stress, attention, expectation, and emotional state all influence this descending modulation.

This multi-level modulation is why pain is context-dependent, why placebo and nocebo effects are real neurophysiological phenomena, and why treating pain as a simple input-output system fails.

records.name: Anthraquinone
records.body:
A class of aromatic organic compounds with a tricyclic ring structure, found in rhubarb, senna, aloe, and Japanese knotweed — characterized by laxative, anti-inflammatory, and antimicrobial activity

Anthraquinones are a class of aromatic organic compounds based on the 9,10-anthracenedione skeleton — a tricyclic structure consisting of three fused six-membered rings with two ketone groups. They are produced by several plant families, most notably [Polygonaceae](../../../../../botany-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/polygonaceae.md) (knotweed, rhubarb), Fabaceae (senna), Asphodelaceae (aloe), and Rhamnaceae (cascara sagrada).

Anthraquinones are the chemical basis of the oldest known class of laxative drugs. Senna, rhubarb root, cascara, and aloe have been used as purgatives across multiple medical traditions for millennia. The laxative mechanism is well characterized: anthraquinone glycosides pass through the small intestine unabsorbed, are hydrolyzed by colonic bacteria to release the potential aglycone, which then stimulates colonic motility and inhibits water reabsorption — producing the cathartic effect.

## Key anthraquinone compounds

**[Emodin](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/emodin.md)** (1,3,8-trihydroxy-6-methylanthraquinone): Found in [Japanese knotweed](../../../../../botany-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/japanese-knotweed.md), rhubarb, and senna. The most pharmacologically studied anthraquinone, with anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, and anticancer activity beyond its laxative effect.

**Chrysophanol**: Found in rhubarb and senna. Laxative and hepatoprotective.

**Rhein**: Found in rhubarb. Anti-inflammatory and nephroprotective in animal studies.

**Aloe-emodin**: Found in aloe. Laxative and potentially anticancer; classified by IARC as possibly carcinogenic to humans (Group 2B).

**Physcion**: Found in Japanese knotweed. Hepatoprotective and antifungal.

## Safety

Chronic use of anthraquinone laxatives can cause electrolyte depletion (particularly potassium), melanosis coli (darkening of the colonic mucosa), and potential hepatotoxicity and nephrotoxicity at high doses. Traditional formularies limit treatment duration and combine anthraquinone-containing herbs with harmonizing agents to buffer their drastic action — a practice that modern toxicology confirms as prudent.

## See also

- [Emodin](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/emodin.md) — the principal anthraquinone in Japanese knotweed

- [Polyphenol](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/polyphenol.md) — the broader chemical class

- [Japanese Knotweed](../../../../../botany-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/japanese-knotweed.md) — a major source

- [Hu Zhang](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/hu-zhang.md) — TCM use of anthraquinone-containing knotweed

records.name: Bioavailability
records.body:
The fraction of an administered drug dose that reaches systemic circulation in pharmacologically active form, expressed as a percentage

**Bioavailability** is the fraction of an administered drug dose that reaches the systemic circulation in an unchanged, pharmacologically active form. It is expressed as a percentage: a drug with 100% bioavailability delivers its entire dose to the bloodstream; a drug with 50% bioavailability delivers half.

Intravenous administration has 100% bioavailability by definition — the drug is placed directly into the bloodstream. Every other route of administration has lower bioavailability because the drug must cross biological barriers and may be degraded or metabolized before reaching systemic circulation.

## Factors affecting oral bioavailability

Oral administration — the most common route — subjects drugs to several barriers:

- **Dissolution and absorption** — the drug must dissolve in the gastrointestinal fluid and cross the intestinal wall. Drugs with poor water solubility, large molecular size, or vulnerability to acid degradation have reduced absorption. Food, gastric pH, and gut motility all influence this step.

- **First-pass metabolism** — after crossing the intestinal wall, orally administered drugs enter the portal vein and pass through the liver before reaching systemic circulation. The liver’s CYP enzymes may metabolize a significant fraction of the drug on this first pass, dramatically reducing bioavailability. This is why some drugs (like nitroglycerin, which is almost entirely destroyed by first-pass metabolism) cannot be given orally and must be administered sublingually, transdermally, or intravenously.

- **Intestinal metabolism** — the gut wall itself contains metabolic enzymes that can degrade drugs before they reach the portal circulation.

- **Efflux transporters** — membrane proteins (like P-glycoprotein) in the intestinal wall actively pump drugs back into the gut lumen, reducing the fraction absorbed.

## Clinical significance

Bioavailability matters because it determines the relationship between the dose administered and the dose that actually reaches the drug’s target. When switching between routes of administration (e.g., from IV to oral), the clinician must adjust the dose to account for bioavailability differences. A drug with 50% oral bioavailability requires twice the oral dose to achieve the same plasma concentration as an IV dose.

Bioavailability also explains variability between patients and between different formulations of the same drug. Generic drugs are required to demonstrate “bioequivalence” — similar bioavailability to the branded version — but small differences can matter for drugs with narrow [therapeutic indices](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/therapeutic-index.md).

In [harm reduction](../../../../services/public-health-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/harm-reduction.md) contexts, bioavailability explains why route of administration dramatically affects both the effect and the risk of a substance. Smoking or injecting a drug bypasses first-pass metabolism, producing higher peak concentrations and faster onset than oral use — which explains both the more intense subjective effect and the higher overdose risk of these routes.

records.name: Cytochrome P450
records.body:
A superfamily of heme-containing enzymes — primarily in the liver — that metabolize the majority of pharmaceutical drugs, dietary compounds, and environmental toxins through oxidation reactions

The cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes are a superfamily of heme-containing monooxygenases found primarily in the endoplasmic reticulum of hepatocytes (liver cells) and enterocytes (intestinal cells). They catalyze the oxidation of a vast range of substrates — pharmaceutical drugs, dietary compounds, endogenous hormones, and environmental toxins — and are responsible for the metabolism of approximately 75% of all clinically used drugs.

The name reflects their biochemistry: “cytochrome” (colored cellular protein), “P450” (the protein absorbs light at 450 nm wavelength when bound to carbon monoxide). Humans have 57 CYP genes organized into 18 families and 44 subfamilies.

## The major drug-metabolizing CYPs

Five CYP enzymes account for the metabolism of most drugs:

Enzyme
% of drug metabolism
Key substrates
Notable inhibitors

**CYP3A4**
~50%
Statins, calcium channel blockers, immunosuppressants, many antibiotics
Grapefruit juice, ketoconazole, [resveratrol](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/resveratrol.md)

**CYP2D6**
~25%
Codeine, tamoxifen, many antidepressants, beta-blockers
Fluoxetine, paroxetine

**CYP2C9**
~10%
Warfarin, NSAIDs, phenytoin
Fluconazole

**CYP2C19**
~5%
Proton pump inhibitors, clopidogrel, diazepam
Omeprazole

**CYP1A2**
~5%
Caffeine, theophylline, some antipsychotics
Fluvoxamine, [resveratrol](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/resveratrol.md)

## Drug interactions

CYP enzymes are the primary mechanism of pharmacokinetic drug interactions. A compound that inhibits a CYP enzyme slows the metabolism of all other drugs that enzyme processes, effectively increasing their blood levels — sometimes to toxic concentrations. A compound that induces a CYP enzyme accelerates metabolism of other drugs, reducing their efficacy.

This is clinically relevant for herbal-drug interactions. [Resveratrol](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/resveratrol.md) inhibits CYP3A4 and CYP1A2, meaning Japanese knotweed preparations can increase blood levels of drugs metabolized by these enzymes. [Emodin](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/emodin.md) also affects CYP-mediated metabolism. These interactions are the pharmacological basis for the contraindication of [Hu Zhang](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/hu-zhang.md) with certain pharmaceutical medications.

## Genetic variation

CYP genes are highly polymorphic — different individuals carry different versions of CYP genes, producing enzymes with different metabolic capacity. CYP2D6 polymorphism is particularly well studied: “poor metabolizers” (lacking functional CYP2D6) accumulate drugs that the enzyme normally clears, while “ultra-rapid metabolizers” (with duplicated CYP2D6 genes) clear drugs so quickly they may not achieve therapeutic levels at standard doses.

## See also

- [First-Pass Metabolism](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/first-pass-metabolism.md) — the process CYP enzymes drive

- [Bioavailability](../../documents/articles/research/2026/07/31/lenticule-import/library/applied-sciences/medicine/archive/bioavailability.md) — what CYP metabolism reduces

- [Resveratrol](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/resveratrol.md) — inhibits CYP3A4 and CYP1A2

records.name: Drug Interaction
records.body:
A modification of one drug's effect by another, altering absorption, metabolism, elimination, or mechanism of action to produce potentiation, antagonism, or novel effects

Requires

- bioavailability
- therapeutic-index

Table of contents

- [Pharmacokinetic interactions](#pharmacokinetic-interactions)

- [Pharmacodynamic interactions](#pharmacodynamic-interactions)

- [Drug interactions and harm reduction](#drug-interactions-and-harm-reduction)

- [Drug-food and drug-herb interactions](#drug-food-and-drug-herb-interactions)

A **drug interaction** occurs when one drug modifies the effect of another — altering its absorption, distribution, metabolism, elimination, or mechanism of action. Drug interactions can increase a drug’s effect (potentiation), decrease it (antagonism), or produce effects that neither drug produces alone.

## Pharmacokinetic interactions

These occur when one drug alters the [pharmacokinetics](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/pharmacokinetics.md) of another:

**Absorption interactions** — one drug alters the absorption of another. Antacids raise gastric pH, reducing the absorption of drugs that require acid for dissolution. Calcium supplements bind to certain antibiotics (tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones) in the gut, forming insoluble complexes that cannot be absorbed.

**Metabolic interactions** — the most clinically significant category. The cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzyme system in the liver metabolizes the majority of drugs. One drug can:

- **Inhibit** a CYP enzyme, slowing the metabolism of every other drug processed by that enzyme. The inhibited drug accumulates, potentially reaching toxic levels at standard doses. Example: fluconazole inhibits CYP3A4, increasing levels of drugs metabolized by CYP3A4 (including some benzodiazepines, statins, and calcium channel blockers).

- **Induce** a CYP enzyme, accelerating the metabolism of every other drug processed by that enzyme. The induced drug is cleared faster, potentially falling below therapeutic levels. Example: rifampin is a potent CYP3A4 inducer that can reduce the levels of oral contraceptives below effective concentrations — a drug interaction with significant consequences that may not be apparent until pregnancy occurs.

**Elimination interactions** — one drug alters the renal or biliary excretion of another. Probenecid blocks the renal tubular secretion of penicillin, increasing penicillin levels. Lithium and NSAIDs interact through renal sodium handling — NSAIDs reduce renal lithium clearance, raising lithium levels toward toxicity.

## Pharmacodynamic interactions

These occur when drugs interact at the receptor or physiological level:

**Additive effects** — two drugs acting on the same system produce a combined effect equal to the sum of their individual effects. Two different sedatives each producing moderate sedation together produce heavy sedation.

**Synergistic effects** — the combined effect exceeds the sum of individual effects. The combination of opioids and benzodiazepines produces respiratory depression far greater than either drug alone — a synergistic interaction responsible for a significant proportion of overdose deaths.

**Antagonistic effects** — one drug opposes the effect of another. Naloxone reverses opioid effects by competitive antagonism at the mu-opioid receptor. Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepine effects by competitive antagonism at the GABA-A receptor. These antagonistic interactions are the pharmacological basis of overdose reversal.

## Drug interactions and harm reduction

The opioid-benzodiazepine interaction is one of the most lethal drug interactions encountered in clinical practice and in the community. Both drug classes depress the brainstem respiratory centers, and their combined effect on respiratory drive is synergistic, not merely additive. This interaction kills through a mechanism that neither drug’s individual dose-response curve predicts — a person who tolerates a given dose of opioid alone and a given dose of benzodiazepine alone may die from the combination.

[Harm reduction](../../../../services/public-health-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/harm-reduction.md) programs address this interaction through:

- **Education** — informing people who use opioids about the specific dangers of combining with benzodiazepines, alcohol, or other CNS depressants

- **Naloxone distribution** — providing opioid antagonist for overdose reversal

- **Supervised consumption** — providing settings where polysubstance interactions can be monitored and reversed

- **Prescriber awareness** — the coprescribing of opioids and benzodiazepines, which remains common in clinical practice, represents an iatrogenic drug interaction that guidelines increasingly warn against

## Drug-food and drug-herb interactions

Interactions are not limited to prescription drugs. Grapefruit juice inhibits intestinal CYP3A4, increasing [bioavailability](../../documents/articles/research/2026/07/31/lenticule-import/library/applied-sciences/medicine/archive/bioavailability.md) of drugs normally partly metabolized in the gut wall. St. John’s Wort induces CYP3A4, reducing levels of oral contraceptives, warfarin, and many other drugs. TCM herbal formulas — which may contain dozens of pharmacologically active compounds — interact with Western pharmaceuticals through mechanisms that are often unstudied.

records.name: Emodin
records.body:
An anthraquinone compound found in Japanese knotweed, rhubarb, and cascara — a laxative in traditional medicine and an anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, and anticancer agent in modern pharmacological research

Table of contents

- [Traditional use](#traditional-use)

- [Modern pharmacology](#modern-pharmacology)

- [Safety](#safety)

- [See also](#see-also)

Emodin (1,3,8-trihydroxy-6-methylanthraquinone) is a naturally occurring anthraquinone found in the roots and rhizomes of several medicinal plants, including [Japanese knotweed](../../../../../botany-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/japanese-knotweed.md) (*Reynoutria japonica*), rhubarb (*Rheum* spp.), cascara sagrada (*Frangula purshiana*), senna (*Senna alexandrina*), and aloe (*Aloe vera*). It is one of the principal bioactive compounds in the Traditional Chinese Medicine herb [Hu Zhang](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/hu-zhang.md) and in Da Huang (rhubarb root), where it contributes to their purgative and heat-clearing actions.

## Traditional use

In TCM, emodin-containing herbs are classified as bitter and cold — herbs that drain heat, dry dampness, and promote downward movement (purgation). Rhubarb root (Da Huang) is the archetypal “drastic purgative” in the Chinese materia medica, used for constipation with heat signs, abdominal distension, and blood stasis. Japanese knotweed rhizome (Hu Zhang) shares these properties. The laxative action of both herbs is attributable primarily to their anthraquinone content, of which emodin is a major component.

The laxative mechanism is well characterized: emodin and related anthraquinones inhibit sodium and chloride absorption in the colon while stimulating chloride secretion, increasing luminal water content. They also stimulate colonic motility through effects on enteric neurons and smooth muscle. This combination — increased secretion and increased motility — produces the cathartic effect that traditional practitioners describe as “draining downward.”

## Modern pharmacology

Beyond its laxative properties, emodin has attracted research attention for several pharmacological activities [[dong2016]](#ref-dong2016):

**Anti-inflammatory**: Emodin inhibits NF-κB activation and suppresses production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6) in both cell culture and animal models of inflammation. It inhibits the NLRP3 inflammasome, a protein complex implicated in chronic inflammatory conditions. These effects provide a pharmacological basis for the traditional use of Hu Zhang for painful, inflammatory conditions.

**Antimicrobial and antiviral**: Emodin has demonstrated activity against several bacterial species in vitro, including *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Streptococcus* spp., and *Helicobacter pylori*. It disrupts bacterial cell membranes and inhibits bacterial enzyme activity. Emodin also shows antiviral activity, including in vitro activity against SARS-CoV-2 — though clinical significance of this in vitro activity remains to be established for both antibacterial and antiviral applications.

**Anticancer**: Emodin inhibits cell proliferation and induces apoptosis in multiple cancer cell lines, acting through inhibition of casein kinase 2, tyrosine kinases, and HER2/neu signaling [[huang2007]](#ref-huang2007). Animal studies show tumor growth inhibition. No human clinical trials have established anticancer efficacy.

**Hepatoprotective and nephroprotective**: Paradoxically, emodin both protects against and can cause liver and kidney injury, depending on dose and duration. At low doses, it reduces oxidative stress in liver tissue. At high doses or with prolonged use, it causes hepatotoxicity and nephrotoxicity — a dose-response relationship that underscores why traditional formularies emphasize short-course use of purgative herbs and always combine them with harmonizing agents.

## Safety

Emodin’s toxicity profile is the reason traditional formulas do not use emodin-containing herbs as long-term monotherapy. Chronic high-dose use can cause diarrhea, electrolyte depletion (hypokalemia), liver enzyme elevation, and kidney damage. The International Agency for Research on Cancer has classified aloe-emodin (a closely related compound) as possibly carcinogenic to humans (Group 2B), and emodin itself is under review. These concerns apply primarily to isolated high-dose emodin or to long-term daily use of anthraquinone laxatives — not to short-course traditional herbal formulas at standard doses, where emodin-containing herbs are buffered by other formula components.

## See also

- [Resveratrol](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/resveratrol.md) — the other major bioactive from Japanese knotweed, with complementary pharmacology

- [Japanese Knotweed](../../../../../botany-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/japanese-knotweed.md) — the plant source

- [Hu Zhang](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/hu-zhang.md) — the TCM herb

## References

[dong2016]
Xin Dong, Jing Fu, Xiao-Bing Yin, Song-Lin Cao, Xiao-Cheng Li, Li-Rong Lin, Jia Ni.
(2016).
Emodin: A Review of its Pharmacology, Toxicity and Pharmacokinetics.
*Phytotherapy Research*, 30, 1207-1218.

[huang2007]
Qian Huang, Guang-Du Lu, Heather M. Shen, Maxey C. M. Chung, Choon Nam Ong.
(2007).
Anti-cancer properties of anthraquinones from rhubarb.
*Medicinal Research Reviews*, 27, 609-630.

records.name: First-Pass Metabolism
records.body:
The phenomenon by which an orally administered drug is extensively metabolized by the liver and intestinal wall before reaching systemic circulation, dramatically reducing the fraction of potential drug available

First-pass metabolism (the first-pass effect) is the metabolic degradation of an orally administered drug as it passes through the intestinal wall and liver before reaching systemic circulation. After absorption from the gut, all blood drains into the portal vein and passes through the liver before entering the general circulation. The liver’s metabolic enzymes — particularly the [cytochrome P450](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/cytochrome-p450.md) family — can convert a large fraction of the drug into inactive metabolites during this first passage, dramatically reducing the drug’s [bioavailability](../../documents/articles/research/2026/07/31/lenticule-import/library/applied-sciences/medicine/archive/bioavailability.md).

First-pass metabolism is the primary reason that many drugs require much higher oral doses than intravenous doses to achieve the same plasma concentration. It is also the primary reason that [resveratrol](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/resveratrol.md) — despite dramatic effects in cell culture — has disappointed in clinical trials: oral resveratrol is rapidly conjugated by glucuronidation and sulfation in the intestinal wall and liver, leaving peak plasma concentrations of free resveratrol orders of magnitude below the concentrations used in vitro.

## The metabolic gauntlet

An orally administered molecule must survive three sequential metabolic barriers:

- **Intestinal lumen**: Gastric acid, digestive enzymes, and gut microbiota can degrade the compound before absorption

- **Intestinal wall**: Enterocytes (intestinal epithelial cells) contain CYP3A4 and other metabolic enzymes, plus efflux transporters (P-glycoprotein) that pump drug molecules back into the lumen

- **Liver**: Hepatocytes contain the full complement of CYP enzymes, glucuronosyltransferases (UGTs), sulfotransferases (SULTs), and other conjugation enzymes

The net result is that for some compounds, less than 1% of the ingested dose reaches systemic circulation in active form.

## Clinical significance

First-pass metabolism explains why:

- Some drugs cannot be given orally (nitroglycerin, lidocaine) — they are almost entirely destroyed on first pass

- Sublingual, transdermal, rectal, and inhaled routes bypass the liver and achieve higher bioavailability

- Grapefruit juice interacts with many drugs — furanocoumarins in grapefruit inhibit intestinal CYP3A4, reducing first-pass metabolism and increasing drug levels

- [Polydatin](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/resveratrol.md) (the glucoside of resveratrol) has better bioavailability than free resveratrol — the glucose moiety allows active transport via SGLT1, bypassing passive diffusion limitations

## See also

- [Bioavailability](../../documents/articles/research/2026/07/31/lenticule-import/library/applied-sciences/medicine/archive/bioavailability.md) — the fraction of drug that survives first-pass metabolism

- [Cytochrome P450](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/cytochrome-p450.md) — the enzyme family responsible for most first-pass metabolism

- [Resveratrol](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/resveratrol.md) — a compound whose clinical utility is limited by first-pass metabolism

records.name: Half-Life
records.body:
The time required for the plasma concentration of a drug to decrease by half, governing dosing frequency, steady-state timing, and elimination duration

Requires

- drug-metabolism
- renal-clearance

**Half-life** (t½) is the time required for the plasma concentration of a drug to decrease by half. It is the fundamental parameter governing how long a drug’s effects last, how frequently it must be dosed, and how long it takes to reach steady state or to be fully eliminated from the body.

## What half-life determines

**Dosing frequency.** A drug with a short half-life must be given more frequently to maintain therapeutic concentrations. A drug with a long half-life can be given less often. This is why some antibiotics are dosed every 4 hours (short half-life) while others are dosed once daily (long half-life).

**Time to steady state.** When a drug is given repeatedly at fixed intervals, plasma concentrations rise with each dose until the amount eliminated between doses equals the amount administered — steady state. This takes approximately 4-5 half-lives. A drug with a 6-hour half-life reaches steady state in about 24-30 hours. A drug with a 24-hour half-life reaches steady state in 4-5 days. Until steady state is reached, the full therapeutic effect may not be apparent.

**Time to elimination.** After a drug is discontinued, it takes approximately 4-5 half-lives for the drug to be effectively eliminated from the body (>96% cleared). A drug with a 4-hour half-life is gone within a day. A drug with a 3-day half-life persists for over two weeks. This matters for [drug interactions](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/drug-interaction.md), for side effect duration after discontinuation, and for drug testing.

## Clinical significance

Half-life interacts with clinical context in ways that pharmacokinetic numbers alone do not capture:

**Withdrawal timing.** The half-life of a substance determines how quickly withdrawal symptoms begin after the last dose. Short-acting opioids (heroin, t½ ~30 minutes; oxycodone, t½ ~3-4 hours) produce withdrawal within hours. Long-acting opioids (methadone, t½ ~24-36 hours) produce withdrawal over days. This pharmacokinetic difference is why methadone and buprenorphine (t½ ~24-60 hours) are used in opioid agonist therapy: their long half-lives provide stable receptor occupancy without the peaks and troughs that drive compulsive dosing of short-acting opioids.

**Accumulation risk.** In patients with impaired elimination (renal failure, hepatic failure, elderly patients with reduced clearance), the effective half-life lengthens. Drugs that would normally be cleared between doses begin to accumulate, potentially reaching toxic concentrations at standard doses. This is why dose adjustment in organ impairment is not optional — it is a pharmacokinetic necessity.

**Context-sensitive half-time.** For drugs administered by continuous infusion (particularly in [airway management](../../documents/articles/research/2026/07/31/lenticule-import/library/applied-sciences/airway/index.md) and critical care), the time for plasma concentration to decrease by half after stopping the infusion depends on how long the infusion ran. Lipophilic drugs redistribute into fat compartments during prolonged infusion, creating a reservoir that extends the effective duration. This is why a patient who received propofol for a brief intubation wakes quickly, but a patient who received propofol for days in the ICU may remain sedated for hours after the infusion stops.

records.name: Pharmacodynamics
records.body:
The study of what a drug does to the body, including receptor binding, dose-response relationships, selectivity, and tolerance

Table of contents

- [Receptor-based mechanisms](#receptor-based-mechanisms)

- [Dose-response relationships](#dose-response-relationships)

- [Selectivity and side effects](#selectivity-and-side-effects)

- [Tolerance and sensitization](#tolerance-and-sensitization)

**Pharmacodynamics** is the study of what a drug does to the body — the mechanisms through which a drug produces its effects. Where [pharmacokinetics](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/pharmacokinetics.md) asks how a drug reaches its target, pharmacodynamics asks what happens when it gets there.

## Receptor-based mechanisms

Most drugs produce their effects by interacting with receptors — proteins on cell surfaces or within cells that normally respond to endogenous signaling molecules (neurotransmitters, hormones, cytokines). A drug that binds to a receptor can:

- **Activate it (agonist)** — mimicking the endogenous ligand. Morphine is an agonist at mu-opioid receptors, mimicking endogenous endorphins to produce analgesia, euphoria, and respiratory depression.

- **Block it (antagonist)** — preventing the endogenous ligand from binding. Naloxone is an antagonist at mu-opioid receptors, reversing opioid effects by displacing agonists from the receptor.

- **Partially activate it (partial agonist)** — producing a submaximal response even at full receptor occupancy. Buprenorphine is a partial agonist at mu-opioid receptors, producing enough activation to prevent withdrawal and craving but not enough to produce the full euphoria or respiratory depression of a full agonist. This pharmacological profile is what makes buprenorphine useful in opioid use disorder treatment — and what connects pharmacodynamics directly to [harm reduction](../../../../services/public-health-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/harm-reduction.md) practice.

## Dose-response relationships

The relationship between drug dose and effect follows a characteristic pattern:

- At low doses, increasing the dose increases the effect approximately proportionally

- At higher doses, the response curve flattens — the receptors are approaching saturation, and further dose increases produce diminishing additional effect

- At some point, a maximal effect (Emax) is reached — no amount of additional drug will produce more of the intended effect, though adverse effects may continue to increase

This curve explains why doubling a dose does not double the effect, why overdose produces toxicity before the therapeutic effect is maximized, and why different drugs that act on the same receptor can have different maximal effects (full vs. partial agonists).

## Selectivity and side effects

No drug acts on a single target. Every drug interacts with multiple receptors, enzymes, or ion channels — some with high affinity (producing the intended therapeutic effect) and some with lower affinity (producing side effects). The [therapeutic index](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/therapeutic-index.md) — the ratio between the dose that produces toxicity and the dose that produces the therapeutic effect — quantifies how much room exists between benefit and harm.

Side effects are not failures of the drug but consequences of its mechanism acting on targets beyond the intended one. Understanding why a side effect occurs (which off-target receptor is being activated or blocked) allows clinicians to predict side effects, choose between drugs with different selectivity profiles, and manage adverse effects when they occur.

## Tolerance and sensitization

With repeated exposure, the body’s response to a drug may change:

- **Tolerance** — the same dose produces less effect, requiring dose escalation to maintain the original response. Mechanisms include receptor downregulation (fewer receptors available), receptor desensitization (receptors less responsive), and compensatory physiological adaptations.

- **Sensitization** — the same dose produces increased effect. This occurs through different mechanisms depending on the drug and the neural circuit involved. Stimulant sensitization is a well-studied example: repeated amphetamine exposure produces progressively larger dopamine responses through neuroplastic changes in reward circuits.

Tolerance and sensitization can occur simultaneously for different effects of the same drug. Opioid users develop tolerance to euphoria (requiring higher doses for the same high) faster than they develop tolerance to respiratory depression (so the dose they need for euphoria approaches the dose that suppresses breathing). This pharmacodynamic asymmetry is the mechanism of opioid overdose death.

records.name: Pharmacokinetics
records.body:
The study of what the body does to a drug: absorption, distribution, metabolism, and elimination (ADME)

**Pharmacokinetics** is the study of what the body does to a drug — how it is absorbed, distributed, metabolized, and eliminated. The four processes are conventionally summarized as ADME:

**Absorption** — the movement of a drug from its site of administration into the bloodstream. A pill dissolves in the gut, crosses the intestinal wall, and enters the portal circulation. An intramuscular injection diffuses from the muscle into capillaries. An intravenous drug bypasses absorption entirely — it is already in the blood. The route of administration determines the speed and completeness of absorption, which determines [bioavailability](../../documents/articles/research/2026/07/31/lenticule-import/library/applied-sciences/medicine/archive/bioavailability.md).

**Distribution** — the movement of a drug from the bloodstream into the body’s tissues. Distribution depends on blood flow (well-perfused organs like the brain, heart, liver, and kidneys receive drug first), protein binding (drugs bound to plasma proteins cannot cross into tissues; only the unbound fraction is pharmacologically active), lipid solubility (lipophilic drugs cross cell membranes readily and accumulate in fatty tissues), and specialized barriers (the blood-brain barrier limits access to the central nervous system).

**Metabolism** — the chemical transformation of a drug, primarily by the liver. Hepatic enzymes — especially the cytochrome P450 (CYP) family — convert lipophilic drugs into more water-soluble metabolites that can be excreted by the kidneys. Metabolism can inactivate a drug, convert an inactive prodrug into its active form, or produce metabolites that are themselves pharmacologically active or toxic. The CYP system is the primary site of [drug interactions](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/drug-interaction.md): drugs that induce or inhibit specific CYP enzymes alter the metabolism of every other drug processed by those enzymes.

**Elimination** — the removal of drug and metabolites from the body. The kidneys are the primary route (renal excretion), with hepatobiliary excretion, pulmonary exhalation, and other minor routes contributing. The rate of elimination determines [half-life](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/half-life.md) and therefore how long a drug’s effects persist and how frequently it must be dosed.

## Clinical significance

Pharmacokinetics determines the practical questions of drug therapy: how much drug to give (dose), how often to give it (dosing interval), how quickly effect onset occurs (route-dependent), how long the effect lasts (half-life-dependent), and what happens when the body’s processing capacity is impaired (dose adjustment in renal or hepatic failure).

Understanding pharmacokinetics also explains why the same dose produces different effects in different patients. Age (pediatric patients have immature metabolic enzymes; elderly patients have decreased renal clearance), body composition (obese patients distribute lipophilic drugs into larger fat compartments), genetic variation (CYP2D6 polymorphisms produce ultra-rapid or poor metabolizers), and organ function (renal or hepatic impairment slows elimination) all alter pharmacokinetics — and therefore alter the drug’s effect at the same dose.

records.name: Phytoalexin
records.body:
A defensive compound synthesized de novo by a plant in response to stress — pathogen attack, UV radiation, or tissue damage — explaining why stressed plants are often more pharmacologically potent than unstressed ones

A phytoalexin is a defensive compound that a plant synthesizes *de novo* in response to stress — pathogen infection, ultraviolet radiation, physical damage, or herbivore attack. Unlike constitutive defenses (compounds always present), phytoalexins are induced: the plant produces them only when threatened. The term was coined by Müller and Börger in 1940 from Greek *phyton* (plant) + *alexein* (to ward off).

Phytoalexins are typically low-molecular-weight antimicrobial compounds that accumulate at the site of infection, creating a localized chemical barrier against the invading pathogen. They belong to diverse chemical classes depending on the plant family: [stilbenoids](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/stilbenoid.md) in Vitaceae (grapes) and [Polygonaceae](../../../../../botany-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/polygonaceae.md) (knotweeds), isoflavonoids in Fabaceae (legumes), sesquiterpenes in Solanaceae (nightshades), indole derivatives in Brassicaceae (mustards).

## Resveratrol as phytoalexin

[Resveratrol](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/resveratrol.md) — the compound that made [Japanese knotweed](../../../../../botany-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/japanese-knotweed.md) pharmacologically famous — is a phytoalexin. The plant produces it in response to fungal infection, UV radiation, and tissue damage. This explains several observations:

- **Why knotweed rhizome is richer in resveratrol than aerial tissue**: The underground rhizome is the plant’s survival organ, under constant microbial challenge from soil organisms

- **Why resveratrol concentration peaks in autumn**: The plant is translocating defensive compounds to the rhizome for winter storage

- **Why stressed plants are more pharmacologically potent**: Traditional herbalists have long observed that wild-harvested plants are often more medicinally active than cultivated ones — the wild plant faces more stress and produces more defensive phytoalexins

## Pharmacological implications

The phytoalexin concept has a practical implication for herbalism and pharmacognosy: the very compounds that make a plant medicinally valuable are the compounds the plant produces to defend itself. The plant’s evolutionary defense strategy is the source of human therapeutic benefit. This is not coincidence — pathogens that attack plants share biochemical targets with pathogens and inflammatory processes that affect humans. An antimicrobial compound effective against a plant fungus may be effective against a human pathogen through the same mechanism.

## See also

- [Resveratrol](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/resveratrol.md) — the most studied phytoalexin

- [Polyphenol](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/polyphenol.md) — the chemical class most phytoalexins belong to

- [Japanese Knotweed](../../../../../botany-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/japanese-knotweed.md) — a major phytoalexin producer

records.name: Polyphenol
records.body:
A large class of plant-produced organic compounds characterized by multiple phenol rings — including flavonoids, stilbenoids, tannins, and phenolic acids — with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and cardioprotective properties

Polyphenols are a large and structurally diverse class of organic compounds produced by plants, characterized by the presence of multiple phenol groups — aromatic rings bearing hydroxyl (-OH) substituents. Over 8,000 polyphenolic compounds have been identified in plants. They are the most abundant [antioxidants](../../../../../../content/text/glossary/terms/inflammation.md) in the human diet, present in fruits, vegetables, tea, coffee, wine, chocolate, and medicinal herbs.

Plants produce polyphenols primarily as defensive compounds — protecting against ultraviolet radiation, pathogens, and herbivores. This defensive function is why stressed or damaged plants often produce higher concentrations of polyphenols than unstressed plants, and why [phytoalexins](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/phytoalexin.md) (stress-induced defensive compounds) are frequently polyphenolic.

## Major classes

**Flavonoids** (~6,000 known compounds): The largest subclass. Includes quercetin, catechins, epicatechin, kaempferol, anthocyanins. Found in virtually all fruits, vegetables, and medicinal herbs. Responsible for many of the colors of flowers and fruits.

**[Stilbenoids](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/stilbenoid.md)**: Includes [resveratrol](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/resveratrol.md) and polydatin (piceid). Found in grapes, peanuts, and most abundantly in [Japanese knotweed](../../../../../botany-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/japanese-knotweed.md). Stilbenoids are produced as phytoalexins — stress-response compounds.

**Tannins**: Large polyphenolic molecules that bind proteins. Responsible for the astringent taste of tea, red wine, and unripe fruit. Divided into condensed tannins (proanthocyanidins) and hydrolyzable tannins (gallotannins and ellagitannins).

**Phenolic acids**: Simple phenol derivatives including gallic acid, caffeic acid, and chlorogenic acid. Abundant in coffee, berries, and whole grains.

**[Anthraquinones](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/anthraquinone.md)**: Include [emodin](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/emodin.md) and related compounds. Found in rhubarb, senna, aloe, and Japanese knotweed. Distinguished by their laxative activity.

## Pharmacological significance

Polyphenols as a class share several pharmacological properties, though the potency and specificity of individual compounds varies enormously:

**Antioxidant activity**: Polyphenols scavenge reactive oxygen species (free radicals) through their phenol hydroxyl groups. This is their most widely promoted property, though the clinical significance of dietary antioxidant supplementation remains debated — the in vitro antioxidant activity of a compound does not predict its in vivo therapeutic benefit, because [bioavailability](../../documents/articles/research/2026/07/31/lenticule-import/library/applied-sciences/medicine/archive/bioavailability.md), metabolism, and the complexity of in vivo redox biology intervene.

**Anti-inflammatory activity**: Many polyphenols inhibit NF-κB, COX-2, and pro-inflammatory cytokine production. This activity is more consistently demonstrated in vivo than pure antioxidant effects and likely accounts for much of the health benefit associated with polyphenol-rich diets.

**Cardiovascular effects**: Epidemiological evidence consistently associates polyphenol-rich diets with reduced cardiovascular risk. Mechanisms include improved endothelial function, reduced platelet aggregation, and anti-inflammatory effects.

## The bioavailability challenge

Most dietary polyphenols have low oral [bioavailability](../../documents/articles/research/2026/07/31/lenticule-import/library/applied-sciences/medicine/archive/bioavailability.md). They are extensively metabolized by intestinal and hepatic enzymes and by the gut microbiome. The compounds that reach systemic circulation are often metabolites rather than the parent compound. This means the therapeutic effects of polyphenol-rich foods and herbs may be mediated by metabolites rather than the compounds measured in vitro — a major challenge for translational research.

## See also

- [Resveratrol](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/resveratrol.md) — a stilbenoid polyphenol from Japanese knotweed

- [Emodin](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/emodin.md) — an anthraquinone polyphenol from Japanese knotweed

- [Phytoalexin](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/phytoalexin.md) — stress-induced compounds, often polyphenolic

- [Bioavailability](../../documents/articles/research/2026/07/31/lenticule-import/library/applied-sciences/medicine/archive/bioavailability.md) — the central challenge for polyphenol pharmacology

records.name: Resveratrol
records.body:
A stilbenoid phytoalexin produced by plants under stress, studied extensively for anti-inflammatory, cardioprotective, and antioxidant properties — most commercially sourced from Japanese knotweed rhizome

Table of contents

- [The French paradox](#the-french-paradox)

- [Molecular targets](#molecular-targets)

- [Bioavailability problem](#bioavailability-problem)

- [Polydatin](#polydatin)

- [Clinical status](#clinical-status)

- [See also](#see-also)

Resveratrol (*trans*-3,5,4’-trihydroxystilbene) is a polyphenolic stilbenoid produced by plants as a phytoalexin — a defensive compound synthesized in response to injury, ultraviolet radiation, or fungal infection. It is found in grape skins, peanuts, blueberries, and most abundantly in the root and rhizome of [Japanese knotweed](../../../../../botany-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/japanese-knotweed.md) (*Reynoutria japonica*), which produces resveratrol at concentrations 50–100 times higher than grape skins and is the primary commercial source for dietary supplements.

## The French paradox

Resveratrol entered Western biomedical consciousness through the “French paradox” — the epidemiological observation, reported by Renaud and de Lorgeril in *The Lancet* in 1992, that French populations had lower rates of coronary heart disease than predicted by their saturated fat intake [[renaud1992]](#ref-renaud1992). Red wine consumption was proposed as the protective factor, and resveratrol — present in grape skins and therefore concentrated in red wine — was identified as a candidate molecule responsible for the cardioprotective effect. Whether resveratrol at the concentrations present in wine is sufficient to explain the epidemiological observation remains contested. The paradox may reflect dietary pattern effects (the Mediterranean diet), reporting artifacts, or multiple interacting factors rather than a single compound.

## Molecular targets

Resveratrol interacts with a broad array of molecular targets, which is both its pharmacological interest and the source of skepticism about its specificity:

**SIRT1 (Sirtuin 1)**: Howitz et al. (2003) reported that resveratrol activates SIRT1, a NAD+-dependent protein deacetylase involved in cellular stress response, metabolism, and aging [[howitz2003]](#ref-howitz2003). This finding launched a wave of aging research and commercial interest. Baur and Sinclair (2006) showed that resveratrol-fed mice on high-calorie diets had improved health markers and extended survival compared to controls [[baur2006]](#ref-baur2006). However, subsequent work revealed that the original SIRT1 activation assay used a fluorescent substrate that produced artifactual results — resveratrol’s activation of SIRT1 is indirect (via AMPK) rather than direct. The downstream metabolic effects are real; the mechanism is more complex than initially proposed.

**NF-κB pathway**: Resveratrol inhibits NF-κB (nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells), a transcription factor that drives inflammatory gene expression. This inhibition underlies many of resveratrol’s anti-inflammatory effects in cell culture and animal models.

**COX-2 (cyclooxygenase-2)**: Resveratrol inhibits COX-2, the same enzyme targeted by NSAIDs like ibuprofen. This provides a molecular basis for the anti-inflammatory and analgesic properties attributed to Japanese knotweed in traditional medicine.

**AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase)**: Resveratrol activates AMPK, a master regulator of cellular energy homeostasis. AMPK activation increases fatty acid oxidation, glucose uptake, and mitochondrial biogenesis — effects that mimic caloric restriction.

## Bioavailability problem

The central limitation of resveratrol pharmacology is bioavailability. Oral resveratrol is rapidly absorbed but extensively metabolized by first-pass metabolism in the intestine and liver, producing glucuronide and sulfate conjugates. Peak plasma concentration of free resveratrol after a 25 mg oral dose is approximately 1–5 ng/mL — orders of magnitude below the concentrations used in most cell culture studies (typically 10–100 μM). This disconnect between in vitro activity and achievable in vivo concentrations is the fundamental challenge for translating resveratrol research into clinical therapeutics.

Several strategies address this: higher dosing (clinical trials have used up to 5 g/day), formulation with absorption enhancers (piperine from black pepper inhibits glucuronidation), nanoparticle delivery, and the use of more bioavailable analogues like pterostilbene (a dimethylated resveratrol derivative found in blueberries).

## Polydatin

Polydatin (piceid) is the glucoside form of resveratrol — resveratrol bonded to a glucose molecule. It is the predominant form in Japanese knotweed rhizome, where it occurs at higher concentrations than free resveratrol. Polydatin achieves serum concentrations 3–4 times higher than free resveratrol at the same oral dose, because it uses the potential SGLT1 (sodium-glucose linked transporter 1) in the intestine rather than relying on passive diffusion. This dramatically better oral bioavailability, combined with greater water solubility and metabolic stability, has led some researchers to argue that polydatin, not free resveratrol, is the therapeutically relevant form in traditional herbal preparations — and that the bioavailability problem afflicting resveratrol research may partly reflect studying the wrong compound [[burns2002]](#ref-burns2002).

## Clinical status

Despite thousands of preclinical studies, resveratrol has not yet produced a breakthrough clinical application. Phase I–III trials have been conducted for cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, Alzheimer’s disease, and various cancers. Results are mixed: some trials show modest improvements in inflammatory markers, insulin sensitivity, or endothelial function; others show no significant effect. No major regulatory body has approved resveratrol as a drug. In the United States, it is sold as a dietary supplement under DSHEA (Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act). In the United Kingdom, trans-resveratrol is authorized as a novel food with a maximum daily intake of 150 mg for adults. It is typically sold as purified extract from Japanese knotweed rhizome, in capsule form at doses of 100–500 mg/day.

The gap between resveratrol’s dramatic effects in cell culture, its promising effects in animal models, and its modest effects in human trials is a case study in translational pharmacology — and in the difference between a compound’s biological activity and its therapeutic utility.

## See also

- [Japanese Knotweed](../../../../../botany-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/japanese-knotweed.md) — the plant source

- [Emodin](../../../../services/pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/emodin.md) — another major bioactive compound from the same plant

- [Japanese Knotweed as Medicine](../../../../services/herbalism-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/japanese-knotweed-as-medicine.md) — comprehensive medicinal text
