- **Cold** → congeals fluids into watery, copious phlegm (phlegm-cold: white, thin, easily expectorated)

## Phlegm and the mind

One of TCM’s most distinctive claims about phlegm is that it can “mist the Heart orifices” (tan mi xin qiao 痰迷心窍), obstructing [Shen](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/shen.md) and producing mental-emotional symptoms: confusion, muddled thinking, mania, incoherent speech, loss of consciousness. This “phlegm misting the mind” pattern is TCM’s framework for understanding certain acute psychiatric presentations, epilepsy, and post-stroke cognitive impairment.

The concept is not as foreign to biomedicine as it might appear. Neuroinflammation, cerebrovascular disease, and metabolic encephalopathy all involve the accumulation of abnormal substances (inflammatory mediators, lipids, metabolic waste) that impair brain function — the biomedical version of “turbid obstruction affecting the mind.”

## Treatment

Phlegm-resolving herbs (hua tan yao 化痰药) are classified by the type of phlegm they address:

- **Cold-phlegm**: Warm, drying herbs — Ban Xia (Pinellia), Bai Jie Zi (white mustard seed)

- **Heat-phlegm**: Cool, clearing herbs — Gua Lou (Trichosanthes), Zhu Ru (bamboo shavings), Bei Mu (Fritillaria)

- **Wind-phlegm** (causing dizziness, tremor): Tian Ma (Gastrodia), Gou Teng (Uncaria)

[Hu Zhang](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/hu-zhang.md) addresses phlegm-heat in the Lung through its bitter, cold properties.

## See also

- [Body Fluids (Jin Ye)](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/jin-ye.md) — the normal fluids that phlegm derives from

- [Qi Stagnation](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/qi-stagnation.md) — a major cause of phlegm formation

- [Damp-Heat](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/damp-heat.md) — dampness that has not yet congealed into phlegm

- [Shen](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/shen.md) — the awareness that phlegm can obstruct

- [Zang-Fu](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/zang-fu.md) — the Spleen and Lung systems central to phlegm pathology

records.name: Qi
records.body:
The circulating operational force in TCM that transforms, transports, protects, and warms — naming what the body does when alive and active

Requires
jing

Qi (氣) is the second of the [Three Treasures](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/san-bao.md) in [traditional Chinese medicine](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/traditional-chinese-medicine.md). It names the circulating operational force — the activity that transforms, transports, protects, and warms.

The character 氣 originally referred to vapor or breath and carries connotations of movement and transformation. In TCM, Qi is not a substance in the Western sense but a functional concept: it is what a body does when it is alive and active. Digestion is Qi at work. Circulation is Qi at work. The immune defense mounted against a pathogen is Qi at work. When TCM says “Qi flows,” it means the body’s functional activities are proceeding — not that an invisible fluid is moving through tubes [@kaptchuk2000].

TCM describes several functional varieties of Qi. Yuan Qi (original Qi) derives from prenatal [Jing](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/jing.md) and drives basic physiological processes. Gu Qi (grain Qi) is extracted from food by the Spleen and Stomach. Zong Qi (gathering Qi) accumulates in the chest and drives respiration and circulation. Wei Qi (defensive Qi) circulates at the body’s surface and protects against external pathogenic factors. These are not different substances but different functional roles of the same operational principle [@unschuld2003].

Qi circulates through the meridian system (jing luo 經絡), which connects the body’s organ-function systems to each other and to the surface. When Qi flows smoothly, functions proceed. When Qi stagnates, functions falter — and stagnation manifests as pain, distension, emotional frustration, or digestive difficulty. When Qi is deficient, the body lacks the operational force to maintain its activities: fatigue, weakness, susceptibility to illness.

Nathan Sivin noted that translating Qi as “energy” is misleading if it implies a measurable physical quantity [@sivin1987]. Qi is closer to a verb than a noun — it names what the body is doing rather than what the body has. The clinical question is not “how much Qi does this patient have?” but “is this patient’s Qi flowing, stagnating, rising when it should descend, or scattering when it should consolidate?”

For information systems, Qi corresponds to operational activity: data flowing through pipelines, queries executing, APIs responding, processes running. A system with Qi is a system whose operations are proceeding. The question TCM’s vocabulary raises is whether operational activity — data circulating, queries returning results, reasoners deriving new triples — is sufficient for a system to be alive in any meaningful sense. A system can have abundant Qi and no [Shen](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/shen.md): it operates but does not reflect. It processes but does not adapt. It runs but does not learn.

records.name: Qi Stagnation
records.body:
气滞 (qi zhi) — the condition where Qi flow is impeded or stuck, producing distension, pain that moves, emotional frustration, and sighing — the most common excess pattern in clinical TCM practice

Table of contents

- [The Liver connection](#the-liver-connection)

- [The cascade: what Qi stagnation produces](#the-cascade-what-qi-stagnation-produces)

- [Treatment principle: soothe the Liver, regulate Qi](#treatment-principle-soothe-the-liver-regulate-qi)

- [Qi stagnation and modern life](#qi-stagnation-and-modern-life)

- [See also](#see-also)

Qi stagnation (qi zhi 气滞) is the condition where [Qi](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/qi.md) flow through the body’s [meridians](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/meridians.md) and [organ-function systems](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/zang-fu.md) is impeded, slowed, or stuck. It is the most common excess pattern in clinical TCM practice — the default pathological response to emotional constraint, chronic stress, and sedentary modern life.

The concept follows directly from TCM’s understanding of Qi as circulating operational force. Qi should flow: smoothly, in the correct direction, through every organ system and meridian. When flow is impeded, the Qi “stagnates” — it accumulates where it should pass through, creating pressure, distension, and dysfunction.

## The Liver connection

Qi stagnation is most commonly associated with the Liver system, because the Liver’s primary function in TCM is to ensure the smooth flow of Qi throughout the body (shu xie 疏泄). When the Liver’s flow-regulating function is impaired — most often by emotional constraint, unexpressed anger, or chronic frustration — Qi flow stagnates throughout the body, producing the pattern known as **Liver Qi stagnation** (gan qi yu jie 肝气郁结).

Liver Qi stagnation is arguably the single most common pattern in modern TCM practice. The characteristic presentation:

- **Distension and fullness**: A feeling of pressure in the chest, hypochondrium (rib-side area), epigastrium, or abdomen — not a sharp pain, but a bloated, pressurized sensation that fluctuates with emotional state

- **Emotional frustration**: Irritability, mood swings, depression, a feeling of being “stuck” or unable to express oneself. The emotional quality and the physical quality mirror each other — the Qi is stuck, and the person feels stuck

- **Sighing**: Spontaneous deep sighing is diagnostic. The sigh is the body’s attempt to move the stagnant Qi in the chest

- **Distension that moves**: Unlike [blood stasis](blood-stasis.md) pain (fixed) or dampness heaviness (settling), Qi stagnation distension can shift location

- **Wiry pulse** (xian 弦): The most reliable pulse finding — the pulse feels taut, like a guitar string, reflecting the tension in the system

- **Symptoms worsen with stress**: The hallmark temporal pattern. The distension, pain, and emotional symptoms increase with emotional stress and decrease with relaxation, exercise, or emotional expression

## The cascade: what Qi stagnation produces

Qi stagnation is clinically significant not just for its own symptoms but because it is the upstream cause of several other pathological patterns:

**Qi stagnation → [Blood stasis](blood-stasis.md)**: Qi moves blood. When Qi stagnates, blood movement slows and eventually stagnates. This is the most common progression — Liver Qi stagnation producing menstrual pain, fixed masses, or cardiovascular dysfunction over time.

**Qi stagnation → Heat**: Stagnant Qi generates heat, the way friction generates warmth. Prolonged Qi stagnation transforms into Liver Fire — the irritability intensifies into outbursts of anger, the face flushes red, headaches become throbbing and temporal.

**Qi stagnation → [Phlegm](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/phlegm.md)**: When Qi stagnation impairs the Spleen’s transformative function, fluids accumulate and congeal into Phlegm. The classic presentation is “plum pit Qi” (mei he qi 梅核气) — a sensation of something stuck in the throat that can neither be swallowed nor expelled. This is TCM’s description of what biomedicine calls globus hystericus.

**Qi stagnation → [Damp-heat](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/damp-heat.md)**: Stagnant Qi impairs fluid metabolism (generating dampness) while simultaneously generating heat. The combined result is damp-heat — commonly settling in the Liver/Gallbladder system.

## Treatment principle: soothe the Liver, regulate Qi

The treatment of Qi stagnation involves herbs that move and regulate Qi flow:

- **Chai Hu** (Bupleurum chinense) — the primary Liver Qi-regulating herb; spreads Liver Qi, relieves constraint

- **Xiang Fu** (Cyperus rotundus) — moves Qi, alleviates pain; called “the general of Qi regulation”

- **Chen Pi** (aged tangerine peel) — regulates Qi in the middle burner, resolves Phlegm

- **Bo He** (peppermint) — disperses Liver Qi, clears the head

- **Yu Jin** (Curcuma wenyujin) — moves Qi and blood, particularly for Liver constraint with blood stasis

The classical formula is **Xiao Yao San** (逍遥散, “Free and Easy Wanderer”) — detailed in [Herbal Medicine](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/herbal-medicine.md) — which soothes Liver Qi stagnation while simultaneously nourishing Blood and supporting the Spleen.

## Qi stagnation and modern life

TCM practitioners note that Qi stagnation has become the background pattern of modern urban life. Sedentary work, emotional suppression in professional settings, chronic screen use, and the mismatch between the body’s need for movement and the reality of desk-bound existence create conditions that the TCM framework identifies as systemic Qi stagnation. This is not a claim about modernity’s pathology — it is an observation that the pattern TCM calls Qi stagnation maps onto the symptom clusters modern medicine sees in stress-related functional disorders: irritable bowel syndrome, tension headaches, non-cardiac chest pain, and functional dyspepsia.

## See also

- [Qi](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/qi.md) — the substance that stagnates

- [Blood Stasis](blood-stasis.md) — the downstream consequence

- [Damp-Heat](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/damp-heat.md) — another downstream consequence

- [Phlegm](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/phlegm.md) — another downstream consequence

- [Zang-Fu](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/zang-fu.md) — the Liver system whose dysfunction causes stagnation

- [Pattern Diagnosis](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/pattern-diagnosis.md) — how stagnation is identified

- [Herbal Medicine](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/herbal-medicine.md) — Xiao Yao San formula for Liver Qi stagnation

records.name: San Bao (Three Treasures)
records.body:
The diagnostic framework of Jing, Qi, and Shen — three layered aspects of vitality used in TCM and Daoist practice to assess the health of a living system

The San Bao (三寶), the Three Treasures, are [Jing](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/jing.md) (essence), [Qi](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/qi.md) (vital energy), and [Shen](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/shen.md) (spirit). Together they form a diagnostic framework for describing layers of vitality in a living system.

The framework is shared between [traditional Chinese medicine](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/traditional-chinese-medicine.md) and Daoist cultivational practice, though each tradition emphasizes different aspects [@schipper1993; @kohn2000]. In TCM, the Three Treasures organize clinical assessment: a practitioner evaluates whether the patient’s substrate is intact (Jing), whether their functional activities are proceeding (Qi), and whether their engagement with the world is coherent and responsive (Shen). In Daoist practice, cultivating the Three Treasures — conserving Jing, circulating Qi, refining Shen — is the path toward integrated vitality.

The three are not independent substances. They are three aspects of a single living process, distinguished by their level of refinement:

Treasure
Character
Layer
Diagnostic question

Jing
精
Stored substrate
Does the system have material to work with?

Qi
氣
Circulating activity
Are the system’s operations proceeding?

Shen
神
Reflective awareness
Is the system responsive to its situation?

The dependencies run upward. Qi draws on Jing: without a substrate, there are no operations to sustain. Shen depends on Qi: without operational activity, there is nothing to be aware of. But the relationship is not additive. More Jing does not automatically produce more Qi, and more Qi does not automatically produce more Shen. Each layer has its own conditions for health and its own modes of failure [@kaptchuk2000].

This layered structure is what makes the framework diagnostically useful. A system can fail at any layer independently:

- **Jing depleted, Qi and Shen present**: the system is aware and active but running out of material. A researcher who is intellectually sharp but physically exhausted. A database approaching storage limits while its query engine runs smoothly.

- **Qi stagnant, Jing and Shen present**: the system has substrate and awareness but its operations are blocked. A person with full reserves but functional paralysis. A well-stocked archive whose search infrastructure has failed.

- **Shen absent, Jing and Qi present**: the system has substrate and operational activity but no reflective capacity. The body moves but does not adapt. The data circulates but the system cannot question whether its own categories still serve.

The third condition — Qi without Shen — is the one that has no standard name in Western systems vocabulary. The system is not broken. It is not inert. It operates, often vigorously. But it operates within frames it cannot examine. It corrects errors but does not question whether the reference state is still appropriate. In [cybernetic terms](../../documents/articles/research/2026/07/31/lenticule-import/library/applied-sciences/information/terms/cybernetics.md), it performs [single-loop learning](../../documents/articles/research/2026/07/31/lenticule-import/library/applied-sciences/information/terms/single-loop-double-loop-learning.md) without [double-loop learning](../../documents/articles/research/2026/07/31/lenticule-import/library/applied-sciences/information/terms/single-loop-double-loop-learning.md). In Daoist folklore, this condition has a figure: the jiangshi (僵尸), the hopping corpse — animated by residual Qi, joints locked, unable to adapt its movement to the situation.

The Three Treasures framework does not rank Shen above Qi or Qi above Jing. A system needs all three. An abundance of Shen without adequate Qi is awareness without the operational capacity to act on what it perceives. The diagnostic value is in identifying which layer is compromised, not in asserting that one layer matters more than the others.

records.name: Shen
records.body:
The capacity for awareness, responsiveness, and coherent engagement with novelty — the third of the Three Treasures, assessed clinically through the patient's eyes, bearing, and affect

Requires
qi

Shen (神) is the third of the [Three Treasures](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/san-bao.md) in [traditional Chinese medicine](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/traditional-chinese-medicine.md). It names the capacity for awareness, responsiveness, and coherent engagement with novelty.

Shen is often translated as “spirit” or “mind,” but neither translation captures the concept’s clinical specificity. In TCM diagnosis, Shen is what a practitioner assesses when they observe the patient’s eyes, complexion, bearing, and responsiveness. Bright eyes, a clear complexion, coherent speech, and appropriate emotional responses indicate that Shen is present. Dull eyes, a waxy complexion, confused speech, and flattened or inappropriate affect indicate that Shen is disturbed or absent [@kaptchuk2000].

This makes Shen a diagnostic category, not a metaphysical claim. The practitioner is not asserting the existence of a soul. They are noting whether the patient’s engagement with the world is responsive and coherent or mechanical and diminished. A person in deep coma has [Jing](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/jing.md) (their body persists) and residual [Qi](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/qi.md) (metabolic processes continue), but their Shen has withdrawn. The body operates at a substrate level; it does not respond to its situation as a situation.

In the *Huang Di Nei Jing*, Shen is associated with the Heart (as a functional system). When the Heart’s Shen is settled, the person sleeps well, thinks clearly, responds to events with appropriate feeling, and can tolerate novelty without rigidity or collapse. When Shen is disturbed — by emotional shock, chronic illness, or constitutional depletion — the person may be anxious, disoriented, or affectively flat. The body continues to function, but its engagement with the world narrows [@unschuld2003].

Kristofer Schipper placed Shen within the Daoist cosmological framework as the most refined layer of vitality: Jing condenses into form, Qi animates that form, and Shen enables the animated form to be aware of itself and its situation [@schipper1993]. This is not a hierarchy of value but a hierarchy of refinement. Shen depends on Qi (without operational activity, there is nothing to be aware of) and Qi depends on Jing (without a substrate, there are no operations to sustain).

The clinical significance is that Shen cannot be restored by adding more Qi. A patient whose Qi is abundant but whose Shen is disturbed will be agitated, restless, operationally active but not coherently responsive. The treatment addresses Shen directly — calming the Heart, settling the spirit — rather than increasing operational throughput. More activity does not produce more awareness.

For information systems, Shen corresponds to what [second-order cybernetics](../../../../../../../../../information-science-services-section/services/cybernetics-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/second-order-cybernetics.md) calls reflexive capacity and what [Argyris and Schön](../../documents/articles/research/2026/07/31/lenticule-import/library/applied-sciences/information/terms/single-loop-double-loop-learning.md) call double-loop learning: the ability to question whether the system’s own categories, schemas, and operational frames still serve the situation they were built for. A system with Shen does not just process data according to its schema. It notices when the schema no longer fits — when the categories have drifted from the phenomena they classify, when the rules produce correct inferences from outdated premises.

This capacity is what the jiangshi lacks, and it is what no amount of operational sophistication can substitute for.

records.name: Wei Qi
records.body:
卫气 (wei qi) — defensive Qi, the protective force that circulates on the body's surface, warms the skin, regulates pore opening, and resists invasion by external pathogenic factors

Wei Qi (卫气, “defensive Qi” or “protective Qi”) is the aspect of [Qi](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/qi.md) that circulates on the body’s surface, between the skin and muscles, protecting against invasion by external pathogenic factors. It is TCM’s concept of the body’s first line of defense — analogous to what biomedicine calls innate immunity and barrier function, though broader in scope.

## Functions

**Warming the skin and muscles**: Wei Qi maintains surface temperature. When Wei Qi is weak, the patient feels cold and is easily chilled — not from internal [Yang deficiency](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/yang-deficiency.md) but from insufficient surface protection.

**Regulating pore opening and closing**: The opening and closing of the pores (cou li 腠理) controls sweating. Wei Qi governs this regulation. When Wei Qi is strong, pores open and close appropriately — sweating when the body needs to cool, closing when the body needs to retain heat. When Wei Qi is weak, pores fail to close properly, producing spontaneous sweating (zi han 自汗) — sweating without exertion or heat.

**Resisting external pathogenic factors**: Wei Qi is the shield against the [six external causes](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/etiology.md) (wind, cold, heat, dampness, dryness, summer heat). When Wei Qi is sufficient, the body surface is sealed and pathogens cannot penetrate. When Wei Qi is weak, the body surface is porous and vulnerable — the patient catches colds easily, is sensitive to drafts, and recovers slowly from upper respiratory infections.

## Production and circulation

Wei Qi is produced by the **Spleen** (from food Qi) and distributed by the **[Lung](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/zang-fu.md)** (which governs the body surface). During the day, Wei Qi circulates on the body’s exterior (yang regions) — this is why people are more alert and resistant during waking hours. At night, Wei Qi retreats to the interior (yin regions) — this is why the body surface is more vulnerable during sleep and why fevers often spike at night.

This day-night circulation also explains why spontaneous sweating (daytime, Wei Qi failing on the surface) differs from night sweats (nighttime, [Yin deficiency](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/yin-deficiency.md) failing to anchor fluids) — they are different pathologies despite both involving sweat.

## Clinical significance

Wei Qi weakness is the TCM framework for understanding recurrent upper respiratory infections, allergic rhinitis, chronic sinusitis, and the general vulnerability to environmental influences that some patients exhibit. A person who “catches everything” and is “always getting sick” has, in TCM terms, weak Wei Qi.

The primary tonifying herb for Wei Qi is **Huang Qi** (Astragalus membranaceus) — sweet, slightly warm, it tonifies Qi with a specific affinity for the body surface. Modern research on astragalus has demonstrated immunomodulatory effects — increased natural killer cell activity, enhanced macrophage function — that correspond to the traditional claim of strengthened surface defense.

## See also

- [Qi](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/qi.md) — the broader concept of which Wei Qi is one variety

- [Zheng Qi](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/zheng-qi.md) — the total defensive capacity, of which Wei Qi is the surface component

- [Etiology](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/etiology.md) — the external pathogenic factors Wei Qi resists

- [Lung](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/zang-fu.md) — the organ system that distributes Wei Qi

- [Yang Deficiency](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/yang-deficiency.md) — deeper warmth deficiency, distinguished from surface Wei Qi weakness

records.name: Wu Xing (Five Phases)
records.body:
A classification system of five functional categories (wood, fire, earth, metal, water) linked by generating and controlling cycles that describe patterns of transformation in TCM

Wu Xing (五行), the Five Phases, is a classification system in [traditional Chinese medicine](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/traditional-chinese-medicine.md) that describes cycles of generation and restraint among five functional categories: wood, fire, earth, metal, and water. The standard translation “Five Elements” is misleading — *xing* means “movement” or “phase,” not “element.” These aren’t substances in the Greek sense but patterns of transformation [@kaptchuk2000].

Each phase corresponds to a cluster of associations: an organ-function system, a season, an emotion, a sensory organ, a taste, a color, a direction. Wood corresponds to the Liver system, spring, anger, the eyes, sourness. Fire corresponds to the Heart system, summer, joy, the tongue, bitterness. Earth corresponds to the Spleen system, late summer, overthinking, the mouth, sweetness. Metal corresponds to the Lung system, autumn, grief, the nose, pungency. Water corresponds to the Kidney system, winter, fear, the ears, saltiness.

The phases relate through two cycles. The *generating cycle* (sheng 生) describes how each phase supports the next: wood feeds fire, fire creates earth (ash), earth yields metal (ore), metal enriches water (minerals), water nourishes wood. The *controlling cycle* (ke 克) describes how each phase restrains another: wood parts earth (roots), earth dams water, water extinguishes fire, fire melts metal, metal cuts wood. Health depends on both cycles operating smoothly. When the generating cycle falters, a downstream phase weakens. When the controlling cycle fails, a phase dominates unchecked.

[Nathan Sivin](../../documents/articles/research/2026/07/31/lenticule-import/humanities/domains/general/domains/people/nathan-sivin.md) observed that the Five Phases operate as a system of correspondences rather than causes [@sivin1987]. A practitioner who identifies a “wood overacting on earth” pattern — irritability, digestive disturbance, a wiry pulse — isn’t claiming that an entity called “wood” is attacking an entity called “earth.” They’re describing a recognizable clinical configuration and using the Five Phases vocabulary to locate it within a system of relationships that suggests both the mechanism and the treatment principle.

records.name: Blood (Xue)
records.body:
血 — the dense, nourishing fluid in TCM that moistens tissues, anchors Shen, and circulates through the meridians — functionally distinct from the biomedical concept of blood, though anatomically overlapping

Requires

- qi
- jing

Table of contents

- [How Blood differs from the biomedical concept](#how-blood-differs-from-the-biomedical-concept)

- [Production](#production)

- [Functions](#functions)

- [Blood pathology](#blood-pathology)

- [See also](#see-also)

Blood (xue 血) in [Traditional Chinese Medicine](../../documents/articles/research/2026/07/31/lenticule-import/library/applied-sciences/medicine/_index.md) is the dense, nourishing fluid that circulates through the [meridians](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/meridians.md) and blood vessels, moistening and nourishing the tissues, organs, skin, hair, and sense organs. It is functionally richer than the biomedical concept of blood — TCM Blood includes not just the red fluid in vessels but the nourishing, moistening, and consciousness-anchoring functions that the fluid performs.

## How Blood differs from the biomedical concept

The TCM concept overlaps with but is not identical to the biomedical concept. Biomedical blood is a tissue: red cells, white cells, platelets, plasma, measurable by CBC and serology. TCM Blood is a functional category: the body’s capacity to nourish, moisten, and anchor awareness. A patient can have a normal CBC and still present with TCM Blood deficiency — pale face, dry skin, poor memory, insomnia, scanty menstruation — because the functional capacity the concept names is broader than the laboratory values.

## Production

Blood is produced through the collaboration of multiple organ-function systems:

- The **Spleen** transforms food into Food [Qi](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/qi.md) (gu qi), the raw material for Blood

- The **Heart** transforms Food Qi into Blood proper through its warming, circulating function

- **[Jing](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/jing.md)** (stored in the Kidney) contributes to Blood production — TCM states “Jing and Blood share a common source”

This production chain explains why Spleen deficiency (poor digestion, poor absorption) leads to Blood deficiency over time: if the raw material is inadequate, the final product is insufficient.

## Functions

**Nourishing**: Blood moistens and nourishes every tissue. Muscles, tendons, skin, hair, nails, and the sense organs all depend on Blood for their vitality. Blood deficiency produces dryness, brittleness, and loss of luster — dry skin, brittle nails, blurred vision, muscle cramps.

**Moistening**: Where [Qi](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/qi.md) warms and moves, Blood cools and moistens. The Qi-Blood pair is another expression of the Yang-Yin dynamic: Qi is the potential, warming, moving principle; Blood is the nourishing, cooling, anchoring principle. Each depends on the other — Qi moves Blood (without Qi, Blood stagnates), Blood nourishes Qi (without Blood, Qi has no substance to animate).

**Anchoring Shen**: The Heart “stores” [Shen](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/shen.md) (awareness, coherent consciousness), and Blood is the medium in which Shen resides. Adequate Heart Blood provides the substrate for settled, coherent awareness. When Heart Blood is deficient, Shen becomes unanchored — producing insomnia, anxiety, restlessness, poor memory, dream-disturbed sleep, and a sense of vague unease.

## Blood pathology

**Blood deficiency** (xue xu 血虚): Insufficient Blood. Pale complexion, dizziness, blurred vision, insomnia, scanty or absent menstruation, pale tongue, thin pulse. Common in women (menstruation depletes Blood), the elderly, and the chronically ill.

**[Blood stasis](blood-stasis.md)** (xue yu 血瘀): Blood that has stopped flowing properly — stagnant, obstructed, or extravasated. Fixed sharp pain, dark complexion, purple tongue, choppy pulse. Treated by blood-invigorating herbs including [Hu Zhang](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/hu-zhang.md).

**Blood heat** (xue re 血热): Heat entering the Blood level, causing reckless bleeding, skin eruptions, agitation. The Blood is “boiling” — moving chaotically rather than in its proper channels.

## See also

- [Qi](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/qi.md) — the motive force that moves Blood

- [Jing](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/jing.md) — the substrate that contributes to Blood production

- [Shen](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/shen.md) — the awareness that Blood anchors

- [Blood Stasis](blood-stasis.md) — the pathological pattern of obstructed Blood

- [Zang-Fu](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/zang-fu.md) — the organ systems that produce and circulate Blood

records.name: Yang Deficiency
records.body:
阳虚 (yang xu) — the depletion of the body's warming, activating, protecting force, producing cold signs, fatigue, fluid accumulation, and a deep slow pulse — the pattern of insufficient metabolic fire

Table of contents

- [Presentation](#presentation)

- [Yang deficiency by organ system](#yang-deficiency-by-organ-system)

- [Causes](#causes)

- [Treatment principle: warm Yang, tonify the Kidney](#treatment-principle-warm-yang-tonify-the-kidney)

- [See also](#see-also)

Yang deficiency (yang xu 阳虚) is the depletion of the body’s Yang — the warming, activating, transforming, protecting aspect of the [Yin-Yang](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/yin-yang.md) dynamic. When Yang is deficient, the body lacks the metabolic fire to warm itself, transform nutrients, circulate fluids, and protect against invasion. Cold signs predominate — not because an external cold pathogen is present, but because the body’s internal warmth is insufficient.

## Presentation

The signs of Yang deficiency reflect the loss of Yang’s qualities — warmth, activity, transformation:

- **Cold**: Feeling cold, especially in the extremities (cold hands and feet), the low back, and the abdomen. The patient seeks warmth — warm rooms, warm drinks, warm clothing

- **Fatigue**: Profound tiredness, worse in the morning, improved somewhat by warmth and gentle activity. The body lacks the activating force to sustain effort

- **Pale complexion**: A bright, white pallor — not the dull paleness of Blood deficiency, but the whiteness of insufficient warming

- **Fluid accumulation**: Yang transforms and moves fluids. When Yang is deficient, fluids accumulate — edema (especially in the legs), copious clear urination, loose watery stools, clear watery nasal discharge

- **Tongue**: Pale, swollen (puffy), often with tooth marks at the margins (the swollen tongue presses against the teeth). Coating is white and moist. The moisture and pallor reflect cold and fluid accumulation

- **Pulse**: Deep (chen 沉) and slow (chi 迟). The pulse retreats from the surface (insufficient Yang to push it outward) and slows (insufficient fire to drive circulation)

## Yang deficiency by organ system

**Kidney Yang deficiency**: The most fundamental. The Kidney is the root of Yang for the whole body — the “gate of vitality” (ming men 命门). Kidney Yang deficiency produces: cold low back and knees, frequent copious clear urination (especially at night — nocturia), impotence or diminished libido, infertility, edema in the legs, dawn diarrhea (wu geng xie 五更泻 — diarrhea at 5 AM, when Yang should be rising but cannot). This pattern describes the metabolic slowdown of advanced aging in TCM terms.

**Spleen Yang deficiency**: The Spleen transforms food and fluids. When Spleen Yang is deficient, transformation fails — producing poor appetite, abdominal bloating after eating, loose stools with undigested food, a heavy feeling in the limbs, and edema. The Spleen “cannot hold” blood in the vessels, so bruising, heavy menstruation, or blood in the stool may occur. This is the pattern underlying many chronic digestive disorders.

**Heart Yang deficiency**: The Heart circulates Blood and houses [Shen](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/shen.md). Heart Yang deficiency produces: palpitations, chest oppression, cold sweats, a feeling of emptiness in the chest, and in severe cases, cyanosis (blue-purple lips and nails). This pattern corresponds to congestive heart failure in biomedical terms.

## Causes

Yang depletes through:

- **Aging**: Yang naturally declines with age, typically after Yin has begun declining. The progressive loss of warmth, vitality, and metabolic vigor in old age is Yang deficiency

- **Chronic illness**: Prolonged disease consumes Yang resources

- **Overexposure to cold**: Living in cold environments, consuming excessive cold or raw foods, cold-water swimming without adequate recovery

- **Overwork**: Physical overexertion (as opposed to the mental overwork that depletes Yin) exhausts Yang

- **Constitutional weakness**: Some individuals are born with weaker Yang — a TCM framework for understanding constitutional variation

## Treatment principle: warm Yang, tonify the Kidney

Yang-tonifying (bu yang 补阳) herbs are warm or hot, often with sweet and pungent tastes. They add warmth and metabolic fire to the depleted system:

- **Fu Zi** (prepared aconite root) — the strongest Yang-warming herb; “rescues devastated Yang.” Toxic if improperly prepared; used only in processed form

- **Rou Gui** (cinnamon bark) — warms the Kidney, strengthens Ming Men fire

- **Du Zhong** (Eucommia bark) — tonifies Kidney Yang, strengthens low back and knees

- **Bu Gu Zhi** (Psoralea fruit) — warms Kidney Yang, stops diarrhea

- **Gan Jiang** (dried ginger) — warms the middle burner, rescues Spleen Yang

The classical formula is **Jin Gui Shen Qi Wan** (金匮肾气丸, “Kidney Qi Pill from the Golden Cabinet”) — Liu Wei Di Huang Wan (the Yin-nourishing base) with added Fu Zi and Rou Gui to warm Yang. This elegant structure — nourishing Yin while warming Yang — reflects the principle that Yang cannot be strengthened without a Yin foundation.

## See also

- [Yin-Yang](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/yin-yang.md) — the dynamic that Yang deficiency disrupts

- [Yin Deficiency](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/yin-deficiency.md) — the complementary deficiency pattern

- [Qi](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/qi.md) — Yang deficiency is a deeper level of Qi deficiency

- [Zheng Qi](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/zheng-qi.md) — the total functional capacity that Yang deficiency weakens

- [Pattern Diagnosis](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/pattern-diagnosis.md) — the diagnostic framework

records.name: Yin Deficiency
records.body:
阴虚 (yin xu) — the depletion of the body's cooling, moistening, anchoring substance, producing heat signs from insufficient cooling rather than excess heat — night sweats, dry mouth, five-palm heat, and a thin rapid pulse

Table of contents

- [Presentation](#presentation)

- [Yin deficiency by organ system](#yin-deficiency-by-organ-system)

- [Causes](#causes)

- [Treatment principle: nourish Yin](#treatment-principle-nourish-yin)

- [See also](#see-also)

Yin deficiency (yin xu 阴虚) is the depletion of the body’s Yin — the cooling, moistening, nourishing, anchoring aspect of the [Yin-Yang](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/yin-yang.md) dynamic. When Yin is deficient, its complementary opposite (Yang — the warming, activating, ascending principle) is relatively unopposed, producing signs of heat. But this is **empty heat** (xu re 虚热) — heat from insufficient cooling, not from excess fire. The distinction is critical because the treatment is completely different: empty heat is treated by nourishing Yin (replenishing the cooling substrate), not by clearing heat (which would further deplete an already deficient system).

## Presentation

The signs of Yin deficiency reflect the loss of Yin’s qualities — moisture, coolness, anchoring:

- **Night sweats**: The body loses its ability to contain fluids, particularly at night when Yin predominates. Sweating during sleep that soaks the sheets is a hallmark

- **Five-palm heat** (wu xin fan re 五心烦热): Heat sensation in the palms of the hands, soles of the feet, and the chest. The extremities radiate heat that the patient describes as “burning from inside”

- **Afternoon/evening fever**: Low-grade temperature elevation in the afternoon or evening, when Yin should be ascending. This tidal fever (chao re 潮热) is characteristic

- **Dry mouth and throat**: Particularly at night. The patient may sip water frequently but without quenching thirst

- **Malar flush**: A reddish flush on the cheekbones — not the full facial redness of excess heat, but a localized, dusky redness

- **Tongue**: Red, with little or no coating. The coating is Yin — when Yin is deficient, the coating thins or disappears, leaving a bare, red tongue body. This is the most reliable diagnostic sign

- **Pulse**: Thin (xi 细) and rapid (shuo 数). The thinness reflects Yin depletion (less fluid volume); the rapidity reflects relative heat

## Yin deficiency by organ system

Each [Zang-Fu](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/zang-fu.md) system has its own Yin deficiency presentation:

**Kidney Yin deficiency**: The archetype. The Kidney stores [Jing](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/jing.md) and is the root of Yin for the whole body. Kidney Yin deficiency produces: low back ache, weak knees, tinnitus, diminished hearing, premature graying, poor memory, night sweats, nocturnal emissions, scanty dark urine. It is the pattern of aging — Yin naturally declines with age, and Kidney Yin is the first to show it.

**Liver Yin deficiency**: The Liver stores [Blood](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/xue.md), and Blood is a Yin substance. Liver Yin deficiency produces: dry eyes, blurred vision, dizziness, numbness or tingling in the limbs, brittle nails, scanty menstruation, irritability from heat. When severe, it progresses to Liver Yang rising — headaches, hypertension, tinnitus.

**Lung Yin deficiency**: The Lung governs moisture distribution. Lung Yin deficiency produces: dry cough (possibly with scanty, sticky, blood-streaked sputum), dry throat, hoarse voice, dry skin. This is the pattern of chronic dry cough that worsens at night.

**Stomach Yin deficiency**: The Stomach needs fluids to digest. Stomach Yin deficiency produces: dry mouth, thirst with desire to sip, poor appetite despite hunger, dry stools, a peeled (mirror-like) tongue coating in the center. This pattern is common after febrile illness that has consumed fluids.

## Causes

Yin depletes through:

- **Chronic illness**: Prolonged disease consumes the body’s resources

- **Overwork without rest**: Yin is restored through rest; chronic overwork without adequate recovery depletes it. TCM specifically identifies excessive mental work (overthinking) as Yin-depleting

- **Aging**: Natural Yin decline is a TCM description of biological aging

- **Blood loss**: Blood is a Yin substance; significant blood loss depletes Yin

- **Unresolved heat disease**: Febrile illness that lingers consumes Yin — “heat scorches Yin”

- **Emotional exhaustion**: Prolonged anxiety, grief, or fear depletes Yin

## Treatment principle: nourish Yin

Yin-nourishing (zi yin 滋阴) herbs are sweet, cool, and moistening. They are the opposite of the bitter, cold, draining herbs used for excess heat — they replenish rather than drain. Key herbs include:

- **Shu Di Huang** (prepared Rehmannia) — the primary Kidney Yin tonic

- **Mai Men Dong** (Ophiopogon) — nourishes Lung and Stomach Yin

- **Gou Qi Zi** (Lycium / goji berry) — nourishes Liver and Kidney Yin

- **Nu Zhen Zi** (Ligustrum) — nourishes Liver and Kidney Yin gently

- **Bai Shao** (white peony) — nourishes Liver Blood and Yin

The classical formula is **Liu Wei Di Huang Wan** (六味地黄丸, “Six-Ingredient Pill with Rehmannia”) — the foundational Kidney Yin tonic formula, consisting of three nourishing herbs and three draining herbs in elegant balance.

## See also

- [Yin-Yang](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/yin-yang.md) — the dynamic that Yin deficiency disrupts

- [Yang Deficiency](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/yang-deficiency.md) — the complementary deficiency pattern

- [Jing](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/jing.md) — the constitutional substrate closely related to Yin

- [Blood (Xue)](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/xue.md) — a Yin substance whose deficiency overlaps with Yin deficiency

- [Pattern Diagnosis](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/pattern-diagnosis.md) — the diagnostic framework

- [Zheng Qi](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/zheng-qi.md) — the total functional capacity that Yin deficiency weakens

records.name: Yin and Yang
records.body:
Complementary relational polarities (shaded/sunlit, rest/activity, cold/heat) used in TCM to describe dynamic balance and diagnose clinical patterns

Yin and Yang (陰陽) are complementary aspects of any phenomenon in [traditional Chinese medicine](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/traditional-chinese-medicine.md). The characters originally referred to the shaded and sunlit sides of a hill — and this concrete image carries the logic: yin and yang are not substances or forces but relative descriptions. Nothing is yin or yang in itself; it is yin or yang in relation to something else.

In TCM, yin and yang organize clinical observation. The body’s processes divide along yin-yang polarities: rest and activity, cold and heat, interior and exterior, depletion and excess, structure and function. Health is dynamic balance between the two. Illness arises when one aspect dominates, the other depletes, or the relationship between them loses its responsiveness [@kaptchuk2000].

The framework is diagnostic, not ontological. When a practitioner identifies a “yin deficiency” pattern — heat signs, dryness, restlessness, a thin rapid pulse — they aren’t claiming that a substance called “yin” has leaked out. They’re describing a configuration: the body’s cooling, moistening, and quieting functions have lost ground relative to its warming, drying, and activating functions. The treatment principle follows from the description: nourish yin, clear deficiency heat, restore the balance.

Yin and yang are not static categories. They transform into each other: extreme cold can produce heat, prolonged activity leads to collapse into rest, acute excess can deplete into deficiency. This dynamic quality distinguishes the framework from simple binary classification. Yin and yang name a relationship, and the diagnostic question is always about the *relationship* — not about which box a symptom falls into [@unschuld2003].

records.name: Zang-Fu (Organ-Function Systems)
records.body:
TCM's organ-function systems — five yin (zang) and six yang (fu) organs defined by functional relationships rather than anatomy, organized through Five Phase generating and restraining cycles

Table of contents

- [Zang and Fu: yin and yang organs](#zang-and-fu-yin-and-yang-organs)

- [Functional relationships, not anatomical descriptions](#functional-relationships-not-anatomical-descriptions)

- [Interactions among Zang-Fu systems](#interactions-among-zang-fu-systems)

- [Diagnostic application](#diagnostic-application)

**Zang-Fu** (臟腑) are the organ-function systems of [traditional Chinese medicine](../../documents/articles/research/2026/07/31/lenticule-import/library/applied-sciences/medicine/archive/index.md). They share names with anatomical organs — Liver, Heart, Spleen, Lung, Kidney, Stomach, and so on — but they are defined by their functional relationships rather than their anatomical location. The TCM Liver is not the anatomical organ in the right upper quadrant; it is a functional system governing the smooth flow of [Qi](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/qi.md), the storage of blood, and the regulation of emotional and somatic tension. Whether the TCM Liver and the biomedical liver refer to the same thing is not a question TCM’s framework is designed to answer [@kaptchuk2000].

## Zang and Fu: yin and yang organs

The system is organized into two categories:

**Zang** (臟) — the five yin organs. These are solid, storage-oriented organs that produce, transform, and store Qi, blood, [Jing](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/jing.md), and body fluids. They are the body’s core functional systems:

Zang organ
Element
Core functions

**Liver** (肝)
Wood
Ensures smooth flow of Qi; stores blood; governs sinews and tendons; opens to the eyes; associated with planning, decision-making, and emotional flexibility

**Heart** (心)
Fire
Governs blood circulation; houses [Shen](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/shen.md) (awareness, coherence); opens to the tongue; associated with joy, clarity, and relational presence

**Spleen** (脾)
Earth
Transforms and transports food and fluids; produces Qi and blood from nourishment; holds blood in vessels; governs muscles and limbs; associated with thought and concentration

**Lung** (肺)
Metal
Governs Qi and respiration; distributes Wei Qi (defensive Qi) to the body surface; regulates water passages; opens to the nose; associated with grief and the capacity to let go

**Kidney** (腎)
Water
Stores Jing (prenatal and postnatal); governs growth, reproduction, and aging; produces marrow (which fills the bones and brain); opens to the ears; associated with will, fear, and constitutional resilience

**Fu** (腑) — the six yang organs. These are hollow, transport-oriented organs that receive, digest, transform, and excrete. They process rather than store:

Fu organ
Paired zang
Core functions

**Gallbladder** (膽)
Liver
Stores and secretes bile; associated with courage and decision-making

**Small Intestine** (小腸)
Heart
Separates pure from impure in digestion; sorts the usable from the waste

**Stomach** (胃)
Spleen
Receives and ripens food; the “sea of grain and water”; initial decomposition

**Large Intestine** (大腸)
Lung
Transports waste and reabsorbs fluids; governs elimination

**Urinary Bladder** (膀胱)
Kidney
Stores and excretes urine; transforms fluids through Kidney Qi

**San Jiao / Triple Burner** (三焦)
Pericardium
Governs water passages and the movement of Qi between the three body cavities (upper, middle, lower); has no anatomical equivalent

The Pericardium (xin bao 心包) functions as a protective envelope for the Heart and is sometimes counted as a sixth zang organ, bringing the total to six pairs along the twelve [meridians](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/meridians.md).

## Functional relationships, not anatomical descriptions

The defining feature of the Zang-Fu system is that it describes what organs do in relation to each other, not what they are as structures. Consider the Spleen:

In biomedicine, the spleen is a lymphoid organ involved in immune function and blood filtration. In TCM, the Spleen is the system responsible for transforming food into usable energy (Qi and blood), transporting fluids, holding blood within the vessels, and maintaining muscle tone. TCM “Spleen deficiency” manifests as fatigue, poor digestion, loose stools, bruising, and a feeling of heaviness — a functional pattern that does not correspond to any single biomedical diagnosis but describes a recognizable clinical presentation.

This functional orientation means that TCM diagnoses are patterns, not diseases. “Liver Qi stagnation” is not a disease entity but a pattern of functional disruption: irritability, sighing, distension in the ribcage, menstrual irregularity, a wiry pulse. The pattern can manifest across multiple biomedical diagnoses (tension headaches, irritable bowel syndrome, premenstrual syndrome, intercostal neuralgia) because it describes a functional dynamic, not a structural pathology.

## Interactions among Zang-Fu systems

The Zang-Fu systems do not operate in isolation. Their interactions follow the generative and restraining cycles of the Five Phases (Wu Xing 五行):

- **Generative cycle** (sheng 生): Wood generates Fire, Fire generates Earth, Earth generates Metal, Metal generates Water, Water generates Wood. Clinically: the Liver supports the Heart; the Heart supports the Spleen; the Spleen supports the Lung; the Lung supports the Kidney; the Kidney supports the Liver.

- **Restraining cycle** (ke 克): Wood restrains Earth, Earth restrains Water, Water restrains Fire, Fire restrains Metal, Metal restrains Wood. Clinically: the Liver restrains the Spleen (excessive Liver Qi can impair digestion); the Spleen restrains the Kidney; and so on.

These cycles provide a framework for understanding how dysfunction in one system affects others. “Liver overacting on Spleen” describes a common clinical pattern where emotional tension (Liver) disrupts digestion (Spleen) — a pattern that biomedical research on the gut-brain axis is now investigating through different vocabulary.

## Diagnostic application

Zang-Fu theory structures clinical assessment in TCM. The practitioner evaluates which systems are involved, whether the pattern is one of excess or deficiency, heat or cold, interior or exterior. A patient presenting with insomnia, anxiety, heart palpitations, and a red-tipped tongue suggests Heart Fire — excess heat in the Heart system disturbing Shen. A patient presenting with fatigue, poor appetite, loose stools, and a pale tongue suggests Spleen Qi deficiency — the Spleen lacking the operational energy to transform and transport.

The diagnostic power of the system lies in its capacity to connect symptoms that biomedicine might distribute across multiple specialists. The TCM practitioner sees one pattern where the biomedical system might see separate consultations for gastroenterology, psychiatry, and gynecology. Whether this integration produces better clinical outcomes is an empirical question; that it produces a different and sometimes illuminating clinical picture is not in dispute.

records.name: Access Intimacy
records.body:
Mia Mingus's concept naming the felt experience of having one's access needs understood and met without constant negotiation or justification.

Requires
labor

Access intimacy is a concept developed by [Mia Mingus](../../../../../../../../../information-science-services-section/services/knowledge-services-section/services/research-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/mia-mingus.md) within the [disability justice](../../documents/articles/research/2026/07/31/lenticule-import/library/applied-sciences/medicine/archive/disability-justice.md) framework. It names the feeling of ease that arises when someone understands your access needs and moves to meet them without requiring you to explain, justify, or prove those needs. Access intimacy is not accommodation in the institutional sense — not the filing of paperwork, the requesting of exceptions, or the provision of services after formal evaluation. It is the trust that access will be anticipated and shared as part of the relationship itself.

Mingus distinguishes access intimacy from other forms of intimacy because it emerges specifically from the experience of navigating a world not built for your body or mind. It can exist between strangers who share an understanding of inaccessibility, or it can be absent in close relationships where access needs go unrecognized. The concept foregrounds the [labor](../../../../../../../../../social-science-services-section/services/sociology-science-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/labor.md) that disabled people perform to secure access — [labor](../../../../../../../../../social-science-services-section/services/sociology-science-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/labor.md) that access intimacy relieves not by eliminating the need but by distributing it across a relationship rather than concentrating it in the person who needs access.

emsenn references access intimacy in “On white-supremacist covid-eugenicist queers” (2025-09-23), connecting it to [Leah Lakshmi Piepzna-Samarasinha](../../../../../../../../../information-science-services-section/services/knowledge-services-section/services/research-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/leah-lakshmi-piepzna-samarasinha.md)’s work in *Care Work*. Collective care infrastructure — the kind that disability justice movements build — depends on access intimacy as its sustaining condition. Without the trust that others will share in access [labor](../../../../../../../../../social-science-services-section/services/sociology-science-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/labor.md), communal care becomes exhausting negotiation rather than mutual support. Access intimacy is what makes collective care sustainable.

records.name: Communitas
records.body:
Roberto Esposito's concept naming the shared obligation, exposure, and vulnerability that bind people into community — not what a community has in common but what it owes.

Requires
obligation

Communitas is a concept developed by [Roberto Esposito](../../documents/articles/research/2026/07/31/lenticule-import/humanities/domains/general/domains/people/roberto-esposito.md) in *Communitas: The Origin and Destiny of Community* (2010) [cite:@esposito_Communitas_2010]. The term derives from the Latin *munus* — obligation, gift, or duty — and names the condition of shared obligation: the exposure, vulnerability, and debt that bind people into community. Communitas does not refer to what a community has in common (shared identity, shared property, shared culture) but to what it owes — the mutual exposure that constitutes relation.

Esposito’s argument is that community has been misunderstood by the modern political tradition. Where liberal theory treats community as a collection of individuals who share attributes, communitas names something prior and more unsettling: the fact that relation itself is constituted by obligation to others, by being exposed to claims one did not choose. Community, in this sense, is not a possession but a dispossession — the condition of owing something to others that cannot be discharged.

This understanding of community stands opposed to [immunitas](immunitas.md), which names the exemption from that obligation. Esposito argues that modern governance operates by immunizing subjects against the demands of communitas — protecting individuals from the exposure, risk, and vulnerability that shared obligation entails.

emsenn uses communitas in “On white-supremacist covid-eugenicist queers” (2025-09-23) to name what COVID-minimizing rhetoric dismantles: collective standards, mask norms, shared care practices — the infrastructure of mutual obligation. When “you do you, I’ll do me” replaces communal care, communitas is pathologized as excessive, intrusive, or authoritarian, and those who cannot protect themselves individually absorb the risks that others refuse to mitigate communally.

records.name: Disability Justice
records.body:
A framework developed by disabled activists of color that grounds disability in intersecting systems of oppression and insists on collective, infrastructural access.

Requires

- communitas
- labor

Disability justice is a political framework developed by disabled activists of color — particularly the performance collective Sins Invalid, [Mia Mingus](../../../../../../../../../information-science-services-section/services/knowledge-services-section/services/research-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/mia-mingus.md), [Leah Lakshmi Piepzna-Samarasinha](../../../../../../../../../information-science-services-section/services/knowledge-services-section/services/research-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/leah-lakshmi-piepzna-samarasinha.md), and [Patty Berne](../../../../../../../../../information-science-services-section/services/knowledge-services-section/services/research-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/patty-berne.md) — that grounds disability in intersecting systems of oppression rather than treating it as an individual medical condition. Where the disability rights movement focused on legal inclusion and accommodation within existing institutions, disability justice insists that those institutions are themselves organized around ableism, racism, [capitalism](../../../../../../../../../social-science-services-section/services/sociology-science-services-section/services/critical-theory-science-services-section/services/anarchism-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/capitalism.md), and [settler colonialism](../../documents/articles/research/2026/07/31/lenticule-import/humanities/domains/sociology/topics/settler-colonialism/index.md). Access cannot be secured by adding ramps to structures built on exclusion.

The framework holds that access is not a special provision for exceptional bodies but a condition that must be built into infrastructure, policies, and norms. Accommodation models place the burden on disabled individuals to request exceptions; disability justice places the burden on communities to build access as a baseline. This shifts the question from “what do you need?” (directed at the individual) to “what have we failed to build?” (directed at the collective).

Piepzna-Samarasinha’s *Care Work: Dreaming Disability Justice* (2018) documents how disability justice communities build care infrastructure through [mutual aid](../../documents/articles/research/2026/07/31/lenticule-import/humanities/domains/sociology/terms/mutual-aid.md), [access intimacy](access-intimacy.md), and collective [labor](../../../../../../../../../social-science-services-section/services/sociology-science-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/labor.md) rather than through institutional channels. emsenn references disability justice in “On white-supremacist covid-eugenicist queers” (2025-09-23) alongside [Alison Kafer](../../../../../../../../../information-science-services-section/services/knowledge-services-section/services/research-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/alison-kafer.md)’s work on disability futures — the insistence that the future must be reimagined through access and interdependence rather than organized around the exclusion and abandonment of those deemed unproductive.

records.name: Immunitas
records.body:
Roberto Esposito's concept naming the exemption from shared obligation that preserves the individual — the dispensation from the claims of communitas.

Immunitas is a concept developed by [Roberto Esposito](../../documents/articles/research/2026/07/31/lenticule-import/humanities/domains/general/domains/people/roberto-esposito.md) in *Immunitas: The Protection and Negation of Life* (2011) [cite:@esposito_Immunitas_2011]. Like [communitas](../../documents/articles/research/2026/07/31/lenticule-import/library/applied-sciences/medicine/archive/communitas.md), it derives from the Latin *munus* — obligation, gift, or duty — but names the opposite orientation. Where communitas is the condition of shared obligation, immunitas is the dispensation from that obligation: the protection that exempts individuals from the claims of the common.

Esposito argues that modern liberal governance operates through immunization. The liberal subject is constituted precisely by being exempted from communal obligation — protected from the demands, risks, and exposures that communitas entails. This immunitary logic extends beyond politics into medicine, law, and everyday life: the body politic, like the biological body, is understood as something that must be defended against intrusion. The etymological link between political immunity and biological immunity is not metaphorical for Esposito — both express the same logic of protecting the individual by negating the claims of the common.

The immunitary paradigm produces a paradox: the mechanisms meant to protect life can, when pushed to their extreme, negate it. Autoimmune disorders — where the body’s defense systems attack the body itself — serve as Esposito’s figure for this political dynamic. A community that immunizes itself against all obligation, all exposure, all vulnerability ceases to be a community at all.

emsenn uses immunitas in “On white-supremacist covid-eugenicist queers” (2025-09-23) to name the logic behind COVID-minimizing rhetoric. “You do you, I’ll do me” sounds liberatory but is immunitarian privatization: it dismantles shared obligation and redistributes risk onto those with least access to individual protection. The result is, in emsenn’s framing, eugenic in effect. Those who cannot immunize themselves individually — because of poverty, disability, or structural abandonment — absorb the risks that others refuse to mitigate communally.

records.name: Meridians (Jing Luo)
records.description: The functional channel network through which Qi circulates in TCM, connecting organ-function systems to each other and to the body surface for diagnosis and treatment

kaptchuk2000.title: The Web That Has No Weaver: Understanding Chinese Medicine

unschuld2003.title: Huang Di Nei Jing Su Wen: Nature, Knowledge, Imagery in an Ancient Chinese Medical Text

records.body:
**Meridians** (jing luo 經絡) are the channels through which [Qi](./qi.md) circulates in [traditional Chinese medicine](traditional-chinese-medicine.md), connecting the body's [organ-function systems](./zang-fu.md) to each other and to the surface. They constitute the body's internal communication and distribution network — not anatomical structures visible on dissection, but functional pathways defined by the patterns of influence they describe.

The meridian system has two components. The **jing** (經, channels or conduits) are the primary pathways — relatively fixed, well-mapped, and clinically significant. The **luo** (絡, network vessels) are finer branches that connect the main channels, distribute Qi to the tissues, and link interior organs to the body surface. Together they form a continuous network that, in TCM's understanding, connects every part of the body to every other part.

## The twelve primary meridians

The core of the system consists of twelve primary meridians (shi er jing mai 十二經脈), each associated with one of the twelve [Zang-Fu](./zang-fu.md) organ-function systems. The twelve meridians are organized into six pairs, each pair linking one yin organ (zang) and one yang organ (fu):

| Yin meridian (zang) | Yang meridian (fu) | Element |
|---|---|---|
| Lung | Large Intestine | Metal |
| Spleen | Stomach | Earth |
| Heart | Small Intestine | Fire |
| Kidney | Urinary Bladder | Water |
| Pericardium | San Jiao (Triple Burner) | Fire (ministerial) |
| Liver | Gallbladder | Wood |

Each meridian follows a specific pathway through the body, with acupuncture points (xue wei 穴位) distributed along its course. These points are where the meridian's Qi is accessible from the surface — where needling, pressure, or moxibustion can influence the flow of Qi within the channel.

The twelve meridians flow in a continuous cycle. Qi circulates through all twelve in a specific sequence over a 24-hour period, with each meridian having a two-hour window of peak activity. This circadian rhythm of Qi flow is used diagnostically: symptoms that recur at specific times of day may indicate dysfunction in the meridian active during that period.

## The eight extraordinary meridians

Beyond the twelve primary meridians, eight extraordinary meridians (qi jing ba mai 奇經八脈) serve as reservoirs and regulators of Qi. The two most clinically significant are:

- **Du Mai** (督脈, Governing Vessel) — runs along the midline of the back, governing all yang meridians
- **Ren Mai** (任脈, Conception Vessel) — runs along the midline of the front, governing all yin meridians

The extraordinary meridians do not have their own organ associations. They function as overflow channels — absorbing excess Qi when the primary meridians are full and releasing stored Qi when the primary meridians are depleted. In Daoist cultivation practice, the Du Mai and Ren Mai form the "microcosmic orbit" through which practitioners circulate refined Qi.

## Meridians as a diagnostic framework

Meridian theory provides a framework for understanding how symptoms in one area relate to dysfunction in another. Pain along the Gallbladder meridian (which runs from the outer corner of the eye, over the temporal region, down the lateral neck and torso, and along the outer leg to the fourth toe) may indicate Liver-Gallbladder disharmony even when the pain itself is in the hip or lateral knee. The meridian pathway connects the symptom to its source.

This connecting function makes meridians diagnostically powerful in ways that anatomical thinking sometimes is not. A headache at the temples, irritability, bitter taste in the mouth, and pain along the lateral ribcage form a recognizable pattern in meridian-based diagnosis: Liver Qi stagnation affecting the Gallbladder meridian. The symptoms are scattered anatomically but unified by the meridian pathway that connects them.

## Meridians and biomedical anatomy

The relationship between meridians and biomedical anatomy remains contested. Research has explored possible correlations with fascial planes, neurovascular bundles, and connective tissue pathways — and some correspondences exist — but no biomedical structure maps cleanly onto the meridian system as TCM describes it [@kaptchuk2000]. The meridian system was not derived from anatomical dissection but from clinical observation of patterns of influence: pressing here affects function there; needling this point relieves that symptom. The map describes functional relationships, not structural ones.

This does not invalidate the meridian framework. It means the framework operates at a different level of description than biomedical anatomy — describing the body's functional geography rather than its structural anatomy. The question is not whether meridians "exist" in the biomedical sense but whether the patterns they describe are clinically useful. For practitioners of acupuncture and related therapies, they demonstrably are.

## Related

- [Zang-Fu](./zang-fu.md) — the organ-function systems that meridians connect
- [Qi](./qi.md) — the circulating force that flows through meridians
- [Traditional Chinese Medicine](traditional-chinese-medicine.md) — the medical tradition that uses meridian theory

records.name: Mixed Depression
records.description: Athanasios Koukopoulos's non-DSM bipolar mixed-state construct: a full depressive episode co-occurring with psychic agitation, marked irritability, and mood lability as core, not excluded, features. It is a distinct framework from the DSM-5 mixed-features specifier, which is built on excluding exactly these three symptoms.

sani2014.title: Koukopoulos' diagnostic criteria for mixed depression: a validation study

mineo2022.title: Which mixed depression model? A comparison between DSM-5-defined mixed features and Koukopoulos' criteria

sani2018.title: The Koukopoulos Mixed Depression Rating Scale (KMDRS): An International Mood Network (IMN) validation study of a new mixed mood rating scale

verdolini2015.title: The State of the Art of the DSM-5 'with Mixed Features' Specifier
verdolini2015.note: PMC4562096; source for the DSM-5 exclusion rationale reused here

records.body:
Mixed depression is Athanasios Koukopoulos's non-DSM diagnostic construct, first described in 1992: a full major depressive syndrome co-occurring with an excitatory process — psychic agitation or inner tension, marked irritability, mood lability or reactivity, and rage or anger. Koukopoulos's central claim is that this excitatory process, not the depressive process itself, is what generates the suicidal ideation, anxiety, and agitation observed in these episodes.

Mixed depression must be kept distinct from the DSM-5 "with mixed features" specifier, which is a different, narrower construct built around the opposite symptom set. Koukopoulos's criteria explicitly include psychomotor agitation, irritability, and mood lability as core, defining symptoms. The DSM-5 specifier's Criterion B explicitly excludes exactly these three symptoms — psychomotor agitation, irritability, and distractibility — from its list of admitted manic/hypomanic symptoms, because the DSM-5 task force judged them to overlap with core depressive/anxiety symptoms and unable to reliably signal manic rather than depressive polarity. The two frameworks are therefore not two names for the same phenomenon but two different symptom sets built on opposite decisions about the same three overlapping symptoms.

A validation study of Koukopoulos's proposed criteria in 435 clinic-referred patients with a major depressive episode (Sani et al. 2014, International Mood Network sites) found the most prevalent individual criteria were absence of psychomotor retardation (84%), mood lability or marked reactivity (78%), and psychic agitation or inner tension (75%); the overall diagnostic model achieved 76.4% sensitivity and 86.3% specificity against clinical correlates used as validators (CGI severity, rapid cycling, substance-abuse history) — concurrent/construct validity against clinical correlates, not diagnostic accuracy against an independent structured-interview gold standard. A head-to-head comparison in 300 patients with a major depressive episode (155 unipolar, 145 bipolar; Mineo et al. 2022) found Koukopoulos's criteria (KMxD) and the DSM-5 mixed-features specifier (MFS) achieved similar overall discrimination of bipolar from unipolar depression by ROC-AUC (KMxD 71.9%, 95% CI 66.2-77.7%; DSM-5 MFS 77.0%, 95% CI 72.0-82.1%), with KMxD more sensitive and DSM-5 MFS more specific — neither framework dominates the other in this single Italian clinical sample.

For measurement, Koukopoulos's criteria have been operationalized as the Koukopoulos Mixed Depression Rating Scale (KMDRS), validated in 350 patients (Sani et al. 2018) with internal consistency Cronbach's α = 0.76, inter-rater reliability κ = 0.73, a two-factor structure (anger, psychomotor excitation) accounting for 80% of variance, and predictive-validity C-statistic 0.82 — an instrument built on a rival, non-DSM construct, whose own authors flag that the validation was cross-sectional. For clinical observation and research design, this means a study or clinician reporting "mixed depression" must specify which framework — Koukopoulos's criteria, the KMDRS, or the DSM-5 specifier — was used, since the two constructs are built on opposite decisions about which symptoms count and yield materially different sensitivity/specificity trade-offs on the same patients.

records.name: Mixed Features Specifier
records.description: The DSM-5/DSM-5-TR course specifier for a major depressive, manic, or hypomanic episode, requiring at least three of seven listed non-overlapping manic/hypomanic symptoms nearly every day for the majority of the episode. Its defining methodological choice is excluding psychomotor agitation, irritability, and distractibility from the admitted symptom list.

verdolini2015.title: The State of the Art of the DSM-5 'with Mixed Features' Specifier

malhi2017.title: Exclusion of overlapping symptoms in DSM-5 mixed features specifier: heuristic diagnostic and treatment implications

perugi2015.title: Mixed features in patients with a major depressive episode: the BRIDGE-II-MIX study

zimmerman2023.title: Identifying the DSM-5 mixed features specifier in depressed patients: a comparison of measures

zimmerman2026.title: How Many Criteria Should Be Required to Define the DSM-5 Mixed Features Specifier in Depressed Patients?

records.body:
The DSM-5 (2013) "with mixed features" specifier applies to a major depressive episode — in either major depressive disorder or bipolar disorder — or to a manic/hypomanic episode, and requires at least three of seven listed manic/hypomanic symptoms present nearly every day for the majority of the days of the episode: elevated or expansive mood, inflated self-esteem or grandiosity, more talkative than usual or pressure to keep talking, flight of ideas or racing thoughts, increase in energy or goal-directed activity, increased or excessive involvement in risky activities, and decreased need for sleep.

The crux of the specifier is what it deliberately excludes. The DSM-5 task force excluded psychomotor agitation, irritability, and distractibility from Criterion B because these symptoms overlap with core depressive and anxiety symptoms and were judged unable to reliably distinguish manic from depressive polarity. This exclusion is the direct point of departure from Koukopoulos's non-DSM mixed-depression construct, whose criteria foreground psychic agitation, irritability, and mood lability as core features rather than excluded ones — the inverse choice from the DSM-5 task force's. Malhi and colleagues have argued in print that removing these three overlapping symptoms may strip out what are in fact core features of mixed states, proposing a return to a Kraepelinian framework that scores mood, ideation, and activity as three semi-independent axes rather than a symptom checklist; this is a published critique and argument, not an empirical demonstration that has displaced the DSM-5 criteria as the operative diagnostic standard.
