Because the specifier's symptom list excludes the three most commonly reported excitatory features of depression, its measured prevalence depends heavily on the operational definition and instrument used. Zimmerman and Mackin (2023), assessing 309 depressed patients against seven different operational definitions (two derived from a dedicated DSM-5 mixed-features interview, five from Young Mania Rating Scale-derived algorithms), found prevalence varying roughly 8-fold across definitions, with poor agreement between the interview-based and YMRS-based approaches despite each showing some independent validity. In the BRIDGE-II-MIX study (Perugi et al. 2015; 2,811 patients with a major depressive episode across 239 centers in 8 countries), only 7.5% met the strict DSM-5 specifier, versus 29.1% meeting a broader research-based "depressive mixed state" definition that permitted overlapping symptoms; the most common individual manic/hypomanic symptoms in the whole sample were irritable mood (32.6%), emotional/mood lability (29.8%), and distractibility (24.4%) — precisely the symptoms the DSM-5 specifier excludes. A later Zimmerman and Mackin study (459 psychiatric outpatients) tested lowering the required count from 3 to 2 criteria: prevalence rose from 3.9% to 13.1%, but the newly captured 2-criteria-only group did not differ meaningfully from the below-threshold group on bipolar family history, functional impairment, comorbidity, or suicide risk, arguing against loosening the threshold. None of this settles whether the 3-criterion threshold is itself well-calibrated relative to non-DSM frameworks, which flag substantially higher rates using different logics (see mixed-depression). For research design, the practical consequence is that a reported prevalence for "mixed features in depression" is not interpretable without naming the exact instrument and criterion count used to generate it.

records.name: Mood Instability
records.description: Mood instability names the degree of moment-to-moment fluctuation in a person's momentary affect — how much it varies in magnitude between one assessment and the next — as measured by ecological momentary assessment, distinct from the average level of that affect. It has been studied as a transdiagnostic marker associated with both depressive and anxiety symptoms.

broome2015.title: Mood instability: significance, definition and measurement

sultson2024.title: Negative affect instability predicts elevated depressive and generalized anxiety disorder symptoms even when negative affect intensity is controlled for: an ecological momentary assessment study

records.body:
Mood instability is defined, in a widely used clinical framing (Broome, Saunders, Harrison & Marwaha, 2015), as rapid oscillations of intense affect together with a difficulty regulating those oscillations or their behavioural consequences. It names the amplitude and frequency of change in momentary affect over short timescales, not the average intensity of that affect: two people can report the same mean level of negative affect across a week while differing sharply in how much that affect swings from one assessment to the next. Broome and colleagues report a population prevalence of 13.9% from the UK Adult Psychiatric Morbidity Survey 2007, higher in women and peaking in the 16–24 age range before declining with age, and argue mood instability has underappreciated potential as a transdiagnostic investigational and therapeutic target — their own interpretive framing rather than a finding derived from a single dataset.

An ecological momentary assessment study of 221 adults from a population-based Estonian sample (Sultson, Murd, Havik & Konstabel, 2024), sampling affect five times daily for a week, found that negative-affect instability predicted elevated depressive and generalized-anxiety symptoms even after statistically controlling for mean negative- and positive-affect intensity (depression odds ratio 2.15, 99% CI 1.08–4.30; generalized anxiety odds ratio 2.16, 99% CI 1.04–4.48) — roughly a doubling of odds per standard-deviation increase in instability, independent of how negative the person's affect was on average. The same predictors held for both depressive and anxiety symptoms, which the authors read as evidence the construct is transdiagnostic rather than disorder-specific, though 62% depression/anxiety symptom overlap in their sample limits how disorder-specific any interpretation can be. The authors' own explicit caution is that despite the word 'predicts' in their title, all of their analyses were cross-sectional: elevated instability and elevated symptoms were measured over the same assessment period, so the finding is an association, not a demonstration that instability precedes or causes later symptom elevation.

Mood instability is a descriptive measure of fluctuation magnitude, and must be kept distinct from early warning signal, the framework built on critical slowing down: mood instability describes how much affect swings, while an early warning signal is a claim about the changing rate and temporal structure of those swings — rising autocorrelation and variance — as a system nears a transition. A person's affect can be highly unstable, with large swings, without those swings showing the slowing-down pattern that early-warning-signal methods look for, and conversely a rising-autocorrelation signal can in principle occur alongside stable-magnitude fluctuation. None of the studies reviewed here identify a neural, hormonal, or other physiological mechanism producing mood instability; it is measured as a statistic over self-reported momentary ratings, not a physiological quantity. The consequence for measurement and research design is that a cross-sectional association between instability and symptom severity, however robust, cannot on its own establish that instability comes before or causes symptom elevation, and that any study using the word 'predicts' for a same-period cross-sectional design should be read for what the analysis actually tested, not for what its title implies.

records.name: Myalgic encephalomyelitis
records.description: A multi-system illness characterized by post-exertional malaise, unrefreshing sleep, cognitive impairment, and often orthostatic intolerance, with onset frequently following infection and case definition varying substantially across epidemiological studies.

fukuda1994.title: The chronic fatigue syndrome: a comprehensive approach to its definition and study

authors: Institute of Medicine Committee on the Diagnostic Criteria for Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome
iom2015.title: Beyond Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome: Redefining an Illness

records.body:
Myalgic encephalomyelitis is a multi-system illness characterized by a constellation of neuroendocrine, autonomic, metabolic, and neuroinflammatory dysfunction. It commonly follows an infection — viral or bacterial, often acute but sometimes insidious — and presents with cardinal symptoms of post-exertional malaise, unrefreshing sleep, cognitive impairment, and orthostatic intolerance, though the prominence of any given symptom varies widely between patients. The name itself asserts inflammation of the brain and spinal cord that has not been consistently demonstrated, and for that reason remains contested among clinicians; the label "systemic exertion intolerance disease" proposed by the 2015 US Institute of Medicine report makes exertional intolerance rather than encephalomyelitis the defining feature.

Case definitions have evolved substantially since the illness was first formally characterized. The 1994 Fukuda definition centered fatigue and required exclusion of alternative explanations; the 2003 Canadian Consensus Criteria made post-exertional malaise a mandatory feature and added immunological, neurological, and endocrine parameters; the 2015 Institute of Medicine report elevated post-exertional malaise to the cardinal diagnostic criterion and required it to be present alongside three of four additional major symptom clusters. These definitions select measurably different populations from clinical samples, which is a leading hypothesis for why ME/CFS research produces inconsistent findings — a study of Fukuda-defined patients is studying a different population than a study of IOM-defined patients, and the biological findings cannot be directly compared.

The distinction between myalgic encephalomyelitis and chronic fatigue as a symptom, or from idiopathic chronic fatigue unrelated to infection or from depression, is clinically essential and scientifically contested. Fatigue is a symptom; the illness is recognized by post-exertional malaise, the specific character of cognitive impairment, and the pattern of autonomic dysfunction, taken together. Depression can coexist with myalgic encephalomyelitis and can superficially resemble it, but the key distinguishing feature is that in myalgic encephalomyelitis, rest and sleep do not restore function — the unrefreshing quality of sleep is itself a cardinal feature — whereas in depression, structured activity and sleep improvement often produce symptomatic relief.

For epidemiological and mechanistic research, the critical consequence is that any study's findings must be read against which case definition was used to recruit and diagnose participants. A study showing normal inflammatory markers in Fukuda-defined ME/CFS patients does not contradict a study showing activated microglia in IOM-defined ones: they are studying different populations. Claims about ME/CFS pathophysiology require explicit statement of the diagnostic criteria used, and systematic reviews must account for definitional heterogeneity rather than treating all fatigue-illness studies as equivalent.

## Related terms

- Post-exertional malaise — the cardinal feature that distinguishes myalgic encephalomyelitis from other chronic fatiguing illnesses
- Two-day cardiopulmonary exercise testing — the closest objective measure of post-exertional malaise and a research assessment tool
- Hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis — the neuroendocrine arm whose dysfunction characterizes the illness
- Sympathoadrenal system — the autonomic arm whose decoupling from HPA axis support drives orthostatic intolerance
- Allostatic load — the cumulative physiological cost framework within which the multi-system dysfunction can be understood

records.name: Neidan
records.description: Inner alchemy: the Daoist discipline that recasts the language of elixir-making as a practice within the body, refining jing into qi, qi into shen, and shen back into emptiness.
records.body:
Neidan (內丹), inner alchemy, is the Daoist discipline that recasts the language of laboratory alchemy as a practice within the body. Laboratory alchemy is *waidan*, "outer elixir": its practitioners compounded mineral elixirs of immortality in furnaces. In neidan, the practitioner's own body is the furnace and cauldron. The ingredients are the [Three Treasures](./san-bao.md), and the "elixir" is formed through breath, attention, and stillness [@pregadio2008].

It took mature form in the Tang and Song dynasties. Its canonical stages are usually told as a sequence of refinements:

1. Refining [jing](./jing.md) into [qi](./qi.md) (liàn jīng huà qì).
2. Refining qi into [shen](./shen.md) (liàn qì huà shén).
3. Refining shen and returning to emptiness (liàn shén huán xū).

Practices along the way include circulating attention along the governing and conception vessels (the "microcosmic orbit") and gathering in the three [dantian](./dantian.md).

Neidan is a path of transformation, not a therapy. It supplied the modern secular [qigong](./qigong.md) of the 1950s with its still, seated, attention-and-breath methods, stripped of their soteriology. The structural reading of neidan as a reversal, returning along the path of generation, is taken up in the philosophy section's [note on Daoism as a second grammar](../../../../../../../../../../../philosophy-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/2026/08/23/2026-08-23-note-on-daoism-as-a-second-grammar.md).

records.name: Neuromodulation
records.description: Altering nervous-system activity by delivering electrical, magnetic or chemical stimulation to targeted sites, from implanted deep-brain and vagus stimulators to skin-surface TENS and transcranial current.

bikson2016.title: Safety of transcranial direct current stimulation: evidence based update 2016

records.body:
Neuromodulation is the deliberate alteration of nervous-system activity by delivering energy or drugs to targeted sites. The electrical and magnetic methods range along two lines: how invasive they are, and whether they fire neurons outright or only bias them.

- **Implanted:** deep brain stimulation for Parkinson's disease, vagus nerve stimulation for epilepsy and depression, spinal cord stimulation for pain. These deliver pulses strong enough to drive neurons.
- **Suprathreshold, non-invasive:** transcranial magnetic stimulation and electroconvulsive therapy fire cortical neurons from outside the skull. At the skin, [TENS](../../../../../../../pain-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/transcutaneous-electrical-nerve-stimulation.md) fires peripheral sensory nerves to mask pain.
- **Subthreshold, non-invasive:** [transcranial electrical stimulation](transcranial-electrical-stimulation.md), including [cranial electrotherapy stimulation](cranial-electrotherapy-stimulation.md), applies weak currents that shift [excitability](../../../../../../../../../neuroscience-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/neuronal-excitability.md) without firing neurons directly [@bikson2016].
- **Peripheral routes to the brain:** [taVNS](transcutaneous-auricular-vagus-nerve-stimulation.md) stimulates a skin branch of the [vagus nerve](../../../../../../../../../physiology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/vagus-nerve.md) in the ear, reaching the brainstem through the nerve instead of through the skull.

The further down this list, the weaker the physical effect and the harder it is to separate a device's action from the [placebo effect](../../../../../../../../content/text/glossary/terms/placebo-effect.md).

records.name: Neuron
records.description: A cell specialized for generating and transmitting electrical signals, serving as the functional unit of the nervous system.
records.body:
A **neuron** is a [cell](../../../../../../../../content/text/glossary/terms/cell.md) specialized for generating and transmitting electrical signals. Neurons are the functional units of the nervous system — every sensation, every movement, every thought, every autonomic adjustment involves neurons carrying information from one part of the body to another.

## Structure

A neuron has three primary components:

**Cell body (soma)** — contains the nucleus and most of the cell's metabolic machinery. The soma integrates incoming signals from other neurons and determines whether to fire an [action potential](./action-potential.md).

**Dendrites** — branching extensions that receive signals from other neurons. A single neuron may have thousands of dendrites, each receiving input from a different source. The dendrites are the neuron's "input" side — where information arrives.

**Axon** — a single, often long extension that carries the action potential away from the cell body toward the next neuron, muscle cell, or gland. Axons can be very short (interneurons in the spinal cord) or very long (motor neurons running from the spinal cord to the toes — up to a meter in length). The axon is the neuron's "output" side — where information is sent.

Many axons are wrapped in **myelin** — a fatty insulating sheath produced by specialized glial cells (Schwann cells in the peripheral nervous system, oligodendrocytes in the central nervous system). Myelin dramatically increases the speed of signal transmission: a myelinated axon conducts impulses at 70-120 meters per second, compared to 0.5-2 meters per second for unmyelinated axons. This speed difference is clinically significant — it is why the fast, sharp "first pain" (carried by thinly myelinated A-delta fibers) arrives before the slow, dull "second pain" (carried by unmyelinated C fibers) when you stub your toe.

At the end of the axon, terminal branches form [synapses](./synapse.md) — junctions where the neuron communicates with its targets.

## Types of neurons

Neurons are classified by function:

- **Sensory (afferent) neurons** — carry information from the body to the central nervous system. [Nociceptors](../../../../../pain-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/nociception.md) (pain-detecting sensory neurons), [proprioceptors](../../../../../somatics-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/proprioception.md) (position-detecting sensory neurons), and the receptors underlying [interoception](../../../../../somatics-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/interoception.md) (internal-state-detecting sensory neurons) are all types of sensory neurons.
- **Motor (efferent) neurons** — carry commands from the central nervous system to muscles and glands. When [somatics](../../../../../somatics-services-section/content/text/glossary/topics/somatics.md) describes restoring cortical control over habitually contracted muscles, it is describing the re-establishment of voluntary motor neuron signaling.
- **Interneurons** — connect neurons to other neurons within the central nervous system. The inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord's dorsal horn are critical to pain modulation — they suppress [nociceptive](../../../../../pain-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/nociception.md) transmission, and their loss contributes to [central sensitization](../../../../../pain-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/central-sensitization.md).

## Glial cells

Neurons do not operate alone. Glial cells — which outnumber neurons roughly 1:1 in the brain — provide structural support, insulation, nutrition, and immune defense. Two types are particularly relevant to this module:

- **Microglia** — the nervous system's immune cells. When activated by injury or sustained nociceptive input, microglia release inflammatory cytokines that maintain neuronal hyperexcitability — a key mechanism in [chronic pain](../../../../../pain-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/chronic-pain.md).
- **Astrocytes** — regulate the chemical environment around synapses, modulate synaptic transmission, and participate in the neuroinflammatory processes that sustain central sensitization.

## Related terms

- [Action Potential](./action-potential.md) — the electrical signal neurons generate
- [Synapse](./synapse.md) — where neurons communicate with their targets
- [Receptor](./receptor.md) — proteins that neurons (and other cells) use to detect signals

records.name: Nociception
records.description: The neural process of encoding and processing noxious stimuli, distinct from the conscious experience of pain
records.body:
**Nociception** is the neural process of encoding and processing potentially harmful (noxious) stimuli. It is the nervous system's threat-detection mechanism — peripheral nerve fibers responding to mechanical, thermal, or chemical stimuli that exceed a threshold indicating potential tissue damage.

Nociception is not pain. This distinction is foundational. Nociception is a neural event: a signal traveling from the periphery through the spinal cord to the brain. Pain is a conscious experience: what the brain produces when it interprets nociceptive and other inputs as indicating threat. The two can dissociate in either direction — nociception without pain (a soldier wounded in combat who feels nothing until the threat passes) and pain without nociception (a person with [central sensitization](./central-sensitization.md) experiencing severe pain from light touch).

## Nociceptive pathways

Nociceptors are free nerve endings distributed throughout the body (skin, muscle, viscera, joints) that respond to stimuli threatening tissue integrity:

- **A-delta fibers** — thinly myelinated, fast-conducting fibers that carry sharp, well-localized "first pain." These produce the immediate, precise pain that makes you withdraw your hand from a hot surface.
- **C fibers** — unmyelinated, slow-conducting fibers that carry dull, diffuse, aching "second pain." These produce the throbbing, poorly localized pain that follows the initial sharp sensation.

The nociceptive signal travels from the peripheral nerve to the dorsal horn of the spinal cord, where it undergoes the first stage of modulation. The dorsal horn is not a passive relay station — it is a processing center where descending signals from the brain, local interneuron activity, and input from other sensory fibers can amplify or suppress the nociceptive signal before it reaches higher centers.

From the dorsal horn, ascending pathways (primarily the spinothalamic tract) carry the signal to the thalamus and then to multiple cortical regions: the somatosensory cortex (localization and intensity), the anterior cingulate cortex (affective/unpleasantness dimension), the insular cortex ([interoceptive](../../../../../somatics-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/interoception.md) integration), and the prefrontal cortex (cognitive evaluation and context).

## Modulation at every level

The clinical significance of nociception is that it is modulated at every stage of transmission. The intensity of the peripheral stimulus does not determine the intensity of the pain experienced. Modulation occurs through:

- **Peripheral sensitization** — inflammatory mediators (prostaglandins, bradykinin, substance P) lower the threshold of nociceptors, making them fire more easily. This is why inflamed tissue is more painful than healthy tissue, even to gentle touch.
- **Spinal gating** — activity in large-diameter mechanoreceptive fibers (A-beta fibers, which carry touch and pressure information) can inhibit nociceptive transmission in the dorsal horn. This is why rubbing a bumped elbow reduces pain — the touch input "closes the gate" on nociceptive input.
- **Descending modulation** — brainstem nuclei (periaqueductal gray, rostral ventromedial medulla) send signals that can either facilitate or inhibit nociceptive transmission at the spinal level. Stress, attention, expectation, and emotional state all influence this descending modulation.

This multi-level modulation is why pain is context-dependent, why placebo and nocebo effects are real neurophysiological phenomena, and why treating pain as a simple input-output system fails.

## Related terms

- [Acute Pain](./acute-pain.md) — pain that serves the protective function nociception evolved to support
- [Central Sensitization](./central-sensitization.md) — what happens when modulation goes wrong
- [Allodynia](./allodynia.md) — pain from non-noxious stimuli, demonstrating nociception-pain dissociation

records.body:
Nuclear factor kappa B is a family of inducible transcription factors, held inactive in the cytoplasm by IκB proteins until a stimulus triggers IκB degradation, whereupon the released dimers enter the nucleus and drive transcription of pro-inflammatory genes. The canonical pathway is activated by pathogen-associated molecules, by tumour necrosis factor and interleukin-1 signalling, and by cellular stress, and its targets include the genes for interleukin-6, tumour necrosis factor alpha, and interleukin-1 beta themselves — a feed-forward arrangement in which the factor's own products re-activate it [hayden2008; liu2017]. **Established**: the pathway's components, its activation logic, and its principal target genes are textbook molecular immunology.

It is a transcription factor, not a cytokine: it does not itself signal between cells but decides which inflammatory messengers a cell will make, which is why a cell can carry a normal cytokine level while its transcriptional program is already committed. The distinction matters for measurement — a serum panel reads the products, while a leukocyte transcriptome reads the program, and the two can disagree.

Two relations asserted on this carrier are sourced here. The factor **delivers** interleukin-6, tumour necrosis factor alpha, and interleukin-1 beta: these are canonical target genes of the pathway [hayden2008; liu2017] (**established**). It is **controlled by** the glucocorticoid receptor, which represses its transcriptional output by tethering, coactivator competition, and induction of IκBα [debosscher2003] (**established as a molecular mechanism**). It is **produced by** reactive oxygen species in the specific sense that oxidants activate the pathway, a crosstalk reviewed with its contradictions intact — reactive oxygen species both activate and, in some settings, inhibit the pathway depending on species, site, and cell type [morgan2010] (**well-supported, context-dependent**).

Because the glucocorticoid receptor terminates an inflammatory episode largely by repressing this factor's transcriptional output, a failure of that repression and a failure of cortisol production produce the same downstream picture and can only be told apart by functional testing. Miller and colleagues found precisely this dissociation in chronic caregivers: heightened transcription of factor-associated genes alongside diminished glucocorticoid-response-element transcription, with ambulatory cortisol output normal [miller2008] (**single well-characterized cohort, replicated in shape by later work**).

records.name: Organ
records.description: A structure composed of two or more tissue types working together to perform a specific physiological function.
records.body:
An **organ** is a structure composed of two or more [tissue](./tissue.md) types working together to perform a specific function. The heart is an organ: cardiac muscle tissue pumps blood, connective tissue provides structural support, epithelial tissue lines the chambers, and nervous tissue regulates the rhythm. No single tissue type could accomplish what the heart does — the organ is the functional unit.

## Organ systems

Organs are grouped into systems that carry out major physiological functions:

| System | Major organs | Primary function |
|---|---|---|
| **Nervous** | Brain, spinal cord, peripheral nerves | Sensation, integration, motor control, cognition |
| **Cardiovascular** | Heart, blood vessels | Circulation of blood; oxygen and nutrient delivery |
| **Respiratory** | Lungs, airways, diaphragm | Gas exchange; oxygen in, carbon dioxide out |
| **Musculoskeletal** | Bones, skeletal muscles, joints, tendons, ligaments | Support, movement, protection |
| **Digestive** | Mouth, esophagus, stomach, intestines, liver, pancreas | Nutrient breakdown, absorption, drug metabolism |
| **Immune/Lymphatic** | Lymph nodes, spleen, thymus, white blood cells | Defense against infection; [inflammation](../../../../../../../../content/text/glossary/terms/inflammation.md) |
| **Endocrine** | Pituitary, thyroid, adrenals, pancreas, gonads | Hormone production; systemic regulation |
| **Urinary** | Kidneys, ureters, bladder | Filtration; waste and drug elimination |
| **Integumentary** | Skin, hair, nails | Barrier; temperature regulation; sensation |
| **Reproductive** | Gonads, uterus, associated structures | Reproduction |

These systems do not operate independently. The cardiovascular system delivers oxygen that the respiratory system acquires. The digestive system absorbs nutrients that the cardiovascular system distributes. The nervous system regulates all of them. Disease in one system affects others — which is why [traditional Chinese medicine](../../../../../traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/traditional-chinese-medicine.md) describes organs not as isolated structures but as functional systems defined by their relationships ([Zang-Fu](../../../../../traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/zang-fu.md)).

## The organ concept in TCM

The distinction between the Western anatomical organ and the TCM functional organ is significant. In Western medicine, "the liver" is a physical structure in the right upper abdomen with specific histological features, identifiable on imaging, and removable by surgery. In TCM, "the Liver" (肝) is a functional system governing the smooth flow of [Qi](../../../../../traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/qi.md), the storage of blood, and the regulation of emotional and somatic tension. The Western liver and the TCM Liver overlap but are not identical — they are defined by different frameworks asking different questions.

This does not mean one framework is right and the other wrong. It means that what counts as an "organ" depends on what you are trying to describe. If you are planning a surgery, the anatomical organ is what matters. If you are trying to understand why a patient's irritability, menstrual irregularity, and rib-side distension form a single clinical pattern, the TCM functional system offers a vocabulary that anatomical description does not.

## Related terms

- [Tissue](./tissue.md) — the components that make up organs
- [Cell](../../../../../../../../content/text/glossary/terms/cell.md) — the units that make up tissues
- [Homeostasis](./homeostasis.md) — the stable conditions that organ systems maintain

records.name: Oxygenation
records.description: The delivery of oxygen from inhaled gas into arterial blood, depending on inspired oxygen concentration, alveolar gas exchange, ventilation-perfusion matching, and hemoglobin transport capacity.
records.body:
**Oxygenation** is the delivery of oxygen from inhaled gas into arterial blood. It depends on inspired oxygen concentration, alveolar gas exchange, ventilation-perfusion matching, and hemoglobin's capacity to bind and transport oxygen.

Oxygenation is monitored at the bedside primarily through pulse oximetry (SpO2), which estimates the percentage of hemoglobin saturated with oxygen. Normal SpO2 is typically 94-100% on room air. Values below 90% indicate significant hypoxemia and warrant immediate intervention — supplemental oxygen, airway repositioning, or escalation to positive-pressure support.

The critical clinical principle is that oxygenation and [ventilation](./ventilation.md) are independent processes. A patient receiving supplemental oxygen may maintain normal SpO2 even while ventilation fails — CO2 rises, respiratory acidosis develops, and the patient's mental status deteriorates, all while the pulse oximeter reads reassuringly. This is why [capnography](./capnography.md) (exhaled CO2 monitoring) is essential alongside pulse oximetry: SpO2 tells you about oxygen in; capnography tells you about CO2 out.

Oxygenation failure can result from:

- **Hypoventilation** — not enough fresh gas reaching the alveoli (opioid toxicity, neuromuscular weakness)
- **Ventilation-perfusion mismatch** — areas of lung that are ventilated but not perfused, or perfused but not ventilated (pulmonary embolism, pneumonia)
- **Shunt** — blood passing through the lung without encountering ventilated alveoli (atelectasis, ARDS)
- **Diffusion impairment** — thickened or damaged alveolar-capillary membrane (pulmonary fibrosis)

Each mechanism responds differently to supplemental oxygen. Shunt physiology, in particular, may not improve significantly with increased FiO2 alone — a distinction that matters when oxygenation fails to improve despite high-flow oxygen.

## Related terms

- [Ventilation](./ventilation.md) — the companion process that must be assessed independently
- [Preoxygenation](./preoxygenation.md) — maximizing oxygen reserves before airway intervention
- [Capnography](./capnography.md) — monitoring that detects ventilation failure when oxygenation is maintained

records.name: Pacing
records.description: An activity management strategy designed to keep exertion within an individual's metabolic capacity, prevent triggering post-exertional malaise, and maintain function through rest, pre-emptive breaks, and self-imposed exercise limits based on symptom response or measurable thresholds like heart-rate ceiling.
records.body:
Pacing is an activity management strategy whose explicit aim is to keep exertion within an individual's current metabolic and autonomic capacity and thereby prevent triggering post-exertional malaise. The strategy operates on the hypothesis that post-exertional malaise is triggered when demand exceeds capacity — when a person attempts exertion their mitochondrial output cannot sustain aerobically, forcing a shift to anaerobic metabolism, or when autonomic demand exceeds the available glucocorticoid and catecholamine support. Pacing aims to identify that threshold and stay beneath it, rather than attempting to expand capacity through progressive exertion.

Implementation of pacing takes several forms, all aimed at the same end of matching exertion to current capacity. One approach is heart-rate-threshold pacing, in which the patient monitors heart rate during activity and stops or reduces intensity when it rises above a predetermined ceiling (typically around 50–60% of age-predicted maximum, well below the threshold for maximal effort). Another is pre-emptive rest: dividing the day into blocks of activity separated by mandated rest periods, acknowledging that even subclinical exertion — thinking, social interaction, standing — carries metabolic cost, and preventing the gradual accumulation of deficit that leads to triggering post-exertional malaise. Symptom-contingent pacing adjusts activity based on the day's symptom baseline: when cognitive fog or fatigue worsens, exertion is reduced regardless of what was planned. The common thread is a discipline of staying within capacity and accepting reduced activity rather than accepting the cost of triggering malaise.

Pacing is often confounded with graded exercise therapy, and the distinction is fundamental and should be stated plainly. Graded exercise therapy prescribes progressive increases in exercise intensity and duration on a predetermined schedule, regardless of symptom response — the rationale being that deconditioning and catastrophic thinking about exercise perpetuate fatigue, and that breaking those cycles requires patients to override their symptoms and steadily increase exertion. The physiological logic of graded exercise therapy is sound in many fatiguing illnesses: deconditioning can be reversed by progressive activity increase, and symptom-focused avoidance can perpetuate disability. In myalgic encephalomyelitis, however, the logic inverts. The core pathophysiology is not deconditioning — it is metabolic and autonomic dysfunction — and the cardinal feature is that exertion beyond capacity triggers a disproportionate and prolonged response. Prescribing progressive exertion that systematically exceeds capacity does not reverse the deconditioning; it repeatedly triggers post-exertional malaise and may consolidate rather than resolve the illness. The two strategies are mechanistically opposite, and applying the wrong one can be harmful.

The evidence base for pacing is limited — there are few randomized controlled trials, and the qualitative evidence and small observational studies show benefit in terms of symptom stability and avoidance of flares. The evidence base against graded exercise in myalgic encephalomyelitis is stronger: the PACE trial, a large randomized controlled trial testing cognitive behavior therapy plus graded exercise versus standard care, had significant methodological problems, including mid-trial changes to outcome measures and recovery thresholds that overlapped with trial entry criteria, which led to overestimation of benefit and led the UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence to withdraw its 2006 recommendation for graded-exercise-based treatment and replace it with a caution that pacing may be more appropriate for myalgic encephalomyelitis. The methodological specifics of the PACE trial are matters of published record, not advocacy — the study had real flaws that affect interpretation of its results.

For patient management and clinical research, the consequence is that an individual with myalgic encephalomyelitis should not be prescribed graded exercise on the assumption that it will restore function. Pacing, with its mechanistic rationale grounded in the actual pathophysiology, is a more defensible starting strategy, though it also requires evidence strengthening and careful long-term outcome measurement.

## Related terms

- Post-exertional malaise — the symptom that pacing aims to prevent by staying within capacity
- Myalgic encephalomyelitis — the illness for which pacing is a proposed management strategy
- Graded exercise therapy — the opposite management strategy, with different mechanistic rationale and risk profile
- Energy envelope — a related concept emphasizing the limitation of total daily energy expenditure
- Allostatic load — the framework of cumulative physiological cost that pacing aims to minimize

records.body:
**Pacing pathogens** is a house term coined by emsenn on 2026-09-02. Pacing pathogens are the pathogens whose acute infection is documented to precipitate the chronic symptom family that infection-associated chronic illness names: post-exertional malaise, unrefreshing sleep, cognitive impairment, orthostatic intolerance, and fatigue that rest does not repair. The name states what the illnesses they leave behind have in common in practice: the one management strategy with consistent patient and guideline support is [pacing](../../../../services/myalgic-encephalomyelitis-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/pacing.md), activity kept inside the limit that avoids [post-exertional malaise](../../../../services/myalgic-encephalomyelitis-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/post-exertional-malaise.md).

## Which pathogens

Membership is evidential, not taxonomic. A pathogen belongs when prospective or well-characterized cohorts show a persistent post-infective syndrome with this symptom shape in a fraction of those infected. Documented members, with the strongest evidence first:

- **Epstein-Barr virus, Ross River virus, and Coxiella burnetii** — the Dubbo prospective cohort followed acute infections with all three and found a post-infective fatigue syndrome in about eleven percent at six months, with a stable case rate independent of which pathogen precipitated it [hickie2006]. That single finding is the empirical basis for grouping the pathogens at all. Infectious mononucleosis in college students has since been followed prospectively into myalgic encephalomyelitis / chronic fatigue syndrome [jason2021].
- **SARS-CoV-2** — long COVID, the condition that supplied the statistical power behind the umbrella; see [infection-associated chronic illness](infection-associated-chronic-illness.md) and the long COVID section.
- **Giardia lamblia** — a protozoan, not a virus: the Bergen waterborne outbreak produced a well-characterized cohort with chronic fatigue syndrome after enteritis [naess2012].
- **Borrelia burgdorferi, Ebola virus, dengue virus, and SARS-CoV-1** — the remaining conditions the National Academies grouped as infection-associated chronic illness, each with its own post-infective syndrome literature cited on the umbrella term's carrier.
- Choutka and colleagues' review of unexplained post-acute infection syndromes is the field's own survey of this set and of the many further pathogens with weaker or single-cohort evidence [choutka2022].

The set is open at its edge. A pathogen with one small cohort belongs provisionally, and the carrier that adds it names the cohort.

## What the term is not

The term names the triggers, not the illnesses: infection-associated chronic illness groups the conditions people are left with, while pacing pathogens groups the agents that start them, across viruses, bacteria, and protozoa alike, which is why it is not a synonym for post-viral. It also makes no mechanistic claim. Whether the pathogens share one pathway or converge on a common downstream state is exactly what the field has not settled, and the term holds that open the way the umbrella term does.

## Consequence

For observation and engineering the precipitating pathogen is one attribute on a person's record, never the key the software is organized around: a pacing measure, a record schema, or a public explainer addresses the symptom family, and a new pathogen joining the set changes a list, not a system. The same holds for the public products: a channel, a newsletter, or a kit built for people with these illnesses serves everyone the set covers, not one virus's patients.

records.name: Pandiculation
records.description: The neuromuscular reset pattern — voluntary contraction followed by slow, controlled release — that somatic education uses to restore cortical control over chronically contracted muscles.

cites: Somatics: Reawakening the Mind's Control of Movement, Flexibility, and Health
Clinical Somatic Education: A New Discipline in the Field of Health Care

hanna1988.title: Somatics: Reawakening the Mind's Control of Movement, Flexibility, and Health

hanna1990.title: Clinical Somatic Education: A New Discipline in the Field of Health Care

records.body:
Pandiculation is the neuromuscular pattern of voluntary contraction followed by slow, controlled lengthening.
It's the movement pattern that animals and humans perform instinctively upon waking — the full-body stretch-and-yawn that resets muscular tone after a period of immobility.
[Thomas Hanna](../../../../../../../../../../../information-science-services-section/services/knowledge-services-section/services/research-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/thomas-hanna.md) made pandiculation the central technique of his Clinical Somatic Education, arguing that it's the only reliable method for reversing sensory-motor amnesia (SMA) — the condition in which habitual muscular contraction drops below the threshold of conscious awareness [@hanna1988].

## Why stretching doesn't work

The standard approach to chronic muscular tightness is stretching: pull the tight muscle to its end range and hold.
The problem, in somatic terms, is that stretching addresses the wrong system.
A chronically contracted muscle isn't short because it lacks mechanical length.
It's contracted because the brain is sending a continuous contraction signal that the person can no longer feel or voluntarily override.

Stretching triggers the stretch reflex — a spinal-level response in which the [muscle spindles](./proprioception.md) detect lengthening and reflexively contract the muscle to protect it from tearing.
This means stretching a chronically tight muscle produces a brief period of increased range (while the stretch reflex is fatigued) followed by a return to the same or greater tension (as the reflexive contraction reasserts itself).
The cortex isn't involved.
The habitual motor pattern remains unchanged.

Pandiculation works differently because it engages the cortex rather than the spinal reflexes.

## The three-phase pattern

Pandiculation consists of three phases:

**Phase 1: Voluntary contraction.**
The person deliberately contracts the chronically tight muscle — moving further into the pattern of tension, not away from it.
This is counterintuitive: if the muscle is already too tight, why make it tighter?
Because voluntary contraction recruits cortical motor neurons.
The act of deliberately producing the contraction pattern re-engages the sensory-motor cortex with the muscle — the same cortical engagement that sensory-motor amnesia has eroded.

**Phase 2: Slow, controlled lengthening.**
From the position of maximum voluntary contraction, the person slowly releases the contraction, lengthening the muscle with continuous cortical control.
This isn't a passive release (letting go suddenly) or a stretch (being pulled by an external force).
It's an active, deliberate deceleration — the cortex controls every increment of lengthening.
The slowness is essential: it maintains cortical engagement throughout the release and gives the sensory-motor system time to recalibrate its baseline tone.

**Phase 3: Complete relaxation.**
At the end of the slow lengthening, the person fully relaxes the muscle and rests.
This allows the nervous system to register the new resting length and tone as the baseline.
Without this rest phase, the system may revert to its habitual contraction pattern.

## Why pandiculation works

The mechanism is cortical, not peripheral.
Sensory-motor amnesia is a loss of voluntary cortical control over a muscle group.
The muscle works fine — it's contracting as instructed by the brain.
The problem is that the instruction has become involuntary and unconscious.
Pandiculation restores voluntary control by making the person produce the contraction pattern consciously and then consciously release it.

This is sensory-motor learning, not mechanical intervention.
Each repetition of the pandiculation pattern strengthens the cortical pathway between voluntary motor command and sensory feedback.
Over repeated practice, the brain's habitual contraction signal weakens and voluntary control reasserts itself.
The muscle relaxes not because it was mechanically stretched but because the brain stopped telling it to contract.

Hanna described this as "the one thing that the sensory-motor system can do that nothing else can do for it" — no amount of massage, manipulation, or stretching can substitute for the brain voluntarily engaging and releasing its own motor patterns [@hanna1990].

## Pandiculation in animals

The instinctive morning stretch is a pandiculation.
Watch a dog or cat wake from sleep: it doesn't passively stretch.
It contracts powerfully — arching the back, extending the limbs, engaging the full musculature — and then slowly releases into relaxation.
This pattern resets neuromuscular tone after the immobility of sleep, restoring the sensory-motor system's readiness for coordinated movement.

Humans pandiculate instinctively too — yawning is a pandiculation of the jaw, face, and respiratory muscles.
But the instinctive pandiculations are limited in scope.
Clinical Somatic Education applies the principle systematically to the full body, using guided movement sequences that address the green-light, red-light, and trauma reflex patterns that Hanna identified as the primary sources of sensory-motor amnesia.

## Relation to other somatic techniques

Pandiculation is distinct from but complementary to other approaches:

**Feldenkrais Method** — [Moshe Feldenkrais](../../../../../../../../../../../information-science-services-section/services/knowledge-services-section/services/research-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/moshe-feldenkrais.md)' Awareness Through Movement uses slow, attentive movement to increase proprioceptive resolution, but doesn't specifically use the contract-then-release pattern.
Feldenkrais works more through exploration and variation; Hanna's method works more through direct engagement with habitual contraction patterns.
Both are cortical approaches; they target different aspects of sensory-motor learning.

**Stretching and yoga** — conventional stretching operates at the spinal reflex level.
Yoga incorporates elements of pandiculation (active engagement followed by release) but typically doesn't emphasize the slow, controlled release phase that makes pandiculation effective for addressing SMA.

**[Somatic Experiencing](./somatic-experiencing.md)** — SE uses discharge (trembling, shaking) to complete interrupted defensive responses.
Pandiculation addresses chronic muscular contraction patterns that may or may not be trauma-related.
Both work through the nervous system rather than on the musculoskeletal system directly, but they address different phenomena.

## Related concepts

- [Somatic Awareness](./somatic-awareness.md) — the perceptual capacity that pandiculation restores and depends on
- [Proprioception](./proprioception.md) — the sensory system that pandiculation recalibrates
- [Tensegrity in Movement](./tensegrity-in-movement.md) — the structural model within which pandiculation rebalances tension distribution

## Sources

- Hanna, T.
  (1988).
  *Somatics: Reawakening the Mind's Control of Movement, Flexibility, and Health.*
  Addison-Wesley [@hanna1988].
- Hanna, T.
  (1990).
  "Clinical Somatic Education: A New Discipline in the Field of Health Care."
  *Somatics*, 8(1), 4–10 [@hanna1990].

records.body:
A percussive massage device (commonly called a massage gun) is a handheld, battery-powered or rechargeable device that delivers rapid repetitive mechanical impacts to muscle tissue. A DC brushless motor drives a rotating cam or eccentric weight, which produces rapid compression and decompression of muscle.

Devices include adjustable frequency (impact rate) and amplitude (depth) controls, rechargeable power, and interchangeable applicator heads (ball for large muscle groups, fork for muscle bellies to avoid bone). Claimed mechanisms include increased blood flow, reduced muscle tension, accelerated muscle recovery, and breakdown of fascial adhesions through myofascial relaxation.

The actual mechanism is mechanical vibration applied to muscle tissue. Vibration activates muscle spindle reflexes and mechanoreceptors, producing transient reflex-mediated muscle relaxation via spinal gating mechanisms [@johnson2022]. Transient local blood flow increase follows mechanical stimulation. These effects are temporary and resolve when stimulation ceases.

Evidence from small trials [@behm2016] [@johnson2022] shows percussive devices produce modest, transient muscle tension relief and increased range of motion during and immediately after use. No evidence supports permanent tissue change, accelerated recovery, or superiority over simpler mechanical massage or heat application. Effects are comparable to manual massage at equivalent depth and duration.

Safety is generally good. Discomfort or transient bruising can occur with intense vibration. The device should be avoided over bone, on thin skin, or in users taking anticoagulants.

records.name: Pharmacodynamics
records.description: The study of what a drug does to the body, including receptor binding, dose-response relationships, selectivity, and tolerance
records.body:
**Pharmacodynamics** is the study of what a drug does to the body — the mechanisms through which a drug produces its effects. Where [pharmacokinetics](./pharmacokinetics.md) asks how a drug reaches its target, pharmacodynamics asks what happens when it gets there.

## Receptor-based mechanisms

Most drugs produce their effects by interacting with receptors — proteins on cell surfaces or within cells that normally respond to endogenous signaling molecules (neurotransmitters, hormones, cytokines). A drug that binds to a receptor can:

- **Activate it (agonist)** — mimicking the endogenous ligand. Morphine is an agonist at mu-opioid receptors, mimicking endogenous endorphins to produce analgesia, euphoria, and respiratory depression.
- **Block it (antagonist)** — preventing the endogenous ligand from binding. Naloxone is an antagonist at mu-opioid receptors, reversing opioid effects by displacing agonists from the receptor.
- **Partially activate it (partial agonist)** — producing a submaximal response even at full receptor occupancy. Buprenorphine is a partial agonist at mu-opioid receptors, producing enough activation to prevent withdrawal and craving but not enough to produce the full euphoria or respiratory depression of a full agonist. This pharmacological profile is what makes buprenorphine useful in opioid use disorder treatment — and what connects pharmacodynamics directly to [harm reduction](../../../../../public-health-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/harm-reduction.md) practice.

## Dose-response relationships

The relationship between drug dose and effect follows a characteristic pattern:

- At low doses, increasing the dose increases the effect approximately proportionally
- At higher doses, the response curve flattens — the receptors are approaching saturation, and further dose increases produce diminishing additional effect
- At some point, a maximal effect (Emax) is reached — no amount of additional drug will produce more of the intended effect, though adverse effects may continue to increase

This curve explains why doubling a dose does not double the effect, why overdose produces toxicity before the therapeutic effect is maximized, and why different drugs that act on the same receptor can have different maximal effects (full vs. partial agonists).

## Selectivity and side effects

No drug acts on a single target. Every drug interacts with multiple receptors, enzymes, or ion channels — some with high affinity (producing the intended therapeutic effect) and some with lower affinity (producing side effects). The [therapeutic index](./therapeutic-index.md) — the ratio between the dose that produces toxicity and the dose that produces the therapeutic effect — quantifies how much room exists between benefit and harm.

Side effects are not failures of the drug but consequences of its mechanism acting on targets beyond the intended one. Understanding why a side effect occurs (which off-target receptor is being activated or blocked) allows clinicians to predict side effects, choose between drugs with different selectivity profiles, and manage adverse effects when they occur.

## Tolerance and sensitization

With repeated exposure, the body's response to a drug may change:

- **Tolerance** — the same dose produces less effect, requiring dose escalation to maintain the original response. Mechanisms include receptor downregulation (fewer receptors available), receptor desensitization (receptors less responsive), and compensatory physiological adaptations.
- **Sensitization** — the same dose produces increased effect. This occurs through different mechanisms depending on the drug and the neural circuit involved. Stimulant sensitization is a well-studied example: repeated amphetamine exposure produces progressively larger dopamine responses through neuroplastic changes in reward circuits.

Tolerance and sensitization can occur simultaneously for different effects of the same drug. Opioid users develop tolerance to euphoria (requiring higher doses for the same high) faster than they develop tolerance to respiratory depression (so the dose they need for euphoria approaches the dose that suppresses breathing). This pharmacodynamic asymmetry is the mechanism of opioid overdose death.

## Related terms

- [Pharmacokinetics](./pharmacokinetics.md) — what the body does to the drug
- [Therapeutic Index](./therapeutic-index.md) — the margin between therapeutic and toxic doses
- [Drug Interaction](./drug-interaction.md) — how drugs modify each other's pharmacodynamics

records.name: Pharmacokinetics
records.description: The study of what the body does to a drug: absorption, distribution, metabolism, and elimination (ADME)
records.body:
**Pharmacokinetics** is the study of what the body does to a drug — how it is absorbed, distributed, metabolized, and eliminated. The four processes are conventionally summarized as ADME:

**Absorption** — the movement of a drug from its site of administration into the bloodstream. A pill dissolves in the gut, crosses the intestinal wall, and enters the portal circulation. An intramuscular injection diffuses from the muscle into capillaries. An intravenous drug bypasses absorption entirely — it is already in the blood. The route of administration determines the speed and completeness of absorption, which determines [bioavailability](./bioavailability.md).

**Distribution** — the movement of a drug from the bloodstream into the body's tissues. Distribution depends on blood flow (well-perfused organs like the brain, heart, liver, and kidneys receive drug first), protein binding (drugs bound to plasma proteins cannot cross into tissues; only the unbound fraction is pharmacologically active), lipid solubility (lipophilic drugs cross cell membranes readily and accumulate in fatty tissues), and specialized barriers (the blood-brain barrier limits access to the central nervous system).

**Metabolism** — the chemical transformation of a drug, primarily by the liver. Hepatic enzymes — especially the cytochrome P450 (CYP) family — convert lipophilic drugs into more water-soluble metabolites that can be excreted by the kidneys. Metabolism can inactivate a drug, convert an inactive prodrug into its active form, or produce metabolites that are themselves pharmacologically active or toxic. The CYP system is the primary site of [drug interactions](./drug-interaction.md): drugs that induce or inhibit specific CYP enzymes alter the metabolism of every other drug processed by those enzymes.

**Elimination** — the removal of drug and metabolites from the body. The kidneys are the primary route (renal excretion), with hepatobiliary excretion, pulmonary exhalation, and other minor routes contributing. The rate of elimination determines [half-life](./half-life.md) and therefore how long a drug's effects persist and how frequently it must be dosed.

## Clinical significance

Pharmacokinetics determines the practical questions of drug therapy: how much drug to give (dose), how often to give it (dosing interval), how quickly effect onset occurs (route-dependent), how long the effect lasts (half-life-dependent), and what happens when the body's processing capacity is impaired (dose adjustment in renal or hepatic failure).

Understanding pharmacokinetics also explains why the same dose produces different effects in different patients. Age (pediatric patients have immature metabolic enzymes; elderly patients have decreased renal clearance), body composition (obese patients distribute lipophilic drugs into larger fat compartments), genetic variation (CYP2D6 polymorphisms produce ultra-rapid or poor metabolizers), and organ function (renal or hepatic impairment slows elimination) all alter pharmacokinetics — and therefore alter the drug's effect at the same dose.

## Related terms

- [Pharmacodynamics](./pharmacodynamics.md) — the companion concept: what the drug does to the body
- [Bioavailability](./bioavailability.md) — the fraction that reaches systemic circulation
- [Half-Life](./half-life.md) — the elimination rate that determines dosing
- [Drug Interaction](./drug-interaction.md) — how drugs modify each other's pharmacokinetics

records.name: Phlegm
records.description: 痰 (tan) — a pathological product of impaired fluid metabolism in TCM, ranging from visible mucus to invisible obstructions that produce nodules, dizziness, mental fog, and masses — 'the source of a hundred diseases'

kaptchuk2000.title: The Web That Has No Weaver

records.body:
Phlegm (tan 痰) is a pathological product of impaired fluid metabolism in [Traditional Chinese Medicine](traditional-chinese-medicine.md).
TCM's concept of phlegm is far broader than the biomedical meaning of respiratory mucus.
It encompasses any abnormal accumulation of thick, turbid fluid in the body — from visible sputum in the lungs to invisible obstructions that produce nodules, masses, dizziness, mental fog, numbness, and psychiatric symptoms.
TCM calls phlegm "the source of a hundred diseases" (bai bing duo you tan zuo sui 百病多由痰作祟) — a recognition of its role in an extraordinary range of conditions.

## Visible and invisible phlegm

**Visible phlegm** (you xing zhi tan 有形之痰): Phlegm you can see or hear — sputum coughed from the lungs, mucus in the throat, nasal discharge, vomited mucoid fluid.
This corresponds roughly to the biomedical concept of mucus and exudate.

**Invisible phlegm** (wu xing zhi tan 无形之痰): Phlegm that cannot be directly seen but manifests through its effects — subcutaneous nodules, goiter, lipomas, atherosclerotic plaque, gallstones, kidney stones, joint swelling, a feeling of obstruction in the throat or chest, dizziness with a heavy head, and mental-emotional symptoms (confusion, mania, epilepsy-like episodes).
This is the distinctively TCM dimension of the concept — the idea that thick, turbid, congealed fluid can obstruct any system in the body, not just the respiratory tract.

## How phlegm forms

Phlegm arises when [body fluids](jin-ye.md) are not properly transformed and transported.
The primary organ responsible is the **Spleen** (which governs fluid transformation), with contributions from the **Lung** (which distributes fluids) and the **Kidney** (which governs water metabolism).
The TCM axiom is: "the Spleen is the source of phlegm; the Lung is the storehouse of phlegm" (pi wei sheng tan zhi yuan, fei wei chu tan zhi qi 脾为生痰之源，肺为储痰之器).

Common pathways to phlegm formation:

- **Spleen [Qi](qi.md) deficiency** → fluids not transformed → accumulation → phlegm
- **[Qi stagnation](qi-stagnation.md)** → impaired fluid movement → accumulation → phlegm
- **Heat** → condenses fluids into thick, sticky phlegm (phlegm-heat: yellow, thick, difficult to expectorate)
- **Cold** → congeals fluids into watery, copious phlegm (phlegm-cold: white, thin, easily expectorated)

## Phlegm and the mind

One of TCM's most distinctive claims about phlegm is that it can "mist the Heart orifices" (tan mi xin qiao 痰迷心窍), obstructing [Shen](shen.md) and producing mental-emotional symptoms: confusion, muddled thinking, mania, incoherent speech, loss of consciousness.
This "phlegm misting the mind" pattern is TCM's framework for understanding certain acute psychiatric presentations, epilepsy, and post-stroke cognitive impairment.

The concept is not as foreign to biomedicine as it might appear.
Neuroinflammation, cerebrovascular disease, and metabolic encephalopathy all involve the accumulation of abnormal substances (inflammatory mediators, lipids, metabolic waste) that impair brain function — the biomedical version of "turbid obstruction affecting the mind."

## Treatment

Phlegm-resolving herbs (hua tan yao 化痰药) are classified by the type of phlegm they address:

- **Cold-phlegm**: Warm, drying herbs — Ban Xia (Pinellia), Bai Jie Zi (white mustard seed)
- **Heat-phlegm**: Cool, clearing herbs — Gua Lou (Trichosanthes), Zhu Ru (bamboo shavings), Bei Mu (Fritillaria)
- **Wind-phlegm** (causing dizziness, tremor): Tian Ma (Gastrodia), Gou Teng (Uncaria)

[Hu Zhang](hu-zhang.md) addresses phlegm-heat in the Lung through its bitter, cold properties.

## See also

- [Body Fluids (Jin Ye)](jin-ye.md) — the normal fluids that phlegm derives from
- [Qi Stagnation](qi-stagnation.md) — a major cause of phlegm formation
- [Damp-Heat](damp-heat.md) — dampness that has not yet congealed into phlegm
- [Shen](shen.md) — the awareness that phlegm can obstruct
- [Zang-Fu](zang-fu.md) — the Spleen and Lung systems central to phlegm pathology

records.name: Photobiomodulation
records.description: The application of red or near-infrared light (600–1000 nm wavelength) to tissue, which penetrates several millimeters below the skin surface and increases ATP production in mitochondria, producing cellular energy, reduced inflammation, and tissue repair effects.

hamblin2017.title: Mechanisms and applications of the anti-inflammatory effects of photobiomodulation

records.body:
Photobiomodulation is the application of red or near-infrared light (typically 600–1000 nm wavelength) to tissue. Red and near-infrared light penetrate to approximately 5–10 mm below the skin surface [@hamblin2017], where they interact with mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase in the electron transport chain.

This interaction increases ATP (cellular energy) production in cells [@hamblin2017]. Downstream effects include increased cellular energy availability for protein synthesis (including collagen), upregulation of anti-inflammatory signaling (reduced TNF-α, IL-6), and angiogenesis (new blood vessel formation).

In controlled laboratory and clinical trials, photobiomodulation produces reproducible effects on tissue repair and inflammation in certain wound models and joint inflammation studies [@hamblin2017]. Evidence is moderate for muscle injury recovery and joint pain; evidence is weaker for cosmetic skin applications and cellulite reduction.

Photobiomodulation does not permanently alter tissue structure or resolve structural problems such as cellulite (subcutaneous fat herniation through connective tissue). While the technique may transiently improve skin appearance through edema reduction and modestly increased collagen turnover, long-term clinical benefit for cosmetic indications is not established.

Safety is generally good. Mild eye strain may occur with direct light exposure; protective eyewear is recommended. Skin irritation is rare. The technique is non-invasive and produces no known serious adverse effects.

records.name: Phytoalexin
records.description: A defensive compound synthesized de novo by a plant in response to stress — pathogen attack, UV radiation, or tissue damage — explaining why stressed plants are often more pharmacologically potent than unstressed ones
records.body:
A phytoalexin is a defensive compound that a plant synthesizes *de novo* in response to stress — pathogen infection, ultraviolet radiation, physical damage, or herbivore attack. Unlike constitutive defenses (compounds always present), phytoalexins are induced: the plant produces them only when threatened. The term was coined by Müller and Börger in 1940 from Greek *phyton* (plant) + *alexein* (to ward off).

Phytoalexins are typically low-molecular-weight antimicrobial compounds that accumulate at the site of infection, creating a localized chemical barrier against the invading pathogen. They belong to diverse chemical classes depending on the plant family: [stilbenoids](stilbenoid.md) in Vitaceae (grapes) and [Polygonaceae](../../../../../../../botany-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/polygonaceae.md) (knotweeds), isoflavonoids in Fabaceae (legumes), sesquiterpenes in Solanaceae (nightshades), indole derivatives in Brassicaceae (mustards).

## Resveratrol as phytoalexin

[Resveratrol](resveratrol.md) — the compound that made [Japanese knotweed](../../../../../../../botany-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/japanese-knotweed.md) pharmacologically famous — is a phytoalexin. The plant produces it in response to fungal infection, UV radiation, and tissue damage. This explains several observations:

- **Why knotweed rhizome is richer in resveratrol than aerial tissue**: The underground rhizome is the plant's survival organ, under constant microbial challenge from soil organisms
- **Why resveratrol concentration peaks in autumn**: The plant is translocating defensive compounds to the rhizome for winter storage
- **Why stressed plants are more pharmacologically potent**: Traditional herbalists have long observed that wild-harvested plants are often more medicinally active than cultivated ones — the wild plant faces more stress and produces more defensive phytoalexins

## Pharmacological implications

The phytoalexin concept has a practical implication for herbalism and pharmacognosy: the very compounds that make a plant medicinally valuable are the compounds the plant produces to defend itself. The plant's evolutionary defense strategy is the source of human therapeutic benefit. This is not coincidence — pathogens that attack plants share biochemical targets with pathogens and inflammatory processes that affect humans. An antimicrobial compound effective against a plant fungus may be effective against a human pathogen through the same mechanism.

## See also

- [Resveratrol](resveratrol.md) — the most studied phytoalexin
- [Polyphenol](polyphenol.md) — the chemical class most phytoalexins belong to
- [Japanese Knotweed](../../../../../../../botany-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/japanese-knotweed.md) — a major phytoalexin producer

records.name: Placebo Effect
records.description: Improvement produced by the context of a treatment (expectation, ritual, the clinician encounter, conditioning) rather than by its specific action; largest for self-reported symptoms such as pain, anxiety, fatigue and nausea.
records.body:
A placebo effect is a genuine change in how a person feels or functions, caused by the context of a treatment rather than by its specific ingredient or mechanism. That context includes expectation, the ritual of treatment, the relationship with a clinician and conditioning from past treatment [@kaptchuk2015]. Its mirror image, the nocebo effect, is harm from negative expectation, such as side effects reported on a placebo.

Placebo effects are largest for symptoms a person reports themselves: pain, anxiety, insomnia, fatigue and nausea. They are smallest or absent for objective measures such as tumour size or bacterial load. The conditions treated by [cranial electrotherapy](../../../../services/medical-technology-services-section/services/electrotherapy-devices-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/cranial-electrotherapy-stimulation.md) and by many practices of [Chinese medicine](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/traditional-chinese-medicine.md) and [qigong](../../../../services/traditional-chinese-medicine-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/qigong.md) sit in the first group. That does not make their effects unreal; it makes them hard to attribute. It is why trials compare the real treatment against a convincing [sham](sham-stimulation.md) under [blinding](blinding.md).

records.name: Platelet Activation
records.description: The sequence of biochemical and morphological changes in a platelet upon exposure to agonists (thrombin, collagen, ADP, thromboxane), producing shape change, granule release, phosphatidylserine externalization, and integrin activation, with phosphatidylserine exposure being the critical membrane change enabling assembly of the coagulation prothrombinase complex.

jackson2005.title: The growing complexity of platelet aggregation

varga2016.title: Mechanisms of platelet function and dysfunction

records.body:
Platelet activation is the sequence of cellular changes that occurs when a
platelet is stimulated by an agonist — a molecule that binds to receptors on
the platelet surface and initiates the activation cascade. The major
physiological agonists are:

1. **Thrombin** — the central coagulation protease, acting through protease-
   activated receptors (PARs)
2. **Collagen** — exposed when blood vessel endothelium is damaged, acting
   through integrin α2β1 and GPVI receptors
3. **Adenosine diphosphate (ADP)** — released from damaged red cells and
   platelets themselves, acting through P2Y1 and P2Y12 receptors
4. **Thromboxane A2** — produced by activated platelets themselves, amplifying
   activation

Each agonist triggers intracellular calcium release, activation of protein
kinase C, and mobilization of phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate. This
leads to a cascade of morphological and biochemical changes:

## Morphological and granule-release changes

Upon activation, a resting discoid platelet undergoes shape change, becoming
spiculated and rounded as its cytoskeleton reorganizes. The platelet contains
two types of granules:

- **Alpha-granules** — storage organelles containing fibrinogen, von Willebrand
  factor, thrombospondin, and platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF)
- **Dense granules** — containing ATP, ADP, serotonin, and divalent cations
  (calcium, magnesium)

Upon activation, both types of granules fuse with the plasma membrane and
release their contents. This is not a side effect; it is a programmed response
amplifying activation. The ADP and ATP released from dense granules activate
nearby resting platelets, propagating the activation response.

## Surface expression of activation markers

Activation brings hidden epitopes to the cell surface:

- **P-selectin** — a cell-adhesion molecule normally sequestered in alpha-granule
  membranes, exposed on the platelet surface upon granule fusion. P-selectin is
  the marker most commonly used clinically to identify activated platelets.
- **Phosphatidylserine (PS)** — normally restricted to the inner (cytoplasmic)
  leaflet of the plasma membrane by ATP-dependent flippase activity. Upon
  activation, calcium-activated scramblase scrambles the membrane, causing PS to
  externalize to the outer (blood-facing) leaflet. PS is an anionic lipid; its
  externalization exposes negative charge on the platelet surface.

## Integrin activation and aggregation

Platelet integrins — particularly αIIbβ3 (GPIIb/IIIa) — undergo conformational
change upon activation, shifting from a low-affinity to a high-affinity state.
This allows them to bind fibrinogen, which has two αIIbβ3 binding sites, one on
each end. A single fibrinogen molecule can therefore bridge two platelets,
linking them together. Multiple such bridges build a platelet aggregate — a
three-dimensional network of activated platelets held together by fibrinogen and
other adhesive proteins.

## Distinction: activation vs. aggregation

Platelet activation and platelet aggregation are often used interchangeably in
casual speech, but they are distinct events:

- **Activation** is the response of a single platelet to an agonist — the shape
  change, granule release, PS externalization, and integrin conformational change.
  Activation can be measured without aggregation by flow cytometry (measuring PS
  exposure or P-selectin surface expression on single cells) or by function assays
  (measuring phosphatidylserine exposure or granule release markers).
- **Aggregation** is the linking of multiple activated platelets into a clump. It
  requires integrin activation and fibrinogen (or another adhesive protein).

A patient can have platelet hyperactivation (elevated P-selectin, elevated PS
exposure) without visible aggregation. Similarly, aggregation assays (such as
light transmission aggregometry) can show reduced aggregation in a patient whose
platelets are actually hyperactivated but have a defect in integrin or in the
adhesive proteins needed for aggregation.

The consequence is that a study reporting "platelet hyperactivation" is saying
something specific — that activation markers are elevated — which is different
from a study reporting "platelet aggregate burden." Both can be true; neither
implies the other.

## The critical consequence: phosphatidylserine externalization

The externalization of phosphatidylserine upon platelet activation is the event
that makes coagulation possible. PS is the anionic membrane surface on which the
prothrombinase complex (factor Xa + factor Va + calcium) assembles. In the healthy
resting state, PS is kept on the inner membrane by flippase activity, and coagulation
complexes cannot form. Upon activation, scramblase externalizes PS, providing the
surface. Clotting then proceeds at the site of the activated platelet. This is why
phosphatidylserine externalization is not a curiosity; it is the essential membrane
change enabling the entire coagulation response.

## Related terms

- Phosphatidylserine — the anionic lipid externalized during activation
- P-selectin — surface adhesion molecule exposed upon activation
- Integrin αIIbβ3 — integrin activated to enable fibrinogen binding
- Platelet aggregation — the linking of multiple activated platelets
- Coagulation cascade — the process enabled by PS externalization
- Thrombin — the principal physiological platelet agonist

records.name: Polyphenol
records.description: A large class of plant-produced organic compounds characterized by multiple phenol rings — including flavonoids, stilbenoids, tannins, and phenolic acids — with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and cardioprotective properties
records.body:
Polyphenols are a large and structurally diverse class of organic compounds produced by plants, characterized by the presence of multiple phenol groups — aromatic rings bearing hydroxyl (-OH) substituents. Over 8,000 polyphenolic compounds have been identified in plants. They are the most abundant [antioxidants](../../../../../../../../content/text/glossary/terms/inflammation.md) in the human diet, present in fruits, vegetables, tea, coffee, wine, chocolate, and medicinal herbs.

Plants produce polyphenols primarily as defensive compounds — protecting against ultraviolet radiation, pathogens, and herbivores. This defensive function is why stressed or damaged plants often produce higher concentrations of polyphenols than unstressed plants, and why [phytoalexins](phytoalexin.md) (stress-induced defensive compounds) are frequently polyphenolic.

## Major classes

**Flavonoids** (~6,000 known compounds): The largest subclass. Includes quercetin, catechins, epicatechin, kaempferol, anthocyanins. Found in virtually all fruits, vegetables, and medicinal herbs. Responsible for many of the colors of flowers and fruits.

**[Stilbenoids](stilbenoid.md)**: Includes [resveratrol](resveratrol.md) and polydatin (piceid). Found in grapes, peanuts, and most abundantly in [Japanese knotweed](../../../../../../../botany-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/japanese-knotweed.md). Stilbenoids are produced as phytoalexins — stress-response compounds.

**Tannins**: Large polyphenolic molecules that bind proteins. Responsible for the astringent taste of tea, red wine, and unripe fruit. Divided into condensed tannins (proanthocyanidins) and hydrolyzable tannins (gallotannins and ellagitannins).

**Phenolic acids**: Simple phenol derivatives including gallic acid, caffeic acid, and chlorogenic acid. Abundant in coffee, berries, and whole grains.

**[Anthraquinones](anthraquinone.md)**: Include [emodin](emodin.md) and related compounds. Found in rhubarb, senna, aloe, and Japanese knotweed. Distinguished by their laxative activity.

## Pharmacological significance

Polyphenols as a class share several pharmacological properties, though the potency and specificity of individual compounds varies enormously:

**Antioxidant activity**: Polyphenols scavenge reactive oxygen species (free radicals) through their phenol hydroxyl groups. This is their most widely promoted property, though the clinical significance of dietary antioxidant supplementation remains debated — the in vitro antioxidant activity of a compound does not predict its in vivo therapeutic benefit, because [bioavailability](bioavailability.md), metabolism, and the complexity of in vivo redox biology intervene.

**Anti-inflammatory activity**: Many polyphenols inhibit NF-κB, COX-2, and pro-inflammatory cytokine production. This activity is more consistently demonstrated in vivo than pure antioxidant effects and likely accounts for much of the health benefit associated with polyphenol-rich diets.

**Cardiovascular effects**: Epidemiological evidence consistently associates polyphenol-rich diets with reduced cardiovascular risk. Mechanisms include improved endothelial function, reduced platelet aggregation, and anti-inflammatory effects.

## The bioavailability challenge

Most dietary polyphenols have low oral [bioavailability](bioavailability.md). They are extensively metabolized by intestinal and hepatic enzymes and by the gut microbiome. The compounds that reach systemic circulation are often metabolites rather than the parent compound. This means the therapeutic effects of polyphenol-rich foods and herbs may be mediated by metabolites rather than the compounds measured in vitro — a major challenge for translational research.

## See also

- [Resveratrol](resveratrol.md) — a stilbenoid polyphenol from Japanese knotweed
