- [Emodin](emodin.md) — an anthraquinone polyphenol from Japanese knotweed
- [Phytoalexin](phytoalexin.md) — stress-induced compounds, often polyphenolic
- [Bioavailability](bioavailability.md) — the central challenge for polyphenol pharmacology

records.name: Post-exertional malaise
records.description: Disproportionate worsening of physical, cognitive, orthostatic, or emotional symptoms following exertion, characteristically delayed 12–72 hours and lasting days to weeks, distinguishing myalgic encephalomyelitis from fatigue, deconditioning, and normal muscle soreness.

stussman2020.title: Characterizing the Experience of Post-Exertional Malaise in Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome: A Qualitative Analysis

records.body:
Post-exertional malaise is the cardinal feature of myalgic encephalomyelitis: a disproportionate worsening of symptoms following physical, cognitive, orthostatic, or emotional exertion. What makes post-exertional malaise distinct from ordinary fatigue, from deconditioning, and from normal delayed-onset muscle soreness is a combination of three features: the severity of the symptom worsening relative to the exertion that triggered it, the characteristic delay of 12 to 72 hours before onset, and the prolonged duration of the flare — typically lasting days to weeks rather than hours. A person with myalgic encephalomyelitis may undertake a modest physical task — a short walk, light housekeeping — that produces no immediate symptoms, then develop profound fatigue, cognitive fog, pain, and autonomic symptoms 24 or 48 hours later that persist for a week or longer. The same task, in a person with ordinary deconditioning or fatigue, either produces immediate symptoms proportional to the effort or produces muscle soreness that resolves within one to three days.

The mechanism of the delay remains unclear but is likely related to the metabolic and immunoinflammatory dysfunction of the illness. Exertion in the absence of adequate aerobic capacity and adequate glucocorticoid-driven substrate mobilization appears to trigger a surge of immune activation — cytokine release from primed microglia and mast cells, reactive oxygen species accumulation, and neuroinflammatory activation — that unfolds over hours rather than minutes and persists for days or weeks. The delayed and prolonged character of this response distinguishes it from the acute inflammatory response to muscle injury, which peaks within 24–48 hours and begins to resolve. Qualitative studies of post-exertional malaise, such as Stussman and colleagues' work, consistently describe patients' characterization of the phenomenon as a "crash" — an abrupt and severe worsening of baseline function that comes on after a symptom-free interval.

For research and clinical assessment, the critical consequence is that a single session's performance — a functional capacity evaluation, a single day of exercise testing, a one-time assessment of activity tolerance — cannot establish a patient's true capacity or characterize their exercise intolerance. Because the response is delayed and sustained, the patient may appear to perform normally on the day of testing and only manifest the deterioration days later, when the clinician or researcher is no longer observing. This is precisely why the two-day cardiopulmonary exercise test, which probes for the characteristic reduced performance on day two, is more informative than a single-day test: the delayed response signature of post-exertional malaise is visible in the test-retest comparison but not in the first-day values.

For clinical management, the existence of post-exertional malaise means that "graded exercise" — steady progressive increases in activity regardless of symptom response — risks repeatedly triggering the flare response, which may then consolidate rather than resolve if the patient continues to exceed their actual aerobic capacity. The alternative framework, activity pacing to stay within an individual energy envelope and avoid triggering malaise, is mechanistically more aligned with the pathophysiology, though its evidence base remains limited.

## Related terms

- Myalgic encephalomyelitis — the illness of which post-exertional malaise is the defining feature
- Two-day cardiopulmonary exercise testing — the objective assessment tool designed to capture post-exertional malaise in controlled conditions
- Pacing — an activity management strategy explicitly designed to prevent triggering post-exertional malaise
- Allostatic load — the framework of cumulative physiological cost that may underlie the prolonged symptom flare
- Dysautonomia — a frequently concurrent symptom cluster whose exertion-intolerance may be distinct from post-exertional malaise or amplified by it

records.name: Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome
records.description: An autonomic disorder characterized by a sustained heart-rate increase of at least 30 bpm within 10 minutes of standing (40 bpm in adolescents), without orthostatic hypotension, and associated with chronic symptoms of dizziness, palpitations, fatigue, and cognitive impairment.
records.body:
Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome is an autonomic disorder characterized by an excessive increase in heart rate upon assuming an upright posture: a sustained heart-rate increase of at least 30 beats per minute within the first 10 minutes of standing or head-up tilt testing (40 beats per minute in adolescents), occurring without the orthostatic hypotension that defines orthostatic intolerance's most common form, the blood-pressure drop upon standing. The tachycardia is accompanied by characteristic symptoms: dizziness, lightheadedness, palpitations, chest discomfort, tremor, anxiety, fatigue, and cognitive impairment (sometimes called "brain fog"), with symptoms typically worsening upon prolonged standing or in warm environments, and improvement with supine posture or lying down. POTS is far more common in women than men, and has a typical onset in adolescence or early adulthood, though it can emerge at any age.

The diagnostic measurement is standardized: a 5–10 minute supine baseline heart rate and blood pressure, followed by active standing or head-up tilt to 60–80 degrees, with continuous heart rate and blood pressure monitoring for 10–20 minutes. The diagnosis requires sustained tachycardia (≥30 bpm increase, or ≥120 bpm standing if baseline is normal) without a concurrent ≥20 mmHg drop in systolic blood pressure. An incidental clinic pulse rate cannot establish or exclude POTS; the diagnosis requires the formal tilt-table or standing test.

POTS presents with three proposed mechanistic subtypes, though these are not cleanly separable and a given individual may show features of more than one. The neuropathic form shows reduced sudomotor and vasomotor function, implying denervation of distal sympathetic fibers; the hyperadrenergic form shows elevated plasma catecholamines at rest or upon standing, suggesting excessive sympathetic outflow; the hypovolemic form shows reduced plasma volume and exaggerated fluid shifts upon tilting. Some patients cannot be categorized into these subtypes (dysautonomic POTS), and the clinical utility of the distinction remains limited. The distinction from inappropriate sinus tachycardia — persistent elevated resting heart rate (>100 bpm) that worsens with minimal exertion — is important: POTS is provoked by postural change and improving with supine rest, while inappropriate sinus tachycardia is resting and exertional, and the two have different management approaches.

POTS frequently co-occurs with myalgic encephalomyelitis, with reported prevalence estimates ranging from 20% to 80% depending on how myalgic encephalomyelitis is defined and how POTS is tested. The relationship between the two conditions is not established as causal in either direction. POTS might be part of the autonomic dysregulation spectrum of myalgic encephalomyelitis, in which case the same underlying pathophysiology (sympathoadrenal-HPA decoupling and reduced glucocorticoid-driven vascular support) would contribute to both conditions. Alternatively, POTS and myalgic encephalomyelitis might be separable conditions that frequently co-occur in some populations, or POTS might in some cases be secondary to the deconditioning imposed by myalgic encephalomyelitis-related exercise intolerance. Disentangling this relationship is an open research question.

For clinical assessment, the consequence is that orthostatic intolerance or tachycardia in a patient with myalgic encephalomyelitis should be formally evaluated with tilt-table testing or standardized standing testing rather than inferred from symptoms. The test itself carries some burden in patients with myalgic encephalomyelitis, as the exertional demand of the test can trigger post-exertional malaise, which is why informed consent and follow-up support are essential.

## Related terms

- Orthostatic intolerance — the symptom POTS produces, and the broader category of dysfunctional blood-pressure and heart-rate responses to postural change
- Orthostatic hypotension — the blood-pressure-drop form of orthostatic intolerance, from which POTS is distinguished by its absence
- Sympathoadrenal system — the autonomic arm whose excessive or dysregulated output appears to drive POTS
- Hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis — the axis whose impaired function may reduce the vascular support needed to compensate for sympathetic tachycardia
- Myalgic encephalomyelitis — the illness with which POTS frequently co-occurs, though causality is unclear
- Dysautonomia — the broader autonomic dysfunction category of which POTS is a specific, measurable form
- Cerebral hypoperfusion — a proposed mechanism for the cognitive symptoms in POTS and their worsening with standing

records.name: Practitioner
records.description: A person attuned in one or more levels of Reiki training who practices energy healing through touch or proximity
records.body:
A **Reiki practitioner** is a person who has received attunement in one or more levels of [Reiki](./reiki.md) training and practices energy healing through touch or proximity.

Practitioners are categorized by degree:
- **Level 1 (Shoden)** — the practitioner can perform hands-on healing on themselves and others, using a standard set of hand positions
- **Level 2 (Okuden)** — the practitioner learns symbols that are used to focus intention and can perform distance healing (sending energy to someone not physically present)
- **Level 3 / Master (Shinpiden)** — the practitioner can perform attunements on others, initiating new practitioners into the practice

The training model is lineage-based: each practitioner traces their attunement through a chain of masters back to Mikao Usui. This lineage structure is significant within the tradition because attunement is understood not as the acquisition of a skill but as the activation of a capacity — the master does not teach the student to generate energy but opens a channel through which energy flows.

In practice, reiki practitioners work in a wide range of settings: private practice, integrative medicine clinics, hospice and palliative care, wellness centers, and personal self-care. The practice requires no specialized equipment — only the practitioner's hands and attention.

records.name: Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder
records.description: A DSM-5 diagnosis of cyclical affective and physical symptoms confined to the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle, whose abrupt onset is experimentally tied to withdrawal from, rather than the absolute level of, ovarian steroids in people with a prior history of the syndrome.

schmidt1998.title: Differential Behavioral Effects of Gonadal Steroids in Women with and in Those without Premenstrual Syndrome

records.body:
Premenstrual dysphoric disorder is a DSM-5 diagnosis requiring at least five of eleven characteristic symptoms present in most menstrual cycles over the preceding year, at least one of which must be a core affective symptom: marked affective lability, marked irritability or anger or increased interpersonal conflict, markedly depressed mood, or marked anxiety and tension. Onset is specifically in the week before menses, with improvement within a few days after the onset of menses and symptoms absent or minimal in the week following menses; the symptoms must cause clinically significant distress or impairment. Irritability is repeatedly described, across independent secondary descriptions of the diagnostic criteria, as the single most commonly reported primary symptom. This criteria summary is standard nosology, cross-checked against multiple independent descriptions rather than a research claim requiring the usual primary-study verification.

What distinguishes premenstrual dysphoric disorder's abrupt, cyclical onset from a general model of hormone-driven mood change is that the trigger is withdrawal from — the change in — ovarian steroid levels, not their absolute level, and this trigger operates only in people with a prior history of the syndrome. Schmidt and colleagues' randomized, placebo-controlled study, published under the pre-DSM label "premenstrual syndrome" that the PMDD diagnostic literature descends from, gave the GnRH agonist leuprolide or placebo to 20 women with premenstrual syndrome and to comparison women without it. Ten of the premenstrual-syndrome women whose symptoms improved on leuprolide, plus 5 further premenstrual-syndrome women and 15 women without the syndrome, then entered a double-blind, crossover add-back phase receiving estradiol and progesterone, each for four weeks, during continued leuprolide administration. The 10 women given leuprolide showed a significant symptom decrease versus both their own baseline and the 10 comparison women given placebo; during hormone add-back, this same group had a significant recurrence of symptoms, while no mood changes occurred in either the 15 women without the syndrome or the 5 premenstrual-syndrome women given placebo hormone during continued leuprolide. Recurrence, in other words, tracked the change in steroid level and required a prior history of the syndrome — not a specific hormone and not an abnormal absolute level. The authors' own conclusion, quoted directly: "In women with premenstrual syndrome, the occurrence of symptoms represents an abnormal response to normal hormonal changes."

The consequence for research design is that this evidence supports an abnormal individual response to a normal, cyclical hormonal transition — not a general model in which hormone change itself produces mood switching in anyone exposed to it, and not evidence about non-cyclical or male populations. A study that treats hormone withdrawal as a general mechanism for affective switching outside this specific reproductive-axis, cyclical, female-specific context extrapolates beyond what the Schmidt and colleagues design established: women without the syndrome given the same leuprolide-and-add-back protocol showed no mood changes at all, so the finding is specifically about a prior-history-dependent vulnerability to change in ovarian steroid level, not a property of the hormones themselves. The original 1998 report available for this entry states these comparisons only as "significant," without exact effect sizes or p-values, which should be sought from the full text before this finding is used to support a specific quantitative claim; later replications have been referenced in the literature but were not independently read for this entry.

records.name: Preoxygenation
records.description: The preparation phase before airway instrumentation that maximizes oxygen reserves in functional residual capacity, extending safe apnea time and reducing desaturation risk during intubation.
records.body:
**Preoxygenation** is the preparation phase before airway instrumentation intended to maximize the body's oxygen reserves, extending the safe duration of apnea and reducing the risk of rapid desaturation during intubation attempts.

The physiological principle is straightforward. The lungs' functional residual capacity (FRC) — the volume of gas remaining at the end of a normal breath — serves as an oxygen reservoir during apnea. On room air (21% oxygen), FRC contains relatively little oxygen. By breathing 100% oxygen for 3-5 minutes (or taking 8 vital-capacity breaths of 100% oxygen), the patient replaces nitrogen in FRC with oxygen, dramatically increasing the available reservoir.

In a healthy adult, adequate preoxygenation can extend the safe apnea time from approximately 1 minute (on room air) to 6-8 minutes. This window allows a clinician to attempt laryngoscopy, reposition, and reattempt if the first pass fails — without the patient desaturating to dangerous levels.

Preoxygenation is less effective — and more critical — in populations with reduced reserves:

- **Pediatric patients** — smaller FRC relative to metabolic rate, faster oxygen consumption, shorter safe apnea times
- **Obese patients** — reduced FRC from abdominal compression, increased oxygen consumption, rapid desaturation
- **Pregnant patients** — reduced FRC and increased metabolic demand
- **Critically ill patients** — shunt physiology, increased metabolic demand, limited response to supplemental oxygen

Techniques include:

- **Tight-fitting non-rebreather mask at high flow** — standard approach for cooperative patients
- **Bag-valve-mask with PEEP valve** — recruits collapsed alveoli and improves FRC
- **Apneic oxygenation** — high-flow nasal cannula continued during laryngoscopy, providing passive oxygen flow during apnea
- **Patient positioning** — head-up or ramped positioning improves FRC, particularly in obese patients

Preoxygenation is not optional. It is the single most important preparation step before any planned airway intervention. A failed first intubation attempt in a well-preoxygenated patient is manageable. A failed first attempt in an inadequately preoxygenated patient may become a [CICO](./cannot-intubate-cannot-oxygenate.md) emergency.

## Related terms

- [Oxygenation](./oxygenation.md) — the process that preoxygenation supports
- [CICO](./cannot-intubate-cannot-oxygenate.md) — the emergency adequate preoxygenation helps prevent
- [Airway](./airway.md) — the passage being instrumented

records.name: Pretest Probability
records.description: The estimated likelihood of a condition being present before a diagnostic test result is known, grounding clinical interpretation in Bayesian reasoning
records.body:
**Pretest probability** is the estimated likelihood of a condition being present before a diagnostic test result is known. It is one of the most important concepts in clinical reasoning — and one of the most frequently violated in informal medical education.

The concept comes from Bayesian reasoning. A test result does not tell you whether a patient has a disease. It tells you how much to update your estimate of the probability that the patient has the disease, given what you already knew before the test. A positive troponin in a patient with crushing chest pain, diaphoresis, and ST-elevation on ECG means something very different from a positive troponin in a young, healthy patient with atypical symptoms and a normal ECG. The test is the same; the pretest probability is different; the clinical meaning is different.

In [FOAM](./foam.md) contexts, pretest probability serves as a cognitive anchor against two common reasoning errors:

- **Availability bias** — overestimating the likelihood of dramatic or memorable diagnoses because FOAM content disproportionately features unusual cases. A podcast episode on a rare cause of chest pain can shift a listener's mental model such that they start considering that diagnosis more often than its actual prevalence warrants. Pretest probability reminds the clinician to ask: how likely is this diagnosis in my patient population, regardless of how vivid the teaching case was?

- **Base-rate neglect** — ignoring the frequency of a condition in the relevant population when interpreting a test result. FOAM content sometimes emphasizes the sensitivity or specificity of a test without discussing the population in which the test is being applied. A highly sensitive test applied to a low-prevalence population generates many false positives — a fact that pretest probability makes explicit.

Pretest probability is not a number that clinicians calculate precisely in most clinical encounters. It is a disciplined habit of thought: before ordering a test, before interpreting a result, before acting on a [FOAMed](./foamed.md) recommendation — ask how likely this diagnosis was before the new information arrived. That estimate shapes what the new information means.

## Related terms

- [Critical Appraisal](./critical-appraisal.md) — the broader discipline of evaluating evidence quality
- [FOAM](./foam.md) — the context in which pretest probability anchors interpretation

records.name: Proprioception
records.description: The sense of body position, movement, and effort — the nervous system's spatial model of itself.

cites: The Integrative Action of the Nervous System
The Man Who Mistook His Wife for a Hat

sherrington1906.title: The Integrative Action of the Nervous System

sacks1985.title: The Man Who Mistook His Wife for a Hat

records.body:
Proprioception is the sense of body position, movement, and effort.
It tells you where your limbs are without looking, how much force you're exerting without measuring, and whether you're upright without checking.
[Charles Scott Sherrington](../../../../../../../../../../../information-science-services-section/services/knowledge-services-section/services/research-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/charles-scott-sherrington.md) coined the term in 1906, combining the Latin *proprius* (one's own) with *-ception* (perception), to name the sensory system by which an organism perceives itself [@sherrington1906].

Proprioception operates through mechanoreceptors distributed throughout muscles, tendons, joint capsules, and fascia.
Muscle spindles detect changes in muscle length and velocity.
Golgi tendon organs detect changes in tension.
Joint receptors detect position and pressure.
Together, these receptors generate a continuous stream of data about the body's spatial configuration — data that the central nervous system integrates into what amounts to a real-time kinematic model.

## How proprioception works

### Peripheral receptors

Three classes of receptor do the primary work:

**Muscle spindles** are stretch-sensitive receptors embedded within skeletal muscle fibers.
They fire in proportion to muscle length and the rate of length change.
When a muscle stretches, its spindles increase their firing rate; when it contracts, they decrease.
This dual sensitivity to position and velocity makes spindles the primary source of dynamic proprioceptive information — they tell the nervous system not just where a limb is but how fast it's moving.

**Golgi tendon organs (GTOs)** sit at the junction between muscle and tendon.
They respond to changes in tension — whether from active contraction or passive loading.
GTOs provide the effort dimension of proprioception: how hard the muscle is working, not just where it is.

**Joint receptors** respond to joint angle, pressure, and extreme positions.
They're most potential at the limits of range of motion, where they contribute to the protective reflexes that prevent hyperextension and dislocation.

### Central integration

Peripheral signals converge on the somatosensory cortex, cerebellum, and brainstem.
The cerebellum integrates proprioceptive input with motor commands to calibrate movement in real time — it's the comparator between intended and actual movement.
The somatosensory cortex maintains the body's spatial map: the felt sense of body shape, size, and position that persists even in the dark.

This central integration is plastic.
Proprioceptive acuity changes with training, injury, and disuse.
Musicians and dancers develop finer proprioceptive resolution in their hands and feet than the general population — not because their receptors are different, but because their cortical maps are more detailed [@bear2015].

### Vestibular interaction

Proprioception doesn't operate in isolation.
The vestibular system — the semicircular canals and otolith organs of the inner ear — provides information about head orientation and angular acceleration.
The brain integrates vestibular input with proprioceptive and visual signals to maintain balance, spatial orientation, and a stable sense of "which way is up."

This integration matters for somatic practice because many movement lessons deliberately alter the relationship between proprioceptive and vestibular input.
[Moshe Feldenkrais](../../../../../../../../../../../information-science-services-section/services/knowledge-services-section/services/research-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/moshe-feldenkrais.md)' lessons frequently involve rolling, turning, and changing orientation relative to gravity.
These movements force the nervous system to recalibrate the relationship between what the proprioceptors report about body configuration and what the vestibular system reports about spatial orientation — producing a more adaptable and accurate composite body-sense.

## Proprioceptive dysfunction

When proprioception degrades, the consequences are immediate and disabling.
[Oliver Sacks](../../../../../../../../../../../information-science-services-section/services/knowledge-services-section/services/research-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/oliver-sacks.md) documented the case of "the disembodied woman" — a patient who lost proprioception through peripheral neuropathy and had to watch her own body constantly to know where it was [@sacks1985].
Without proprioception, even standing requires visual monitoring; walking becomes a deliberate, effortful calculation rather than an automatic process.

Less dramatic but more common is the proprioceptive degradation that accompanies chronic pain, aging, and disuse.
When a joint is injured, the surrounding proprioceptive receptors are damaged or desensitized.
The nervous system compensates with altered movement patterns — guarding, limping, bracing — that become habitual even after the tissue heals.
This is one pathway into what [Thomas Hanna](../../../../../../../../../../../information-science-services-section/services/knowledge-services-section/services/research-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/thomas-hanna.md) called sensory-motor amnesia: the proprioceptive signal degrades, the cortex stops monitoring the area, and the compensatory pattern becomes invisible to the person producing it.

## Proprioception in somatic practice

Somatic practices treat proprioception as trainable.
[Moshe Feldenkrais](../../../../../../../../../../../information-science-services-section/services/knowledge-services-section/services/research-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/moshe-feldenkrais.md) designed his Awareness Through Movement lessons around a principle from psychophysics: the Weber-Fechner law, which states that the ability to detect a change in a stimulus is proportional to the magnitude of the stimulus [@feldenkrais1972].
If you're carrying a heavy load, you can't feel the addition of a small weight.
If you're carrying nothing, you can feel the addition of a feather.

Applied to movement: if you're exerting great effort, you can't detect small differences in position or tension.
If you reduce effort to near-zero, your proprioceptive resolution increases.
This is why Feldenkrais lessons use slow, small, gentle movements — not to protect the body but to increase the signal-to-noise ratio in proprioceptive input.
The goal is cortical: create conditions under which the brain can build a more detailed motor-sensory map.

## Proprioception and the stability framework

The [neurophysiological embodiment of information-theoretic stability](../../../../../../../neuroscience-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/neurophysiological-embodiment-of-information-theoretic-stability.md) describes the nervous system as minimizing divergence between predicted and actual sensory states.
Proprioception contributes the motor-spatial terms in this process: the brain predicts where the body will be after issuing a motor command, and proprioceptive feedback provides the error signal — the difference between predicted and actual position.
The cerebellum computes this prediction error in real time, adjusting motor output to minimize it.

When proprioceptive input degrades — through injury, disuse, or sensory-motor amnesia — the prediction-error signal becomes noisy.
The system can still function, but with less precision and more compensatory effort.
Somatic practices that sharpen proprioceptive acuity improve the quality of this error signal, allowing the nervous system to operate closer to its stability manifold with less metabolic and attentional cost.

## Related concepts

- [Somatic Awareness](./somatic-awareness.md) — the broader capacity that proprioception feeds into
- [Interoception](./interoception.md) — the complementary sense of internal physiological state
- [Tensegrity in Movement](./tensegrity-in-movement.md) — the structural model that proprioception monitors and modulates

## Sources

- Sherrington, C.S. (1906).
  *The Integrative Action of the Nervous System.*
  Yale University Press [@sherrington1906].
- Bear, M.F., Connors, B.W., & Paradiso, M.A. (2015).
  *Neuroscience: Exploring the Brain.*
  4th ed. Wolters Kluwer [@bear2015].
- Sacks, O.
  (1985).
  *The Man Who Mistook His Wife for a Hat.*
  Summit Books [@sacks1985].
- Feldenkrais, M.
  (1972).
  *Awareness Through Movement.*
  Harper & Row [@feldenkrais1972].

records.name: Psychomotor Agitation
records.description: A nonspecific excess of restless motor activity accompanying mental tension, tracked separately across medication-activation, hypoglycemic, and mood-episode contexts, and readily confounded with drug-induced akathisia unless separately assessed.

amitai2015.title: SSRI-Induced Activation Syndrome in Children and Adolescents — What Is Next?

records.body:
Psychomotor agitation is excessive, non-goal-directed motor activity — pacing, restlessness, an inability to remain still — that accompanies mental tension and is tracked as a named, separate symptom across several distinct clinical contexts. The U.S. FDA's black-box warning language for antidepressants, issued in 2004, lists anxiety, agitation, panic attacks, insomnia, irritability, hostility, aggressiveness, impulsivity, akathisia, hypomania, and mania as reported symptoms following antidepressant initiation (regulatory text reported here as characterized by search results for this entry, not independently re-fetched from FDA.gov). The clinical literature groups much of this presentation under the label "activation syndrome" (Amitai et al. 2015), most documented in children and adolescents and most concentrated in the early weeks of treatment or after a dose change. Agitation is also part of the neuroglycopenic symptom cluster of hypoglycemia, in which brain glucose deprivation produces confusion, difficulty concentrating, irritability, and a combative or agitated presentation sometimes mistaken for intoxication — a cluster distinguished, in standard endocrinology teaching, from the earlier-warning autonomic symptoms of hypoglycemia (sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger) that are mediated by catecholamine and cholinergic release rather than by glucose deprivation of the brain itself.

The FDA's own black-box list is itself evidence for the distinction this term exists to hold: it names "agitation" and "akathisia" as separate items in the same symptom list, rather than treating one as a subtype of the other. Crowner and colleagues' 1990 observational study makes the same distinction operational: a closed-circuit television camera was installed in each corner of the dayroom of a locked unit for violent psychiatric patients, and incidents of assault, together with the five minutes preceding each one, were recorded on videotape; all parties present were then rated specifically for akathisia's motor component, separately from any global judgment of how agitated the ward was. Psychomotor agitation is the nonspecific clinical sign — motor restlessness from any cause, including the underlying psychiatric illness itself — while akathisia is a specific, drug-induced motor state that can produce or mimic that sign and can be rated as its own variable, as Crowner and colleagues did.

The clinical and research consequence is that psychomotor agitation is a nonspecific sign that cannot be attributed to illness severity, or to any single mechanism, without first considering reversible medical causes and medication effects. The hypoglycemic neuroglycopenic pattern is reported in standard clinical teaching as an established pattern, but no primary study located for this entry gives a specific numeric prevalence of irritability or agitation as a hypoglycemia symptom; it remains, nonetheless, a reversible cause to exclude before agitation is read as psychiatric. And because a specific, ratable motor state — akathisia — can itself produce or be mistaken for agitation, an assessment or research design that records "agitation" as one undifferentiated sign, without separately rating for akathisia's motor component, risks treating a medication effect as evidence of worsening illness.

records.name: Psychomotor Retardation
records.description: A clinically and instrumentally measurable slowing of movement and speech occurring in depressive illness, distinguished from subjective slowness by objective actigraphic, kinematic, and ground-reaction-force correlates, and only inconsistently predictive of antidepressant response depending on drug class.

bennabi2013.title: Psychomotor Retardation in Depression: A Systematic Review of Diagnostic, Pathophysiologic, and Therapeutic Implications

bennabi2020.title: Psychomotor Retardation and the prognosis of antidepressant treatment in patients with unipolar Psychotic Depression

treadway2011.title: Reconsidering anhedonia in depression: Lessons from translational neuroscience

records.body:
Psychomotor retardation is an objectively measurable slowing of movement and speech that occurs in depressive illness, distinct from a patient's subjective report of feeling slowed down. Per Bennabi and colleagues' systematic review, which synthesizes a large body of prior work (the review's own methods describe drawing on 116 papers, a scope reported by the review itself rather than independently re-derived from its full text for this entry), psychomotor abnormalities in depressed patients have been instrumented with actigraphy (wrist-worn accelerometry of spontaneous movement), cinematographic and kinematic analysis of movement, and ground-reaction-force platforms measuring gait and posture, in addition to the retardation subscales carried by standard clinician-rated depression scales. The review explicitly notes the field's lack of one standardized measurement approach across these methods: actigraphic counts, kinematic movement-time parameters, and force-platform indices are not interchangeable operationalizations of the same underlying slowing, and a study reporting "psychomotor retardation" without naming its measurement method is reporting one of several only loosely comparable things.

The review associates psychomotor retardation with abnormalities of prefrontal cortex function and of dopaminergic transmission specifically — a synthesis claim of the review, not a single controlled study demonstrating a causal prefrontal-dopamine-to-retardation chain. This places psychomotor retardation in the same neighborhood as, but not the same construct as, motivational anergia: the reduced willingness to exert effort for reward that is operationalized behaviorally by effort-discounting tasks such as the Effort Expenditure for Rewards Task, and argued by Treadway and Zald's reconsideration of anhedonia to be dissociable from consummatory pleasure and traceable to the same mesolimbic dopamine literature. Psychomotor retardation is a directly observed or instrumented slowing of actual movement and speech; motivational anergia is an effort-allocation computation inferred from choice behavior on a task. The two are read against the same accumbens-dopamine and prefrontal literature and plausibly share mechanism, but psychomotor retardation is not itself measured by, and does not reduce to, an effort-discounting task.

The consequence for research design is that treatment-response evidence for psychomotor retardation is genuinely mixed rather than settled, and should be reported as such rather than smoothed into one rule. In a cohort of 122 patients with unipolar psychotic depression, presence of psychomotor retardation at baseline predicted lower remission rates and greater persistence of delusions; baseline prevalence was 73%, falling to 35% after six weeks of treatment (Bennabi et al. 2020). Yet a more recent secondary analysis pooling nine randomized controlled trials states, in its own framing, that it remains unclear whether psychomotor retardation is independently associated with poorer prognosis — the authors of the largest pooled analysis located for this entry do not claim a settled answer. The 2013 review additionally reports a split by drug class: baseline retardation predicted response to milnacipran, a serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor, in at least one cited trial, while similarly designed studies found psychomotor retardation did not predict response to SSRIs. A research design that treats "psychomotor retardation predicts poor antidepressant response" as one general, drug-class-independent finding is not supported by this literature; a study should specify measurement method and antidepressant class before drawing a prognostic claim from baseline retardation.

records.name: Qi
records.description: The circulating operational force in TCM that transforms, transports, protects, and warms — naming what the body does when alive and active

kaptchuk2000.title: The Web That Has No Weaver: Understanding Chinese Medicine

sivin1987.title: Traditional Medicine in Contemporary China
sivin1987.publisher: Center for Chinese Studies, University of Michigan

unschuld2003.title: Huang Di Nei Jing Su Wen: Nature, Knowledge, Imagery in an Ancient Chinese Medical Text

records.body:
Qi (氣) is the second of the [Three Treasures](./san-bao.md) in [traditional Chinese medicine](traditional-chinese-medicine.md). It names the circulating operational force — the activity that transforms, transports, protects, and warms.

The character 氣 originally referred to vapor or breath and carries connotations of movement and transformation. In TCM, Qi is not a substance in the Western sense but a functional concept: it is what a body does when it is alive and active. Digestion is Qi at work. Circulation is Qi at work. The immune defense mounted against a pathogen is Qi at work. When TCM says "Qi flows," it means the body's functional activities are proceeding — not that an invisible fluid is moving through tubes [@kaptchuk2000].

TCM describes several functional varieties of Qi. Yuan Qi (original Qi) derives from prenatal [Jing](./jing.md) and drives basic physiological processes. Gu Qi (grain Qi) is extracted from food by the Spleen and Stomach. Zong Qi (gathering Qi) accumulates in the chest and drives respiration and circulation. Wei Qi (defensive Qi) circulates at the body's surface and protects against external pathogenic factors. These are not different substances but different functional roles of the same operational principle [@unschuld2003].

Qi circulates through the meridian system (jing luo 經絡), which connects the body's organ-function systems to each other and to the surface. When Qi flows smoothly, functions proceed. When Qi stagnates, functions falter — and stagnation manifests as pain, distension, emotional frustration, or digestive difficulty. When Qi is deficient, the body lacks the operational force to maintain its activities: fatigue, weakness, susceptibility to illness.

Nathan Sivin noted that translating Qi as "energy" is misleading if it implies a measurable physical quantity [@sivin1987]. Qi is closer to a verb than a noun — it names what the body is doing rather than what the body has. The clinical question is not "how much Qi does this patient have?" but "is this patient's Qi flowing, stagnating, rising when it should descend, or scattering when it should consolidate?"

For information systems, Qi corresponds to operational activity: data flowing through pipelines, queries executing, APIs responding, processes running. A system with Qi is a system whose operations are proceeding. The question TCM's vocabulary raises is whether operational activity — data circulating, queries returning results, reasoners deriving new triples — is sufficient for a system to be alive in any meaningful sense. A system can have abundant Qi and no [Shen](./shen.md): it operates but does not reflect. It processes but does not adapt. It runs but does not learn.

## Related terms

- [Jing](./jing.md) — stored substrate, the material Qi draws upon
- [Shen](./shen.md) — reflective awareness, the capacity Qi alone does not provide
- [San Bao](./san-bao.md) — the Three Treasures as a diagnostic system
- [Cybernetic feedback](../../../../../../../../../../../information-science-services-section/services/cybernetics-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/cybernetic-feedback.md) — the mechanism through which operational activity self-regulates

records.name: qi qing
records.description: 七情 — the Seven Affects (joy, anger, worry, pensiveness, grief, fear, fright), TCM's internal causes of disease, each assigned to a Zang organ and pathogenic only when excessive, prolonged, or suppressed
records.body:
Qi Qing (七情, the Seven Affects) are Traditional Chinese Medicine's category of internal (as opposed to external or dietary) causes of disease: joy (喜, xi), anger (怒, nu), worry (憂, you), pensiveness (思, si), grief (悲, bei), fear (恐, kong), and fright (驚, jing). Each affect is associated with a specific Zang organ and a characteristic direction of effect on Qi, and each becomes pathogenic not by occurring — normal emotional response is not disease — but by being excessive, prolonged, or chronically suppressed.

## Classical basis

Individual emotion-organ correspondences appear scattered through the *Huang Di Nei Jing*, most systematically in *Su Wen* Chapter 5, 陰陽應象大論 (*Yin Yang Ying Xiang Da Lun*), which embeds each affect within the Five Phase correspondence tables — for instance "在志為思，思傷脾，怒勝思" (in the emotions [Earth] is Pensiveness; Pensiveness injures the Spleen; Anger overcomes Pensiveness), giving each affect both an organ target and a place in the Five Phase restraining cycle. The systematic collection and formalization of the seven affects specifically as a category of internal causation, distinguished from external and dietary causes, is credited to the Song-dynasty physician Chen Yan (陳言, courtesy name Wuze, 陳無擇) in his *San Yin Ji Yi Bing Zheng Fang Lun* (《三因極一病證方論》, c. 1174 CE, "Treatise on the Three Categories of Causes, Symptoms, and Formulas Extending to Unity"). Chen Yan's tripartite etiology divides all disease causation into external causes (外因, the Six Excesses of wind, cold, heat, dampness, dryness, and summer heat), internal causes (內因, the seven affects), and causes neither internal nor external (不內外因, such as dietary irregularity or parasitic damage) — establishing the seven affects as medicine's first systematically named internal-cause category.

## The seven affects and their organs

| Affect | Character | Organ | Effect on Qi |
|---|---|---|---|
| Joy | 喜 (xi) | Heart | Slows and scatters Qi |
| Anger | 怒 (nu) | Liver | Makes Qi rise |
| Worry | 憂 (you) | Lung | Knots and depletes Qi |
| Pensiveness | 思 (si) | Spleen | Knots Qi |
| Grief | 悲 (bei) | Lung | Dissolves Qi |
| Fear | 恐 (kong) | Kidney | Makes Qi descend |
| Fright | 驚 (jing) | Heart/Kidney | Scatters Qi |

Worry and grief are both assigned to the Lung but are classically distinguished — worry as a knotting, anxious anticipation, grief as a dissolving, depleting sorrow — even though they share an organ target and their clinical presentations (chest tightness, shallow breathing, fatigue for worry; shortness of breath, weak voice, pale complexion for grief) overlap considerably.

## The pathogenicity criterion

The seven affects' defining clinical principle is that emotion itself is not disease. Anger felt and expressed appropriately is a normal physiological response; anger that is chronic, suppressed, or grossly disproportionate produces the pathological pattern of Liver Qi stagnation. Grief appropriate to genuine loss is a normal process; grief that remains prolonged and unresolved depletes Lung Qi and produces chronic fatigue and immune vulnerability. This criterion — magnitude, duration, and whether the affect is expressed or bottled — rather than the mere presence of feeling, is what makes the seven affects a medical category rather than a moral judgment about emotional life.

## Clinical significance

Because each affect targets a specific organ, a patient's emotional history is, in TCM diagnostic practice, direct clinical data pointing toward which organ system is likely disturbed — chronic unresolved anger toward Liver patterns, chronic anxious rumination toward Spleen patterns, chronic unprocessed fear toward Kidney patterns. This is not a claim that emotion is the only or even the primary cause of any given organ pattern (diet, overwork, and external pathogenic factors all contribute independently), but the seven affects give TCM a structured way to ask about a patient's emotional life as part of the same diagnostic inquiry used to ask about digestion, sleep, and pain — rather than treating psychological history as a separate domain outside the medical interview.

## Biomedical convergence, honestly graded

The seven affects' organizing principle — that the pathogenic ingredient is duration and suppression, not the emotion's mere occurrence — resonates with the psychoneuroimmunological finding that chronic, unresolved stress states (not acute emotional response) drive the sustained sympathetic and inflammatory signaling documented in the modern social-genomics literature (the Conserved Transcriptional Response to Adversity, chronic social-defeat paradigms in animal models, and related work). That resonance is at the level of a shared clinical principle — chronicity and non-resolution matter more than acute intensity — and does not extend, on current evidence, to the specific organ assignments: biomedicine has not established that worry-predominant chronic stress produces a Spleen-congruent physiological signature distinguishable from anger-predominant or fear-predominant chronic stress (see Hypothesis 3 in "Marrow, Spleen, and the Transport of Substances" for a concrete, falsifiable version of this open question). The seven affects' organ-specificity is a testable hypothesis that current biomedical research is positioned to examine, not yet a confirmed finding.

records.name: Qi Stagnation
records.description: 气滞 (qi zhi) — the condition where Qi flow is impeded or stuck, producing distension, pain that moves, emotional frustration, and sighing — the most common excess pattern in clinical TCM practice

kaptchuk2000.title: The Web That Has No Weaver

records.body:
Qi stagnation (qi zhi 气滞) is the condition where [Qi](qi.md) flow through the body's [meridians](meridians.md) and [organ-function systems](zang-fu.md) is impeded, slowed, or stuck.
It is the most common excess pattern in clinical TCM practice — the default pathological response to emotional constraint, chronic stress, and sedentary modern life.

The concept follows directly from TCM's understanding of Qi as circulating operational force.
Qi should flow: smoothly, in the correct direction, through every organ system and meridian.
When flow is impeded, the Qi "stagnates" — it accumulates where it should pass through, creating pressure, distension, and dysfunction.

## The Liver connection

Qi stagnation is most commonly associated with the Liver system, because the Liver's primary function in TCM is to ensure the smooth flow of Qi throughout the body (shu xie 疏泄).
When the Liver's flow-regulating function is impaired — most often by emotional constraint, unexpressed anger, or chronic frustration — Qi flow stagnates throughout the body, producing the pattern known as **Liver Qi stagnation** (gan qi yu jie 肝气郁结).

Liver Qi stagnation is arguably the single most common pattern in modern TCM practice.
The characteristic presentation:

- **Distension and fullness**: A feeling of pressure in the chest, hypochondrium (rib-side area), epigastrium, or abdomen — not a sharp pain, but a bloated, pressurized sensation that fluctuates with emotional state
- **Emotional frustration**: Irritability, mood swings, depression, a feeling of being "stuck" or unable to express oneself.
  The emotional quality and the physical quality mirror each other — the Qi is stuck, and the person feels stuck
- **Sighing**: Spontaneous deep sighing is diagnostic.
  The sigh is the body's attempt to move the stagnant Qi in the chest
- **Distension that moves**: Unlike [blood stasis](../../../../../../content/text/glossary/terms/blood-stasis.md) pain (fixed) or dampness heaviness (settling), Qi stagnation distension can shift location
- **Wiry pulse** (xian 弦): The most reliable pulse finding — the pulse feels taut, like a guitar string, reflecting the tension in the system
- **Symptoms worsen with stress**: The hallmark temporal pattern.
  The distension, pain, and emotional symptoms increase with emotional stress and decrease with relaxation, exercise, or emotional expression

## The cascade: what Qi stagnation produces

Qi stagnation is clinically significant not just for its own symptoms but because it is the upstream cause of several other pathological patterns:

**Qi stagnation → [Blood stasis](../../../../../../content/text/glossary/terms/blood-stasis.md)**: Qi moves blood.
When Qi stagnates, blood movement slows and eventually stagnates.
This is the most common progression — Liver Qi stagnation producing menstrual pain, fixed masses, or cardiovascular dysfunction over time.

**Qi stagnation → Heat**: Stagnant Qi generates heat, the way friction generates warmth.
Prolonged Qi stagnation transforms into Liver Fire — the irritability intensifies into outbursts of anger, the face flushes red, headaches become throbbing and temporal.

**Qi stagnation → [Phlegm](phlegm.md)**: When Qi stagnation impairs the Spleen's transformative function, fluids accumulate and congeal into Phlegm.
The classic presentation is "plum pit Qi" (mei he qi 梅核气) — a sensation of something stuck in the throat that can neither be swallowed nor expelled.
This is TCM's description of what biomedicine calls globus hystericus.

**Qi stagnation → [Damp-heat](damp-heat.md)**: Stagnant Qi impairs fluid metabolism (generating dampness) while simultaneously generating heat.
The combined result is damp-heat — commonly settling in the Liver/Gallbladder system.

## Treatment principle: soothe the Liver, regulate Qi

The treatment of Qi stagnation involves herbs that move and regulate Qi flow:

- **Chai Hu** (Bupleurum chinense) — the primary Liver Qi-regulating herb; spreads Liver Qi, relieves constraint
- **Xiang Fu** (Cyperus rotundus) — moves Qi, alleviates pain; called "the general of Qi regulation"
- **Chen Pi** (aged tangerine peel) — regulates Qi in the middle burner, resolves Phlegm
- **Bo He** (peppermint) — disperses Liver Qi, clears the head
- **Yu Jin** (Curcuma wenyujin) — moves Qi and blood, particularly for Liver constraint with blood stasis

The classical formula is **Xiao Yao San** (逍遥散, "Free and Easy Wanderer") — detailed in [Herbal Medicine](../../documents/articles/notes/herbal-medicine.md) — which soothes Liver Qi stagnation while simultaneously nourishing Blood and supporting the Spleen.

## Qi stagnation and modern life

TCM practitioners note that Qi stagnation has become the background pattern of modern urban life.
Sedentary work, emotional suppression in professional settings, chronic screen use, and the mismatch between the body's need for movement and the reality of desk-bound existence create conditions that the TCM framework identifies as systemic Qi stagnation.
This is not a claim about modernity's pathology — it is an observation that the pattern TCM calls Qi stagnation maps onto the symptom clusters modern medicine sees in stress-related functional disorders: irritable bowel syndrome, tension headaches, non-cardiac chest pain, and functional dyspepsia.

## See also

- [Qi](qi.md) — the substance that stagnates
- [Blood Stasis](../../../../../../content/text/glossary/terms/blood-stasis.md) — the downstream consequence
- [Damp-Heat](damp-heat.md) — another downstream consequence
- [Phlegm](phlegm.md) — another downstream consequence
- [Zang-Fu](zang-fu.md) — the Liver system whose dysfunction causes stagnation
- [Pattern Diagnosis](../../documents/articles/notes/pattern-diagnosis.md) — how stagnation is identified
- [Herbal Medicine](../../documents/articles/notes/herbal-medicine.md) — Xiao Yao San formula for Liver Qi stagnation

records.name: Qigong
records.description: The family of Chinese practices that cultivate the body's functional activity (qi) by coordinating posture or movement, breath, and attention; a twentieth-century name for methods descended from daoyin, breath cultivation, and inner alchemy.

palmer2007.title: Qigong Fever: Body, Science, and Utopia in China

kohn2008.title: Chinese Healing Exercises: The Tradition of Daoyin

jahnke2010.title: A comprehensive review of health benefits of qigong and tai chi

records.body:
Qigong (氣功, "qi work" or "the skill of qi") names a family of practices that cultivate the body's functional activity, [qi](./qi.md), by coordinating three things at once: the body's posture or movement, the breath, and the mind's attention. Chinese teaching calls this coordination the [three regulations](./san-tiao.md): regulating the body, the breath, and the mind.

The word is modern. Its practices are old. Therapeutic stretching and breathing, *daoyin* (導引, "guiding and pulling"), is depicted in a silk chart buried at Mawangdui in 168 BCE, and the *Zhuangzi* already mocks practitioners of "bear hangings and bird stretches" [@kohn2008]. "Qigong" became the umbrella term only in the 1950s, when state clinics gathered [daoyin](./daoyin.md), breath cultivation, and simplified [inner alchemy](./neidan.md) under one secular, medical name. The mass "qigong fever" of the 1980s and 1990s followed [@palmer2007]. The history is traced in the [2026-09-24 note on qigong as a practice system](../../documents/articles/notes/2026/09/24/2026-09-24-note-on-qigong-as-a-practice-system.md).

Practices divide along three lines, which cross-cut:

- **Moving and still.** Moving forms (dong gong) such as [Baduanjin](./baduanjin.md) sequence postures with breath. Still forms (jing gong) such as [standing post](./zhan-zhuang.md) and seated breath-and-attention practice hold one posture.
- **Medical, martial, and contemplative.** Medical qigong treats or maintains health within [traditional Chinese medicine](./traditional-chinese-medicine.md). Martial qigong conditions the body for combat arts; its movement overlaps with [taijiquan](../../../../../medical-services-section/services/health-services-section/services/fitness-services-section/services/martial-arts-services-section/services/tai-chi-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/taijiquan.md). Contemplative and Daoist qigong aims at transformation of the person, not treatment.
- **Self-practice and emitted qi.** Most qigong is done by the practitioner for themself. "External qi" healing, where a master directs qi into a patient, is a distinct and far more contested claim.

Within Chinese medicine's own terms, qigong works on the [Three Treasures](./san-bao.md). It conserves [jing](./jing.md), keeps qi circulating instead of stagnating, and settles [shen](./shen.md). Attention is often gathered in the lower [dantian](./dantian.md). This section records that account as the tradition's own theory of the practice.

Biomedical research treats qigong as low-to-moderate intensity mind-body exercise with slowed breathing. Across dozens of randomized trials it reports benefits for balance, physical function, blood pressure, mood, and quality of life [@jahnke2010]. The trials' strength and limits are weighed in the [2026-09-24 note on the clinical evidence for qigong and taiji](../../documents/articles/notes/2026/09/24/2026-09-24-note-on-the-clinical-evidence-for-qigong-and-taiji.md). The breathing component has its own physiology in [slow-paced breathing](../../../../../../../physiology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/slow-paced-breathing.md).

records.name: Rapid Cycling
records.description: A bipolar-disorder course specifier defined by Dunner and Fieve as four or more mood episodes within twelve months, originally proposed as a predictor of lithium-prophylaxis failure. DSM adopted the same threshold essentially unchanged; it names a course pattern that can wax and wane, not a fixed subtype.

dunner1974.title: Clinical factors in lithium carbonate prophylaxis failure
dunner1974.note: PMID 4589148; the ~44/96 lithium-treated patient count is reported in secondary sources and was not independently confirmed against the original abstract

miola2023.title: Prevalence and outcomes of rapid cycling bipolar disorder: Mixed method systematic meta-review

schneck2004.title: Phenomenology of rapid-cycling bipolar disorder: data from the first 500 participants in the Systematic Treatment Enhancement Program

records.body:
Rapid cycling names a bipolar-disorder course specifier: four or more mood episodes (manic, hypomanic, or depressive) within twelve months. The definition originates with Dunner and Fieve (1974), who proposed it as a predictor of lithium-prophylaxis treatment failure in a retrospective clinical-factor analysis of lithium non-responders; secondary sources describe roughly 44 of 96 lithium-treated patients as meeting the definition, though this could not be independently verified against the original abstract. The same four-episodes-per-year threshold was later adopted essentially unchanged as a DSM course specifier.

Rapid cycling is a course specifier, not a separate diagnosis or a fixed subtype: DSM-5 states it can wax and wane over the course of the illness rather than marking a stable, permanent illness form. This distinguishes it from proposed sub-thresholds inside the same spectrum — "ultra-rapid" cycling (roughly 48-hour cycles) and "ultradian" cycling (polarity changes faster than once every 24 hours) — which some researchers describe as the outer edge of the rapid-cycling spectrum but which have never themselves been adopted into DSM or ICD (see ultradian-cycling).

A 2023 mixed-method systematic meta-review aggregating 22 reviews (30 underlying studies, 13,698 bipolar-disorder patients) found 27.6% (3,777 patients) met rapid-cycling criteria, with rapid-cycling patients showing greater illness severity, lower functioning, and higher rates of suicide attempts, hypothyroidism, and substance use than non-rapid-cycling patients. A cross-sectional cohort of the first 500 enrollees in the Systematic Treatment Enhancement Program for Bipolar Disorder (STEP-BD) found 20% met rapid-cycling criteria in the preceding year; rapid cyclers were disproportionately female, had earlier illness onset, presented with more depressive symptoms, had poorer functioning, and had significantly more depressive and hypomanic/manic episodes in the preceding year than non-rapid-cyclers.

For research design, the consequence is that these prevalence and correlate figures come from help-seeking, largely tertiary-referral or research-registry samples (STEP-BD, and reviews aggregating similarly ascertained cohorts) — they are cross-sectional estimates in clinical populations, not population-representative incidence figures, and because rapid cycling is a course specifier that can wax and wane, a single cross-sectional assessment characterizes a patient's status during the assessed year, not a permanent trait.

records.name: Reactive Aggression
records.description: Aggression triggered by perceived threat, frustration, or provocation, distinguished from planned proactive aggression and modeled via an amygdala-hypothalamus-periaqueductal-gray circuit whose rodent causal evidence and human correlational evidence point in conflicting directions.

lin2011.title: Functional identification of an aggression locus in the mouse hypothalamus

coccaro2007.title: Amygdala and Orbitofrontal Reactivity to Social Threat in Individuals with Impulsive Aggression

deveney2013.title: Neural Mechanisms of Frustration in Chronically Irritable Children

records.body:
Reactive aggression is aggression triggered by perceived threat, frustration, or provocation — an angry, retaliatory response to a proximate trigger — distinguished in the theoretical literature from proactive (instrumental) aggression, which is planned and reward-directed rather than triggered by an immediate provocation. It is modeled as arising from an amygdala–hypothalamus–periaqueductal-gray threat circuit, modulated (or insufficiently modulated) by attentional and prefrontal regulation circuits — an integrative theoretical account, referred to in this literature as the Blair model, synthesizing multiple imaging and lesion findings rather than a single confirmed causal pathway demonstrated end-to-end in humans; this dossier did not verify a specific Blair primary source directly, and the attribution should be checked before further use.

The clearest causal evidence for a specific node in this circuitry is rodent-only. Lin, Boyle, Dollar, Lee, Lein, Perona, and Anderson (2011) found that optogenetic stimulation of a subpopulation of neurons in the ventrolateral ventromedial hypothalamus (VMHvl) of male mice is sufficient to trigger attack on females, males, and inanimate objects, while pharmacogenetic silencing of the same region reversibly inhibits inter-male aggression — a bidirectional, activate-to-cause and silence-to-block, design that licenses a genuinely causal claim about this hypothalamic node in mice. No equivalent causal manipulation exists, or could ethically exist, in humans; any extension of the VMHvl findings to a human "aggression circuit" claim is extrapolation, not evidence.

Human evidence is correlational, cross-sectional imaging. Coccaro, McCloskey, Fitzgerald, and Phan (2007) found exaggerated amygdala reactivity to angry faces and diminished amygdala–orbitofrontal functional connectivity in 10 unmedicated adults with intermittent explosive disorder relative to 10 healthy matched comparison subjects, consistent with a model of impulsive aggression as amygdala hyperreactivity under insufficient prefrontal regulation. This runs in the opposite direction from a separate, developmental literature on frustrative nonreward (see frustrative-nonreward): Deveney and colleagues (2013), studying 42 children (19 with severe mood dysregulation, 23 healthy comparison) under a rigged-feedback frustration task, found chronically irritable children showed reduced, not exaggerated, amygdala and striatal activation to frustrating negative feedback. The two paradigms probe different things — social-threat faces in adults with a reactive-aggression diagnosis, versus non-social frustrating feedback in irritable children — and this directionality conflict is real and unresolved in the literature; it should not be papered over with one unified "hyperactive amygdala" story for blocked-goal-to-rage.

The consequence for research design is to keep the two evidentiary channels separate rather than substituting one for the other: a causal claim about a specific circuit node, as in the rodent VMHvl work, cannot be read onto a human correlational group-difference finding, as in the IED amygdala work, and a finding in one population or paradigm should not be assumed to generalize, in direction or magnitude, to a different population or paradigm without directly testing it.

records.name: Receptor
records.description: A protein that detects a specific chemical signal and initiates a cellular response, serving as the molecular target for neurotransmitters, hormones, and most drugs.
records.body:
A **receptor** is a protein — usually embedded in a [cell](../../../../../../../../content/text/glossary/terms/cell.md) membrane or located inside a cell — that detects a specific chemical signal and initiates a cellular response. Receptors are the molecular targets through which neurotransmitters, hormones, and most drugs produce their effects. They are the locks to which signaling molecules are the keys.

## How receptors work

A receptor has a **binding site** — a region whose three-dimensional shape is complementary to the shape of its specific signaling molecule (called its **ligand**). When the ligand binds, the receptor changes shape (a conformational change), which triggers a cascade of events inside the cell. This might mean opening an ion channel, activating an enzyme, or initiating a gene expression program.

The specificity of the binding site is what makes receptor-mediated signaling precise. The mu-opioid receptor responds to endorphins (and to morphine, which mimics their shape) but not to serotonin. The serotonin 5-HT1A receptor responds to serotonin but not to dopamine. This specificity is also why drugs have "off-target" effects: at higher concentrations, a drug may begin binding to receptors it does not normally interact with at lower concentrations, producing side effects.

## Major receptor families

**Ligand-gated ion channels** — receptors that are also ion channels. When the ligand binds, the channel opens, allowing ions (sodium, potassium, calcium, chloride) to flow across the membrane. These produce fast responses (milliseconds). Examples: GABA-A receptors (chloride channels; inhibitory; enhanced by benzodiazepines), NMDA receptors (calcium channels; excitatory; involved in [central sensitization](../../../../../pain-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/central-sensitization.md)).

**G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs)** — the largest family of receptors and the most common drug targets. When the ligand binds, the receptor activates an intracellular G-protein, which triggers a signaling cascade. These produce slower responses (seconds to minutes) but can amplify the signal enormously. Examples: mu-opioid receptors, adrenergic receptors, dopamine receptors, most serotonin receptors.

**Receptor tyrosine kinases** — receptors that, when activated, add phosphate groups to intracellular proteins, initiating cascades that affect cell growth, differentiation, and survival. These are the targets of many cancer drugs. Responses are slow (hours to days).

**Nuclear receptors** — located inside the cell; bind ligands that can cross the cell membrane (steroid hormones, thyroid hormone, vitamin D). When activated, they directly regulate gene expression. Responses are the slowest (hours to days) but can produce lasting changes in cell behavior.

## Receptors and sensory systems

The term "receptor" is used in two related but distinct ways in medicine:

1. **Molecular receptors** — the proteins described above; the targets of neurotransmitters and drugs
2. **Sensory receptors** — specialized nerve endings or cells that detect physical stimuli (touch, pressure, temperature, stretch, chemicals) and convert them into electrical signals

Sensory receptors include:
- **Mechanoreceptors** — detect pressure, vibration, stretch (Merkel cells in skin, [muscle spindles](../../../../../somatics-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/proprioception.md) in muscles, Golgi tendon organs in tendons)
- **Thermoreceptors** — detect temperature changes
- **Nociceptors** — detect potentially damaging stimuli ([nociception](../../../../../pain-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/nociception.md))
- **Chemoreceptors** — detect chemical changes (oxygen/CO2 levels in blood, pH)

The connection between the two uses: sensory receptors contain molecular receptors. A nociceptor's sensitivity to heat is mediated by a specific molecular receptor (TRPV1) that opens an ion channel in response to high temperature. Capsaicin (the compound that makes chili peppers hot) activates the same TRPV1 receptor, which is why hot peppers produce a sensation of burning — the molecular receptor cannot distinguish between actual heat and capsaicin.

## Receptors as the basis of drug action

Nearly all of [pharmacodynamics](../../../../../pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/pharmacodynamics.md) is receptor physiology applied to clinical practice. Agonists activate receptors. Antagonists block them. Partial agonists partially activate them. The [therapeutic index](../../../../../pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/therapeutic-index.md) reflects the difference between the dose that activates the desired receptor and the dose that begins activating unintended receptors. [Drug interactions](../../../../../pharmacology-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/drug-interaction.md) often involve two drugs competing for the same receptor or affecting the same receptor system through different mechanisms.

## Related terms

- [Cell](../../../../../../../../content/text/glossary/terms/cell.md) — where receptors are located
- [Synapse](./synapse.md) — where receptor-mediated communication between neurons occurs
- [Neuron](./neuron.md) — cells that use receptors to communicate

records.name: Reiki
records.description: A Japanese healing practice developed by Mikao Usui in which a practitioner channels energy through their hands to support healing
records.body:
**Reiki** (Japanese: 霊気, literally "spiritual energy" or "universal life energy") is a healing practice developed by Mikao Usui in Japan in the early 1920s. It centers on the idea that a [practitioner](../../../../services/reiki-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/practitioner.md) can channel energy through their hands — by direct touch or proximity — to support healing in the recipient.

A reiki session typically involves the recipient lying down, clothed, while the practitioner places their hands on or near a series of positions on the body, each held for several minutes. The practitioner does not manipulate tissue (as in massage) or apply pressure (as in acupressure); the practice is based on energy transfer rather than physical intervention.

Reiki is organized into levels or degrees. First Degree introduces the basic hand positions and self-treatment. Second Degree introduces symbols and the concept of distance healing. Third Degree (Master level) qualifies the practitioner to teach and attune others. The attunement process — in which a Reiki master performs a ritual to "open" a student's capacity to channel energy — is central to the tradition's transmission model.

From a biomedical perspective, there is limited evidence for reiki's efficacy beyond placebo effects and the general benefits of relaxation and compassionate attention. From the perspective of those who practice it, reiki operates on a dimension of experience that biomedical measurement does not capture. The practice continues to be widely used in integrative medicine settings, hospice care, and personal wellness.

records.name: Resveratrol
records.description: A stilbenoid phytoalexin produced by plants under stress, studied extensively for anti-inflammatory, cardioprotective, and antioxidant properties — most commercially sourced from Japanese knotweed rhizome

renaud1992.title: Wine, alcohol, platelets, and the French paradox for coronary heart disease

howitz2003.title: Small molecule activators of sirtuins extend Saccharomyces cerevisiae lifespan

baur2006.title: Resveratrol improves health and survival of mice on a high-calorie diet

burns2002.title: Plant foods and herbal sources of resveratrol
burns2002.publication: Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry

records.body:
Resveratrol (*trans*-3,5,4'-trihydroxystilbene) is a polyphenolic stilbenoid produced by plants as a phytoalexin — a defensive compound synthesized in response to injury, ultraviolet radiation, or fungal infection. It is found in grape skins, peanuts, blueberries, and most abundantly in the root and rhizome of [Japanese knotweed](../../../../../../../botany-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/japanese-knotweed.md) (*Reynoutria japonica*), which produces resveratrol at concentrations 50–100 times higher than grape skins and is the primary commercial source for dietary supplements.

## The French paradox

Resveratrol entered Western biomedical consciousness through the "French paradox" — the epidemiological observation, reported by Renaud and de Lorgeril in *The Lancet* in 1992, that French populations had lower rates of coronary heart disease than predicted by their saturated fat intake [@renaud1992]. Red wine consumption was proposed as the protective factor, and resveratrol — present in grape skins and therefore concentrated in red wine — was identified as a candidate molecule responsible for the cardioprotective effect. Whether resveratrol at the concentrations present in wine is sufficient to explain the epidemiological observation remains contested. The paradox may reflect dietary pattern effects (the Mediterranean diet), reporting artifacts, or multiple interacting factors rather than a single compound.

## Molecular targets

Resveratrol interacts with a broad array of molecular targets, which is both its pharmacological interest and the source of skepticism about its specificity:

**SIRT1 (Sirtuin 1)**: Howitz et al. (2003) reported that resveratrol activates SIRT1, a NAD+-dependent protein deacetylase involved in cellular stress response, metabolism, and aging [@howitz2003]. This finding launched a wave of aging research and commercial interest. Baur and Sinclair (2006) showed that resveratrol-fed mice on high-calorie diets had improved health markers and extended survival compared to controls [@baur2006]. However, subsequent work revealed that the original SIRT1 activation assay used a fluorescent substrate that produced artifactual results — resveratrol's activation of SIRT1 is indirect (via AMPK) rather than direct. The downstream metabolic effects are real; the mechanism is more complex than initially proposed.

**NF-κB pathway**: Resveratrol inhibits NF-κB (nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells), a transcription factor that drives inflammatory gene expression. This inhibition underlies many of resveratrol's anti-inflammatory effects in cell culture and animal models.

**COX-2 (cyclooxygenase-2)**: Resveratrol inhibits COX-2, the same enzyme targeted by NSAIDs like ibuprofen. This provides a molecular basis for the anti-inflammatory and analgesic properties attributed to Japanese knotweed in traditional medicine.

**AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase)**: Resveratrol activates AMPK, a master regulator of cellular energy homeostasis. AMPK activation increases fatty acid oxidation, glucose uptake, and mitochondrial biogenesis — effects that mimic caloric restriction.

## Bioavailability problem

The central limitation of resveratrol pharmacology is bioavailability. Oral resveratrol is rapidly absorbed but extensively metabolized by first-pass metabolism in the intestine and liver, producing glucuronide and sulfate conjugates. Peak plasma concentration of free resveratrol after a 25 mg oral dose is approximately 1–5 ng/mL — orders of magnitude below the concentrations used in most cell culture studies (typically 10–100 μM). This disconnect between in vitro activity and achievable in vivo concentrations is the fundamental challenge for translating resveratrol research into clinical therapeutics.

Several strategies address this: higher dosing (clinical trials have used up to 5 g/day), formulation with absorption enhancers (piperine from black pepper inhibits glucuronidation), nanoparticle delivery, and the use of more bioavailable analogues like pterostilbene (a dimethylated resveratrol derivative found in blueberries).

## Polydatin

Polydatin (piceid) is the glucoside form of resveratrol — resveratrol bonded to a glucose molecule. It is the predominant form in Japanese knotweed rhizome, where it occurs at higher concentrations than free resveratrol. Polydatin achieves serum concentrations 3–4 times higher than free resveratrol at the same oral dose, because it uses the potential SGLT1 (sodium-glucose linked transporter 1) in the intestine rather than relying on passive diffusion. This dramatically better oral bioavailability, combined with greater water solubility and metabolic stability, has led some researchers to argue that polydatin, not free resveratrol, is the therapeutically relevant form in traditional herbal preparations — and that the bioavailability problem afflicting resveratrol research may partly reflect studying the wrong compound [@burns2002].

## Clinical status

Despite thousands of preclinical studies, resveratrol has not yet produced a breakthrough clinical application. Phase I–III trials have been conducted for cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, Alzheimer's disease, and various cancers. Results are mixed: some trials show modest improvements in inflammatory markers, insulin sensitivity, or endothelial function; others show no significant effect. No major regulatory body has approved resveratrol as a drug. In the United States, it is sold as a dietary supplement under DSHEA (Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act). In the United Kingdom, trans-resveratrol is authorized as a novel food with a maximum daily intake of 150 mg for adults. It is typically sold as purified extract from Japanese knotweed rhizome, in capsule form at doses of 100–500 mg/day.

The gap between resveratrol's dramatic effects in cell culture, its promising effects in animal models, and its modest effects in human trials is a case study in translational pharmacology — and in the difference between a compound's biological activity and its therapeutic utility.
