kaptchuk2000.title: The Web That Has No Weaver: Understanding Chinese Medicine

unschuld1985.title: Medicine in China: A History of Ideas

scheid2002.title: Chinese Medicine in Contemporary China: Plurality and Synthesis

records.name: Transcranial Alternating Current Stimulation
records.description: Weak sinusoidal current at a chosen frequency through scalp electrodes, intended to entrain brain oscillations of that frequency.

herrmann2013.title: Transcranial alternating current stimulation: a review of the underlying mechanisms and modulation of cognitive processes

voroslakos2018.title: Direct effects of transcranial electric stimulation on brain circuits in rats and humans

records.body:
Transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) delivers a weak sinusoidal [alternating current](../../../../../../../../../../../physical-science-services-section/services/physics-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/alternating-current.md), typically 1–2 mA peak to peak, at a frequency matched to a brain rhythm: [alpha](../../../../../../../../../neuroscience-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/alpha-rhythm.md) at 10 Hz, gamma at 40 Hz, and so on. The aim is [entrainment](../../../../../../../../../neuroscience-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/neural-entrainment.md). A rhythmic field too weak to fire neurons can still pull the timing of an ongoing [oscillation](../../../../../../../../../neuroscience-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/neural-oscillation.md) toward the stimulation frequency, and so, in principle, change the functions that oscillation supports [@herrmann2013].

The debate is whether enough field reaches the cortex. Direct recordings suggest scalp tACS at common intensities produces fields near the lower limit of what affects neurons. Some reported effects may instead come from rhythmic stimulation of nerves in the scalp or of the retina, which is sensed as flicker [@voroslakos2018]. Careful studies now control for these routes.

records.name: Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation
records.description: Constant weak current (typically 1–2 mA for 20–30 minutes) through two scalp sponge electrodes; the anode tends to raise and the cathode to lower the excitability of the cortex beneath.

nitsche2000.title: Excitability changes induced in the human motor cortex by weak transcranial direct current stimulation

bikson2016.title: Safety of transcranial direct current stimulation: evidence based update 2016

records.body:
Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) passes a constant [current](../../../../../../../../../../../physical-science-services-section/services/physics-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/electric-current.md), typically 1–2 mA for 20–30 minutes, between two saline-soaked sponge electrodes on the scalp. The electrodes are usually 25–35 cm², which keeps the [current density](../../../../../../../../../../../physical-science-services-section/services/physics-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/current-density.md) at the skin low. The montage (where the anode and cathode sit) decides which cortex receives the strongest field.

Its modern form comes from Nitsche and Paulus's demonstration that a few minutes of 1 mA over the motor cortex changed its [excitability](../../../../../../../../../neuroscience-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/neuronal-excitability.md) beyond the stimulation period itself: raised under the anode, lowered under the cathode [@nitsche2000]. It has since been studied for depression, chronic pain, stroke rehabilitation and cognition, with mixed and often modest results.

A large evidence review found no serious adverse effects across tens of thousands of sessions at conventional parameters. Tingling, itching and mild skin redness were common and transient [@bikson2016]. Its currents are of the same order as those of [cranial electrotherapy stimulation](cranial-electrotherapy-stimulation.md) devices. CES differs in its waveform (pulsed alternating current, not direct current) and in its small electrodes on or near the ears.

records.name: Transcranial Electrical Stimulation
records.description: Weak current (about 0.5–4 mA) applied through scalp or head electrodes to shift brain excitability or rhythms without firing neurons directly; the family that includes tDCS, tACS and cranial electrotherapy.

bikson2016.title: Safety of transcranial direct current stimulation: evidence based update 2016

voroslakos2018.title: Direct effects of transcranial electric stimulation on brain circuits in rats and humans

datta2013.title: Cranial electrotherapy stimulation and transcranial pulsed current stimulation: a computer based high-resolution modeling study

records.body:
Transcranial electrical stimulation (tES) passes a weak [current](../../../../../../../../../../../physical-science-services-section/services/physics-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/electric-current.md), usually 0.5–4 mA, between electrodes on the head. Some of that current crosses the skull and sets up a small [electric field](../../../../../../../../../../../physical-science-services-section/services/physics-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/electric-field.md) in the brain. Such fields are far too weak to fire neurons outright. They shift [membrane potentials](../../../../../../../../../neuroscience-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/membrane-potential.md) by fractions of a millivolt, which can bias [excitability](../../../../../../../../../neuroscience-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/neuronal-excitability.md) or the timing of [oscillations](../../../../../../../../../neuroscience-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/neural-oscillation.md) [@bikson2016].

The family is named by waveform:
- **[tDCS](transcranial-direct-current-stimulation.md):** constant direct current.
- **[tACS](transcranial-alternating-current-stimulation.md):** sinusoidal alternating current at a chosen frequency.
- **Random-noise stimulation (tRNS):** current that fluctuates randomly across a band of frequencies.
- **Pulsed stimulation:** trains of pulses, the waveform most [cranial electrotherapy stimulation](cranial-electrotherapy-stimulation.md) devices use through ear or temple electrodes [@datta2013].

The central scientific question is dose. Measurements show most applied current is shunted through the scalp. At common intensities the brain field is a fraction of a volt per metre, near or below what reliably affects neurons [@voroslakos2018]. Effects may therefore depend on electrode placement, on the brain's own state, and on repeated sessions, which is part of why results vary so much between studies. The methods are generally safe at these intensities [@bikson2016].

records.name: Transcutaneous Auricular Vagus Nerve Stimulation
records.description: Electrical stimulation applied to the auricular branch of the vagus nerve via electrodes placed on the ear, intended to modulate autonomic nervous system tone and produce anti-inflammatory and analgesic effects through vagal afferent signaling.

butt2019.title: The anatomical basis for transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation

kaniusas2019.title: Current Directions in the Auricular Vagus Nerve Stimulation II – An Engineering Perspective

shekelle2018.title: Benefits and Harms of Cranial Electrical Stimulation for Chronic Painful Conditions, Depression, Anxiety, and Insomnia

records.body:
Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) is electrical stimulation applied to the auricular branch of the vagus nerve via ear-placed electrodes. The auricular branch is a documented cutaneous sensory pathway [@butt2019] that innervates the ear. taVNS devices deliver electrical current at frequencies intended to activate this nerve branch, which sends afferent (sensory) signals into the brainstem via the vagus nerve nucleus [@butt2019].

Vagal afferent signaling has reproducible effects on autonomic nervous system tone (increased parasympathetic activity), anti-inflammatory cytokine release, and pain modulation [@butt2019]. These effects are well-documented with implanted vagus nerve stimulation in clinical settings. Stimulation parameters (frequency, intensity, pulse width) determine the magnitude and nature of vagal activation [@kaniusas2019], and anatomical targeting of the auricular branch increases likelihood of afferent vagal recruitment compared to non-targeted stimulation [@kaniusas2019].

Evidence for taVNS effectiveness is emerging. Anatomical studies confirm that transcutaneous stimulation at identified auricular landmarks reliably activates the vagus nerve [@butt2019]. Clinical trials for specific taVNS indications (depression, anxiety, pain, seizures) are ongoing but limited in number and scale; reported effect sizes are modest and study quality varies. (Cranial electrotherapy stimulation, a distinct diffuse-current technology reviewed by Shekelle et al. (2018) [@shekelle2018] for chronic pain, depression, anxiety, and insomnia, found insufficient evidence for any indication; that finding does not transfer to taVNS's targeted peripheral-nerve mechanism.)

Mechanistic studies demonstrate that appropriately parameterized taVNS increases parasympathetic tone (measured by heart rate variability), reduces inflammatory markers (TNF-α, IL-6), and produces modest analgesic effects in laboratory pain models. These effects align with known vagal physiology.

Safety is generally good. Mild skin irritation at the electrode site can occur. No serious adverse effects are well-documented. Users with implanted pacemakers or other implanted electrical devices should consult a physician before use.

records.name: Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation
records.description: A portable electrical device delivering stimulation through skin electrodes to modulate pain perception, theorized to work through gate control or endogenous opioid release depending on frequency.

johnson2022.title: Efficacy and safety of transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) for acute and chronic pain in adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 381 studies (the meta-TENS study)

records.body: Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) delivers electrical current through skin electrodes to modulate pain perception. A TENS device is a small battery-operated unit with leads connected to surface electrodes; the user adjusts frequency, intensity, and pulse width. TENS is widely used for acute pain, chronic pain, postoperative pain, and musculoskeletal conditions. Two primary mechanisms are proposed: (1) Gate control theory application — Low-frequency high-intensity TENS activates large-diameter A-beta fibers that inhibit nociceptive transmission at the spinal cord; (2) Endogenous opioid release — High-frequency TENS may activate descending opioid-sensitive pathways, triggering release of endogenous opioid peptides. These mechanisms are not mutually exclusive; different TENS parameters engage different pathways. TENS effectiveness depends critically on stimulus parameters — frequency, intensity, and pattern determine which mechanism is engaged. Biomedical evidence for TENS shows it reduces pain compared to sham TENS or no treatment, though effect sizes vary across studies. TENS is most effective when applied according to principles matching one of the proposed mechanisms. TENS differs from electroacupuncture in that it uses surface electrodes without point-specific targeting and is grounded in gate control and neurochemical theories, while electroacupuncture targets specific points through needle insertion at depth.

records.name: Trauma
records.description: An event or condition that overwhelms the organism's capacity to cope, leaving the nervous system stuck in a defensive state that was never completed and resolved.
records.body:
Trauma is defined not by the event but by the organism's response to it. A traumatic experience is one that overwhelms the [nervous system's](../../../../../human-body-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/the-nervous-system.md) capacity to process, integrate, and resolve the threat. The same event — a car accident, an assault, a natural disaster — may be traumatic for one person and not another, depending on their resources, support, history, and nervous system capacity at the time.

What makes trauma pathological is the failure of resolution. In a normal threat response, the autonomic nervous system mobilizes for defense (fight or flight), the threat passes, and the system discharges the mobilization energy and returns to baseline. In trauma, this cycle does not complete. The defensive energy remains stored in the body — the person remains physiologically in the threat state even after the threat has passed. This is [Somatic Experiencing's](../concepts/somatics/somatic-experiencing.md) central framework: trauma is a physiological event, and it must be resolved physiologically.

**Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)** is the clinical syndrome that results: re-experiencing (intrusive memories, flashbacks), avoidance (of reminders and of emotional engagement), hyperarousal (the nervous system stuck in chronic threat-detection), and negative alterations in cognition and mood.

**Complex trauma** (developmental trauma) results from prolonged, repeated traumatic experiences, especially during childhood within caregiving relationships. It alters not just memory but the developing nervous system itself — stress-response architecture, [attachment](./attachment.md) patterns, affect regulation capacity, and physical health across the lifespan. Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) research demonstrates dose-response relationships between childhood adversity and adult disease.

Trauma history is a significant factor in [chronic pain](../../../../../pain-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/biopsychosocial-model.md): ACEs alter stress-axis regulation, immune function, and pain processing, contributing to conditions the biomedical model cannot explain through tissue damage alone.

## Related terms

- [Affect](../../../../../../../../../../../philosophy-services-section/services/relationality-services-section/services/agency-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/undated/affect.md) — the felt dimension of traumatic states
- [Attachment](./attachment.md) — early relational patterns shaped by traumatic and non-traumatic caregiving
- [Defense Mechanism](./defense-mechanism.md) — psychological processes that manage traumatic material
- [Somatic Experiencing](../concepts/somatics/somatic-experiencing.md) — resolving trauma through the autonomic nervous system
- [The Biopsychosocial Model of Pain](../../../../../pain-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/biopsychosocial-model.md) — trauma as a factor in chronic pain
- [Disability Justice](../../../../../../content/text/glossary/terms/disability-justice.md) — structural conditions that produce and compound trauma

records.name: Treatment-Emergent Affective Switch
records.description: A manic or hypomanic episode beginning during or shortly after antidepressant treatment of a depressive episode. Its estimated rate disagrees sharply between short randomized trials (low, non-significant excess risk) and large naturalistic cohorts (meaningfully elevated risk, especially under antidepressant monotherapy).

gijsman2004.title: Antidepressants for bipolar depression: a systematic review of randomized, controlled trials

oliva2025.title: Switch to mania after acute antidepressant treatment for bipolar depression: a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials

tondo2010.title: Mania associated with antidepressant treatment: comprehensive meta-analytic review

viktorin2014.title: The risk of switch to mania in patients with bipolar disorder during treatment with an antidepressant alone and in combination with a mood stabilizer

olgiati2023.title: Antidepressant emergent mood switch in major depressive disorder: onset, clinical correlates and impact on suicidality

records.body:
Treatment-emergent affective switch names a manic or hypomanic episode that begins during or shortly after antidepressant treatment of a depressive episode. It is defined by its temporal relationship to antidepressant exposure rather than by a fixed rate or a settled mechanism — as the evidence below shows, its measured frequency depends heavily on study design. This distinguishes treatment-emergent affective switch from a baseline mixed depressive episode: the switch is defined by its temporal relationship to antidepressant exposure, not by excitatory symptoms already present before treatment began, even though the two are empirically associated, as below.

The estimated risk genuinely disagrees across designs, and neither side has displaced the other. Short randomized controlled trials of antidepressants in bipolar depression, pooled in meta-analysis, find switch rates that are low and not significantly different from placebo: a 2004 systematic review of 12 short-term RCTs (1,088 patients) found 3.8% switch on antidepressant versus 4.7% on placebo (risk ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.47-2.13), and the authors explicitly note too few manic events occurred to have adequate power to detect a real difference — a null result under low power, not demonstrated safety. A 2025 network meta-analysis of 13 RCTs (1,362 patients) likewise found no individual antidepressant with a significantly higher switch risk than placebo, rating overall confidence in the evidence as low. Large naturalistic cohort and registry studies, by contrast, report meaningfully elevated risk: a comprehensive meta-analytic review pooling 109 studies (114,521 patients total, 35 in the pooled random-effects analysis) found 12.5% mania/hypomania risk with antidepressant exposure versus 7.5% without; a Swedish national-registry cohort of 3,240 bipolar patients found antidepressant monotherapy carried a hazard ratio of 2.83 for mania, while an antidepressant added to an existing mood stabilizer carried no increased — and, over the longer period studied, apparently protective — risk.

The two literatures are not simply contradictory; they answer different practical questions. The RCT literature is short in duration, frequently requires or permits mood-stabilizer co-treatment, often excludes patients judged at high switch risk, and has too few manic events for adequate statistical power. The registry/cohort literature captures real-world monotherapy use — which most current guidelines already discourage — over longer follow-up with larger event counts, but is subject to confounding by indication: patients placed on antidepressant monotherapy without a mood stabilizer may differ systematically (for example, in diagnostic certainty about bipolarity or in clinical monitoring) from those on combination treatment, a possibility none of the cohort studies can fully rule out. Neither literature shows that antidepressants cause switch in a given individual case.

A related complication concerns baseline mixed depression: a post-hoc analysis of the CO-MED trial (425 outpatients) found mixed depressive episodes more common among patients who later switched than among those who did not (11.7% vs. 5.9%, p=0.032), while self-reported irritability and psychomotor agitation showed no significant difference between switchers and non-switchers in that same dataset — a finding that complicates any simple claim that irritability itself predicts switch, even though irritability is repeatedly named a hallmark of mixed states in the conceptual literature (see mixed-depression). For clinical observation and research design, the consequence is that a reported switch rate is only interpretable alongside its study design and treatment condition: RCT-derived rates under mood-stabilizer co-treatment and registry-derived rates under real-world monotherapy are not measuring the same clinical scenario, and neither generalizes to the other's scenario.

records.name: Tumor necrosis factor alpha
records.description: A cytokine produced chiefly by activated macrophages that both drives inflammatory transcription through NF-κB and directly impairs mitochondrial oxidative capacity, existing in distinct membrane-bound and soluble forms with different receptor preferences.

kalliolias2015.title: TNF biology, pathogenic mechanisms and emerging therapeutic strategies
kalliolias2015.note: PMID 26656660; resolved against CrossRef and PubMed 2026-09-02

hayden2008.title: Shared Principles in NF-κB Signaling
hayden2008.note: PMID 18267068; resolved against CrossRef and PubMed 2026-09-02

zell1997.title: TNF-alpha and IL-1 alpha inhibit both pyruvate dehydrogenase activity and mitochondrial function in cardiomyocytes: evidence for primary impairment of mitochondrial function

records.body:
Tumor necrosis factor alpha is a cytokine produced chiefly by activated macrophages that signals through two receptors to drive inflammatory gene transcription, cell survival, or programmed cell death depending on receptor and context [kalliolias2015]. Its own gene is an NF-κB target and its signalling activates that pathway in turn [hayden2008], which is the **produced-by** relation asserted here (**established**).

Unlike the interleukins it is synthesized as a membrane-bound precursor cleaved to a soluble form, and the two forms preferentially engage different receptors, so the same molecule delivers different signals depending on whether it acts at a cell contact or at a distance [kalliolias2015]. **Established.**

The **impairs** relation to oxidative phosphorylation is sourced in Zell and colleagues' cardiomyocyte work, which found this cytokine together with interleukin-1 alpha inhibiting both pyruvate dehydrogenase activity and mitochondrial function, and argued the mitochondrial impairment was primary rather than secondary to the enzyme block [zell1997]. **Single in-vitro study in cardiomyocytes**: the direction is consistent with a wider literature on cytokine-induced mitochondrial dysfunction, but this specific pairing of enzyme and organelle impairment rests on that work and has not been reproduced in human tissue under this paradigm's conditions.

Because this cytokine impairs mitochondrial respiration directly as well as amplifying inflammatory transcription, an inflammatory episode that is not terminated imposes a metabolic cost that outlasts the signalling itself.

records.name: Two-day cardiopulmonary exercise testing
records.description: A test-retest exercise protocol performed on consecutive days, where people with myalgic encephalomyelitis characteristically show reduced oxygen consumption and workload at ventilatory threshold on day two, while healthy controls and those with other fatiguing conditions reproduce day-one values.

fluge2014.title: Metabolic dysfunction in myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome: A window into an energy starved brain and muscle

records.body:
Two-day cardiopulmonary exercise testing is a maximal or near-maximal exercise protocol performed on two consecutive days, with the critical feature being test-retest comparison 24 hours apart. In healthy people and in people with other fatiguing illnesses — fibromyalgia, post-viral fatigue from conditions other than myalgic encephalomyelitis, depression-related fatigue — performance on day two reproduces values from day one: VO₂ max, anaerobic threshold, maximum heart rate, and workload are stable across the two sessions. In myalgic encephalomyelitis, the characteristic finding is a second-day decrement: a reduced oxygen consumption at ventilatory threshold, a reduced anaerobic threshold workload, and a lower maximum VO₂ achieved. This pattern — normal or near-normal day-one values with day-two decline — is the signature of post-exertional malaise made objective and measurable in a controlled setting. The first day's demand appears to impose a cost that impairs capacity on the second day.

Why the two-day protocol matters scientifically is that single-day cardiopulmonary exercise testing in myalgic encephalomyelitis typically appears unremarkable: the day-one values fall within normal ranges or show only modest reductions. It is only when the test is repeated that the pathology becomes visible. This makes the two-day CPET a more sensitive instrument for myalgic encephalomyelitis than standard exercise testing, but it also makes it a substantial and potentially harmful research intervention. The test itself is maximal or near-maximal effort, which means it places demand on already-compromised metabolic and autonomic systems, and the predictable consequence is a prolonged post-exertional malaise flare in the days following testing. For research purposes, the benefit of an objective measure that captures the core pathophysiology has justified this cost, but it means two-day CPET is a research tool rather than a routine clinical assessment.

The mechanistic interpretation of the two-day CPET remains debated. The leading hypothesis, advanced by Fluge and colleagues, posits that reduced pyruvate dehydrogenase activity limits aerobic capacity and forces cells into anaerobic metabolism at low workloads, accumulating lactate and producing the post-exertional flare. Repeated use of this compensatory mechanism exhausts the anaerobic reserve, explaining the day-two decline. An alternative or complementary hypothesis implicates autonomic dysfunction: the sympathetic surge required for maximal exercise on day one is sustained into day two, producing vascular dysregulation and cerebral hypoperfusion that impairs exercise tolerance. Both mechanisms may operate; the evidence supporting each is limited and replication has been mixed.

For clinical and research practice, the consequence is clear: two-day CPET offers currently the closest thing to an objective, reproducible measure of the core pathophysiology of myalgic encephalomyelitis. However, modest sample sizes in published studies, inconsistent replication of the day-two effect, and the real risk of inducing prolonged symptom worsening mean that it remains a specialized research instrument appropriate for carefully-conducted studies with informed consent and follow-up support, not a routine or screening assessment.

## Related terms

- Post-exertional malaise — the phenomenon two-day CPET is designed to measure objectively
- Myalgic encephalomyelitis — the illness in which the two-day pattern distinguishes it from other fatiguing conditions
- Pyruvate dehydrogenase — the metabolic node in one leading mechanistic hypothesis for the day-two decline
- Anaerobic glycolysis — the compensatory mechanism proposed to operate when aerobic capacity is exhausted
- Ventilatory threshold — the exercise intensity marker most consistently showing the two-day decline
- Mitochondrial respiration — the upstream system whose compromise may limit aerobic capacity

records.name: Ultradian Cycling
records.description: Reported bipolar mood-polarity changes occurring faster than once every 24 hours, described at the outer edge of the rapid-cycling spectrum. It has never been admitted into DSM-5 or ICD-11 as a recognized diagnostic category, and its discriminant validity against other causes of rapid mood variability is disputed.

kramlinger1996.title: Ultra-rapid and ultradian cycling in bipolar affective illness

goldberg2011.title: Ultra-rapid cycling bipolar disorder: a critical look
goldberg2011.note: secondary critical commentary; read in summarized secondary form, not quoted directly from primary text

records.body:
Ultradian cycling names reported bipolar mood-polarity changes occurring faster than once every 24 hours — an extension, past "ultra-rapid" cycling (cycles of roughly 48 hours), of the rapid-cycling course specifier (four or more episodes per year) to its outer, sub-daily edge. It has never been admitted into DSM-5 or ICD-11 as a recognized diagnostic specifier or subtype.

The primary descriptive source is a case series of five hospitalized bipolar patients studied by retrospective life-charting and prospective daily mood ratings during extended inpatient evaluation, reporting a spectrum of cycle frequencies from annual down to distinct, abrupt mood shifts under 24 hours in duration in patients without evidence of personality disorder — offered by the authors as evidence against a simple reinterpretation of the pattern as borderline personality disorder. As a case series of five patients, this establishes that such patterns are observable and documentable in careful inpatient study, not their population prevalence or their status as a distinct nosological entity; the authors themselves frame it as an open descriptive question about the outer edge of the rapid-cycling spectrum, not a settled category.

A critical secondary commentary argues the construct lacks demonstrated content and discriminant validity relative to other conditions with intrinsic moment-to-moment mood variability — ordinary affective lability seen in borderline personality disorder or ADHD-associated mood reactivity — and warns of the risk that a diagnostically fashionable label gets over-applied to non-bipolar mood instability once an "ultra-rapid" specifier is available for clinicians to reach for; this critique was read in summarized secondary form, not quoted directly from its primary text.

For clinical observation and research design, the consequence is that a report of sub-24-hour mood-polarity change should not be treated as an established, DSM/ICD-recognized bipolar course specifier: because DSM-5 and ICD-11 have never admitted ultradian cycling, and because its discriminant validity against other sources of rapid mood variability is disputed rather than demonstrated, distinguishing it from borderline personality disorder-associated lability or other non-bipolar mood instability requires an independent structured assessment, not the presence of fast mood swings alone.

records.name: Vacuum Cupping Device
records.description: A small handheld silicone or rubber cup that creates localized negative pressure (partial vacuum) when applied to skin, drawing tissue upward and producing transient analgesia, hyperemia, and mechanical mobilization.

cao2012.title: An Updated Review of the Efficacy of Cupping Therapy

lauche2012.title: The Effect of Traditional Cupping on Pain and Mechanical Thresholds in Patients with Chronic Nonspecific Neck Pain: A Randomised Controlled Pilot Study

records.body:
A vacuum cupping device made of silicone or rubber creates localized negative pressure by manual suction (squeezing the cup sides) when applied to skin. The negative pressure draws skin and superficial muscle tissue into the cup, dilates local capillaries, and mobilizes tissue temporarily. The cup is removed by releasing the vacuum.

The mechanisms are: (1) local capillary dilation and increased blood flow, which produces transient hyperemia; (2) activation of mechanoreceptors via negative pressure, triggering gate-control analgesia (transient pain relief); and (3) tissue mobilization via suction. All effects are temporary and resolve when the cup is removed.

Marketing claims that cupping removes stagnant blood or breaks up fascia lack mechanistic support. Fascia is not a discrete target amenable to mechanical breakup. Negative pressure mobilizes tissue temporarily but does not produce lasting structural change.

Evidence from small randomized trials [@cao2012] [@lauche2012] shows cupping produces modest, transient pain reduction comparable to massage or heat application. No evidence supports superiority over simpler methods or long-term benefit. Cupping combined with acupuncture showed slightly larger effects than cupping alone in some trials, but the independent contribution of cupping versus acupuncture is unclear.

Safety is generally good. Bruising is expected and dose-dependent; extreme negative pressure or prolonged application can produce blistering. Users on anticoagulants have increased bruising risk.

records.name: Ventilation
records.description: The movement of gas in and out of the lungs — the process by which fresh gas reaches the alveoli and carbon dioxide is eliminated, driven by respiratory muscles and regulated by brainstem centers.
records.body:
**Ventilation** is the movement of gas in and out of the lungs — specifically, the process by which fresh gas reaches the alveoli and carbon dioxide is eliminated from the body. Adequate oxygen saturation does not guarantee adequate ventilation; these are independent processes that must be assessed separately.

Ventilation is driven by the respiratory muscles — primarily the diaphragm — creating negative intrathoracic pressure that draws air into the lungs. It is regulated by brainstem respiratory centers responding to CO2 levels, pH, and oxygen tension. When ventilation fails, CO2 accumulates (hypercapnia), leading to respiratory acidosis, altered mental status, and eventually respiratory arrest.

Ventilation is monitored at the bedside through:

- **Respiratory rate and pattern** — tachypnea, bradypnea, irregular patterns, or apnea
- **Tidal volume assessment** — visible chest rise, auscultation of breath sounds
- **[Capnography](./capnography.md)** — the most direct bedside measure of ventilation adequacy, tracking exhaled CO2 over time
- **Arterial blood gas (ABG)** — PaCO2 provides definitive measurement but requires blood sampling

Ventilation failure can result from:

- **Central drive depression** — opioids, sedatives, brainstem pathology reducing respiratory drive
- **Neuromuscular weakness** — myasthenia gravis, Guillain-Barre syndrome, residual paralysis
- **Mechanical obstruction** — upper-airway obstruction, severe bronchospasm, tension pneumothorax
- **Chest wall restriction** — obesity, flail chest, massive pleural effusion

The clinical trap is supplemental oxygen masking ventilation failure. A patient on high-flow oxygen may maintain SpO2 of 95% while their CO2 climbs to dangerous levels. Without capnography or serial blood gases, this deterioration is invisible until the patient becomes obtunded or arrests.

## Related terms

- [Oxygenation](./oxygenation.md) — the companion process assessed independently
- [Capnography](./capnography.md) — the primary bedside monitor for ventilation
- [Airway](./airway.md) — the passage through which ventilation occurs

records.name: Verbena hastata
records.description: Verbena hastata (blue vervain, Blue Verbena): a slightly cooling, drying, relaxing herb in the herbal materia medica, used as bitter, diaphoretic, diuretic, expectorant; nausea from very large doses.
records.body:
*Verbena hastata*, known as blue vervain, Blue Verbena, Simpler's Joy, Swamp Verbena, is recorded in this section's herbal materia medica as follows. Its properties and uses are the herbal tradition's account, drawn from the sources listed; they are not clinical evidence, and the warnings should be read before any use.

## Energetics

- slightly cooling
- drying
- relaxing

## Properties

- bitter
- diaphoretic
- diuretic
- expectorant
- hypotensive
- nervine
- relaxant
- opening

## Dosage forms

- **weak infusion:**
  - For nervine properties, 1 cup up to 3 times daily.
- **southern decoction:**
  - leaf or roots for lymphatic or diaphoretic properties
  - 1 cup as needed
- **tincture:**
  - Fresh leaf and flowers (1:2, 60% alcohol); dried leaf and flowers (1:5, 40% alcohol); 5-10 drops
  - If no results are seen, increase to 1-2 ml (0.2-0.4 tsp.) up to 4 times daily
- **glycertie:**
  - Dried leaf and flowers (1:6); 1-5 ml (0.2-1 tsp.) as needed 3-4 times daily
- **notes:**
  - **uses:**
    - nervous exhaustion after long-term stress
    - helpful for anger and tension, especially before period
    - some types of headaches, including migraines associated with PMS.
    - it's also a great herb for migraine headaches, especially combined with mad-dog skullcap (Scutellaria lateriflora) and other herbs as appropriate
    - surface and peripheral nervous systems
    - neuralgias and skin problems
    - It is helpful for many spasmodic nervous disorders, including tics, palsy, and Tourette's syndrome.
    - mild pain
    - colds, flu, and respiratory congestion
    - It is great for tight and tense muscles in stressed-out people who are holding themselves stiffly.
    - diaphoretic to sweat out fever
    - relax tension in nervous system
    - relax people who tend to hold onto anger and frustration for too long
  - **harvest:**
    - mid-summer, full bloom
    - Harvest the entire plant just below the lowest usable leaves and the stem down to where it starts getting tough and woody.

## Warnings

- nausea from very large doses
- large doses may promote miscarriage during pregnancy

## Sources

- The Modern Herbal Dispensatory
- Southeast Medicinal Plants

records.name: Waidan
records.description: External alchemy: the Chinese laboratory art of compounding elixirs from minerals such as cinnabar, mercury, and lead to confer health and immortality; the practice neidan later internalized.
records.body:
Waidan (外丹), external alchemy, is the Chinese laboratory art of making elixirs. It is "external" in contrast to [neidan](./neidan.md), inner alchemy. Its practitioners heated and transformed minerals in sealed crucibles in search of an elixir (dān, 丹, also "cinnabar") that would confer long life or immortality. The chief minerals were cinnabar (mercuric sulphide), mercury, lead, sulphur, and arsenic compounds.

Its classic early statement is Ge Hong's fourth-century *Baopuzi*, which ranks the elixir above every other method of transcendence. The art flourished through the Tang dynasty [@pregadio2008]. It was also dangerous. Several Tang emperors are believed to have died of elixir poisoning, and the toxicity of mercurial and arsenical preparations was part of why the language of the furnace, the ingredients, and the firing times turned inward. From the Song dynasty onward, neidan read that same language as a description of breath, attention, and the body's own [Three Treasures](./san-bao.md).

Waidan also left practical chemistry in Chinese pharmacy and technology. The early recipe for gunpowder is recorded in an alchemical context.

records.name: Waxy flexibility
records.description: One of the twelve DSM-5-TR catatonic signs: a limb or posture that yields to passive repositioning and is then held in place, associated with the retarded pole and, together with catalepsy, part of the clinical pattern distinguishing malignant catatonia from neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

philbrick1994.title: Malignant catatonia
philbrick1994.publication: Journal of Neuropsychiatry and Clinical Neurosciences

bush1996a.title: Catatonia. I. Rating scale and standardized examination

records.body:
Waxy flexibility is one of the twelve psychomotor signs named in the DSM-5-TR's three-of-twelve-sign diagnostic threshold for catatonia, listed alongside catalepsy, stupor, mutism, negativism, posturing, mannerism, stereotypy, agitation not influenced by external stimuli, grimacing, echolalia, and echopraxia. It belongs to the hypokinetic cluster of signs most associated with the retarded pole of the syndrome, though DSM-5-TR does not require it specifically for diagnosis — any three of the twelve signs suffice.

Waxy flexibility, together with catalepsy, features in the clinical pattern that reviews describe as distinguishing malignant catatonia from neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): malignant catatonia tends to show waxy flexibility and catalepsy along with a preceding prodrome of excitement or agitation before rigidity develops, while NMS classically begins with "lead-pipe" rigidity — a different quality of resistance, without the yielding, maintained-posture quality of waxy flexibility — and no preceding excited prodrome, tied temporally to antipsychotic exposure. This differential pattern is stated consistently across clinical reviews, but no single primary study establishing it with reported sensitivity or specificity was located, so it is best treated as clinical teaching rather than a validated instrument.

Because waxy flexibility is a qualitative, examiner-elicited sign — present or absent on passive manipulation of a limb — reliable use requires an operationalized definition and trained rating rather than unaided impression. The Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale was developed and validated to give catatonic signs operationalized definitions and a standardized examination technique, achieving high interrater reliability in its validation study: a 23-item total-score reliability of 0.93 (mean per-item agreement 88.2%) and a 14-item screening-instrument reliability of 0.95 (mean per-item agreement 92.7%). Absent that structure, waxy flexibility's presence, and its role in the malignant-catatonia/NMS differential, remain matters of individual clinical judgment rather than a validated, reproducible measurement.

## Related terms

- Catatonia — the syndrome this sign is one of twelve diagnostic criteria for
- Retarded catatonia — the pole most associated with this sign
- Malignant catatonia — the variant whose differential from neuroleptic malignant syndrome turns partly on this sign
- Bush-Francis catatonia rating scale — the instrument that operationalizes this sign for reliable rating

records.name: Wei Qi
records.description: 卫气 (wei qi) — defensive Qi, the protective force that circulates on the body's surface, warms the skin, regulates pore opening, and resists invasion by external pathogenic factors

kaptchuk2000.title: The Web That Has No Weaver

records.body:
Wei Qi (卫气, "defensive Qi" or "protective Qi") is the aspect of [Qi](qi.md) that circulates on the body's surface, between the skin and muscles, protecting against invasion by external pathogenic factors.
It is TCM's concept of the body's first line of defense — analogous to what biomedicine calls innate immunity and barrier function, though broader in scope.

## Functions

**Warming the skin and muscles**: Wei Qi maintains surface temperature.
When Wei Qi is weak, the patient feels cold and is easily chilled — not from internal [Yang deficiency](yang-deficiency.md) but from insufficient surface protection.

**Regulating pore opening and closing**: The opening and closing of the pores (cou li 腠理) controls sweating.
Wei Qi governs this regulation.
When Wei Qi is strong, pores open and close appropriately — sweating when the body needs to cool, closing when the body needs to retain heat.
When Wei Qi is weak, pores fail to close properly, producing spontaneous sweating (zi han 自汗) — sweating without exertion or heat.

**Resisting external pathogenic factors**: Wei Qi is the shield against the [six external causes](../../documents/articles/notes/etiology.md) (wind, cold, heat, dampness, dryness, summer heat).
When Wei Qi is sufficient, the body surface is sealed and pathogens cannot penetrate.
When Wei Qi is weak, the body surface is porous and vulnerable — the patient catches colds easily, is sensitive to drafts, and recovers slowly from upper respiratory infections.

## Production and circulation

Wei Qi is produced by the **Spleen** (from food Qi) and distributed by the **[Lung](zang-fu.md)** (which governs the body surface).
During the day, Wei Qi circulates on the body's exterior (yang regions) — this is why people are more alert and resistant during waking hours.
At night, Wei Qi retreats to the interior (yin regions) — this is why the body surface is more vulnerable during sleep and why fevers often spike at night.

This day-night circulation also explains why spontaneous sweating (daytime, Wei Qi failing on the surface) differs from night sweats (nighttime, [Yin deficiency](yin-deficiency.md) failing to anchor fluids) — they are different pathologies despite both involving sweat.

## Clinical significance

Wei Qi weakness is the TCM framework for understanding recurrent upper respiratory infections, allergic rhinitis, chronic sinusitis, and the general vulnerability to environmental influences that some patients exhibit.
A person who "catches everything" and is "always getting sick" has, in TCM terms, weak Wei Qi.

The primary tonifying herb for Wei Qi is **Huang Qi** (Astragalus membranaceus) — sweet, slightly warm, it tonifies Qi with a specific affinity for the body surface.
Modern research on astragalus has demonstrated immunomodulatory effects — increased natural killer cell activity, enhanced macrophage function — that correspond to the traditional claim of strengthened surface defense.

## See also

- [Qi](qi.md) — the broader concept of which Wei Qi is one variety
- [Zheng Qi](zheng-qi.md) — the total defensive capacity, of which Wei Qi is the surface component
- [Etiology](../../documents/articles/notes/etiology.md) — the external pathogenic factors Wei Qi resists
- [Lung](zang-fu.md) — the organ system that distributes Wei Qi
- [Yang Deficiency](yang-deficiency.md) — deeper warmth deficiency, distinguished from surface Wei Qi weakness

records.name: Wheeze
records.description: A musical, usually expiratory breath sound produced by turbulent airflow through narrowed lower airways, most commonly from bronchospasm but also from mucosal edema, mucus plugging, or foreign body.
records.body:
**Wheeze** is a musical breath sound, usually expiratory, produced by turbulent airflow through narrowed lower airways. It is most commonly associated with bronchospasm (as in asthma or reactive airway disease) but can result from any process that narrows the airways below the vocal cords.

Common causes of wheezing:

- **Bronchospasm** — smooth muscle contraction in the bronchial walls, as in acute asthma, COPD exacerbation, or anaphylaxis
- **Mucosal edema** — swelling of the airway lining from inflammation or allergic reaction
- **Mucus plugging** — excessive secretions partially obstructing airway lumens
- **Foreign body** — lodged in a bronchus, producing localized wheeze (unilateral wheezing is a red flag for foreign body aspiration)

The clinical interpretation of wheeze requires attention to several features:

- **Timing** — expiratory wheeze is typical of bronchospasm; inspiratory wheeze may indicate more severe obstruction or a different mechanism
- **Distribution** — diffuse bilateral wheeze suggests a systemic process (asthma, COPD); localized or unilateral wheeze suggests a focal obstruction (foreign body, tumor, mucus plug)
- **Severity** — the absence of wheeze in a patient with severe respiratory distress can indicate airflow so reduced that turbulence cannot be generated ("silent chest"), which is more dangerous than loud wheezing

Wheeze should be distinguished from [stridor](./stridor.md), which is typically inspiratory and indicates upper-airway narrowing. Both represent turbulent airflow through a narrowed passage, but stridor localizes the problem above the vocal cords while wheeze localizes it below.

Treatment depends on the underlying cause. Bronchospasm responds to bronchodilators (beta-agonists such as albuterol) and, in severe cases, systemic corticosteroids and epinephrine. Foreign body obstruction may require bronchoscopic removal. The sound itself is a sign, not a target — treating the wheeze means treating its cause.

## Related terms

- [Stridor](./stridor.md) — upper-airway narrowing sound
- [Airway](./airway.md) — the passage whose narrowing produces wheeze
- [Ventilation](./ventilation.md) — the process that lower-airway narrowing impedes

records.name: Wu Xing (Five Phases)
records.description: A classification system of five functional categories (wood, fire, earth, metal, water) linked by generating and controlling cycles that describe patterns of transformation in TCM

kaptchuk2000.title: The Web That Has No Weaver

records.body:
Wu Xing (五行), the Five Phases, is a classification system in [traditional Chinese medicine](traditional-chinese-medicine.md) that describes cycles of generation and restraint among five functional categories: wood, fire, earth, metal, and water.
The standard translation "Five Elements" is misleading — *xing* means "movement" or "phase," not "element."
These aren't substances in the Greek sense but patterns of transformation [@kaptchuk2000].

Each phase corresponds to a cluster of associations: an organ-function system, a season, an emotion, a sensory organ, a taste, a color, a direction.
Wood corresponds to the Liver system, spring, anger, the eyes, sourness.
Fire corresponds to the Heart system, summer, joy, the tongue, bitterness.
Earth corresponds to the Spleen system, late summer, overthinking, the mouth, sweetness.
Metal corresponds to the Lung system, autumn, grief, the nose, pungency.
Water corresponds to the Kidney system, winter, fear, the ears, saltiness.

The phases relate through two cycles.
The *generating cycle* (sheng 生) describes how each phase supports the next: wood feeds fire, fire creates earth (ash), earth yields metal (ore), metal enriches water (minerals), water nourishes wood.
The *controlling cycle* (ke 克) describes how each phase restrains another: wood parts earth (roots), earth dams water, water extinguishes fire, fire melts metal, metal cuts wood.
Health depends on both cycles operating smoothly.
When the generating cycle falters, a downstream phase weakens.
When the controlling cycle fails, a phase dominates unchecked.

[Nathan Sivin](../../general/people/nathan-sivin.md) observed that the Five Phases operate as a system of correspondences rather than causes [@sivin1987].
A practitioner who identifies a "wood overacting on earth" pattern — irritability, digestive disturbance, a wiry pulse — isn't claiming that an entity called "wood" is attacking an entity called "earth."
They're describing a recognizable clinical configuration and using the Five Phases vocabulary to locate it within a system of relationships that suggests both the mechanism and the treatment principle.

## Related terms

- [Yin and Yang](./yin-yang.md) — the complementary polarity framework that operates alongside the Five Phases
- [Qi](./qi.md) — the circulating force whose behavior the Five Phases classify
- [San Bao](./san-bao.md) — the Three Treasures, another diagnostic axis
- [Traditional Chinese Medicine](traditional-chinese-medicine.md) — the medical tradition that uses this framework
