records.name: Blood (Xue)
records.description: 血 — the dense, nourishing fluid in TCM that moistens tissues, anchors Shen, and circulates through the meridians — functionally distinct from the biomedical concept of blood, though anatomically overlapping

kaptchuk2000.title: The Web That Has No Weaver

records.body:
Blood (xue 血) in [Traditional Chinese Medicine](traditional-chinese-medicine.md) is the dense, nourishing fluid that circulates through the [meridians](meridians.md) and blood vessels, moistening and nourishing the tissues, organs, skin, hair, and sense organs.
It is functionally richer than the biomedical concept of blood — TCM Blood includes not just the red fluid in vessels but the nourishing, moistening, and consciousness-anchoring functions that the fluid performs.

## How Blood differs from the biomedical concept

The TCM concept overlaps with but is not identical to the biomedical concept.
Biomedical blood is a tissue: red cells, white cells, platelets, plasma, measurable by CBC and serology.
TCM Blood is a functional category: the body's capacity to nourish, moisten, and anchor awareness.
A patient can have a normal CBC and still present with TCM Blood deficiency — pale face, dry skin, poor memory, insomnia, scanty menstruation — because the functional capacity the concept names is broader than the laboratory values.

## Production

Blood is produced through the collaboration of multiple organ-function systems: - The **Spleen** transforms food into Food [Qi](qi.md) (gu qi), the raw material for Blood - The **Heart** transforms Food Qi into Blood proper through its warming, circulating function - **[Jing](jing.md)** (stored in the Kidney) contributes to Blood production — TCM states "Jing and Blood share a common source"

This production chain explains why Spleen deficiency (poor digestion, poor absorption) leads to Blood deficiency over time: if the raw material is inadequate, the final product is insufficient.

## Functions

**Nourishing**: Blood moistens and nourishes every tissue.
Muscles, tendons, skin, hair, nails, and the sense organs all depend on Blood for their vitality.
Blood deficiency produces dryness, brittleness, and loss of luster — dry skin, brittle nails, blurred vision, muscle cramps.

**Moistening**: Where [Qi](qi.md) warms and moves, Blood cools and moistens.
The Qi-Blood pair is another expression of the Yang-Yin dynamic: Qi is the potential, warming, moving principle; Blood is the nourishing, cooling, anchoring principle.
Each depends on the other — Qi moves Blood (without Qi, Blood stagnates), Blood nourishes Qi (without Blood, Qi has no substance to animate).

**Anchoring Shen**: The Heart "stores" [Shen](shen.md) (awareness, coherent consciousness), and Blood is the medium in which Shen resides.
Adequate Heart Blood provides the substrate for settled, coherent awareness.
When Heart Blood is deficient, Shen becomes unanchored — producing insomnia, anxiety, restlessness, poor memory, dream-disturbed sleep, and a sense of vague unease.

## Blood pathology

**Blood deficiency** (xue xu 血虚): Insufficient Blood.
Pale complexion, dizziness, blurred vision, insomnia, scanty or absent menstruation, pale tongue, thin pulse.
Common in women (menstruation depletes Blood), the elderly, and the chronically ill.

**[Blood stasis](../../../../../../content/text/glossary/terms/blood-stasis.md)** (xue yu 血瘀): Blood that has stopped flowing properly — stagnant, obstructed, or extravasated.
Fixed sharp pain, dark complexion, purple tongue, choppy pulse.
Treated by blood-invigorating herbs including [Hu Zhang](hu-zhang.md).

**Blood heat** (xue re 血热): Heat entering the Blood level, causing reckless bleeding, skin eruptions, agitation.
The Blood is "boiling" — moving chaotically rather than in its proper channels.

## See also

- [Qi](qi.md) — the motive force that moves Blood
- [Jing](jing.md) — the substrate that contributes to Blood production
- [Shen](shen.md) — the awareness that Blood anchors
- [Blood Stasis](../../../../../../content/text/glossary/terms/blood-stasis.md) — the pathological pattern of obstructed Blood
- [Zang-Fu](zang-fu.md) — the organ systems that produce and circulate Blood

records.name: Yang Deficiency
records.description: 阳虚 (yang xu) — the depletion of the body's warming, activating, protecting force, producing cold signs, fatigue, fluid accumulation, and a deep slow pulse — the pattern of insufficient metabolic fire

kaptchuk2000.title: The Web That Has No Weaver

records.body:
Yang deficiency (yang xu 阳虚) is the depletion of the body's Yang — the warming, activating, transforming, protecting aspect of the [Yin-Yang](yin-yang.md) dynamic.
When Yang is deficient, the body lacks the metabolic fire to warm itself, transform nutrients, circulate fluids, and protect against invasion.
Cold signs predominate — not because an external cold pathogen is present, but because the body's internal warmth is insufficient.

## Presentation

The signs of Yang deficiency reflect the loss of Yang's qualities — warmth, activity, transformation:

- **Cold**: Feeling cold, especially in the extremities (cold hands and feet), the low back, and the abdomen.
  The patient seeks warmth — warm rooms, warm drinks, warm clothing
- **Fatigue**: Profound tiredness, worse in the morning, improved somewhat by warmth and gentle activity.
  The body lacks the activating force to sustain effort
- **Pale complexion**: A bright, white pallor — not the dull paleness of Blood deficiency, but the whiteness of insufficient warming
- **Fluid accumulation**: Yang transforms and moves fluids.
  When Yang is deficient, fluids accumulate — edema (especially in the legs), copious clear urination, loose watery stools, clear watery nasal discharge
- **Tongue**: Pale, swollen (puffy), often with tooth marks at the margins (the swollen tongue presses against the teeth).
  Coating is white and moist.
  The moisture and pallor reflect cold and fluid accumulation
- **Pulse**: Deep (chen 沉) and slow (chi 迟).
  The pulse retreats from the surface (insufficient Yang to push it outward) and slows (insufficient fire to drive circulation)

## Yang deficiency by organ system

**Kidney Yang deficiency**: The most fundamental.
The Kidney is the root of Yang for the whole body — the "gate of vitality" (ming men 命门).
Kidney Yang deficiency produces: cold low back and knees, frequent copious clear urination (especially at night — nocturia), impotence or diminished libido, infertility, edema in the legs, dawn diarrhea (wu geng xie 五更泻 — diarrhea at 5 AM, when Yang should be rising but cannot).
This pattern describes the metabolic slowdown of advanced aging in TCM terms.

**Spleen Yang deficiency**: The Spleen transforms food and fluids.
When Spleen Yang is deficient, transformation fails — producing poor appetite, abdominal bloating after eating, loose stools with undigested food, a heavy feeling in the limbs, and edema.
The Spleen "cannot hold" blood in the vessels, so bruising, heavy menstruation, or blood in the stool may occur.
This is the pattern underlying many chronic digestive disorders.

**Heart Yang deficiency**: The Heart circulates Blood and houses [Shen](shen.md).
Heart Yang deficiency produces: palpitations, chest oppression, cold sweats, a feeling of emptiness in the chest, and in severe cases, cyanosis (blue-purple lips and nails).
This pattern corresponds to congestive heart failure in biomedical terms.

## Causes

Yang depletes through: - **Aging**: Yang naturally declines with age, typically after Yin has begun declining.
The progressive loss of warmth, vitality, and metabolic vigor in old age is Yang deficiency - **Chronic illness**: Prolonged disease consumes Yang resources - **Overexposure to cold**: Living in cold environments, consuming excessive cold or raw foods, cold-water swimming without adequate recovery - **Overwork**: Physical overexertion (as opposed to the mental overwork that depletes Yin) exhausts Yang - **Constitutional weakness**: Some individuals are born with weaker Yang — a TCM framework for understanding constitutional variation

## Treatment principle: warm Yang, tonify the Kidney

Yang-tonifying (bu yang 补阳) herbs are warm or hot, often with sweet and pungent tastes.
They add warmth and metabolic fire to the depleted system:

- **Fu Zi** (prepared aconite root) — the strongest Yang-warming herb; "rescues devastated Yang."
  Toxic if improperly prepared; used only in processed form
- **Rou Gui** (cinnamon bark) — warms the Kidney, strengthens Ming Men fire
- **Du Zhong** (Eucommia bark) — tonifies Kidney Yang, strengthens low back and knees
- **Bu Gu Zhi** (Psoralea fruit) — warms Kidney Yang, stops diarrhea
- **Gan Jiang** (dried ginger) — warms the middle burner, rescues Spleen Yang

The classical formula is **Jin Gui Shen Qi Wan** (金匮肾气丸, "Kidney Qi Pill from the Golden Cabinet") — Liu Wei Di Huang Wan (the Yin-nourishing base) with added Fu Zi and Rou Gui to warm Yang.
This elegant structure — nourishing Yin while warming Yang — reflects the principle that Yang cannot be strengthened without a Yin foundation.

## See also

- [Yin-Yang](yin-yang.md) — the dynamic that Yang deficiency disrupts
- [Yin Deficiency](yin-deficiency.md) — the complementary deficiency pattern
- [Qi](qi.md) — Yang deficiency is a deeper level of Qi deficiency
- [Zheng Qi](zheng-qi.md) — the total functional capacity that Yang deficiency weakens
- [Pattern Diagnosis](../../documents/articles/notes/pattern-diagnosis.md) — the diagnostic framework

records.name: Yijinjing
records.description: The "Sinew-Changing Classic": a set of strengthening and stretching exercises, legendarily from Bodhidharma at Shaolin, historically a late-Ming text, and one of the four standardized health qigong forms.

shahar2008.title: The Shaolin Monastery: History, Religion, and the Chinese Martial Arts

records.body:
Yijinjing (易筋經), the "Sinew-Changing Classic", is a moving [qigong](./qigong.md) set. Its exercises alternate sustained effort against the body's own resistance with stretching, and they aim, in their own account, to transform the sinews: weak and slack into strong and supple.

Its legend credits Bodhidharma, the Indian monk said to have brought Chan Buddhism to the Shaolin monastery. The attribution does not survive historical study. The text is a Ming-dynasty composition, dated to the 1620s, that joins Daoist [daoyin](./daoyin.md) and inner-alchemical ideas to the Shaolin martial tradition's growing prestige [@shahar2008].

The Chinese Health Qigong Association's 2003 standard form has twelve movements. Examples are "Wei Tuo presenting the pestle", "plucking a star", and "nine ghosts drawing sabres". It is practised slowly, with sustained stretches and twists of the spine, and like every form it regulates body, breath, and mind together, as the [three regulations](./san-tiao.md) describe. Of the four standard forms it is the most muscular.

records.name: Yin Deficiency
records.description: 阴虚 (yin xu) — the depletion of the body's cooling, moistening, anchoring substance, producing heat signs from insufficient cooling rather than excess heat — night sweats, dry mouth, five-palm heat, and a thin rapid pulse

kaptchuk2000.title: The Web That Has No Weaver

records.body:
Yin deficiency (yin xu 阴虚) is the depletion of the body's Yin — the cooling, moistening, nourishing, anchoring aspect of the [Yin-Yang](yin-yang.md) dynamic.
When Yin is deficient, its complementary opposite (Yang — the warming, activating, ascending principle) is relatively unopposed, producing signs of heat.
But this is **empty heat** (xu re 虚热) — heat from insufficient cooling, not from excess fire.
The distinction is critical because the treatment is completely different: empty heat is treated by nourishing Yin (replenishing the cooling substrate), not by clearing heat (which would further deplete an already deficient system).

## Presentation

The signs of Yin deficiency reflect the loss of Yin's qualities — moisture, coolness, anchoring:

- **Night sweats**: The body loses its ability to contain fluids, particularly at night when Yin predominates.
  Sweating during sleep that soaks the sheets is a hallmark
- **Five-palm heat** (wu xin fan re 五心烦热): Heat sensation in the palms of the hands, soles of the feet, and the chest.
  The extremities radiate heat that the patient describes as "burning from inside"
- **Afternoon/evening fever**: Low-grade temperature elevation in the afternoon or evening, when Yin should be ascending.
  This tidal fever (chao re 潮热) is characteristic
- **Dry mouth and throat**: Particularly at night.
  The patient may sip water frequently but without quenching thirst
- **Malar flush**: A reddish flush on the cheekbones — not the full facial redness of excess heat, but a localized, dusky redness
- **Tongue**: Red, with little or no coating.
  The coating is Yin — when Yin is deficient, the coating thins or disappears, leaving a bare, red tongue body.
  This is the most reliable diagnostic sign
- **Pulse**: Thin (xi 细) and rapid (shuo 数).
  The thinness reflects Yin depletion (less fluid volume); the rapidity reflects relative heat

## Yin deficiency by organ system

Each [Zang-Fu](zang-fu.md) system has its own Yin deficiency presentation:

**Kidney Yin deficiency**: The archetype.
The Kidney stores [Jing](jing.md) and is the root of Yin for the whole body.
Kidney Yin deficiency produces: low back ache, weak knees, tinnitus, diminished hearing, premature graying, poor memory, night sweats, nocturnal emissions, scanty dark urine.
It is the pattern of aging — Yin naturally declines with age, and Kidney Yin is the first to show it.

**Liver Yin deficiency**: The Liver stores [Blood](xue.md), and Blood is a Yin substance.
Liver Yin deficiency produces: dry eyes, blurred vision, dizziness, numbness or tingling in the limbs, brittle nails, scanty menstruation, irritability from heat.
When severe, it progresses to Liver Yang rising — headaches, hypertension, tinnitus.

**Lung Yin deficiency**: The Lung governs moisture distribution.
Lung Yin deficiency produces: dry cough (possibly with scanty, sticky, blood-streaked sputum), dry throat, hoarse voice, dry skin.
This is the pattern of chronic dry cough that worsens at night.

**Stomach Yin deficiency**: The Stomach needs fluids to digest.
Stomach Yin deficiency produces: dry mouth, thirst with desire to sip, poor appetite despite hunger, dry stools, a peeled (mirror-like) tongue coating in the center.
This pattern is common after febrile illness that has consumed fluids.

## Causes

Yin depletes through: - **Chronic illness**: Prolonged disease consumes the body's resources - **Overwork without rest**: Yin is restored through rest; chronic overwork without adequate recovery depletes it.
TCM specifically identifies excessive mental work (overthinking) as Yin-depleting - **Aging**: Natural Yin decline is a TCM description of biological aging - **Blood loss**: Blood is a Yin substance; significant blood loss depletes Yin - **Unresolved heat disease**: Febrile illness that lingers consumes Yin — "heat scorches Yin" - **Emotional exhaustion**: Prolonged anxiety, grief, or fear depletes Yin

## Treatment principle: nourish Yin

Yin-nourishing (zi yin 滋阴) herbs are sweet, cool, and moistening.
They are the opposite of the bitter, cold, draining herbs used for excess heat — they replenish rather than drain.
Key herbs include:

- **Shu Di Huang** (prepared Rehmannia) — the primary Kidney Yin tonic
- **Mai Men Dong** (Ophiopogon) — nourishes Lung and Stomach Yin
- **Gou Qi Zi** (Lycium / goji berry) — nourishes Liver and Kidney Yin
- **Nu Zhen Zi** (Ligustrum) — nourishes Liver and Kidney Yin gently
- **Bai Shao** (white peony) — nourishes Liver Blood and Yin

The classical formula is **Liu Wei Di Huang Wan** (六味地黄丸, "Six-Ingredient Pill with Rehmannia") — the foundational Kidney Yin tonic formula, consisting of three nourishing herbs and three draining herbs in elegant balance.

## See also

- [Yin-Yang](yin-yang.md) — the dynamic that Yin deficiency disrupts
- [Yang Deficiency](yang-deficiency.md) — the complementary deficiency pattern
- [Jing](jing.md) — the constitutional substrate closely related to Yin
- [Blood (Xue)](xue.md) — a Yin substance whose deficiency overlaps with Yin deficiency
- [Pattern Diagnosis](../../documents/articles/notes/pattern-diagnosis.md) — the diagnostic framework
- [Zheng Qi](zheng-qi.md) — the total functional capacity that Yin deficiency weakens

records.name: Yin and Yang
records.description: Complementary relational polarities (shaded/sunlit, rest/activity, cold/heat) used in TCM to describe dynamic balance and diagnose clinical patterns

kaptchuk2000.title: The Web That Has No Weaver: Understanding Chinese Medicine

unschuld2003.title: Huang Di Nei Jing Su Wen: Nature, Knowledge, Imagery in an Ancient Chinese Medical Text

records.body:
Yin and Yang (陰陽) are complementary aspects of any phenomenon in [traditional Chinese medicine](traditional-chinese-medicine.md). The characters originally referred to the shaded and sunlit sides of a hill — and this concrete image carries the logic: yin and yang are not substances or forces but relative descriptions. Nothing is yin or yang in itself; it is yin or yang in relation to something else.

In TCM, yin and yang organize clinical observation. The body's processes divide along yin-yang polarities: rest and activity, cold and heat, interior and exterior, depletion and excess, structure and function. Health is dynamic balance between the two. Illness arises when one aspect dominates, the other depletes, or the relationship between them loses its responsiveness [@kaptchuk2000].

The framework is diagnostic, not ontological. When a practitioner identifies a "yin deficiency" pattern — heat signs, dryness, restlessness, a thin rapid pulse — they aren't claiming that a substance called "yin" has leaked out. They're describing a configuration: the body's cooling, moistening, and quieting functions have lost ground relative to its warming, drying, and activating functions. The treatment principle follows from the description: nourish yin, clear deficiency heat, restore the balance.

Yin and yang are not static categories. They transform into each other: extreme cold can produce heat, prolonged activity leads to collapse into rest, acute excess can deplete into deficiency. This dynamic quality distinguishes the framework from simple binary classification. Yin and yang name a relationship, and the diagnostic question is always about the *relationship* — not about which box a symptom falls into [@unschuld2003].

## Related terms

- [Qi](./qi.md) — the circulating force whose yin-yang balance determines its clinical behavior
- [Wu Xing](./wu-xing.md) — the Five Phases, a complementary classification system
- [San Bao](./san-bao.md) — the Three Treasures, another axis of TCM assessment
- [Traditional Chinese Medicine](traditional-chinese-medicine.md) — the medical tradition that uses this framework

records.name: ying qi
records.description: 營氣 — Nutritive Qi, the refined portion of Food Qi that circulates inside the vessels alongside Blood, nourishing the organs and forming part of Blood's own substance
records.body:
Ying Qi (營氣, Nutritive Qi or Construction Qi) is the refined, clear portion of the Qi extracted from food and drink that circulates inside the blood vessels, nourishing the internal organs and the whole body, and contributing directly to the formation of Blood. It is paired throughout TCM literature with Wei Qi (衛氣, Defensive Qi), the coarser, more mobile portion of the same source Qi that circulates outside the vessels and at the body's surface — the two together forming a single system distinguished by location and function rather than substance.

## Classical basis

The foundational description of both Ying Qi and Wei Qi, and of their shared origin and contrasting circulation, is given in the *Huang Di Nei Jing, Ling Shu*, Chapter 18, 營衛生會 (*Ying Wei Sheng Hui*, "The Meeting of Nutritive and Defensive Qi"): "人受氣於穀，穀入於胃，以傳與肺，五藏六府，皆以受氣，其清者為營，濁者為衛。營在脈中，衛在脈外" — a person receives Qi from grain; grain enters the stomach and is transmitted to the Lung; the five Zang and six Fu organs all receive Qi from it; its clear portion becomes Ying, its turbid portion becomes Wei; Ying travels inside the vessels, Wei travels outside the vessels. The same chapter gives Ying Qi's specific function: "營氣者，泌其津液，注之於脈，化以為血，以榮四末，內注五臟六腑" — Nutritive Qi secretes body fluid, pours it into the vessels, transforms it into Blood, nourishes the four limbs, and flows inward to irrigate the five Zang and six Fu organs.

## Relationship to Blood

Ying Qi's defining clinical significance is its direct participation in the formation of Blood — the *Ling Shu* passage above states explicitly that Ying Qi "transforms into Blood" (化以為血). TCM textbooks accordingly describe Ying Qi and Blood as closely related, near-interchangeable substances circulating together within the same vessels: where Qi in general is said to move Blood, and Blood is said to nourish Qi, Ying Qi in particular is described as inseparable from Blood in circulation, to the point that clinical patterns are sometimes named jointly as "Ying-Blood level" disorders, especially in the Four Levels (衛氣營血) framework used to track the progression of febrile disease from the body's surface to its interior.

## Circulation

Ying Qi circulates in a fixed, cyclical pathway through the twelve regular meridians, moving in sequence from one meridian to the next and completing a full circuit of the body in coordination with Wei Qi's separate, day-night-alternating circulation pattern. This orderly, unceasing circulation is described in the *Ling Shu* passage's closing image: "營周不休，五十而復大會，陰陽相貫，如環無端" — nutritive Qi circulates without cease, completing fifty circuits before the great reunion [of Ying and Wei], yin and yang penetrating each other continuously, like a ring without end.

## Clinical significance

Ying Qi deficiency presents similarly to Blood deficiency, given the two substances' close relationship: pallor, fatigue, numbness of the limbs, and poor nourishment of tissue generally. Because Ying Qi is drawn from the same source (Gu Qi, extracted by Spleen transformation) as Wei Qi, chronic Spleen dysfunction that impairs Yun Hua reduces both Ying and Wei Qi together, though a patient's presentation may emphasize one deficiency pattern over the other — poor surface defense and susceptibility to colds pointing toward Wei Qi weakness, versus pallor and numbness pointing toward Ying Qi/Blood weakness.

## Biomedical convergence, honestly graded

The Ying/Wei division — one portion of a shared source circulating within vessels and nourishing tissue, the other circulating outside vessels in a surface-defensive role — bears a loose structural resemblance to the biomedical distinction between the intravascular compartment (plasma proteins, circulating nutrients, and cells confined to the bloodstream) and tissue-level or surface-level immune and barrier function (skin, mucosa, innate surface defenses). This is, at most, a resonance of structure: TCM arrived at the Ying/Wei division from the observation that some qualities of vitality track with circulation-in-the-vessels and others track with the body's exterior resilience against invasion, not from any anatomical distinction between plasma and interstitial or surface compartments. The two frameworks are not describing the same substances by different names; they are two independent systems that both found it useful, for their own diagnostic purposes, to separate an "inside the vessel" function from an "at the surface" function.

records.name: yun hua
records.description: 運化 — the Spleen's function of transforming ingested food and fluid into usable Qi, Blood, and Body Fluids, and transporting the resulting essence to the rest of the body
records.body:
Yun Hua (運化) names the Spleen's core physiological function in Traditional Chinese Medicine: the transformation (化, hua) of ingested food and drink into usable substance, and the transportation (運, yun) of that substance to where the body needs it. The two characters are conventionally paired as a single compound term, but they name two distinct operations that the Spleen performs together — extraction and distribution — and TCM clinicians distinguish failures of one from failures of the other when a patient's presentation calls for it.

## Classical basis

The physiological sequence Yun Hua describes is given directly in the *Huang Di Nei Jing, Su Wen*, Chapter 21, 經脈別論 (*Jing Mai Bie Lun*): "飲入於胃，游溢精氣，上輸於脾，脾氣散精，上歸於肺" — drink enters the stomach; its essential qi overflows and is transmitted upward to the Spleen; the Spleen's qi disperses that essence upward to the Lung. This single sentence is the standard textbook citation for the mechanism, and later passages in the same chapter extend the same logic to solid food. The Spleen and Stomach's joint role as the digestive seat of the body is given its classical administrative metaphor in *Su Wen* Chapter 8, 靈蘭秘典論 (*Ling Lan Mi Dian Lun*): "脾胃者，倉廩之官，五味出焉" — the Spleen-Stomach is the Granary Official, from which the five flavors emerge. The formula that elevates this function to the center of TCM physiology as a whole is Li Dongyuan's (李東垣) *Pi Wei Lun* (《脾胃論》, *Treatise on the Spleen and Stomach*, Jin-Yuan dynasty): "脾胃為後天之本，氣血生化之源" — the Spleen-Stomach is the root of postnatal life, the source from which Qi and Blood are engendered and transformed.

## The two operations

**Transformation (化)**: The Spleen extracts the essential, usable portion of ingested food and drink — termed Gu Qi (穀氣, grain qi) — separating it from what cannot be used. This extracted essence is the raw material for Qi, Blood, and Body Fluids (Jin Ye); without adequate transformation, the raw material for all three is insufficient regardless of how much food is eaten.

**Transportation (運)**: The Spleen distributes the transformed essence to the Lung (which further disperses it to the skin and body surface), to the Heart (which further transforms Food Qi into Blood proper), and to the muscles and limbs, which the Spleen is separately said to govern. Transportation also includes the Spleen's role in moving fluids as part of the body's overall water metabolism, working alongside the Lung and Kidney.

The Spleen's transformation and transportation together are also credited with keeping fluids and blood moving in their proper channels rather than pooling or leaking — a function closely related to, but classically distinguished from, the Spleen's separately named function of Tong Xue (統血, holding Blood within the vessels).

## Clinical significance

Yun Hua failure is one of the most common findings in TCM clinical practice, presenting as poor appetite, bloating and distension after eating, loose stools, fatigue, a heavy or foggy sensation in the head and limbs, and a pale, possibly swollen tongue with a thin white coating. Because Yun Hua supplies the raw material for Qi, Blood, and Jin Ye, its failure cascades: inadequate transformation produces Qi deficiency and Blood deficiency downstream, while inadequate transportation of fluids produces Dampness, and — if the Dampness thickens and congeals over time — Phlegm. The saying "the Spleen is the source of Phlegm" describes exactly this progression: a Spleen that fails at Yun Hua does not merely under-produce nourishment, it also fails to move the fluids it cannot use, leaving them to accumulate pathologically.

Because Yun Hua is functionally so close to digestion and absorption in the biomedical sense, TCM treatment for its failure — tonify Spleen Qi, dry Dampness, use warming and aromatic herbs that support digestive transformation — overlaps substantially with dietary and digestive management in a biomedical frame, even though the underlying theoretical accounts (Qi transformation versus enzymatic digestion and intestinal absorption) describe the process at entirely different levels.

## Biomedical convergence, honestly graded

Yun Hua's clinical picture — poor appetite, bloating, loose stools, fatigue following meals — overlaps substantially with what biomedicine would investigate as malabsorption, dysbiosis, or functional dyspepsia, and TCM's historical anatomical category 脾 is documented to have spanned both the biomedical spleen and the pancreas (see the *Nan Jing*, Difficulty 42, and Wang Qingren's *Yi Lin Gai Cuo* on this history), which makes a functional resemblance to pancreatic exocrine digestion unsurprising rather than mysterious. This is a resonance of clinical picture and historical anatomy, not of mechanism: Yun Hua as TCM describes it is a single unified process of extraction-and-distribution attributed to one organ-function system, where biomedicine distributes the same territory across gastric digestion, pancreatic exocrine enzyme secretion, small-intestinal absorption, and hepatic/portal processing — several separately regulated systems rather than one. The overlap is real and clinically useful to notice; it is not evidence that TCM's single-organ account was secretly a biomedical account in disguise.

records.name: Zang-Fu (Organ-Function Systems)
records.description: TCM's organ-function systems — five yin (zang) and six yang (fu) organs defined by functional relationships rather than anatomy, organized through Five Phase generating and restraining cycles

kaptchuk2000.title: The Web That Has No Weaver: Understanding Chinese Medicine

unschuld2003.title: Huang Di Nei Jing Su Wen: Nature, Knowledge, Imagery in an Ancient Chinese Medical Text

records.body:
**Zang-Fu** (臟腑) are the organ-function systems of [traditional Chinese medicine](traditional-chinese-medicine.md). They share names with anatomical organs — Liver, Heart, Spleen, Lung, Kidney, Stomach, and so on — but they are defined by their functional relationships rather than their anatomical location. The TCM Liver is not the anatomical organ in the right upper quadrant; it is a functional system governing the smooth flow of [Qi](./qi.md), the storage of blood, and the regulation of emotional and somatic tension. Whether the TCM Liver and the biomedical liver refer to the same thing is not a question TCM's framework is designed to answer [@kaptchuk2000].

## Zang and Fu: yin and yang organs

The system is organized into two categories:

**Zang** (臟) — the five yin organs. These are solid, storage-oriented organs that produce, transform, and store Qi, blood, [Jing](./jing.md), and body fluids. They are the body's core functional systems:

| Zang organ | Element | Core functions |
|---|---|---|
| **Liver** (肝) | Wood | Ensures smooth flow of Qi; stores blood; governs sinews and tendons; opens to the eyes; associated with planning, decision-making, and emotional flexibility |
| **Heart** (心) | Fire | Governs blood circulation; houses [Shen](./shen.md) (awareness, coherence); opens to the tongue; associated with joy, clarity, and relational presence |
| **Spleen** (脾) | Earth | Transforms and transports food and fluids; produces Qi and blood from nourishment; holds blood in vessels; governs muscles and limbs; associated with thought and concentration |
| **Lung** (肺) | Metal | Governs Qi and respiration; distributes Wei Qi (defensive Qi) to the body surface; regulates water passages; opens to the nose; associated with grief and the capacity to let go |
| **Kidney** (腎) | Water | Stores Jing (prenatal and postnatal); governs growth, reproduction, and aging; produces marrow (which fills the bones and brain); opens to the ears; associated with will, fear, and constitutional resilience |

**Fu** (腑) — the six yang organs. These are hollow, transport-oriented organs that receive, digest, transform, and excrete. They process rather than store:

| Fu organ | Paired zang | Core functions |
|---|---|---|
| **Gallbladder** (膽) | Liver | Stores and secretes bile; associated with courage and decision-making |
| **Small Intestine** (小腸) | Heart | Separates pure from impure in digestion; sorts the usable from the waste |
| **Stomach** (胃) | Spleen | Receives and ripens food; the "sea of grain and water"; initial decomposition |
| **Large Intestine** (大腸) | Lung | Transports waste and reabsorbs fluids; governs elimination |
| **Urinary Bladder** (膀胱) | Kidney | Stores and excretes urine; transforms fluids through Kidney Qi |
| **San Jiao / Triple Burner** (三焦) | Pericardium | Governs water passages and the movement of Qi between the three body cavities (upper, middle, lower); has no anatomical equivalent |

The Pericardium (xin bao 心包) functions as a protective envelope for the Heart and is sometimes counted as a sixth zang organ, bringing the total to six pairs along the twelve [meridians](./meridians.md).

## Functional relationships, not anatomical descriptions

The defining feature of the Zang-Fu system is that it describes what organs do in relation to each other, not what they are as structures. Consider the Spleen:

In biomedicine, the spleen is a lymphoid organ involved in immune function and blood filtration. In TCM, the Spleen is the system responsible for transforming food into usable energy (Qi and blood), transporting fluids, holding blood within the vessels, and maintaining muscle tone. TCM "Spleen deficiency" manifests as fatigue, poor digestion, loose stools, bruising, and a feeling of heaviness — a functional pattern that does not correspond to any single biomedical diagnosis but describes a recognizable clinical presentation.

This functional orientation means that TCM diagnoses are patterns, not diseases. "Liver Qi stagnation" is not a disease entity but a pattern of functional disruption: irritability, sighing, distension in the ribcage, menstrual irregularity, a wiry pulse. The pattern can manifest across multiple biomedical diagnoses (tension headaches, irritable bowel syndrome, premenstrual syndrome, intercostal neuralgia) because it describes a functional dynamic, not a structural pathology.

## Interactions among Zang-Fu systems

The Zang-Fu systems do not operate in isolation. Their interactions follow the generative and restraining cycles of the Five Phases (Wu Xing 五行):

- **Generative cycle** (sheng 生): Wood generates Fire, Fire generates Earth, Earth generates Metal, Metal generates Water, Water generates Wood. Clinically: the Liver supports the Heart; the Heart supports the Spleen; the Spleen supports the Lung; the Lung supports the Kidney; the Kidney supports the Liver.
- **Restraining cycle** (ke 克): Wood restrains Earth, Earth restrains Water, Water restrains Fire, Fire restrains Metal, Metal restrains Wood. Clinically: the Liver restrains the Spleen (excessive Liver Qi can impair digestion); the Spleen restrains the Kidney; and so on.

These cycles provide a framework for understanding how dysfunction in one system affects others. "Liver overacting on Spleen" describes a common clinical pattern where emotional tension (Liver) disrupts digestion (Spleen) — a pattern that biomedical research on the gut-brain axis is now investigating through different vocabulary.

## Diagnostic application

Zang-Fu theory structures clinical assessment in TCM. The practitioner evaluates which systems are involved, whether the pattern is one of excess or deficiency, heat or cold, interior or exterior. A patient presenting with insomnia, anxiety, heart palpitations, and a red-tipped tongue suggests Heart Fire — excess heat in the Heart system disturbing Shen. A patient presenting with fatigue, poor appetite, loose stools, and a pale tongue suggests Spleen Qi deficiency — the Spleen lacking the operational energy to transform and transport.

The diagnostic power of the system lies in its capacity to connect symptoms that biomedicine might distribute across multiple specialists. The TCM practitioner sees one pattern where the biomedical system might see separate consultations for gastroenterology, psychiatry, and gynecology. Whether this integration produces better clinical outcomes is an empirical question; that it produces a different and sometimes illuminating clinical picture is not in dispute.

## Related

- [Meridians](./meridians.md) — the channels connecting Zang-Fu systems to each other and to the body surface
- [Qi](./qi.md) — the circulating force that Zang-Fu systems produce, transform, and distribute
- [Jing](./jing.md) — the stored substrate that the Kidney system governs
- [Shen](./shen.md) — the reflective awareness that the Heart system houses
- [San Bao](./san-bao.md) — the Three Treasures framework
- [Traditional Chinese Medicine](traditional-chinese-medicine.md) — the medical tradition that uses Zang-Fu theory

records.name: Zhan Zhuang
records.description: "Standing like a post": still qigong in which one posture, often the arms rounded as if embracing a tree, is held for minutes while breath and attention settle.
records.body:
Zhan zhuang (站樁), "standing like a post", is still [qigong](./qigong.md). The practitioner holds one standing posture for minutes at a time, from a few minutes at first to half an hour or more, and does not move.

The best-known posture, "embracing the tree" (chēng bào zhuāng), goes like this. Feet shoulder-width apart, knees softly bent, pelvis dropped so the lower back lengthens, arms raised and rounded in front of the chest as if holding a large ball or tree trunk, shoulders and elbows sunk, gaze level. Breath is natural and gradually lengthens, and attention rests in the lower [dantian](./dantian.md) or on the body as a whole.

Standing practice belongs to both the martial and the health lineages. In twentieth-century martial arts it was central to Yiquan, developed by Wang Xiangzhai, where it trains structural alignment and relaxed strength. In health qigong it is taught as the simplest complete exercise of the [three regulations](./san-tiao.md). The body is regulated by alignment. The breath is regulated by letting it slow. The mind is regulated by staying with sensation.

The load is isometric and sustained, mostly in the thighs and shoulders. Beginners typically notice trembling, heat, and fatigue there long before anything else. Teachers treat these as expected and advise standing shorter and more often rather than forcing duration.

records.name: Zheng Qi
records.description: 正气 — 'righteous qi,' the body's total functional capacity to maintain health, resist disease, and recover from illness — the concept that determines whether exposure to a pathogenic factor results in disease

kaptchuk2000.title: The Web That Has No Weaver

unschuld2003.title: Huang Di Nei Jing Su Wen: Nature, Knowledge, Imagery in an Ancient Chinese Medical Text

records.body:
Zheng Qi (正气, "righteous Qi" or "upright Qi") is [Traditional Chinese Medicine's](traditional-chinese-medicine.md) term for the body's total functional capacity to maintain health, resist pathogenic factors, and recover from illness.
It encompasses all the body's defensive, regenerative, and self-regulating functions — what biomedicine distributes across concepts like immune function, homeostatic regulation, tissue repair, and physiological reserve.

The *Huang Di Nei Jing* states the foundational principle: "When Zheng Qi is sufficient internally, pathogenic factors cannot invade" (正气存内，邪不可干).
Disease, in this framework, is not caused by the pathogenic factor alone but by the interaction between the pathogenic factor (*xie qi* 邪气, "evil Qi") and the body's Zheng Qi.
A strong Zheng Qi can resist or expel a pathogen; a weak Zheng Qi allows the pathogen to establish and cause disease.

## What Zheng Qi comprises

Zheng Qi is not a separate substance.
It is the aggregate functional capacity of all the body's vital substances and organ systems working together:

- **[Qi](qi.md)** — the circulating operational force (the body's potential capacity)
- **[Blood (Xue)](xue.md)** — the nourishing, moistening medium
- **[Jing](jing.md)** — the constitutional reserve (stored potential)
- **[Shen](shen.md)** — the awareness and adaptive capacity
- **[Yin and Yang](yin-yang.md)** in proper balance
- **[Zang-Fu](zang-fu.md)** organ systems functioning harmoniously

When any of these components is deficient, Zheng Qi as a whole is weakened, and the body becomes vulnerable to disease.

## Zheng Qi and Xie Qi

TCM [etiology](../../documents/articles/notes/etiology.md) frames disease as the contest between Zheng Qi and Xie Qi (邪气, "pathogenic Qi" or "evil Qi").
The outcome depends on the relative strength of each:

- **Strong Zheng Qi, weak Xie Qi**: The pathogen is expelled.
  No disease occurs, or illness is mild and brief.
- **Weak Zheng Qi, strong Xie Qi**: The pathogen overwhelms the body's defenses.
  Disease occurs — severity depends on the degree of imbalance.
- **Zheng Qi and Xie Qi in prolonged contest**: The struggle produces the signs and symptoms of disease — fever (the body's heat-generating defense), inflammation (Zheng Qi mobilizing to the site of invasion), fatigue (Zheng Qi being consumed in the fight).

This framework has a clinical consequence: TCM treatment does not only target the pathogen (Xie Qi).
It also supports the body's Zheng Qi — strengthening what is deficient, restoring what is depleted, ensuring the body has the functional capacity to complete its own recovery.
The phrase "support the righteous and expel the pathogenic" (fu zheng qu xie 扶正祛邪) describes the dual treatment principle.

## Clinical significance

Zheng Qi determines prognosis.
Two patients with the same pathogenic exposure may have dramatically different outcomes depending on their Zheng Qi.
A person with robust Zheng Qi who encounters Wind-Cold (a common cold) mounts a brief defensive response and recovers quickly.
A person with depleted Zheng Qi — from overwork, chronic illness, poor nutrition, emotional exhaustion — may develop a prolonged illness or see the pathogen penetrate to deeper levels (from exterior to interior pattern).

This is why TCM places so much emphasis on tonification — strengthening Qi, nourishing Blood, enriching Yin, warming Yang — even in the treatment of apparently infectious conditions.
Killing the pathogen is insufficient if the body lacks the capacity to heal the damage and prevent recurrence.

## See also

- [Qi](qi.md) — the potential aspect of Zheng Qi
- [Blood (Xue)](xue.md) — the nourishing component
- [Jing](jing.md) — the constitutional reserve
- [Etiology](../../documents/articles/notes/etiology.md) — how disease arises from the Zheng Qi / Xie Qi interaction
- [Pattern Diagnosis](../../documents/articles/notes/pattern-diagnosis.md) — assessing whether the pattern is excess (Xie Qi strong) or deficient (Zheng Qi weak)
